    take 269 MENUS   n=34  lum mean 0.0143  p99 0.3037  frac>0.15  1.92%
    ratio 1.03x mean luminance

So X4 does not draw the map darker than its other menus, and nothing before the
composite is dimming it. If #44's darkness is still present it lives after this
point, or it is contrast rather than luminance. **Patola did not report on the
map's appearance this run**, so that half of #44 is still unanswered.

### Two of my own errors, recorded

* I first correlated the identity-pose episodes against map opens using the
  `vr pose:` channel and reported "6 of 24 within 2 s". That channel samples
  every **9.3 s**; the event is 0.2-0.5 s long. It could not have resolved it
  and the number meant nothing. WITHDRAWN. `poselag` at 11 ms was the right
  channel and it was in the same log.
* My first `poselag` regex ended `.*valid=(\d)` — greedy, so it matched
  `rawvalid=1` and reported `valid=1` for all 31499 samples. The corrected
  count, 10103, matches what score_run.py had printed on the same file. **The
  cross-check was available the whole time.**

**P4 -- #44's darkness gets a free discriminator, from the dumps.** The UI
dumps are the UI-ONLY target, before compositing. So:

    map content dark IN THE DUMP     -> X4 draws it that way, upstream
    map content normal in the dump   -> our composite darkens it, ours to fix

That question has never been asked and it costs nothing. It also splits "dark"
from "blurry", which have been one word since #44 was written.

**P5 -- #78, view recentring.** With the head held still across an open/close
cycle, any yaw change in X4's camera is X4's doing. `camread` and `poselag`
record it, so this is measured rather than remembered -- which is why the
protocol asks for a still head on the first three cycles.

**Deliberately still not covered:** the cockpit-fitting and station-building
menus, at Patola's choice — they contain 3D views and are their own case.

**The instrument is the UI dump, not the #82 report.** `ui mvp #82` latches
ONCE (`ui_mvp_logged`), so it fires in the cockpit and says nothing about menu
draws -- the same once-flag shape that cost take 264. Making it re-report per
surface is a layer change and would need the harness first, so it is not in
this take. The dumps answer the question categorically instead: a full-screen
menu either fills the frame or sits inside the middle 52.5% of it, and nobody
needs a reference to tell those apart.

**P1 -- regression, and it must hold.** The cockpit HUD stays fixed to the
cockpit exactly as in take 268. If this fails, nothing else in the run counts.

**P2 -- menus are ORTHOGRAPHIC, so the w-gate should leave them ALONE.** They
are full-screen 2D overlays, the same population as the object markers, which
means `w == 1` and `t == 0` and no scale. **So menus should look exactly as
they did before #81 existed -- unshrunk, filling the frame.** If they come back
shrunk to ~52%, they are perspective, the two-population model is incomplete,
and #82 needs a third case. This is the prediction most likely to be wrong and
it is the reason for the run.

**P3 -- #44 is expected and is NOT news.** The map drew dark and blurry with a
1-2 s smear on exit long before the scale existed. **Do not ask whether it is
worse** -- that is a magnitude against memory, and Patola's eye is not the
instrument for it. The answerable questions are categorical: is anything
SHEARED into a wedge, is text legible at 2816, does anything slide against the
cockpit that should not.

**P4 -- shear needs a straddle.** A primitive is sheared only when its vertices
sit on both sides of `w = 1 +- 0.02`. A pure orthographic quad (all w == 1) and
a pure perspective one (all w >> 1) are each gated as a unit and come out
clean. So shear should appear only where X4 draws something at roughly ONE
METRE of view depth. Patola already saw it on the corner brackets in take 267
and liked it, which means those vertices do straddle -- so the mechanism is
live, and menus are worth checking for it specifically.

**If P2 fails, the follow-up is an A/B, not a fix.** Re-run this command with
`X4VR_UI_FOV=0` and compare the same screens. That separates "our scale did it"
from "it was always like that" without either of us judging a magnitude.

## TAKE 268 — #83's resolution call. PREDICTIONS, WRITTEN BEFORE THE RUN

**Why 2816 and not some other number.** The UI scale is **0.5252**, from take
267's own log, not from arithmetic here: `ui field: X4VR_UI_FOV=1.0000 -> X4
lays the UI out at half 36.87 deg (tan 0.7500) against a rendered half of 55.00
deg, so the UI pass is scaled by 0.5252`. A HUD glyph therefore keeps `0.5252 x
render_width / 1408` of the pixels it had at 1408x1408 **before #81 existed** --
the state Patola could read. Parity is at `1408 / 0.5252 = 2681`; 2816 is the
next clean doubling and clears it at **1.05x**. The runtime asks for 3096x3243
per eye anyway, so 1408 was never near what the panel wanted.

**The second knob change, declared rather than smuggled:** `X4VR_UI_DUMP`
drops from `600:6:150` to `1800:2:150`. Not a measurement choice -- take 267's
dumps are 2.0 GB and /tmp has 5.6 GB free, so the same budget at 4x the bytes
would fill the disk mid-run. `X4VR_MV_DUMP` stays set only to keep the dump
filenames per-run; in burst mode the ring owns both the ui and the present
dump, so they cannot be separated.

**P1 -- extents.** `X4 renders 2816x2816, eye 2816x2816 (from X4VR_RES),
composite 5632x2816`. If it still reads 1408x1408 the run measured nothing.

**P2 -- the premise, and the most informative line in the run.** `ui img #N
carries the UI -- 2816x2816`. The scorer prints the UI target's own extent. If
X4 sizes that target from the render, resolution buys HUD pixels and #83 is a
settings question. **If it stays 1408x1408, resolution cannot buy them and #83
needs an entirely different answer** -- that possibility has never been tested,
because every stored log is 1408x1408.

**P3 -- readability.** Given P2, the HUD should read at least as well as it did
before #81 existed. Not "better than take 267" -- that is a magnitude against
memory, which Patola's eye is not the instrument for. The question is absolute
and binary: *can you read the notification panel text?*

**P4 -- cost. 6.05 ms (165 fps).** Take 267's GAMEPLAY was 4.20 ms (238 fps);
the only measured 1x->4x ratio we own is take 158->159, 6.80 -> 9.82 = 1.44x.
Falsifier: materially above ~7.5 ms means the fov-1.4917 scene scales worse
than the fov-2.21 scene did. Take 160 already showed the curve going
superlinear by 9x, so this is a live possibility rather than a formality, and
above 11.1 ms the setting fails a 90 fps budget outright.

**P5 -- the FAIL will fire again.** `X4VR_ROLL_STEREO was set but the pose
channel is down` is inherited from `X4VR_POSE=0` and is about #77. It is not
this run failing.

**P6 -- an unknown settled for free.** `X4VR_HEADLOOK_GAIN=0.115` is
degrees-per-mouse-count, and it has only ever been tuned at 1408x1408. Nothing
in this tree records whether X4's mouse-look is resolution-normalised. The loop
is closed (`X4VR_CAMREAD` / `X4VR_CAMLOOP`), so a wrong gain model changes
speed and damping, not the fixed point -- at worst head-look feels sluggish or
twitchy. `poselag |declared - X4| yaw` read median 0.345 deg / p90 0.805 in take
267; a large rise there is a gain-model failure, **not** a #83 result.

from the render extent, so resolution does buy HUD pixels. #83's premise was

## #84 — BELOW THRESHOLD AT 2816, AND THE INSTRUMENT CANNOT YET SAY MORE

Patola, unprompted and having tried to provoke it: *"flew with the ship and
tried lots of ships and stations; the brackets were in sync the entire time.
Tried really hard and having them at the extreme, could see no deviation
whatsoever, always perfectly centered, both large and small ships, green
brackets and blue brackets."* On take 267 he found #84 without being asked to
look, so this is the same observer on the same question.

**Do not record #84 as fixed.** Two scalings survive that report and they have
different consequences:

    offset constant in PIXELS  -> still 24 px at 2816, but half the ANGLE
                                  (1.87 deg -> 0.94 deg): invisible, still there
    offset constant in ANGLE   -> 48 px at 2816, same angle: he would see it
                                  -- this one is already hard to reconcile
    offset genuinely zero      -> something about 1408 caused it

### The re-frame is DONE and verified. #84 is still unsettled, and it is my fault.

`bracket_pair.py` now reads its frame from the data -- the decoded image width
and the burst spacing the layer itself logged -- and `reframe()` documents what
scales by S, by S^2, by S*T, and what does not scale at all. Verified two ways:

* **A bit-exact no-op at 1408.** Re-run against take 267: 47 pairings, 91
  ambiguous, 204 candidates, 2 rejected, 9 unreadable, and all four bins to the
  digit. Every stored verdict still means what it meant.
* **Twelve selftest cases pass**, four of them new: `reframe(1408)` moves
  nothing, `reframe(2816)` doubles lengths and quadruples areas, `NEAR_PX`
  follows W (35.1 -> 70.1 px, because a threshold in METRES must), and take
  268's actual frame is refused.

**Take 268 cannot settle #84, and the reason is a knob I chose.** Three
independent failures, any one of them fatal:

    only 3 adjacent pairs carry a bracket (n6-n11) against take 267's 365
    1-2 bracket clusters per frame, so <=6 candidate pairings before any test
    the pairs are 1216 ms apart, against the 178 ms the method was built on

The third is the one that matters and it is a consequence of dropping the burst
from `600:6:150` to `1800:2:150`. **I made that change to save disk, and never
asked what it did to the measurement.** At 1216 ms `MOVE_R` becomes 822 px, the
search window blows past `MAX_BLOB`, and no ship is ever re-found -- so the tool
reported "0 accepted, 0 dropped" with both failure modes looking identical. It
now counts `whose ship was never re-found` separately, because "no bracket" and
"bracket whose ship vanished" have opposite diagnoses.

That counter immediately showed something about take 267 that was invisible for
the whole of #84's history: **61 brackets there also lost their ship**, against
47 accepted and 91 ambiguous. Not a defect and not a reason to re-open anything
-- but a third of the population was being discarded through a path that printed
nothing, and no conclusion should rest on a denominator nobody has seen.

**The disk arithmetic that drove the change was wrong.** I priced `600:6:150`
at 2816 by scaling take 267's file COUNT, forgetting that the burst count falls
with the frame rate: at ~56 fps average instead of ~133, the same period yields
27 bursts rather than 73. Take 267's own dump spec at 2816 costs ~2 GB, not 8.
There was never a reason to change it.

**`pairing_is_local()` is the guard that would have caught it**, and it is
written to be able to fail: it compares the frame-to-frame search radius against
the offset being measured and refuses above 3x. Take 267 sits at 0.67, take 268
at 4.57. This is the third time the pair spacing has been the defect -- 257 too
far, 258 too close, 268 too far again -- so the band is now checked by the tool
instead of by me remembering.

**What a take that settles #84 must do.** `X4VR_UI_DUMP=300:6:150` at
2816x2816: ~54 bursts x 5 adjacent pairs = 270 pairs, ~35 pairings at take 267's
rate, ~4 GB against 8.9 GB free. **Prediction to check first, from the run's own
first burst line:** the 6-slot ring should bring the spacing back to ~178 ms
(the layer will report a 380 MB burst buffer, up from 90 MB). If it still logs
~1200 ms, then the write cost at 2816 dominates rather than the ring depth, and
#84 is not measurable at that resolution by this method at all -- which is worth
knowing before spending the rest of the take.

## #84: DO NOT PROPOSE A FOURTH MECHANISM FOR THE CENTRE BIN

Three hypotheses, three refutations, each costing a full re-measurement:

    lone-candidate loophole -> centre unchanged (46.52 -> 45.11), -65% pairings
    absolute brightness floor -> EVERY bin worse (3.5-6.9 -> 55-67)
    cockpit depth rejection -> centre identical to the digit

Three STRUCTURAL limits are now pinned by tests in `tools/bracket_pair.py`, and
they are properties of the method rather than bugs:

* co-movement is blind between two objects at infinity (a star and a distant
  ship share a velocity)
* brightness cannot both exclude stars and admit a dim ship beside a console
* a disparity window wide enough to SEARCH is too wide to be LOCAL

Anyone resuming: characterise what those 16 centre pairings actually latch onto
BEFORE proposing a mechanism. Every attempt so far built the hypothesis and the
fix in the same step.

## WITHDRAWN TODAY — do not resurrect any of these

* **"the HUD moves 1.7x the scene"**, and with it the multiplicative shape and
  the chi2 refutation of #75. All three divided by one global "scene motion"
  over a scene whose parts do not move together. **#75 is UNDECIDED, not
  refuted.**
* **take 260's `X4VR_POSE=0` elimination.** The pose channel was uploading
  IDENTITY in both runs -- "identity until #33 drives it", budget 0.00 -- so the
  test could only come out one way. The pose subsystem is NOT ruled out.
* **"the brackets are pinned to the canvas at 1.37 m."** Measured on a window
  holding 640x more chrome pixels than bracket pixels; the colour split
  reversed it. Brackets read dx +0, untouched.
* **"the bracket offset grows toward the sides."** From nearest-blob pairing
  whose middle bins carried sd ~26 px. Co-movement pairing says mostly CONSTANT.
* **my predicted #82 split of ~2940/2934.** Measured 1254 perspective / 4788
  orthographic.

## THE INSTRUMENT RULES THIS SESSION ADDED

* **Drive new layer code on the GPU before spending a take.** Takes 263, 264
  and 265 were lost to instrument bugs a harness run catches in a second:
  a publish gated on an unrelated knob, a report that latched a premature zero,
  and a lock-order inversion the comment above the edit forbade.
  `tests/run-wgate.sh` is that harness for the w-gate.
* **A silent instrument must say WHICH way it was silent.** "rejected nothing"
  and "could not read" are the same output and mean opposite things.
* **Change ONE thing, and verify a revert actually reverts.** One attempt
  changed three things, measured the combination, then "reverted" one of them
  and produced a THIRD configuration that read as new information.
* **Record the prediction before the run.** It is what turned three centre-bin
  attempts into clean refutations instead of ambiguous outcomes.

# Earlier banner — state as of take 261 (RUN and scored)

## #76 IS SOLVED IN PRINCIPLE — #45 is the mechanism, confirmed by prediction

**X4 lays its UI out against its DEFAULT field (fov=1.0, 73.7399 deg, half-tan
0.75) whatever `<fov>` we set, while rendering the world at the field we asked
for.** A UI element X4 places at NDC `n` therefore means angle `atan(n*0.75)`
but is displayed at `atan(n*tan(half_world))` — pushed outward, and moving by
`tan(half_world)/0.75` as much as the world under any camera rotation. At
X4VR_FOV=1.4917 that ratio is **1.904**. That is the sliding HUD.

Take 260's field-dependence fit predicted `gain = tan(half_world)/0.75`, a
function of X4VR_FOV alone, and take 261 ran fov=1.0 to test it:

                              take 260 (1.4917)   take 261 (1.0)   predicted
    matched slope, n=143            1.40              1.05          1.00+-0.10
    matched median over pairs       1.51              1.02          ~1.00
    IQR across pairs                0.32              0.07          small
    per-cell range (9 cells)     1.21..1.88        1.00..1.12       flat ~1.00
    global slope (hud_slide)        1.81              1.02          ~1.00
    intercept                      -2.9 px           +0.5 px        ~0

**The field dependence vanished too**, 1.21..1.88 down to 1.00..1.12 — which is
what the two-field model requires and what nothing else on the table predicts.
Corroborated in the same log by an unrelated line: the canvas reads 21.5 px
against 11.3, the same 1.904. And Patola, in the headset, unprompted: *"for the
first time the HUD was fixed to the cockpit in a very comfortable/ideal
distance."*

**RESIDUAL, unexplained:** 1.05 not 1.00, edges 1.07-1.12 against centre
1.00-1.02, implying a UI field of fov 0.964. Inside the measurement's own IQR
of 0.07, so possibly nothing. Do not build on it without re-measuring.

**THE FIX IS TASK #81**, in `make_canvas_k`, whose `k[0]/k[5]` scale slots
already exist and sit at 1.0 on the non-canted path:
`k[0] = k[5] = 0.75 * sx_screen`. **fov=1.0 is a DIAGNOSTIC, never the fix** —

    pose residual: X4VR_FOV=1.4917 renders 110.0 deg, runtime wants 94.0 x 99.0
        deg per eye -> budget 0.00 deg of head rotation. ... so a budget under
        ~2.3 clamps the ordinary case — WHICH THIS ONE DOES

and all 20 `vr pose:` samples in take 259 logged `residual 0.00,0.00 applied`.

## WHAT TAKE 260 DID ESTABLISH

**P260.0 — the flush fix, MISSED HIGH but working.** Predicted 100-150 ms/frame;

~1.1 s, not the predicted "under 1 s".

The miss is now explained and the explanation is offline-verified: the residue is

sparse UI layer costs ~56 ms for both layers, the dense present layer ~127 ms.

## #76 — MEASURED TWICE, REPRODUCED. Ratio ~1.7, MULTIPLICATIVE.

**Report the SLOPE, not the median of per-pair ratios.** `hud_slide.py` prints
both since this session. The median is dominated by small-motion pairs, whose
ratios are mostly noise; the slope is not, and it is the number that survives a
change of run:

                  pairs   median   slope   slope |scene|>=40   intercept
      take 259      49    +1.77    1.756       1.701           -2.4 px
      take 260     133    +1.90    1.811       1.694           -2.9 px

The medians look 7% apart and the well-measured slopes agree to **0.4%**. Take
260 simply has 3x the pairs and proportionally more small ones. `scene` carries
error like `ui` does, so the slope is quoted as the geometric mean of the
`ui~scene` and `1/(scene~ui)` fits, which brackets the errors-in-variables bias.

**MULTIPLICATIVE, now by two independent routes.** First, `--span-scan`, pairing
frames k apart WITHIN each burst so k*dt covers the same physical head motion —
five time scales from one run, needing no control over Patola's head speed:

    take 259   span 1..5: +1.77 +1.91 +1.72 +1.91 +1.83   trend +0.012/step
    take 260   span 1..5: +1.90 +1.91 +1.96 +1.95 +1.88   trend +0.001/step

Second, and not derived from the span scan: **the regression intercept**. A
fixed per-pair offset would appear as a large intercept, and both runs give
`ui = 1.7*scene - 2.5 px`. Every fixed-offset and fixed-lag mechanism is
excluded twice over.

**#75 stays refuted as the cause.** "The head rotation counted twice" predicts
exactly +2.00 and constant. chi2 against a constant +2.00 is **66 per dof** on
take 260 and 89 on take 259, and the well-measured slope is 1.69.

**THE SCATTER IS REAL AND STILL UNEXPLAINED.** Observed spread is **4.9x** the
stated per-pair error (259: 4.6x), and chi2 against the BEST constant is still
33 per dof. No single constant fits. Something varies pair to pair that neither
quantisation nor the controls account for — this is the live thread, and the
two open questions below both attack it.

**Where it can still be.** With the pose channel known inert (see the take 260
section above) and the canvas contributing only a CONSTANT per-eye offset
(+-11.3 px, identical in consecutive frames of one eye, so it cancels in every
difference), **our layer applies no per-frame differential between the scene and
the UI in either run.** Both are drawn by X4 into one image and reprojected
together by the compositor. So the 1.7x is X4's own rendering, or the
servo/compositor interaction — not a transform of ours. Earlier text here
claimed the difference was "what OUR patches do to one and not the other"; that
was written when the pose channel was believed live.

## #76's two open questions, both answerable OFFLINE from take 260's dumps

`tools/hud_tiles.py` (new, selftested against synthetic rigid and mixed cases):

1. **Is the UI one object, or a mixture?** `--channel ui`. **A MIXTURE**: 35
   pairs, median IQR across tiles 0.56, 26/35 past the bar.
2. **Is the SCENE one object?** `--channel scene`. **ALSO A MIXTURE, and this
   is the one that matters**: 202 pairs, median IQR 0.64, 185/202 past the bar.

The rigid control — the same frames displaced by a KNOWN amount, same tiles,
same search — reads **0.00**, so the correlator is not the source. Nor is the
mask: #76's scene channel punches UI-shaped holes that MOVE WITH THE UI, so a
tile containing one would carry a signal at the UI's rate. Filling them
(`--raw-scene`) changes the channel — pair 88->89's global shift moves +34 to
+32 — and leaves the disagreement intact, **0.67 against 0.64**, 185/200 past
the bar.

**The per-tile-position map says what it is** (median over 160-199 pairs/cell):

    +1.55 +1.00 +1.64
    +1.69 +0.97 +1.53
    +1.39 +0.93 +1.31

Stable and left-right symmetric: centre column 1.00, both edge columns 1.3-1.7.
**That is mostly PROJECTION GEOMETRY, not a defect.** A 110 deg rectilinear
projection scales image displacement as `(1 + tan^2 θ)` under yaw — averaged
over a tile that is 1.98 at the edges against 1.075 at the centre, so
**predicted outer/centre 1.84, measured 1.57**. Same sign, same order. The 17%
shortfall is NOT accounted for (content is not uniform within a tile, and pitch
contributes a different pattern), so this is "mostly explained", not closed.

**CONSEQUENCE — the biggest withdrawal in this file.** Dividing UI motion by ONE
global scene number averages over that field dependence, so **"the HUD moves
1.7x the scene" is not a property of the HUD.** Withdrawn, and with it the
MULTIPLICATIVE shape and the chi2 refutation of #75 — all three were computed
against that denominator. The 4.9x scatter called unexplained above was the
denominator moving.

**The replacement is `--channel both`**: both channels, SAME pair, SAME tile, so
the field dependence cancels whatever causes it.

## #45 IS THE MECHANISM — the UI is laid out against X4's DEFAULT field

**The FOV sweep cannot be done offline.** All three takes that carry UI dumps
(258, 259, 260) ran `X4VR_FOV=1.4917`. There is no stored variation to exploit;
say so rather than manufacture one.

What IS available offline is the FIELD DEPENDENCE of the matched gain, and it
is sharper. Fitting `log(gain)` on `log(1+x^2)` over the matched map's cells
with n >= 10:

    beta - 1 = -0.523   ->  beta = 0.48      gain at field 1.0:  G = 1.90

and G is not an arbitrary number:

    tan(55.00 deg)  /  tan(36.87 deg)  =  1.4281 / 0.7500  =  1.904
    rendered field     X4's DEFAULT fov=1.0        measured G =  1.90

**X4 lays its UI out against its DEFAULT 73.74 deg field while rendering the
world at the 110 deg we asked for.** That is exactly task #45's suspicion, and
it agrees with #56's finding that the shadow splits follow `<fov>` while the
atlas does not — different X4 subsystems honour the knob differently.

The same two-field model predicts the gain FALLS toward the edges, 1.90 at the
centre tile to 1.25 at the outer tiles, against ~1.33 measured. Sign and order
right. **It predicts beta = 0.31 where 0.48 was measured, and that gap is NOT
explained** — the cells carry only n = 12..32 each and the medians are coarse,
but do not record the model as confirmed.

**THE PREDICTION THIS MAKES, and it is a strong one:** the gain should be
`tan(half_world) / 0.75`, so it is a function of `X4VR_FOV` alone —

    X4VR_FOV  1.0 -> 1.00   1.2 -> 1.30   1.3426 -> 1.56   1.4917 -> 1.90

(1.37 appeared here first and was WRONG -- written without computing it.
tan(44.24 deg)/0.75 = 1.30.)

**At X4VR_FOV=1.0 the slide should VANISH.** A predicted null at a knob we
already have, and the cheapest possible discriminator: if the HUD still slides
at fov=1.0 the two-field model is dead. Note #70 parks wide-fov shading defects
with a floor at 1.3426, so 1.0 is outside the range the project wants to ship —
this is a DIAGNOSTIC setting, not a candidate fix.

**THE OLDER TEST, now superseded but still valid:** correlate the per-pair matched ratio
against the HEAD TRANSLATION for that pair, which `X4VR_POSELOG` already
records. Translation is read from the LOG, not derived from the image, so this
is not the ratio-against-its-own-denominator trap. Parallax predicts the ratio
rises with translation at fixed rotation; flat refutes it and sends the search
back to how the canvas is transformed. Only after that does `X4VR_CANVAS_M`
become a question. Note that dividing the two
separate per-position maps does NOT do this — they are built over different pair
populations (scene 200 pairs, UI only the 35 under `MAX_UI`, which are the
small-motion pairs whose ratios run high).

    UI     dx median -23.0 px  ->  1.37 m, flat in every frame (the canvas)
    SCENE  40.7% at infinity · median 1.50 m · 10% nearer than 0.57 m
           nearest at the -60 px SEARCH BOUND (0.53 m) — not a measurement

Anchor 1 passes: 40.7% of tiles read |dx| <= 2 px, which is the starfield; 0%

**42.8% of scene tiles are nearer than the UI plane, and that is NOT an
occlusion finding.** Scene tiles are sampled where the UI is NOT drawn, by
construction, so this is the depth of the scene AROUND the UI, never behind it.
Testing an occlusion conflict needs `X4VR_HUDLESS=1` or a pre-composite dump —
a different run, not this data. The tool says so itself; do not re-derive the
claim it refuses.

**Then, and only then, the vanilla baseline** — the same measurement with the

**A WITHDRAWN claim of mine — do not resurrect it.** I reported that the ratio

## The dump cadence — settled, and the trap it replaced

`X4VR_UI_DUMP=PERIOD[:BURST[:GAPMS]]`, gap in WALL CLOCK, default **150 ms**.
Parsed once in `common/x4vr_dumpspec.hpp`, pinned by `tests/dumpspec.cpp`.

**The measurable band is 15..300 px of image motion** — MIN_MOTION at the
bottom, the +-320 px search at the top. At 12.8 px/deg that is 1.2..23 deg.
This tool has now failed from BOTH ends:

    take 257   one dump per period, ~1.3 s apart   motion PAST +-320 px
    take 258   six CONSECUTIVE presents, 8.5 ms    motion UNDER 15 px
    take 259   150 ms asked, 209.7 ms achieved     49 pairs, in band
    take 260   150 ms asked, 180.0 ms achieved    133 pairs, in band

Take 258 is the sharper lesson: at 117 presents/s a pair is 8.5 ms apart, and
clearing 15 px needs a **138 deg/s** head turn. **No head speed could have
produced a measurement**, so Patola's pauses — which I first blamed — were
irrelevant. The spacing was an unstated default, not a decision. The layer now
records `t_capture` per slot and logs the ACHIEVED milliseconds, so a bad gap is
visible in the first burst rather than after the take.

**The overshoot is real but shrank with the flush fix: 40% on take 259, 20% on
take 260.** Consistent with the flush itself having been part of the delay.
Watch it; if a run needs a specific dt, calibrate from the previous run's line.

## The flush — was 2378 ms/frame, now 185. VERIFIED in take 260.

Take 259's own breakdown, after three offline hypotheses had each been measured
and each been wrong:

    QueueWaitIdle 2 ms · eye 1098 · ui write 203 · coverage 1076 · OTHER 0

**OTHER is zero**, so that is the whole cost. Both hot terms read the
write-combined readback buffer ONE BYTE AT A TIME — `write_ppm8` did
`rgb[...] = bgra ? p[2 - c] : p[c]`, and the flush counted UI coverage in a
SECOND per-pixel pass over the same bytes.

Now: one bulk memcpy per layer into RAM, per-pixel work from there, coverage
folded into the pass `write_ui8` already made (`common/x4vr_dumpio.hpp`).
Offline A/B on real WC memory: **519.9 -> 25.7 ms, 20.2x**, and 519.9 matches
the 549 measured in situ. `tests/dumpio.cpp` holds the ORIGINAL per-pixel code
verbatim and requires byte-for-byte agreement (76 checks).

**No memory-type change was needed.** An earlier test concluded the type was
worth 3.5% — it benchmarked `write_png_n`, a BULK read, which neither hot path
does. `t_cov` is kept and should now read ~0: a term that vanishes from the log
is indistinguishable from one nobody measured.

**Take 260 measured it: median 185 ms/frame over 71 bursts** (min 96, max 433;
eye 127, ui 56, cov 0). That is 12.9x, against a prediction of 100-150 — **the
prediction missed high** and a burst is ~1.1 s rather than "under 1 s".

**Why it missed, verified offline rather than guessed.** The residue is PNG
deflate, not readback. `tests/readback_speed.cpp` puts `write_png_n` at **121.6
ms per 1408x1408 layer even from CACHED RAM**, while the bulk read of the same
bytes is 80x faster than the old scalar path and no longer material. So the
remaining cost cannot be attacked from the readback side at all; it needs a
compression-level change. Real frames beat the synthetic figure because deflate
is content-dependent — the sparse UI layer costs ~56 ms for both layers against
the dense present layer's ~127 ms.

The fix paid for itself in data: **71 bursts / 425 frames in 4 minutes**, against
34 bursts / 197 frames in 8 minutes for take 259.

## #80 — CONFIRMED offline. Not started; #76 has priority.

*"Rolling my head does not make the HUD adapt the eye separation as it does
with the cockpit."* Measured on take 258's dumps by `tools/roll_disparity.py`,
per-tile disparity ANGLE:

    n102 (control)  scene  +0.0 deg  MAD 0.0  11 tiles   UI 0 deg   log roll  +0.48
    n108            scene -48.9 deg  MAD 1.8  12 tiles   UI 0 deg   log roll -49.35
    n114            scene +46.5 deg  MAD 1.5   7 tiles   UI 0 deg
    n132            scene  -9.8 deg  MAD 0.6   8 tiles   UI 0 deg

Three code facts, each read before the measurement: `make_canvas_k` puts the UI
disparity in `k[12]` alone (no k[13], no roll input, built once at pipeline
creation); the scene's stereo goes through the pose channel gated by
`roll_active()`; and **`quat_of_angles(decl_yaw, decl_pitch, q)` carries no
roll**, so the head's roll reaches the display entirely as compositor
reprojection, rotating the image by -phi. The scene therefore lands at +0.45
deg (correct) and the UI at +phi — **17.1 px of VERTICAL disparity at 49 deg,
~1.15 deg of divergence, which eyes cannot fuse.** Not cosmetic.

Fix shape: rotate the canvas disparity with the head, `k[12] = -ax*d*cos(phi)/z`
and `k[13] = -ay*d*sin(phi)/z`, delivered per frame through the pose channel the
scene already uses. **The SIGN must come from a measurement** —
`roll_disparity.py` reads both channels' angles directly, so a take with the fix
supplies it.

## X4's UI target (img #65) — how to read the dumps

* 1408x1408, fmt 50 (B8G8R8A8_SRGB), **DOUBLED to 2 layers (per-eye)**.
* **`alpha` alone is the WRONG mask.** X4 writes the weapon arcs and the
  weapon-bracket rectangles with **colour and ZERO alpha** — 1.19% of frame
  n45. Invisible in any viewer, which is why Patola reported them "missing".
  `--mask union` (alpha OR colour) is the default and the right one.
* The reverse exists too: ~1.47% has alpha and no colour, a dimming scrim over
  the lower console.
* Coverage varies enormously by scene — 2.3% cockpit, 68% menu, 99.3% map — so
  an average across scenes is meaningless.

## HELD by Patola's decision: the per-eye separation at the corners

*"It is something more visible on the corners."* The bright start-screen quad
did NOT look wrong, only the menu overlay and the savegame loadscreen — **which
rules out the mono loadscreen lead**.

**Every offline measurement is structurally blind to it.** The present dump is
copied inside `composite()` and the VR blit sends that same image, so the dumps
are exactly the bytes handed to the compositor and everything the runtime does
is downstream. That is why 81 frames measure 1.02x while he sees it wrong.

Three corner-weighted candidates, NOT discriminated, to be varied INDEPENDENTLY
(a 2x2, not a sequence of single guesses):

1. **Declared frustum vs the runtime's** — runtime wants 94.0 x 99.0 deg,
   canted 15.04 deg, vertically ASYMMETRIC; the layer declares symmetric +-55.
2. **The declared viewpoint does not follow the head** — `t_head vs d_scene
   r=+0.925` in take 257, +0.846 in take 259.
3. **The compositor warps each frame by an angle it was not drawn with** —
   `poselag ... LEADS the pixels by up to 11.96 deg`.

## Instrument rules earned the hard way

* **A control must match the DIFFICULTY of the measurement**, not just have a
  known answer. `roll_disparity.py`'s control carries a dx as well as a dy for
  exactly this reason.
* **A control proves the channel correlates with itself**, not that it is what
  you think.
* **Render any mask and LOOK at it.**
* **A discrimination metric only discriminates over the range it was built
  for.** `ncc_shift`'s margin measures peak ISOLATION; gating a +-6 px
  refinement on it rejected all 24 of take 257's pairs while their controls read
  +1.00. **The gate belongs on the wide search, always.**
* **Range failures have TWO ends.** Fixing "too far apart" produced "too close
  together". Before changing a spacing, write down the acceptable band and the
  value the change will produce, and check containment.
* **Never print a verdict that fires whatever the number is** — and never key
  one on an EXTREME when the hypothesis is about coherence. `roll_disparity.py`
  first printed CONFIRMED from `max(|dy|)`; its own table refuted it. A
  rotation is coherent, so only a coherence statistic can test one.
* **A goodness-of-fit statistic can be weakest exactly where the effect is
  strongest.** r2 of dy against dx scored 0.30 on the frame whose twelve tiles
  agreed to 1.8 deg, because cockpit tiles sit at similar depth.
* **Never correlate a derived ratio against its own numerator or denominator.**
* **Benchmark the operation the code performs**, not a convenient proxy.
* **A cap or argument silently ignored is a defect.** The shell here is
  **zsh**, which does NOT word-split unquoted parameters.
* **Quote any value with a space in a handed-over command.** Take 258's
  `X4VR_WATCH_WANT=ui dump: burst frames` starts no shell. Fixed at
  `common/x4vr_shquote.hpp`; `env: run =` now round-trips.
* **No mid-run check Patola has to perform.** `X4VR_WATCH=1` arms
  `tools/watch_run.sh`; **notify-send only — speech is FORBIDDEN.**
* **Verify a cleanup, do not report it.**
* **A watcher must not observe itself** — and `pkill -f <pattern>` in the same
  command line as the relaunch kills the launching shell.
* **Cache per burst, not per run.** `channels()` returns ~95 MB a frame.
* **`X4VR_UI_DUMP` does not turn on layer B.**
* **UI dumps are RGBA, always PNG**, ignoring `X4VR_DUMP_PPM`.
* `14.17 px/deg` still has NO recorded derivation.

## Take 202 — #56 ANSWERED, and the FAIL was my own instrument

Take 202 ran and FAILed: *"the frame's object slots carry 2 distinct cascade
scales"*. **Both halves of that line were wrong** — the invariant it asserted
and the walk it asserted it about — and #56 turned out to be answerable from
logs already on disk, with no run at all.

### The answer

**X4's cascade split distances DO respond to `<fov>`. The atlas does not.**

`V_csmthresholds` is a `vec4` in the camera block at float 232, and X4's own
`common_frag.glsl:1071` does `if (depth < V_csmthresholds[i])` — so these are
the cascade split distances in view metres, read live from X4 rather than
derived by us.

| fov | fov-sensitive set | also present |
|---|---|---|
| 1.4917 | `[5.2 23.9 195.1 1338.7]` — **takes 190–199, 201, 202** | `[7.2 33.3 269.9 1856.4]` |
| 1.75 | `[4.7 21.1 173.6 1189.6]` — take 200 | `[7.2 33.3 269.9 1856.4]` |

The control was already run **eleven times**: every stored take at fov 1.4917
gives the identical set to the printed precision, across different yaw, shear
and classification knobs. Takes 200 and 202 differ in `X4VR_TAKE`, `X4VR_LOG`
and `X4VR_FOV` and **nothing else** — a single-variable comparison.

`mapsize` 2048, `maxdist` 5000 and `factors` [1 1 1 1 1] are unchanged at both
fields, as is the 10 × 2048² D16 atlas.

**So the splits move NEARER as the field widens** — ×0.888 for a ×1.173
widening. That is neither hypothesis in #56's framing: fitted-to-frustum would
make cascade 0 *grow* with the field, fixed-extent would leave it alone. With
the atlas fixed and the splits pulled inward, the last cascade covers
1189.6→5000 m instead of 1338.7→5000 m on the same texels — **the guard band's
shadow price lands on the far field, not the near one.**

**Direction established, law NOT.** ×0.888 matches neither `tan(θ/2)` (0.681)
nor `1/sx` (0.681) nor `cos` (0.751). Two points cannot fit a law and I am not
going to pretend otherwise; a third field would discriminate and costs one
take, whenever the law actually matters for a decision.

### Why `<fov>` reaches X4's CPU at all

Because `X4VR_FOV` is a **config override**, not a projection patch
(`injector/x4vr_config.hpp:109`) — the injector serves X4's own `<fov>` tag, so
X4 computes its splits from it. That is task #24's non-intrusive path paying
off in a place it was not designed for.

### The camera that carries the shadows is not the one we widen

In take 202, **85 camera slots only ever show `sx=1.33333`** and **38 only ever
show `sx=0.70024`** — disjoint, zero overlap, so these are two real populations
and not one slot sampled before and after our own rewrite. **All 58
shadow-configured slots are in the 1.33333 group; none is in the widened one.**
X4 never attaches a cascade configuration to the camera whose field we widen,
yet the splits it uploads still respond to the setting.

### What the FAIL actually was

Two separate defects, both mine.

**The invariant was false.** The warning said *"the CSM is light-space and
should be identical in every slot"*. X4's shipped GLSL refutes it: there is
exactly **one** declaration of `M_shadowCSM0`, member 3 of the per-**object**
`BUFFER_BINDING_SLOT_WORLD` block — and X4 feeds it three different source
frames. `mul(vec4(Pos,1), M_shadowCSM0)` with object-space `Pos` in 186 vertex
entry points, `mul(vec4(IO_world_pos,1), …)` in others, and
`mul(vec4(view_pos,1), …)` in 54 fragment ones. It carries the draw's own
transform composed with the cascade, so **a spread is the expected reading**,
and `|row0|` is a cascade scale only for a view-space reader. Fifty-odd takes
of `csm0-scale` were chasing a quantity that never had the meaning assumed.

**And the walk was reading dead memory.** `obj_sets` appended one entry per
descriptor write and was **never cleared**; `obj_bound` was never cleared
either. X4 re-points set 3 binding 0 at a fresh sub-allocation per draw — 13748
binds in this take — so the walk accumulated 167 slots and credited *all of
them on every draw*. About half had been recycled by the time the report ran,
which is where `csm0-scale=inf` came from, and the "2 distinct scales" was
`{0.154204, inf}`. A descriptor write **replaces** a binding; the layer now
models it that way, keyed by `dstBinding`, and clears `obj_bound` at
`vkBeginCommandBuffer`.

`tests/run-multiview-render.sh` gained `X4VR_TEST_OBJ_REWRITE`, which writes
one binding twice and asserts the second wins with **one** distinct scale. It
fails on the old code and passes on the new. The pre-existing cases pass either
way — the fixture only ever wrote once, which is exactly why this hid.

**The same rewrite silently disarmed three negative controls**, because they
grepped for wording I deleted (`cascade 0 spans`, `OBJBLOCK: WARNING`). All
three are re-pointed at the current text with a note to move them together.

### The rule this broke, again

**Sweep the stored logs for the line a proposed run would produce, before
specifying the run.** The three-take plan for #56 asked for a fixed-field
control that eleven takes already contained. This is the second time; the first
cost a measurement ten prior takes already had.

### What is still open

`kObjBlockBytes` was `576`, a guess from a dump. X4 binds **768** — measured,
13748 binds, no other range at set 3. The declared members reach ~560 bytes and
768 is that rounded to a 256-byte alignment. Corrected.

**CORRECTION, made while building #67.** This section first said *"`g_track.bound`
(the camera slots) has the identical never-cleared defect"*. **That named the
wrong member.** `bound` **replaces** on each bind (`bound = it->second`) — I
inferred the defect from the absence of a `.clear()` without reading the
assignment at the bind site, which is the same mistake the false CSM invariant
was.

The camera path's staleness is real but lives in **`g_track.sets`**: it appends
one entry per descriptor write, dedupes on (buffer, offset), and is never
cleared *or capped*. `bound` then copies that whole accumulated list and
`credit_draw` credits every entry on every draw. Take 202 decoded **600 slots**
with **125 of them carrying three distinct projections each** — that is the
signature, and it is the likeliest explanation for *"cam#N is a UBO slot, not a
camera"*.

Still not fixed, deliberately. Every settled camera number was measured through
the accumulating walk, and the one thing that could not be established offline
is *how much* flipping it moves. So **task #67 reports instead of acting**:
`sets_live` records the same writes with the semantics `vkUpdateDescriptorSets`
actually has, and one `proj LIVESETS` line per run says what the superseding
walk *would* have picked. Nothing above it uses that walk. The default flips
once a real X4 frame has shown the size of the change — and that line rides
free on whatever take runs next, so it confounds nothing.

`tests/run-multiview-render.sh` runs it twice: written once the two walks must
agree (an instrument that invents differences is useless), and with one binding
re-pointed at a region nothing else names they must differ in **both** the slot
count and the winner. Before that second case the `DIFFERS` branch had never
been seen to fire.

## #33: the log sweep — residual, and X4's clamp is 65/35 not 56.5

Swept before scoping any work, and it answered the design question without a
run. **The runtime pose is already located, converted and published** —
`locate_views` every VR frame, `views[0].pose.orientation` → `head_angles()` →
`head_share_write()`, which drives X4's own free-look through the injector. The
#59 channel (`g_pose`) is the *only* thing still fed a static Euler.

So the question was never "which OpenXR call". It is **what job the shader
conjugation does now that the camera-driving path exists**, since both rotate
the view and nothing guards against having both on.

### The instrument was already there

`inject camread: X4 <y>,<p> deg (raw …) | cmd <y>,<p> | head <y>,<p>` carries
all three angles. **6962 samples across 16 takes.**

**Two-thirds of them are a dead read-back** — 4564 of 6962 have `raw 0.0000,
0.0000`, X4 reporting nothing rather than reporting zero. Taken at face value
they would have said "the residual is ≈0" and closed the question backwards.
Only the 2398 live samples mean anything.

### The residual has two regimes

`|head − X4|` yaw, live samples only, binned by `|head|`:

| bin (deg) | n | median | p90 | max |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0–10 | 1625 | 0.31 | 22.15 | 74.74 |
| 10–20 | 249 | 3.32 | 24.73 | 81.64 |
| 20–30 | 156 | 1.99 | 28.80 | 91.28 |
| 30–40 | 110 | 1.15 | 15.16 | 56.30 |
| 40–50 | 110 | 0.22 | 3.27 | 54.43 |
| 50–56.5 | 21 | 0.54 | 3.67 | 10.79 |
| 56.5–70 | 19 | 1.18 | 12.06 | 12.78 |
| **70–200** | **108** | **27.15** | **48.67** | **79.37** |

Take 149 alone (n=571, all `CLOSED`, the cleanest session): median **0.22°**,
p90 **2.27°**, max 14.28°. The high p90 in the low bins is fast-motion
transient plus four early takes whose servo was not tracking at all (136, 139,
141, 147 have medians of 63°, 21°, 12°, 6°) — those are in the table because
excluding them would be selecting on the outcome.

**So: below the clamp the servo tracks to a few tenths of a degree. Past it the
residual is unbounded** — head reaches 136°, X4 stops, and the difference is
everything above ~27° median.

### X4's clamp is 65.00 / 35.00, and three comments said 56.5

`|X4 yaw|` never exceeds **65.00°** in any of the 2398 live samples, and 65.00
occurs **129 times exactly** while every other value above 60 occurs once.
`|X4 pitch|` never exceeds **35.00°**. Round numbers, hard stops.

**CORRECTION — that paragraph is circular on its own, and I published it as
confirmation.** The largest |command| in the same 2398 samples is *also*
exactly 65.00: the servo clamps its own target there, so "X4 never exceeded 65"
partly restates our own ceiling. An instrument whose subject cannot exceed the
limit it is being tested for cannot establish that limit.

**What is not circular is the overshoot.** 303 samples show X4's camera going
PAST the command and still pinning to exactly 65.00 — furthest is **X4 65.00
against a command of 53.04** — and 256 do the same in pitch, **35.00 against
26.83**. A ceiling that were merely ours would be sailed straight through by an
overshoot. That, plus take 136 (which ran with the OLD 56.5/40 limits and still
read 65.00/35.00), is the evidence. The maximum never was.

That matches `yaw_limit_deg = 65.0f` / `pitch_limit_deg = 35.0f`, which
`x4vr_headlook.hpp` has used all along — **the constants were right and three
comments were wrong**, all repeating take 117's superseded 56.5: the header's
own rule 2, twenty lines above the constant that contradicts it;
`x4vr_layer.cpp`'s declared-pose comment; and `tests/headlook.cpp`, whose case
`head_look_step(mild, {56.5f, 0.0f}); // exactly at the clamp` was **not at the
clamp at all**, so it never exercised `clamped`. All corrected, test still
passes.

### What this decides

**Residual, not replacement.** The conjugation is a sub-degree correction
almost always, which is the regime reprojection handles well. Its real job is
the region past X4's clamp.

**And that region is bounded by the guard band, not by the conjugation.** At
`X4VR_FOV=1.4917` the rendered half-field is ~55°. A head 71° past where X4 is
pointing (136 − 65) is asking to see something X4 never drew — reprojection
cannot invent it, and the result is the black edge. So "look past the clamp"
is a **#24 guard-band question wearing a #33 costume**, and the two have to be
sized together.

Caveat on frequency: ~5% of live samples sit past the clamp, but these are
takes where the extremes were being deliberately exercised. That fraction says
nothing about normal play.

## Is X4's 65/35 reachable? It is DATA, and there is an 85/85 beside it

The guard band cannot buy the past-the-clamp region at any price, so the clamp
itself was the only lever left. It turns out not to be compiled in.

**`libraries/parameters.xml`** (inside `08.cat`), under `<playercamera>`:

    <lookaround>
      <internal maxpitch="35" maxyaw="65" anglespeed="200" angleacc="500"
                trackmaxpitch="85" trackmaxyaw="85"/>
      <external maxpitch="85" .../>
      ...
    </lookaround>

`maxyaw="65"` and `maxpitch="35"` are **exactly** the measured stops, to the
digit. So the limit is data X4 parses, not a constant in the executable — and
that is the first requirement for reaching it non-intrusively.

**And the same element carries `trackmaxpitch="85" trackmaxyaw="85"`.** The
`track` prefix reads as head-tracking, and 85/85 would convert most of the
expensive region into something X4 renders *properly* — no reprojection, no
guard band, free.

**SETTLED: do not pursue `trackmax*`.** It is a VR-shaped name in a binary
whose entire VR surface is residue, and the section *"The residue is much wider
than `IsVRMode`"* above ends with an instruction I did not follow before
spending on this: **"Before spending anything on a VR-shaped name in this
binary, re-read this section."**

Re-reading it answers the question. What would have to switch X4 into "tracked"
mode is its head-tracker path — the twenty-two `*ActiveHeadTracker*` accessors,
`IsHeadTrackingActive`, `GetOpenTrackConnectionStatus`, and the
`enableopentrack` config tag sitting at `false` in the player's own file. All of
it is listed there as residue, reopened four separate times, and OpenTrack is a
forbidden path besides.

And the evidence I had gathered for `trackmax*` is exactly the class that
section names as insufficient. `trackmaxyaw` and `trackmaxpitch` DO appear in
the binary — but in an **alphabetically sorted attribute-name interning table**
(`…sway, tactical, takeoff…`), which is consistent with the names being
data-derived and proves only that they were *named*. X4's own
`libraries/parameters.xsd` does not cover this section at all, so the schema
adds nothing either. Quoting the rule it broke: *"an exported symbol, a
vocabulary string and a config tag are each evidence that a feature was named,
never that it is implemented here."*

**So #68 raises `maxyaw`/`maxpitch` directly.** Those are proven live to the
digit — the overshoot pins to exactly 65.00 and 35.00 — and depend on no
VR-shaped name at all. The 85/85 pair is recorded here only so the next person
does not re-find it and think it is a door.

### The delivery problem, which is the real open question

`parameters.xml` lives **inside `08.cat`**, not loose. The injector interposes
`fopen`/`open`/`openat`, which is how `<fov>` and `inputmap.xml` are served,
and both of those are loose files. An archive member is not reachable that way.

Three routes, in order of how much they respect "the player's files are read
once and never written":

1. **Synthesise an extension in memory.** X4 enumerates `extensions/` and
   merges `extensions/<name>/libraries/parameters.xml`. Interposing
   `opendir`/`readdir` alongside the existing `open` family would let the
   injector present an extension that exists nowhere on disk. Nothing written,
   same mechanism class as everything else the injector does.
2. **Archive-level interception** — hook the reads into `08.dat` and substitute
   bytes at the member's offset. Doable (the `.cat` index is plain text and the
   offset is a running sum) but it means owning X4's archive format.
3. **Write a real extension directory.** Simplest, and the only one that
   modifies the player's install. Against the standing constraint.

Route 1 is the one that fits. It is not built.

### What #68 carries

`maxyaw` and `maxpitch`, raised directly. Not `trackmax*` — see above.

The value to raise them *to* is open and is a comfort question, not a technical
one: `<external>` and `<externalengine>` in the same file already use
`maxpitch="85"`, so 85 is a number X4 itself considers reasonable for a
look-around, but the internal view has cockpit geometry behind it and the
honest answer is what the canopy actually shows. That is Patola's eye, not a
measurement.

**The one thing that could still refuse:** that these values are read once into
a camera object and clamped again somewhere downstream. Nothing suggests it,
but #68's first take is what would show it — X4's own readback going past 65.00
is the whole acceptance test, and it needs no new instrument.

Extracted to `/tmp/x4-libs` with `/tmp/x4cat.py`. **X4's content — never
committed**, same rule as the shaders and the Lua.

## Measuring the seam from a screenshot, if it ever comes up again

Count the **fraction of rows** carrying a sign-consistent column-to-column
step. **Do not use the median over rows** — that needs the seam to span >50% of
the height and returned a false ABSENT on takes 198b/198c when a station
covered part of the view. Compare guard-to-seam **separation**, never absolute
x: the PNGs differ in height between sessions and content cross-correlation
gave three different offsets.
