## The pattern that dominated this stretch — ELEVEN instances

**Every instrument here recorded a different event than the question asked.**
`NEVER REACHED` meant "not while watched"; the give-up sat inside the branch its
own failure mode skips; the test fixture was ordered so the bug could not occur;
the harness rendered one frame; the pipe inventory keyed on pipeline *creation*
rather than use; the bind description was keyed on `out[i]` before
`vkCreateGraphicsPipelines` wrote it; the module_map message keyed on parsed
modules rather than lines; the bind-time case counted passes and was blind to
content; `frag-invproj-check` could not see the term it exists to check; and
the check that retired the reconstruction hypothesis asked whether the patch
*applies* when the question was whether the patched module *runs*; and I
refuted the take-70 rule by matching `g_shear_nodepth` to the wrong env var
from memory instead of grepping the two lines that define it.

**The newest one is the cheapest to avoid: `grep` what a variable reads before
reasoning about the branch it gates.** `X4VR_SHEAR_LIGHTS` and
`X4VR_SHEAR_NODEPTH` are different knobs at different granularities — one
per-module, one per-pass — and assuming they were the same produced a
confident, published, wrong refutation.

**Before trusting any instrument here, ask which event it records.** And a
green case is worth nothing until it has been seen to fail — the negative
control caught four of these, the newest being the whole-sweep flip run that
proved no module had silently missed the `R⁻¹` term.

## Method note

Elimination has outperformed instrumentation. Take 195 killed a hypothesis in
one run by changing a knob and re-measuring. Five runs of capture and
attribution produced one name and no cause. Prefer "switch it off and
re-measure" over "build a probe to watch it".

# #77 REGRESSION — the vertex map rotated, the fragment map did not

Found while estimating #74 (head translation), by reading the code rather than
from a run.

`patch_vertex_eye_offset` with roll on displaces the eye along
`(cos φ, sin φ)`. `patch_fragment_invproj_eye` computes a **scalar** d and
applies `T(d)` along x only — and in current runs it cannot do otherwise,
because it is called with `pose_set = pose_rotate() ? ... : 0xffffffff` and
`pose_rotate()` is OFF, so the fragment side has no pose access at all.

The call site states the invariant it violates:

> the affine applied to gl_Position and the affine undone before the deferred
> reconstruction have to be the same map or the reconstruction is wrong by the
> difference

Residual: `d·(cos φ − 1, sin φ)`. **Zero at φ = 0**, so every pre-#77 tag and
all level-headed play is unaffected — but |residual| = 1.08·d at 65 deg, larger
than the eye offset itself. It corrupts `view_pos`, so it lands in per-eye
deferred lighting and shadows. Take 221 judged stereo geometry and comfort and
would not have shown it.

Shipped and defaulted ON in c3e7689. Confirmable offline in the harness before
any take.

**The fix is also #74's prerequisite.** Threading a per-frame 2D offset into
the fragment correction is the same machinery head translation needs, because
translation is the same vector from a different source.

# Take 235 — the dump comparison CANNOT work while the servo follows the head

The protocol asked Patola to hold head poses and dumped the presented eye image
at each. The correlation came out clean -- n13/14/15 are the roll hold at -42
deg, n20-23 pitch up, n28-31 yaw +40 -- and the measurement is still worthless.

At `X4VR_FOV=1.4917` the scale is **8.60 px per degree** near the centre
(`704 * sx * pi/180`, sx = 0.70024). Within a single held pose the declared
camera moved:

    roll -42 hold    yaw  -1.15 ..  +3.32  ( 38.5 px)   pitch +0.34 .. +7.22  (59.2 px)
    pitch-up hold    yaw -10.89 ..  -5.27  ( 48.4 px)   pitch +21.6 .. +34.1  (107.8 px)
    yaw +40 hold     yaw +34.61 .. +43.77  ( 78.8 px)   pitch +1.08 .. +3.14  (17.7 px)

The drift under investigation is "ever so slightly". The confound is an order
of magnitude bigger, and no amount of predict-and-subtract rescues it: the dump
timestamps are file mtimes, uncertain by a good fraction of a second, during
which the pose moves degrees.

**The flaw is structural, not a matter of holding stiller.** The servo makes
X4's camera follow the head, so any head motion moves the entire rendered scene;
asking for a held head pose is asking for a held camera, and 1 degree is 8.6 px.

Two further notes for whoever measures dumps next:

* phase correlation on a space scene returns **zero** for the inter-eye
  disparity, because the modal shift is the far field at 0 -- the scorer's own
  `eye` section reports the same pairs as "22 with parallax, spread 39 px". A
  global peak is the wrong statistic when the quantity varies with depth, which
  is the aggregates-hide-local-defects trap in a new place.
* the dumps carry no log line, so correlation runs through file mtimes against
  the log's monotonic clock. That is good to a second, which is fine for a held
  pose and useless during motion.

The way out is to stop moving the head at all: `X4VR_ROLL_FORCE` changes the
published roll with the head level and still, so the camera pose is genuinely
constant and the only difference between dumps is the shear.

# Take 237 — the drift is LOCALISED: submission side, not render side

Two phases, each with the confounding variable structurally absent rather than
asked to be small. The design is Patola's: he proposed the numpad half.

    Phase A   head rotates, X4's camera does NOT   (X4VR_HEADLOOK unset)
              -> the cockpit drifts, same directions, no Z
    Phase B   X4's camera rotates via numpad, head still
              -> NO drift. "rotation is perfectly pivoted"

**Phase B clears everything upstream of layer submission.** X4's rendering, the
stereo shear, the SPIR-V patches, the projection arithmetic and the servo are
all geometrically correct under camera rotation. Six takes of elimination end
here: the drift requires the HEAD to move relative to the DECLARED pose, and
does not require X4's camera to move at all.

The scorer pins the configuration: `pose 0 driven, 32 identity`, `world-locked
all run`, `poselag nothing to compare`. The declared pose was identity
throughout, so the only mechanism acting was the compositor reprojecting our
layer by the full head rotation.

## The obvious suspect there is CLEAN

    declared   vr_declared_fov() = +/-55 deg on all four sides
               (X4VR_FOV 1.4917 * 73.7399 = 110.0 deg)
    rendered   sx = sy = 0.70024  ->  110.0 deg on both axes at 1:1

The declared frustum matches what X4 renders, on both axes. Not an FOV
mismatch.

## What is eliminated, cumulatively

    1  the head-translation path        present with X4VR_HEAD_TRANSLATE off
    2  the neck orbit in our shift      present with the shift at zero
    3  the declared POSITION            take 234, knob confirmed live
    4  servo lag / timing warp          persists while the pose is HELD
    5  X4's own camera orbiting         vanilla rotates in place, no parallax
    6  everything upstream of submit    take 237 phase B
    7  declared vs rendered FOV         both 110 deg, checked above

## A caution for whoever resumes this

Phase A is NOT a clean read of "drift". With head-look off and an identity
declared pose, rotating the head is exactly like looking around a fixed screen
floating in space -- the image swings through the view because you are looking
away from it, and that is expected. The drift is an EXTRA displacement on top
of that, and separating the two by eye is a much harder judgement than the
phase-B null, which is unambiguous.

So phase B is the load-bearing half. Phase A says "something remains"; it does
not say how much.

The magnitude also failed to behave as a reprojection would: in take 233 with
head-look ON, the servo makes the declared orientation follow the head, so the
reprojection angle for yaw and pitch is near zero (poselag median 0.000, p90
0.115) -- yet drift was reported on those axes too. In take 237 every axis was
reprojected by the FULL head angle, and the drift was described in similar
terms rather than dramatically worse. A reprojection artifact should scale with
the reprojection angle. This one does not appear to, which is the next thing to
pin down and the reason no mechanism is named here.

# Take 238 — the Z artifact was the declared position, and it is GONE

`X4VR_HEAD_TRANSLATE=1` together with `X4VR_DECLARE_RENDERED_POS=1`, a
combination that had never run: take 231 had translation with the headset's own
position declared, and takes 233/234 tested the declared position with the
shift at zero, where it has almost nothing to correct. Testing a fix in the one
configuration where it cannot act is a mistake worth naming.

Patola: *"this time there was no Z artifact, only the X/Y artifacts."*

So the mechanism was exactly what it looked like. With translation on we render
from a SHIFTED eye and were declaring the UNSHIFTED one; a compositor handed a
positional difference reprojects it, and a positional reprojection reads as
apparent depth. Declaring the position we actually rendered from removes the
difference and the artifact with it.

**Still open:** the rotation-coupled X/Y drift, which take 237 localised to the
submission side and which nothing here touches.

## Can the artifact be turned into Z translation? No -- but its honest form is available

Patola asked whether the effect could be used deliberately. It cannot, for two
reasons, and both matter:

* **Without depth a positional delta can only shift the image RIGIDLY**, as if
  every pixel were at one distance. Moving forward makes near things grow while
  far things barely change; a rigid shift feels like the world sliding past
  rather than being approached. It is not the effect, only a cousin of it.
* **What a runtime does with a declared position that disagrees with the pixels
  is unspecified.** Building on it is building on behaviour that a WiVRn update
  may change -- the same class of mistake as building on VR residue.

**The real version is available though**, and take 238's log records it:
`XR_KHR_composition_layer_depth` is among the 62 instance extensions WiVRn
offers. Submitting X4's depth beside the colour lets the compositor do true
positional reprojection with parallax -- near moving more than far -- which is
genuine Z and would sharpen X/Y as well.

Why X/Y were nearly free and Z is not is GEOMETRY, not an implementation gap:
a lateral eye shift is exactly a projection shear (`x_ndc = sx*(x-d)/z`), an
exact operation on what X4 already drew, while moving along the view axis
rescales by `z/(z-dz)`, which is depth-dependent and has no exact shear form.

Costs, so the route is not remembered as free:

    disocclusion   reprojection can only show what was rendered; lean far enough
                   and geometry behind the cockpit frame should appear, and
                   there is no data for it. A VISIBLE defect, bounded by how far
                   you move -- negligible at centimetres, not at 25 of them
    plumbing       the depth exists (the deferred passes read it) but getting it
                   into a per-eye depth swapchain at present time is real work
    performance    an extra swapchain and copy per frame
    scope          it does nothing for the X/Y rotation drift

A fourth route, recorded so it is not rediscovered: write `M_view`'s
translation so X4 genuinely renders from the moved eye. Exact, no disocclusion,
no extra swapchain -- but a per-frame write into a block 500+ slots share,
needing slot selection, and X4's CPU-side culling would not move with it.

DEFERRED, not rejected. #74 is not clean while the X/Y drift stands, #76 gates
#71, and depth reprojection would introduce a visible-artifact class into the
territory that killed the previous attempts.

# #76/#57 — X4 ALREADY SEPARATES THE HUD, and ships the switch to prove it

Found by reading X4's shipped GLSL rather than by instrumenting the frame. The
same technique that found `B_csmdebugcolor` for #70.

## Why one layer can never fix #76

X4 renders with **no roll** -- we never drive roll into its camera -- so the
declared layer pose has two choices and both are wrong:

    declare roll = 0      world stays level (right), HUD counter-rotates (wrong)
    declare roll = head   HUD stays put (right), world rolls with the head (wrong)

Patola confirmed the first directly: *"all the HUD elements always stay
perfectly level to the world and accompany the roll of my head, rolling to the
opposite side."* One layer cannot satisfy both, which is exactly why #57 asks
for a second one. #30/#40's canvas does NOT solve this: it is shader-side
stereo placement, putting the UI at a chosen depth, and the UI still travels in
the same composition layer and is still reprojected.

## The composite, from `copy_gamma.frag.glsl`

    if (U_fsr3g_useuitexture) {
        // FFX will own UI composition, so feed only HUDLESS into swapchain
        OUT_RT0 = hudless;
    } else {
        OUT_RT0 = hudless;
        vec4 ui = texelFetch(S_diffuse_map, ivec2(gl_FragCoord.xy), 0);
        OUT_RT0.rgb = ui.rgb + (1.0 - ui.a) * hudless.rgb;
    }

**The scene arrives at this pass already HUD-less**, in every AA mode including
the plain fallback -- the variable is called `hudless` throughout. The UI is a
separate texture, premultiplied alpha, `texelFetch`ed 1:1 with no filtering.
`test/dlssg_ui_verify.frag.glsl` states the same law independently, because
DLSS frame generation needs a HUD-less input:

    reconstructed = ui.rgb + (1.0 - ui.a) * LinearFromSRGB_Deprecated(hudless.rgb)

**So the separation #57 needs already exists inside X4**, maintained for
somebody else's feature, and `U_fsr3g_useuitexture` is the switch that hands us
the hudless image alone.

## Where the switch lives, verified the way #70 taught

    member       21 of BLOCK_BUFFER_BINDING_SLOT_DYNAMIC
    location     descriptor set 4, binding 0, byte 512 (uint index 128)
    declared by  4 modules, ALL agreeing on offset 512
                 -- which is a TAUTOLOGY, not reassurance: those four are the
                 four copy_gamma permutations. See the correction below.
    SAMPLED by   mod-0012 -- one of the composite's own fragment modules --
                 as OpAccessChain %_ptr_Uniform_uint %__0 %int_21
    type         uint, so any non-zero word is true

The sampled check is not a formality: `M_shadowCSM0Clip` is declared by 370
modules and sampled by zero, and that cost this project takes.

## What is NOT yet established

* that setting it leaves the UI texture intact and reachable -- the branch says
  FFX would own composition, and X4 may or may not keep feeding the texture
* how to locate `S_diffuse_map` at that draw and copy it into a swapchain of
  our own -- but see below: its bindless index is member 16 of the same block,
  and there is a cheaper source than the block

**ANSWERED below:** whether set 4 binding 0 is writable the way the camera
block is. The mechanism transfers; the addressing does not.

## Is set 4 binding 0 writable the way the camera block is?

Offline, no run. **The mechanism transfers. The addressing does not, and that
retires the write as the route.**

### The mechanism transfers -- all four properties the camera write needs hold

1. **No dynamic offsets.** Despite the name, X4 never passes
   `pDynamicOffsets`: descriptor sets are baked -- 1652 allocations, static
   `(buffer, offset)` pairs, set state appearing in renderdoc as *Initial
   Contents* (`docs/frame-analysis.md`, the capture). The descriptor's own
   offset IS the address.
2. **Same arena, same access.** Memory 793/829 are ~268 MB host-coherent
   persistently mapped; X4 updates constants by plain CPU memcpy, with zero
   `vkCmdUpdateBuffer` in the whole frame.
3. **The layer's walk already reaches a per-draw block.** `proj OBJBLOCK`
   reports up to **331 slots readable, winner range 768, `set3/range768
   x13748`** in one frame. That is set 3, the *per-object* block, reached
   through the same `buf_binding -> mapped` walk. Per-draw is not the obstacle.
4. **The write window is the same.** `X4VR_CSM_DEBUG` writes from the submit
   hook -- after X4 has recorded every draw and memcpy'd its constants, before
   the GPU reads them.

### The addressing does not -- measured, not reasoned

`tools/block_offset_census.py` was written for this and is the test to run
before writing any block offset ever again:

    tools/block_offset_census.py 4 0 --at 512

The camera block is safe to write **by offset** because every slot has ONE
layout. The DYNAMIC block is generated per shader family by
`MACRO_BUFFER_DYNAMIC`, exactly like set 2's MATERIAL block: **38 distinct
layouts across the 370 modules that declare it**, sizes from 432 to 3824 bytes.

Byte 512, across all 370:

| modules | type | member at byte 512 |
|---|---|---|
| 54 | float | `U_patternstr` |
| 32 | vec4 | `U_pattern_color` |
| 14 | float | `U_diffuse_tiling` |
| 8 | float | `U_diffusestr` |
| 6 | vec4 | `S_color_glow_color` |
| **4** | **uint** | **`U_fsr3g_useuitexture`** |
| 2 | float | `U_waterlevel` |
| 2 | float | `U_override_normal_pattern` |
| 1 | vec4 | `S_shad_color` |

**123 modules have a member starting exactly at byte 512, 19 more straddle it,
and in only 4 is it the switch.** Writing `uint 1` into the other 119 writes
float `1.4e-45` -- a denormal that reads as zero -- so a blind write by offset
zeroes pattern strength, diffuse tiling, glow colour and water level across the
frame. Not "might not work": a global visual corruption with nothing to do with
the HUD. Byte 480 is worse -- **13** different members, `S_diffuse_idx` in 4
against `S_pattern_tiling` (36), `S_pattern_color` (32), `U_diffusestr` (14).

**The negative control, run first.** Same tool, the block whose write is known
to work -- `X4VR_CSM_DEBUG` writes byte 1520 and takes 229/230 saw it on
screen:

    set 1 binding 0  ->  1 distinct layout, 370 modules, 72 members
    byte 1520        ->  370 modules, ALL uint B_csmdebugcolor, 0 straddling

One name at one byte in every module that has it. The instrument separates the
two cases, so its reading on set 4 is a measurement rather than a shape.

(That control also caught a real thing about the dump set: **four of the 409
dumps are OURS**, not X4's -- the cursor shim declares `g_tCursor` at set 1
binding 0. Counted naively they appeared as a second camera-block "layout" with
zero members. Any count over `/tmp/x4vr-shaders` is 405 X4 modules plus 4 of
ours.)

**Correction to this file.** The line above says the switch is "declared by 4
modules, ALL agreeing on offset 512" and offers the agreement as
reassurance. It is a tautology: the four are the four `copy_gamma`
permutations, so of course they agree. The number that decides the question is
the 119 that put something *else* there, and it had not been measured. The
consistent-offset test is the right test for the CAMERA block, where one layout
covers every slot; it is the wrong test here.

Writing it safely would mean aiming at the exact slot bound for the
`copy_gamma` draw -- per-draw pipeline-to-descriptor tracking the layer does
not have (`obj_bound` is hardcoded to set index 3, and
`x4vr_CmdBindDescriptorSets` passes `dynCount`/`dyn` straight through without
recording them).

### And that is moot, because the module is one we already patch

    take 235:  mv final: rp #0 <- frag module #12 (mod-0012.spv)
               samples set 0 binding 5[53306], set 0 binding 5[53306]
               [index-offset APPLIED]

**`mod-0012` is the present pass's fragment module, it runs every frame, and
the layer already rewrites it.** Two bindless samples -- exactly `copy_gamma`'s
`hudless` and `ui`. This was never a candidate module; it is one we have been
modifying since task #13.

So force the branch in the SPIR-V instead of in the buffer. The switch is read
once, as `OpAccessChain %_ptr_Uniform_uint %block %int_21` then `OpLoad %uint`.
`OpLoad` is four words (op, type, result, pointer) and `OpCopyObject` is four
words (op, type, result, operand), so it is an **in-place substitution** --
same word count, no re-layout, no new ids beyond one `uint` constant. Against
per-draw descriptor tracking, that is not a close call.

### Where the UI texture comes from

`S_diffuse_idx` -- member 16, byte 480, `uint`, read by the fragment stage --
is the bindless index of `S_diffuse_map`, so the UI texture's identity is in
the same block as the switch. Reading it host-side has the same addressing
problem, and **we probably do not need to**: the UI has its own render pass
(the capture's 2816x1385 `B8G8R8A8_SRGB`, 232 draws, immediately before the
1-draw final blit), and the layer already hooks `vkCreateFramebuffer` and knows
every pass's attachments.

### One thing still to settle

**The no-dynamic-offsets fact rests on one renderdoc capture**, and it is the
only direct evidence about how set 4 is bound. It does not change the
recommendation -- the aliasing table retires the write either way -- but if we
ever do need to read that block host-side it wants confirming. One counter on
`dynCount` in `x4vr_CmdBindDescriptorSets` rides along free on any take.

## The `#103` contradiction: RESOLVED, and it was never a contradiction

`docs/frame-analysis.md` called `#103` *"LDR composition (scene + UI)"* while
`copy_gamma.frag.glsl` says the UI arrives as a separate premultiplied-alpha
texture. **`#103` is the UI texture.** The two were not competing measurements:
one is X4's current shipped source, the other a **label inferred from shape**
in an old capture -- an SRGB LDR target after the HDR chain, with a fullscreen
textured quad drawn into it, therefore "something copies the scene in".

The step that fails is the fullscreen quad, and it fails because that draw can
now be **named** instead of inferred.

### Naming a module from its own block

`tools/name_module.py`. The DYNAMIC block's tail (byte 432 on) is generated
from the shader's `<properties>` list in `shadergl/ogl/*.xml`, so the member
names ARE the property names with a type prefix. That is a fingerprint from a
dump to a source file. Validated on a module identified independently:
`mod-0012` matches `copy_gamma.xml` EXACT and nothing else, and we already knew
it was `copy_gamma` from the layer's own log and its two bindless samples.

    mod-0022   ->  visual_transition.xml     X4's full-screen UI fade
    mod-0261   ->  xu_ui_unlit_sdf.xml       SDF text
    mod-0263   ->  xu_ui_unlit.xml           UI quads
    mod-0265   ->  xu_ui_unlit.xml
    mod-0345   ->  xu_ui_unlit.xml

`visual_transition.frag.glsl` ends by **premultiplying alpha** --
`rgb *= U_useralphascale; OUT_RT0 = saturate(vec4(rgb, a * F_alphascale))` --
which is precisely the format `copy_gamma` consumes. It is a UI overlay, not a
scene blit.

### The whole writer set, in our own configuration

Take 203 numbers the same target `#65`, 1408x1408 `fmt=50 B8G8R8A8_SRGB`, and
its framebuffer lines name **both** its passes:

    fb  rp #33: 1408x1408 attachments=1 imgs=[#65]   <- visual_transition
    fb  rp #45: 1408x1408 attachments=1 imgs=[#65]   <- xu_ui_unlit*, SDF text

**Nothing but UI writes it.** rp #33 is also the only pass the layer tags
`canvas` that is not a present pass, and rp #45's modules were bound as
`-> original`, i.e. treated as unsheared. Two instruments already agree it is
the UI.

Note those four UI modules are classified **`World,live-sx`** by the layer.
That is the documented false positive -- X4's UI vertex shaders read member 0
of the set-3 block exactly as world geometry does -- and it is the reason "what
is this module" has to be answered by naming and not by classification. Reading
the classification as the answer is what produced the "scene + UI" label in the
first place.

### What this changes for #57/#76

**The separation exists in the frame already**, not only in the shader source:
one image holding UI alone with alpha, and a scene that reaches `copy_gamma`
HUD-less. The remaining unobserved link is that `copy_gamma`'s `S_diffuse_idx`
resolves to that image -- a runtime bindless value, not readable offline. The
take that forces `U_fsr3g_useuitexture` settles it for free: HUD gone, scene
intact.

One caution for the design, not for this finding: the UI target is logged
`MASKED`, so the layer is already doubling it per eye.

## The branch-force patch: BUILT, offline-validated, not yet run

`patch_fragment_force_block_uint`, wired to `X4VR_HUDLESS`. It replaces every
load of one `uint` block member with a constant, so the branch it feeds is
statically known.

    %343 = OpAccessChain %_ptr_Uniform_uint %__0 %int_21
    %343 = OpLoad  %uint %342          ->   %343 = OpCopyObject %uint %uint_1_0
    %344 = OpINotEqual %bool %343 %uint_0_0        (untouched)
           OpBranchConditional %344 ...            (untouched)

Both are four words, the result id is kept, and on `mod-0012` the constant
already existed -- so the patched module is **1431 words, exactly as many as
X4 shipped**. Nothing is renumbered and nothing downstream is touched.

### The signature, and what it selects

Deliberately over-determined: set 4 binding 0, a member at byte **exactly 512**,
whose type is a 32-bit **unsigned** int, whose `OpMemberName` is
`U_fsr3g_useuitexture`, and which is actually **loaded**. The member INDEX is
not used -- it is 21 in this build, and an index means different things in
different families.

Type alone would also select the right four today, since every other member at
byte 512 is a float or a vec4. That is an observation about this build, so the
name is required as well; if a future X4 strips `OpMemberName` this refuses and
changes nothing, which is the safe direction to fail.

Run against **X4's own dumps**, not only against a fixture we wrote:

    4 of 409 matched — mod-0011, 0012, 0184, 0185 — all valid SPIR-V,
    exactly 1 load rewritten each, and the module's OTHER uint load
    (S_diffuse_idx, the UI texture's bindless index) left alone.

That assertion is now in `tests/run-multiview-render.sh` and skips loudly when
`/tmp/x4vr-shaders` is absent.

### `X4VR_HUDLESS=0` is the control, and it is the point

The value is a parameter so that 0 forces the switch to its **shipped** value.
That exercises every step -- same four modules matched, same instruction
rewritten, same driver recompile -- and must look identical to leaving the knob
unset. An A/B between 1 and 0 differs in one thing; an A/B between 1 and unset
differs in two. If forcing 0 changes the screen, the patch is landing somewhere
it should not and nothing about forcing 1 is interpretable.

The value is parsed strictly: exactly `"0"` or exactly `"1"`. `strtoul` returns
0 for anything it cannot read, so a typo would have silently selected the
control arm and the run would have come back reporting that forcing the switch
changed nothing. That confusion has cost a take before.

### Where it is applied, and why there

**Before the unsheared-twin snapshot.** The present pass is all-LDR, so
`classify_unsheared` marks it unsheared and every one of its pipelines takes
the TWIN. A patch applied after that point would be created, logged, and never
bound -- which this project has done before. `hudless_patched` is threaded into
the twin snapshot, the module recreate and the canvas variant, and is kept
SEPARATE from `frag_patched`, which is published as "index-offset APPLIED" and
would otherwise name a transform that never ran.

### A defect found while wiring it

The fog knob's report claimed to be *"reported unconditionally, including the
0"* and sat inside `bindless_report()`, whose first statement returns unless a
bindless knob is on. So `X4VR_DISABLE_FOG=1` with the bindless knobs off printed
**nothing at all**, and the two readings that line exists to separate -- "fog
still on" and "fog disabled and it changed nothing" -- stayed
indistinguishable. #76's report had inherited the same gate, which is how it
surfaced: the harness ran the knob and no line appeared.

Both now live in `shader_knob_report()`, outside every gate. This is take 173's
failure again -- two unrelated features on one gate, with no log line saying so
-- and the comment naming that failure is three functions away in the same file.

### Take 239: it works, completely

`X4VR_HUDLESS=1`, and Patola's report:

> starting loadscreen didn't appear, all black. On the 3D menu, the text
> overlay where you select continue, options, etc was not drawn. [...] the
> savegame loadscreen was also not drawn. Started in the cockpit, HUD was not
> there. Pressed M to bring the map, the cockpit was blurred but nothing
> appeared. [...] I exited the game blind.

and with the knob off, *"all the above elements were back."*

**The patched module IS the one X4 binds** -- the last thing that had not been
verified anywhere. And the switch does exactly what the GLSL says: `OUT_RT0 =
hudless`, with the whole UI composite dropped.

Three things follow, and the second and third are design constraints rather
than confirmations:

1. **Every scrap of X4's UI lives in that one texture.** Menus, load screens,
   the map, the HUD -- all gone together, all back together. Nothing UI-shaped
   survived in `hudless`, so the separation #57 needs is total, not partial.
2. **X4's menu blur is in the SCENE chain, not the UI.** Pressing M blurred the
   cockpit and drew nothing. So when the UI moves to its own layer, the scene
   layer will still blur behind it. That is arguably the right behaviour -- the
   depth cue survives -- but the blur will be locked to the scene's frame and
   the menu to the head's.
3. **Load screens are UI in their entirety**, so during a load our scene layer
   is black and everything the player sees is on the UI layer.

**Not yet observed: that X4 still RENDERS the UI texture.** The composite stops
sampling it; nothing tells X4's CPU side that, since the switch is now a shader
constant rather than game state, so its UI passes should be untouched. That is
a strong inference and not a measurement -- the next step samples the texture,
which settles it directly.

**The tight control was not run.** 239b was launched with `X4VR_HUDLESS=-`, and
the strict parse rejected it: *"is neither 0 nor 1 — IGNORED, nothing is
patched"*. So the control arm was an UNSET run, not a forced-to-0 one. What is
shown is patch-vs-no-patch; what is not shown is that rewriting the load with
the shipped value is invisible. Worth having, not worth a run of its own -- the
composite we build next is a stronger test of the same thing. (The strict parse
earning its place on its first outing is the small mercy here: `strtoul("-")` is
0, so without it the run would have silently taken the control arm and reported
that forcing the switch changed nothing.)

### The acceptance rule was wrong, and it FAILed a run that answered perfectly

The scorer demanded the count be exactly 4 and 239a reported **2**, so a run
whose screen answered the question completely was scored FAIL.

**X4 creates the copy_gamma permutations lazily.** Two were patched 3 ms before
the first present and the other two **9.8 seconds later**:

    356269.102  hudless #1
    356269.102  hudless #2
    356269.105  mv first present   <- the aggregate line says 2 here
    356278.948  hudless #3
    356278.948  hudless #4

The number the rule wanted exists only in the *final* report, and these runs do
not reach teardown -- which `score_run.py` **already says**, about the pose
channel, two sections above the one I wrote. The offline "4 of 409" ranges over
the dump corpus; the live count ranges over one run's module creations, and I
equated them.

Fixed in both places: the layer now labels the first-present figure a snapshot,
and the scorer counts the per-module `hudless #N` lines, which are monotonic
and available without a teardown. Four is a **ceiling**, not a target -- fewer
means X4 did not need every permutation, and only *more* invalidates the
screen. 239a now reads `4 module(s) patched (ceiling 4)`.

Same shape as take 202 and the four earlier false FAILs in that file: a
rule of mine, about a number my own instrument produced, contradicting an
observation that was never in doubt.

### The pose FAIL in both arms is the map, and it is not #76

Both 239a and 239b FAIL on *"the pose fell back to identity N times AFTER it
had been driven"*. It is in **both** arms, so it has nothing to do with the
switch -- and every late identity sample sits inside a map-or-menu window:

    239a   M down 356402.347   identity 356402.487, 356409.154
           ESC   356411.580/356412.850   identity 356415.829
    239b   M down 356635.327   identity 356636.710, 356643.377, 356650.043
           ESC   356654.425/356655.601   identity 356656.708

Identity is *correct* there -- there is no cockpit camera with the map up. The
defect is that head-look announces itself idle for external/floating view and
not for the map, so the scorer cannot tell a legitimate drop-out from a real
one. That is #72's territory and the scorer already has a `map` section holding
the intervals it would need. **Not fixed here**, deliberately: absorbing it into
the exclusion during a commit about something else is how a real dropout would
later get hidden by a rule written to make a different run go green.

### What is verified, and what is not

* **Verified offline**: the transform, on X4's own bytes, 4 of 409, valid, one
  load each, the right load.
* **Verified on a GPU under validation**: the value parse, the report firing at
  zero and when unset, and a knob-set run being otherwise unchanged. 202 cases,
  no failures. No fixture there declares X4's block, so the harness does not
  test MATCHING -- the dumps do.
* **Verified live, take 239**: that the patched module is the one X4 BINDS, and
  that the UI is separable in its entirety.
* **Still not verified**: that X4 keeps rendering the UI texture (inference),
  and that forcing the shipped value is invisible (the control that was not
  run).

## #57 step 1: naming the UI render target

Written **before** the run that tests it.

### The predicate

    an image is the UI target iff
      every pass that has written it is one the canvas predicate calls UI
      AND it is not a swapchain image
      AND its format is 8-bit LDR

**Both of the first two clauses are load-bearing.** X4's present passes are
*also* canvas passes -- take 203 has rp #0/#1/#4/#7/#10 all reading
`+PRESENT-CAND +CANVAS` -- and the only thing separating them from the UI pass
by shape is which image they write. Drop the swapchain clause and the predicate
returns five present targets alongside the one that matters.

Paper check against take 203's inventory, which selects exactly one image:

    img #65 writers — masked rp [33,45] unmasked rp []
    rp #33.0: 1 colour [50L] no-depth ... +CANVAS   <- visual_transition
    rp #45.0: 1 colour [50L] no-depth ... +CANVAS   <- xu_ui_unlit*

Every other canvas pass in that frame wrote a `44L` swapchain image.

### Two things the harness caught that a live run would have hidden

* **The lookup ran after the images were gone.** The first version resolved the
  image's format and extent from `g_images` at report time. `mv_report("final")`
  fires from `vkDestroyInstance`, by which point every `VkImage` has been
  destroyed -- so the target reported *"no ImageInfo (untracked image)"* at
  teardown while resolving perfectly at first present. A report that works at
  one of its two call sites and degrades at the other is worse than one that
  never works, because the working half makes the broken half look like data.
  The image's properties are now COPIED into the writer record when the writer
  is recorded.
* **The identification could not be a teardown line.** `mv_report` runs at
  first present -- where the writer map is still empty, take 203 logged
  `img #65 writers — masked rp []` there -- and at teardown, which these runs
  never reach. That is exactly what made #76's first acceptance rule
  unsatisfiable, one section up. So the headline is **latched** at the
  framebuffer, fires once, and needs neither a present nor a clean exit.

### What the run must say

    ui: TARGET img #N — WxH fmt=F, DOUBLED to 2 (per-eye), K masked writer(s)

`DOUBLED` is the number #57 depends on: the layer already masks the UI pass, so
X4's UI is rendered **twice, once per view**, and the second composition layer
can be a projection layer rather than a quad. If it comes back `NOT doubled`
the design changes, and the scorer FAILs on it rather than letting a mono UI
reach both eyes silently.

Exactly 1 is required. Zero and many are different failures and are reported as
such; every rejected candidate names *its own* reason, because "no UI pass ran"
and "the image I want is a swapchain image" want opposite responses.

Asserted in the harness on a real GPU, with the negative control **in the same
frame** as the positive: img #1 is accepted, img #0 rejected for having a world
pass among its writers, img #2 for having no writer. Dropping `X4VR_CANVAS_M`
was tried as the negative arm and does not work -- the pass is still classified
`+CANVAS`, so both arms found the same image and the control asserted nothing.

### Take 240: img #65, and it is per-eye

    ui: TARGET img #65 — 1408x1408 fmt=50, DOUBLED to 2 (per-eye),
        1 masked writer(s) so far.

The predicate resolved to **exactly one** image, at the size of the eye, format
`50` = `B8G8R8A8_SRGB`, and **doubled** -- so X4's UI is already rendered twice,
once per view, and layer B can be a projection layer rather than a quad. And it
is `#65`, the same serial take 203 named, from a completely different
configuration.

The latch fired **9.6 s after the first present**, which is the design being
right rather than lucky: `mv_report`'s first-present call had
`img #65 writers — masked rp []`, and the run never reached teardown. A
teardown-only report would have come back empty, exactly as #76's first
acceptance rule did.

**A weakness the run exposed.** The latch says `1 masked writer(s) so far`
while take 203's finished frame has **two** passes writing that image. A latch
reports the first moment the answer is 1, not a settled answer -- so a later
non-canvas writer would invalidate an announcement already made. There is now a
retraction check for that, and it is **UNEXERCISED**: nothing in X4's frame or
in the render test writes an image with a canvas pass and then a non-canvas
one, so its silence is the absence of a test rather than a confirmation.

### Does X4 keep rendering the UI? Counted, not inferred

Take 240 ran with `X4VR_HUDLESS=1`, so it is tempting to read "the UI target
was found" as "X4 still draws into it". **It is not the same claim.** Writers
are recorded at `vkCreateFramebuffer`, and creating a framebuffer is not
drawing through it -- the same distinction as `nm -D` proving a symbol is
imported rather than called.

`X4VR_PIPE_INVENTORY=1` would have answered it, but a counter answers it better
and needs no knob:

    ui: X4 has RECORDED N render pass(es) into img #65 since it was identified

Two one-shots, at N=1 and N=600. The first says X4 draws the UI at all; the
second, about ten seconds of frames later, says it keeps doing so rather than
having drawn it once at load. Both are free after they fire, and neither needs
a teardown the runs never reach.

It says **RECORDED**, not *drew*: this counts `vkCmdBeginRenderPass`, and a
command buffer could in principle be built and never submitted. X4 presents
every frame so the gap is small, but the two are different words for a reason.
Exercised in the harness, which is what stops it shipping as a line nobody has
seen fire.

### X4 recentres the view when the map opens

Patola, take 240: *"when I bring up the (invisible) map, before or during the
blur, the game also centers the view of the cockpit."*

That is X4's own behaviour and it explains the pose dropout that has FAILed
every run since 239: the identity samples all sit inside map/menu windows
because X4 has taken the camera back to centre and there is no cockpit camera
to read. It is #78's mechanism, named -- and it is more than a scorer problem, since
head-look's neutral moves underneath it every time a menu opens.

## #57 step 2: layer B — the plan, before the code

Layer A exists: `X4VR_HUDLESS=1` makes X4 emit the hudless scene, and the
compositor blits it into the runtime's swapchain every frame. Layer B is
`img #65`, submitted as a **second projection layer** -- projection rather than
quad because take 240 measured the image `DOUBLED to 2`, so X4 already renders
the UI once per view.

    layer A   hudless scene, declared with the pose it was RENDERED from
    layer B   the UI target, alpha-blended over it, in the SHIP's frame at a
              finite distance — NOT the head pose (take-241 correction)

`frame_end()` already takes an array and a count, so submitting two layers
needs no change there. `proj_ui` gets
`XR_COMPOSITION_LAYER_BLEND_TEXTURE_ALPHA_BIT` and **premultiplied** alpha --
which is what X4 produces: `visual_transition` ends `rgb *= U_useralphascale`
and `copy_gamma` consumes `ui.rgb + (1-ui.a)*hudless.rgb`.

### The copy, and where the risk actually is

The hard part is not the layer, it is getting `#65`'s bytes without corrupting
an image X4 owns. Copying at present time means guessing the layout X4 left it
in, and a wrong `oldLayout` is undefined behaviour rather than an error.

**That problem is already solved in this file.** The MV probe captures an
attachment at `vkCmdEndRenderPass`: it barriers from `a.final_layout` -- the
layout the render pass itself declared, recorded by `record_final_layouts()` --
to `TRANSFER_SRC_OPTIMAL`, copies, and barriers back to exactly that layout.
Nothing is guessed, and the moment is the one where the UI image is complete.

So layer B copies at the end of every pass that writes the UI target.

**And the premise is measured, not assumed.** `final=N` in the pass inventory
is `VkAttachmentDescription::finalLayout`, straight from X4's own render-pass
create info -- the code is four lines above the log line. Take 203's UI pass
reads:

    rp #33.0: 1 colour [50L] no-depth final=2 ...

`2` is `VK_IMAGE_LAYOUT_COLOR_ATTACHMENT_OPTIMAL`, **not** `5`
(`SHADER_READ_ONLY_OPTIMAL`). So X4 issues its own barrier somewhere between
that pass and `copy_gamma` sampling the image -- a barrier the layer does not
track. A present-time copy would therefore have to guess, and would guess
`COLOR_ATTACHMENT_OPTIMAL` when the image is by then in `SHADER_READ_ONLY`.
Wrong `oldLayout` is undefined behaviour, not an error, so it would not even
fail loudly.

That is the whole argument for capturing at the pass end rather than at
present, and it is worth having checked: had `final` read `5`, the staging
image below would be unnecessary and the copy would be one step instead of two.

### Two things that follow from that, both costs

* **The swapchain image is not acquired yet.** Acquisition happens on the
  present thread, and writing an unacquired image is invalid. So the UI pass
  copies into a **layer-owned staging image**, and the compositor copies
  staging -> XR swapchain at present, where acquisition already happens and the
  existing eye blit already does exactly this.
* **Which UI pass is last is not known a priori.** Take 203's frame has two
  (rp #33 then rp #45, creation order, which is not execution order). Copying
  at every UI pass end means the last one wins, at the price of one redundant
  copy: 1408x1408x4x2 layers = 15.9 MB, so ~48 MB/frame across the three copies
  rather than 32. **That is a real number against "performance is king"** and it
  is written down here so the first measurement is compared against a
  prediction rather than against nothing. If it costs, the fix is to learn the
  last UI pass from frame 1 and copy only after it.

### What must be true before this is judged by eye

The identification has a latch and the latch has a blind spot (above). Once
layer B is wired, a wrong identification stops being a line in a log and
becomes a wrong image in the headset -- so `ui_retract_if_disqualified()` needs
its fixture built at that point, not left UNEXERCISED as it is now.

### Then, and not before

Layer A is already there: `X4VR_HUDLESS=1` makes X4 emit the hudless scene, and
the layer blits it into the runtime's swapchain every frame. Layer B is the UI
target, copied into a second swapchain and submitted with
`XR_COMPOSITION_LAYER_BLEND_TEXTURE_ALPHA_BIT` and **premultiplied** alpha --
which is what X4 produces, since `visual_transition` ends
`rgb *= U_useralphascale` and `copy_gamma` consumes `ui.rgb + (1-ui.a)*hudless`.
Declared with the head pose rather than the rendered one, which is the whole
point.

## CORRECTION, take 241: layer B's frame was WRONG, and repeatedly

Everything below that says the UI layer is declared **with the head pose** is
wrong, and it is wrong in the same way in several places because I wrote it
once and re-read my own note as if it were settled.

Patola:

> the HUD was **never** intended to follow my head in the cockpit, and **this
> is not the first time you insist on it**. Instead it was meant to stay fixed
> relative to the cockpit. It should be world-locked, but not in the infinity;
> it should behave as floating widgets projected in a plane or sphere
> representing the view of the cockpit.

**The record said so before any of this was written.** #57's title is
*"Separate screen-locked from world-at-infinity with a **finite canvas**"*, and
#30/#40 was *"UI on a **floating canvas**"*. Head-locking is the obvious VR
idiom and the cheap one — the pose is already in hand and no distance has to be
chosen — and that is exactly why it kept winning over the title.

**The distinction is modal**, and it is his to make, not mine: in the cockpit
the HUD belongs to the **ship**, like real instruments, so turning the head
leaves it behind. In walking mode a minimal head-locked HUD *is* right.

### What take 241 does establish

The mechanism works end to end — identification, capture, blit, submission —
and the pose is demonstrably being honoured, because the **savegame load screen
came out head-locked**, which is what a head-pose layer B does.

* The **starting load screen appeared again**, where take 239 had it black. The
  UI is genuinely coming back through layer B and not through `copy_gamma`.
* **Roll is correct**: the HUD followed the head's roll.
* **Pitch and yaw are inverted.** A sign error on top of the frame error — and
  worth keeping, because whatever frame is chosen the convention still has to
  be right. #77 was a sign error of exactly this shape.
* **The start-menu text is still missing** while the load screen is not. Two UI
  things behaving differently, unexplained.

### What the frame has to become

    layer B pose = the SHIP's orientation, not the head's and not the
                   rendered camera's (which contains the head-look servo)
                 = rendered_pose  o  headlook^-1

and at a **finite distance**, which a projection layer cannot express — it has
no depth, so the compositor treats it as infinitely far. That points at a
**quad layer** per eye (`XrCompositionLayerQuad` carries `eyeVisibility` and a
`size` in metres), not the projection layer take 241 submits.

Two interactions to settle before building it, neither of them mine to decide
alone:

* **The distance.** "A plane or sphere representing the view of the cockpit"
  needs a number, and it wants to sit where the cockpit glass is rather than
  where the instruments are.
* **Double parallax.** #30/#40 already bakes a per-eye shift into the UI image
  to place it at a chosen depth. Putting that image on a quad at a finite
  distance would apply parallax twice. One of the two has to go, and which one
  depends on the distance above.

## Take 242: the frame is RIGHT, two defects remain

The quad, in the ship's frame at 0.70 m. Patola's report, and it is the most
informative one this task has had.

### The identity claim is CONFIRMED, from the log

    ui: SUBMITTING a quad at 0.70 m ... orientation IDENTITY
    vr pose: declared yaw=-8.02 pitch=6.19 deg

Layer A's pose tracks the head-look command while the quad sits at identity, so
the two poses differ by exactly that command -- which is what the claim
predicted and what the line was written to be able to refute. **The frame is
not the problem**, and that rules out a whole class.

**Roll is FIXED**: *"rolling my head would not roll the HUD (it stayed level
with the cockpit), which is good"*. That is the quad's identity orientation
doing its job.

### Defect 1: yaw and pitch still double

*"the HUD moves in the opposite direction of my head, does not become fixed in
space... I imagine that it might be doing that twice."*

Patola's reading, and the roll/yaw asymmetry is the evidence for it: the servo
drives yaw and pitch only, while #77's roll is a shear rather than a geometric
rotation -- so a mechanism living in the SERVO would leave roll clean and break
exactly these two.

The candidate is the image CONTENT, not the layer. X4 draws the HUD in screen
space against a camera the servo has already turned by +theta to follow the
head, so inside the image the HUD sits at (ship + theta); pinning that to a quad
at the ship's direction displaces it by -theta while the head is at +theta.

**The arithmetic is NOT settled and must not be guessed at a fourth time.** I
have talked myself round this loop in both directions in one sitting, and the
frame has already been wrong twice. Settle the sign on paper against
`head_angles()` and the servo's own convention -- the way #77 was eventually
settled -- before spending a take. If the paper says the current arrangement is
already correct, then something else supplies the second rotation and the paper
will say what.

### Defect 2: the stereo separation is wrong EVERYWHERE

Consistent across the start-up load screen, the savegame load screen and the
map, which is what makes it separable from defect 1: the map *"behaved
correctly"* in framing and still had the wrong separation.

**Suspect, and it is mine.** The quad submits `imageArrayIndex = 0` with
`XR_EYE_VISIBILITY_BOTH`, and **layer 0 is the LEFT eye's render** -- the UI
pass is masked, so it is drawn per-eye with per-eye transforms. Showing the left
eye's image to both eyes gives a left-biased picture, and the quad then adds its
own parallax on top of a disparity that is already baked in.

A quad needs a genuinely **eye-neutral** source. Dropping the #30/#40 canvas map
was necessary but not sufficient: the pass is still masked and still sheared.
The fix is to make the UI pass eye-neutral, not to pick the other array layer.

### Also: 0.70 m is too close

*"It look uncomfortably close"*, on every panel. A knob, not a rebuild --
`X4VR_CANVAS_M`. Try 1.2-1.5 m. Judge it only after defect 2 is fixed, because
wrong separation and wrong distance both read as "uncomfortably close".

## The shape of the fix

    layer A   hudless scene, declared with the pose it was RENDERED from
    layer B   the UI texture, declared with the SHIP's frame at a FINITE
              distance -- NOT the head pose. See the take-241 correction
              above; head-locking is right in walking mode and wrong in the
              cockpit, and I built the wrong one twice.

which is #57 exactly, and it also gates #71: aiming is guided by HUD markings,
so a HUD that slides cannot be aimed through however free the mouse is. That

## Settled on paper, no take: what take 242 actually measured

The banner said defect 1 was paper work and defect 2 was concrete. **Both were
wrong that way round.** Defect 1 is settled below and the fix is three lines;
defect 2's mechanism is refuted by the code and is retracted.

### #55's open half is ANSWERED, and take 242 was the experiment

#55 measured every HUD element at **zero** disparity against −20 to −43 px on
the cockpit beside it, and then said exactly what it could not conclude:

> 0 px is what screen-locked content reads *and* what world geometry at
> infinity reads. Under a head rotation those diverge: screen-locked follows
> the head, world-at-infinity rotates correctly. **This method cannot separate
> them** [...] What separates them is a canvas at a *finite* distance —
> `X4VR_CANVAS_M=2`, which moves screen-space content and leaves world alone.
> Filed rather than guessed.

Take 242 put the UI on a canvas at a finite distance. **The falsifier fired.**

    quad at the ship's direction, head and X4 camera both at +C:

      screen-locked content   sits at image angle 0
                              -> displayed at ship angle 0     ship-fixed, correct
      world-at-infinity       sits at image angle -C
                              -> displayed at ship angle -C    head at +C, so 2C apart

Patola saw the second: *"the HUD moves in the opposite direction of my head,
does not become fixed in space... it might be doing that twice."* Had the HUD
been screen-locked, the identity quad would have made it ship-fixed and he
would have called it correct — which is what he called the **map**.

**So X4's cockpit HUD is world-anchored in angle and drawn at infinity.** Both
halves at once, which is the third possibility #55 could not reach with one
frame. It is also the only self-consistent reading of the older roll report,
*"all the HUD elements always stay perfectly level to the world"* — level to
the **world**, not to the screen.

That closes #55's open half and it retires the "X4 draws the HUD in screen
space" sentence in the take-242 section above, which was written as an
unsettled candidate and is now refuted.

### Defect 1: the servo's sign is CORRECT — the quad's declaration is not

The banner sent me to check `head_angles()` against the servo. Done, and the
servo is innocent. `head_look_step()` applies `sign_yaw` **twice**:

    d.dx          = lround(sign_yaw * step_yaw * weight / gain)
    s.cmd_yaw_deg += sign_yaw * (float)d.dx * gain

`sign_yaw² = 1`, so `cmd_yaw_deg` accumulates in **head convention** (+ = left)
and not in the mouse convention. It has to: the next frame forms
`err_yaw = want_yaw - cmd_yaw_deg` against a `want_yaw` derived from
`head.yaw_deg`, and a loop cannot close across two conventions.
`tests/headlook.cpp` pins the other end — `quat_of_angles` round-trips through
`head_angles`. So `cam_yaw_deg`, `decl_yaw`, and layer A's declared quaternion
are all in head convention and all correct.

**There is no sign error anywhere in the chain.** The doubling is not a sign; it
is a missing rotation, and the arithmetic above says which:

    HUD displayed angle = Q + (content angle in the texture)
                        = Q + (-C)

    Q = 0 (today)   ->  -C    wrong by 2C, which is what take 242 saw
    Q = C           ->   0    ship-fixed, which is what #57 asks for

**The quad must declare the same orientation layer A declares.** Not because
the HUD lives there, but because the quad is a re-projection of an image
rendered through X4's camera, and the honest declaration for such an image is
the pose it was rendered from — which is the rule layer A already follows. The
image is the same image; only the depth differs.

**This is NOT the head-locking Patola rejected twice, and the difference must
be stated so it is not re-read as one.** Head-locked means the HUD's displayed
angle equals the head's. Here it is `Q − C = 0`: the quad's *frame* turns with
the camera while the content inside it counter-turns by exactly as much, and
the HUD lands on the ship and stays there. The behavioural test is the same one
Patola has given twice — **turn your head and the HUD must leave the view.**
Identity was the arrangement that could not do that, because it declared "this
image was rendered from the ship's forward axis", which is false the moment the
camera turns.

The take-242 log line was not wrong; it was answering a smaller question than I
credited it with. It asked *are the two declared poses different?* and they
were. Nothing in it observed the frame the **content** was in, and that is the
frame that decides the behaviour. I wrote "the frame is CONFIRMED right" from a
line that could only ever confirm the declaration.

### Defect 2: RETRACTED — the source is already eye-neutral

The claim was: *"the quad submits `imageArrayIndex = 0` and layer 0 is the LEFT
eye's render — the UI pass is masked, so it is drawn per-eye and sheared."*

**The second half is false, and `classify_unsheared()` says so:**

    unsheared[i] = any && all_ldr;      // every colour attachment 8-bit

The UI pass is all-LDR, so it is `unsheared` — the pipelines bound in it take
the **original, unpatched** twins. No K, no cant, no per-eye anything. Both
array layers of img #65 carry identical pixels, so `imageArrayIndex = 0` is
eye-neutral by construction and has been since long before layer B existed.

What misled me is real and worth keeping: X4's UI vertex shaders *are*
classified `World, live-sx`, because they read set-3 member 0 exactly as world
geometry does. That is about the variant **emitted** for a module. Which variant
gets **bound** is a per-pass decision, and in this pass it is the original.
Emitted is not bound — the same distinction that cost a take before.

**So there is nothing to fix here, and one less thing to build.** The residual
"wrong stereo separation" has a simpler cause with no code in it: content X4
drew **at infinity** is being presented at **0.70 m**. Zero disparity in the
source, 0.70 m of vergence demand from the quad — a reticle over a ship 5 km
away asks the eyes to converge at arm's length. That is not a defect in the
quad; it is the canvas distance, and it is why every panel showed it equally.

Defect 2 and "0.70 m is too close" were one defect all along, exactly as that
section feared they might be. They are not separable because they are not two.

## Take 243: P243.1 REFUTED. The fix was half a placement.

*"The HUD still goes to the opposite side of the head without staying fixed
relative to the cockpit"* — in both arms, and 243b was indistinguishable from
243a except for distance. The run was properly exercised: `ui quad 23
submission sample(s), largest declared angle 10.08 deg`, so the quad really did
carry a turned pose and the change really did reach the headset.

**The geometry says it could not have worked, and I should have seen it before
spending the take.** `XrCompositionLayerQuad` is a rectangle **centred at
`pose.position`** and turned about that centre by `pose.orientation`. I changed
the orientation and left the centre pinned at `neutral + (0, 0, -zm)`. Turning
a panel about its own centre does not move the content near that centre — so
the HUD's world direction was identical in 242 and 243a, which is exactly what
Patola reported twice in the same words.

    242    centre dead ahead, orientation identity   HUD at -C
    243a   centre dead ahead, orientation C          HUD at -C   <- no-op
    243b   ditto, panel further away                 HUD at -C

**What 243 did establish, and it is worth the take.** The panel's centre was
FIXED in the reference space in both arms, and the HUD still moved. Content on
a fixed panel can only appear to move if it moves **within the texture**. So
X4's cockpit HUD is world-anchored in angle — no longer an inference from one
observation, but forced by two takes with a stationary panel. The take-242
conclusion survives; only my implementation of it was wrong.

**The fix: place the panel where X4's image plane was.** Position *and*
orientation are one rigid placement and have to move together. The centre now
orbits the neutral point to sit `zm` along the camera's own forward axis:

    off      = R(C) * (0, 0, -zm)
    position = neutral + off
    orient   = R(C)

Then a HUD element the texture holds at `-C` lands at `C + (-C) = 0` and sits
on the ship. `tests/headlook.cpp` asserts the orbited centre lands on the
camera axis, and asserts it *as a contrast against 243a's pinned centre*,
because "the centre is straight ahead" on its own is true by construction and
would be a check that cannot fail.

**How this was missed.** The take-242 arithmetic was done entirely in the angle
domain, where a frame is a rotation and nothing else. That is the right domain
for the question "which frame", and it silently drops the question "where is
the origin of that frame". A quad has both, and I declared one of them. The
lesson generalises past this task: **a transform is not applied until every
component of it is applied**, and an angle-domain derivation cannot tell you
that a translation is missing.

### The stereo separation, which is now the OTHER finding

*"Eye separation still feels wrong"* in both arms, *"improved slightly"* at
1.4 m. Distance changes it but does not fix it, which is the signature of a
scale error rather than a placement one.

**Nothing has ever compared the runtime's own eye separation with the number
the scene is sheared by.** `X4VR_IPD=0.064` sets the shear that gives the SCENE
its stereo; the quad has no shear at all, and the runtime derives its stereo
from the two eye poses it reports. Two layers, two different separations, and
if they disagree the UI cannot sit convincingly in front of the scene at ANY
distance — while moving it further away shrinks the disparity and so shrinks
the disagreement, which is precisely "slightly better at 1.4 m".

A line now reports both at the first located frame. It is a real comparison and
not a guard that can only agree: one side is a pose WiVRn measured from the
headset, the other is a number from the environment, and they have no common
ancestor. **This is measurement, not a fix** — if they differ, which number
should win is #25's question and Patola's to judge, and the answer may be to
stop baking an IPD at all.

## Take 244: STOP. Three takes, three placements, one unchanged report.

Patola: *"We're again stuck in that situation where you change random knobs and
they don't have an effect... the HUD on the cockpit still goes to the opposite
direction of my head (why nothing has an effect on this?)"*

He is right, and the question is the correct one to ask. The answer is that all
three placements were built on an **assumption about where the HUD sits inside
X4's UI texture as the camera turns**, and the assumption was different every
time — while nothing ever measured it:

    take 242   assumed screen-locked   content at 0     -> quad at identity
    take 243   assumed world-anchored  content at -C    -> quad rotated
    take 244   ditto                                    -> quad rotated + orbited

If the content is at neither 0 nor −C, all three are wrong and none of them
could have worked. Their joint result — *"opposite the head"* at every
placement — is consistent with content at **−2C**, which no take has tested,
because no take has measured the number.

**#55 said this in writing and I did not act on it.** It measured the HUD's
disparity, found zero, and stated that zero cannot separate screen-locked from
world-at-infinity — *"under a head rotation those diverge"*. It filed the
distinguishing experiment. Three takes later I am building it.

### What was eliminated first, so the list is honest

* **Stale binary — NO.** Take 244's log carries the `ipd:` line, which exists
  only in the orbit build. It ran the code it was meant to.
* **The pose being zero — NO.** `cam_valid` is 0 for the first 113 s (loading,
  expected) and 1 through the cockpit window; the quad's declared angle reaches
  27.61°.
* **A scale error in the quad — NO.** X4's half-angle at `X4VR_FOV=1.4917` is
  `1.4917 × 73.7399 / 2 = 55.0°`, and the panel is 4.00 m wide at 1.40 m, i.e.
  `atan(2.0/1.4) = 55.0°`. They agree exactly, so the texture is not being
  magnified.

That leaves the content's own frame, which is the one thing never measured.

### `tools/hud_vs_camera.py` — the measurement, and its control

Cross-correlate consecutive present dumps in two channels: `hud` (X4's
green/cyan overlay) and `grey` (the cockpit, overlay removed). `grey` is the
WORLD's motion in the same image at the same instant, so it calibrates
pixels-per-degree with no knowledge of the field, and the verdict is the ratio:

    dx_hud / dx_grey ~ 1   world-anchored
    ~ 0                    screen-locked
    ~ 2                    X4 counter-rotates it twice — what 242/243/244 imply

**Validated on take 237's 74 dumps as a negative control** — that run had no
head-look and X4's camera never left 0.00, so every pair must come back
unusable. Three defects were found doing it, all of which produced
confident-looking wrong answers:

* It halved every image as if it were an SBS composite. The present dumps are
  written one file per array layer and are already 1408×1408, so the search
  window no longer fit and `shift()` returned `None` — printed as "no signal"
  and summarised as *"the camera did not turn"*. A geometry mistake was exiting
  through the same door as a real null; it now raises.
* It correlated everything against file [0], which is the black start-up frame.
  Consecutive pairs instead, with scene breaks not bridged.
* **It had no margin gate**, though the docstring quotes #55's reason for one.
  Four scene-change pairs with correlation margins of 0.000–0.009 were folded
  into a headline median of −0.65 — a confident number assembled from noise.
  Static pairs read 0.34–0.52, so the gate separates them cleanly.

### The pivot artefact, which Patola says I under-weighted — he is right

*"as if the pivot was wrong or there was a larger rotation arm than my neck,
making the cockpit shift up, the sides of the cockpit get more distant when I
look at them... doing that for a long time might cause VR motion sickness"*

There is a mechanism and it is in the log. Layer A declares its position as

    off = head_to_world(R(C), (±ipd/2) + g_reye.sx, g_reye.sy, 0)
    position = neutral + off

so the head-translate shift is **rotated by the camera angle**. Take 244's
scorer reports `translate |published| max x 0.1412 y 0.1715 m`. That is a 17 cm
lever swinging with every turn of the head, fed to the compositor as the point
the pixels were rendered from — which is exactly "a larger rotation arm than my
neck". #74 is documented as *"built, default OFF, not clean... a small
deterministic-in-angle drift remains, seven hypotheses eliminated"*, and it has
been ON in every recent take.

It is eliminable with a knob and no code: `X4VR_HEAD_TRANSLATE=0`. That is
Patola's own method — switch the candidate off and re-measure — and it should
have been tried the first time he described the artefact.

things asked for: the overlays further away, and the 17 cm arm gone.

**P245.2.** The ratio is one of the three named values. I am not predicting
