## Take 245: the 17 cm arm was real, and 245B's instrument was not ready

### 245A — the elimination WORKED, and it closes more than it aimed at

Patola: *"the pitch up shifting the quad in the savegame loadscreen is solved
and now turning my head doesn't push the cockpit away like before to a
noticeable degree. So it's much better now. Stereo separation feels better now
too, only looking up at the borders in the overlay seem to be a bit wrong."*

Three complaints improved from removing **one** thing: `X4VR_HEAD_TRANSLATE`.
Layer A had been declaring

    position = neutral + R(C) · (±ipd/2 + head_shift)

with the shift measured at **0.17 m** in take 244. That whole vector is rotated
by the camera angle, so the point the compositor is told the pixels came from
swung on a 17 cm lever with every turn of the head. Consequences, all three of
which Patola reported separately and I had been treating as three problems:

* **the cockpit "pushed away" and its sides stretched** — the compositor was
  reprojecting for a viewpoint that moved when the real head barely had;
* **the load screen drifted on pitch up** — the quad's centre does NOT use the
  shift, so it stood still while the WORLD swung under it. The relative motion
  was read as the quad drifting. Only pitch-up because that is where the shift
  got large enough to see;
* **stereo separation felt wrong** — the declared eye positions carried the
  swinging vector on top of the IPD.

**#74's head translation, as implemented, is harmful and stays OFF.** It is not
"built, default OFF, not clean" any more; it is a known cause of the artefact
Patola identified as the nausea risk. The seven eliminated hypotheses in its
notes were all looking for a small drift, and the thing to look at was the lever
arm the declaration multiplies it by.

This is Patola's method and it should have been run the first time he described
the artefact, not the third.

### 245B — no usable pair, and the instrument is why

`hud_vs_camera.py` reported NO USABLE PAIR over 25 dumps of a run whose log
shows X4's camera moving through 62°. Two causes, both mine:

**1. The protocol I specified defeats the measurement.** I asked Patola to HOLD
each position ~6 s so a dump would land in it. Dumps land every ~4 s, so
consecutive dumps fall inside the SAME hold and the world has not moved between
them — `dx_grey = 0` with good confidence, correctly reported as unusable. The
pairs that matter are across DIFFERENT holds, which a consecutive-pairs tool
never forms.

**2. The `hud` channel does not survive a nebula.** Inherited from
`hud_frame.py`: `(G+B)/2 - R`, correct for take 162's frame. Take 245b's cockpit
looks out at a blue-purple nebula, and that expression scored **66% of the
frame** as HUD. Both channels then carried the same content and every margin
collapsed to ~0.001.

X4's HUD is **cyan** (G ≈ B); the nebula is blue-purple (B > G). Requiring
`G >= 0.9B and G > 1.3R` gives **0.09%** coverage on the same frame and picks
out the radar arc and the target brackets. On take 237's static control the
margin rises from 0.34 to **0.876**. Fixed, with the counter-example recorded in
the docstring.

**What 245b hints at but does NOT establish:** in three of five cockpit pairs
`dx_hud` lands within a few px of `dx_grey` (68/73, 188/191, 20/21), which is
ratio ≈ 1, i.e. world-anchored. **Every one of those margins is ~0.000.** It is
recorded as a hint and nothing is built on it; reading a verdict out of
zero-margin correlations is the exact mistake this tool's margin gate exists to
prevent.

**The better instrument, if the measurement is still needed:** dump the UI
target on its own — `X4VR_MV_DUMP_AFTER_RP=33,56`, the two passes take 244's
inventory shows writing `img #65` — instead of the composited present. There is
then no nebula, no stars and no cockpit in the image, so no colour trick is
needed and the contamination question does not arise.

## The HUD's frame, MEASURED at last — and the defect is 10% in yaw only

Patola recorded two 20 s clips at 30 fps. `tools/hud_vs_camera.py` cross-
correlates consecutive frames in a cyan-only HUD channel against a HUD-removed
luma channel, so the cockpit in the same image calibrates pixels-per-degree and
the verdict is a ratio. A clip is a far better instrument than take 245b's
dumps: 4 s apart the head has moved through a large unknown angle and nothing
correlates, while at 30 fps consecutive frames differ by a few px.

    clip                       yaw            pitch
    vanilla X4, no mod         1.00 (84)      1.00 (78)
    VR, take 245A config       0.90 (55)      1.00 (97)

**X4's cockpit HUD is WORLD-ANCHORED, exactly, on both axes.** 84 usable pairs
in vanilla X4, median 1.00, 79 verdicts "world-anchored" and **zero** reading
screen-locked or doubled. #55's open half is closed with a number, and takes
243/244 had the right premise after all — the content really is at −C.

**In VR it tracks at 0.90 in yaw and 1.00 in pitch.** 55 pairs with the world
moving ≥8 px, sd 0.115, and direction-independent: 0.890 for one sense of the
turn, 0.900 for the other. That is a clean scale factor on ONE AXIS, not a
lag (a lag reproduces the same rate under constant velocity) and not a sign
error.

**Verified before believing it:** the cyan mask on the VR frames selects only
the target-bracket cluster — 0.024% coverage — and NOT the cockpit's own
emissive cyan panels, which would have biased the ratio toward 1.0 by measuring
the cockpit twice. The mask image was inspected, not assumed.

### The structural suspect, from the code

    pv[e].fov = oat.on ? oat.fov[e] : g_vr_fov;   // scene: the RUNTIME's
                                                  // per-eye ASYMMETRIC frustum
    const XrFovf &f = g_vr_fov;                   // quad: X4's SYMMETRIC fov

**The two layers carrying one camera's image are described by two different
fields.** This run's runtime reports eye0 `l=-54 r=+40 u=+44 d=-55` — strongly
asymmetric horizontally — while `g_vr_fov` is X4's symmetric ±55.0°
(`x4_half_for_fov(1.4917) = 1.4917 × 73.7399 / 2`). The scene's pixels are
remapped onto the runtime's frustum by the affine; the quad's are placed at
X4's angles. Nothing makes those agree.

Taking the measurement at face value, HUD motion / world motion =
`tan(assumed) / tan(true)`, so `tan(true) = tan(55.0°)/0.90 = 1.587` and X4's
true horizontal half-angle is about **57.8°** while its vertical is exactly the
55.0° we assume. X4's UI is not square in angle even though it renders into a
square 1408×1408 target.

**That is task #45, open since before any of this: "Check whether X4 lays the
HUD out against the window rather than the render extent."** X4 is told its
window is 2816×1408 — the SBS composite, aspect 2:1 — while it renders
1408×1408. A horizontal field derived from the window and a vertical one
derived from the render is exactly the shape of a yaw-only error.

**Not yet established, and not to be guessed:** whether 57.8° is right, and
whether the fix is the quad's width, `x4_half_for_fov`, or what X4 is told
about its window. The next step reads X4's own projection for the UI camera
(`X4VR_DUMP_MATRICES=1` gives sx = 1/tan(half)) and compares it to 55.0° —
paper, from a run we may already have.

### The honest gap

10% over a 50° turn is about 5° of slip. That is a real defect and it is the
right shape, but it is smaller than *"goes to the opposite side of my head"*
sounds. Either the recording does not capture the runtime's final reprojection
(so his eyes see more than the capture does), or the slip feels far larger in a
headset than the number suggests, or there is a second effect the clip does not
show. **Recorded as a discrepancy rather than resolved**, because the last four
takes were spent on explanations that fitted a description instead of a
measurement.

## CONFIRMED: Patola's recording IS what he sees, and the number is the defect

*"The VR recording is exactly what I see in the headset."* So the 10% measured
in the clip is the whole of *"the HUD still goes to the opposite direction of my
head, not becoming fixed in relation to the cockpit"*.

**His description was accurate and my reading of it was not.** "Goes to the
opposite side" is what correct world-locked content does; the load-bearing half
was always *"not becoming fixed in relation to the cockpit"*, which is exactly a
0.90 tracking ratio. The DOUBLING was my inference — he offered it once as
*"I imagine that it might be doing that twice"* and three takes were built on my
promotion of that guess to a premise.

### X4's projection is square — so the asymmetry is ours

From `proj CAMERA` walks in takes 106 and 112, every camera but one 4-draw
group reports `|sy/sx| = 1.0000`:

    25-29 draws   sx=1.33333  ratio=1.0000    ignores <fov>
    19    draws   sx=0.75405  ratio=1.0000    HONOURS <fov>
    4     draws   sx=3.78085  ratio=1.5000

`1/0.75405 = 1.326 = tan(52.98°)` and `x4_half_for_fov(1.437) = 1.437 ×
73.7399/2 = 52.98°` — **exact**. So `x4_half_for_fov` is validated against X4's
own matrix, and X4's render is angularly SQUARE on both axes.

### The number that matches

    runtime eye0 frustum   l=-54 r=+40 u=+44 d=-55
      horizontal tan-span  tan54 + tan40 = 2.2155
      vertical   tan-span  tan55 + tan44 = 2.3938
      h/v                                  0.9255

    measured HUD tracking  yaw 0.90 (sd 0.115, n=55)   pitch 1.00
    predicted              0.9255                       difference 0.025

And the vanilla clip, which has no affine and no runtime frustum in it, reads
**1.00 on both axes** — the control the prediction requires.

### What this does and does NOT establish

**Established:** the scene and the UI are displayed through mappings that differ
by the runtime frustum's aspect. The UI pass is deliberately `unsheared`, so it
keeps X4's original symmetric ±55° framing and the quad reproduces that
faithfully; the scene is remapped by the affine onto a frustum whose horizontal
and vertical spans differ by 7.5%. Nothing makes those agree, and the HUD is
what reveals it.

**NOT established, and a ratio cannot establish it: WHICH SIDE IS WRONG.** The
measurement says the two disagree, not which one is at its true angle. Two
readings fit equally:

* the quad is faithful and the **WORLD is horizontally wrong by 7.5%** — an
  aspect error in #35's affine, invisible against a starfield and exactly the
  kind of thing that costs comfort. Note `make_canvas_k`'s neighbours already
  carry `sy_s = -sx_s`, deriving one axis from the other, which is the habit
  that would produce this;
* the affine is right and the **quad should be sized from the runtime frustum**
  rather than from X4's symmetric field.

**Do not pick one by argument.** Separating them needs an ABSOLUTE angular
reference — something whose true angular size is known — not another ratio.
The cheap candidate is a rigid cockpit feature measured in both clips against a
HUD element beside it, which cancels the unknown per-axis scale. That is the
next piece of paper, and it is not a take.

This also **retracts the #45 suggestion made one message earlier**: X4 does not
lay the HUD out non-square, so "against the window rather than the render
extent" is not this defect. #45 remains open on its own merits.

## RETRACTED, one commit later: the frustum-aspect explanation is REFUTED

The section above derived the 10% from the runtime frustum's h/v tan-span ratio
of 0.9255 against a measured 0.90, called the vanilla clip's 1.00 the control,
and committed it. **`X4VR_OFFAXIS` is not set in take 245A.** There is no
`offaxis` line anywhere in its log, so `oat.on` is false, the affine never runs,
and

    pv[e].fov = oat.on ? oat.fov[e] : g_vr_fov;   // -> g_vr_fov
    const XrFovf &f = g_vr_fov;                   // quad

**both layers are declared with the SAME symmetric ±55.0° field.** The runtime's
asymmetric frustum, from which 0.9255 was computed, is not used by anything in
that run. The agreement was a coincidence, and I checked the code for the
mechanism only after the number matched.

That is the failure mode this file already names twice — a matching number
ending the search. It got past me because 0.925 against 0.90 was a *good* match
and I went looking for confirmation instead of for the configuration.

**What survives, because it was measured rather than derived:**

* X4's cockpit HUD is world-anchored: vanilla 1.00 on both axes, 84 pairs.
* In VR it tracks at 0.90 in yaw, 1.00 in pitch, 55 pairs, sd 0.115,
  direction-independent.
* The SAME HUD element is tracked in both clips — the target-bracket cluster,
  confirmed by rendering the mask for one frame of each and looking at it.
* X4's projection is angularly square (`|sy/sx| = 1.0000` on every camera but a
  4-draw group), and `x4_half_for_fov` is exact against its own matrix.

**What is now open, and it is smaller and sharper than before:** with the affine
off, the scene layer and the quad share a pose, a field and a source image.
There is no mapping difference left to explain 0.90, so the cause is something
neither pose nor field:

1. **Parallax asymmetry.** The quad is real geometry at a finite distance and
   the compositor gives it full head-translation parallax; a projection layer is
   a 2D reprojection and gets none. Take 244 measured 0.17 m of real head
   motion. At 2.5 m that is ~3.9°. **This is task #75's shape.** It predicts the
   effect scales with 1/distance — and Patola reports the HUD behaving the same
   at 0.70, 1.40 and 2.50 m, which argues against it. Testable without a new
   run only if a clip exists at another distance; none does.
2. **A measurement bias not yet found.** The `grey` channel is the whole frame
   (cockpit + nebula + stars); the `hud` channel is ~220 sparse pixels. They are
   not weighted alike.

**No third fix is going to be proposed from this.** Two mechanisms remain, the
evidence does not choose between them, and the last four takes were spent on
mechanisms that fitted a number.

### Take 246 — the 0.70 m clip, and what it decides

245A's line verbatim with **`X4VR_CANVAS_M` 2.5 → 0.7** and the take/log names
moved on. Nothing else changes, so the canvas distance is the only variable
against a clip that has already been measured.

    X4VR_TAKE=246-CANVAS070 X4VR_CANVAS_M=0.7 X4VR_STEREO=1 X4VR_BINDLESS_PATCH=1 X4VR_DECLARE_RENDERED_POS=1 X4VR_ROLL_STEREO=1 X4VR_HEADLOOK_LEAD=1.0 X4VR_HUDLESS=1 X4VR_RES=1408x1408 X4VR_VR=1 X4VR_GAMESCOPE=1 X4VR_SBS_RIGHT_LAYER=1 X4VR_HEADLOOK=1 X4VR_SBS_LAYERS=2 X4VR_POSE=1 X4VR_HEADLOOK_RAW=191 X4VR_HEADLOOK_KP=0.25 X4VR_POSELOG=1 X4VR_MV=1 X4VR_PROJ_LIVE=1 X4VR_SBS=1 X4VR_LOG=/tmp/x4vr-take246.log X4VR_UI_LAYER=1 X4VR_MASK_PRESENT=1 X4VR_IPD=0.064 X4VR_FOV=1.4917 X4VR_BINDLESS_MIRROR=1 X4VR_CAMREAD=1 X4VR_MV_INVENTORY=1 X4VR_CAMLOOP=1 X4VR_HEADLOOK_GAIN=0.115 ./launch/x4vr-launch.sh

Record the same clip as `/dados/x4-vr.mp4`: in the cockpit, ~20 s at 30 fps,

    python3 tools/hud_vs_camera.py <clip> --fps 15
    python3 tools/score_run.py /tmp/x4vr-take246.log

**P246.1 — the whole point.** Parallax scales as 1/distance, so if it is the
cause the yaw ratio moves from 0.90 to about **0.64**:

    parallax share at 2.5 m = 1 - 0.90 = 0.10
    at 0.70 m                = 0.10 x 2.5/0.7 = 0.357  ->  ratio 0.64

**P246.2 — the falsifier, and it is the likely one.** If the yaw ratio comes
back at **0.90 again**, parallax is dead and the remaining suspect is my own
instrument: the `grey` channel is the whole frame while `hud` is ~220 sparse
pixels, and nothing has shown that asymmetry is harmless.

**Already awkward for the parallax hypothesis, stated before the run so it is
not claimed afterwards:** pitch measured exactly 1.00 at 2.5 m. Head
translation during a turn is not purely horizontal, so parallax should have
degraded pitch as well and it did not. Patola also reports the HUD behaving the
same at 0.70, 1.40 and 2.50 m across takes 242–245, which is the same
observation from the other side. **The expected outcome of this run is the
falsifier**, and it is worth running because it converts "two candidates" into
one, cheaply, with a clip he already knows how to record.

If P246.2 fires, the next step is auditing `hud_vs_camera.py` against a

check both report it — rather than another take.

## Take 246: BOTH predictions missed, and the instrument is now audited

    canvas    yaw (all usable)   yaw (|dx_grey|>=8)      pitch
    2.50 m    0.92               0.90  sd 0.115  n=55    1.00
    0.70 m    1.00               0.95  sd 0.154  n=45    1.00

**P246.1 is REFUTED.** Parallax predicted 0.64 at 0.70 m and would have made the
near canvas *worse*. It came back better. The scene layer's missing
head-translation parallax is not the cause, and #75 loses this as a symptom.

**P246.2 is not confirmed either.** It predicted 0.90 unchanged; the point
estimate moved to 1.00.

**The confounds were checked and eliminated, in order:**

* **Config.** `diff` of the two `env: run =` lines: only `X4VR_CANVAS_M`,
  `X4VR_LOG` and `X4VR_TAKE`. A genuine single-variable pair.
* **Servo gain.** Fitting `declared` against X4's own readback over the paired
  `poselag` lines gives slope **0.9964 / 0.9951 / 0.9966** for takes 245A / 246
  / 244. No gain error, and no difference between runs.
* **The clamp.** 245A's clip reached ±65° (the servo's stop) and 246's only
  −44..+32, so the excursions differed. But binning 245A's ratio by accumulated
  travel gives 0.910 / 0.825 / 0.880 / **1.000**, best at the largest
  excursion — the opposite of a clamp signature.
* **The same HUD element** is tracked in every clip: the target-bracket cluster,
  confirmed by rendering the mask and looking at it.

### The tool is now audited rather than trusted

`--selftest` runs two audits on a real frame, and the second is the one that
matters:

    rigid         shift the whole frame by a known dx; both channels must
                  return exactly it
    differential  move the HUD and the background by DIFFERENT known amounts
                  and check the reported ratio is A/B

Rigid passes exactly at 3/5/8/12/20/35 px on all three clips. **Differential
recovers 0.80, 0.90 and 1.00 to three decimals** on both VR clips. So the
instrument carries no bias in the only regime it is ever used in, and the
numbers above are real.

**The rigid test alone would have been useless and nearly shipped as
reassurance** — it cannot see a bias that appears only when the two channels
disagree, which is the entire use. `grey` is the whole frame and `hud` is a
couple of hundred sparse pixels; that asymmetry is now measured harmless rather
than assumed harmless.

### What the numbers can and cannot support

Compared like-for-like on the strong-pairs subsets, 0.90 ± 0.115 (n=55) against
0.95 ± 0.154 (n=45) are **not statistically distinct**, and the verdict flips
with the subset — 245A reads 0.92 over all usable pairs and 0.90 over strong
ones; 246 reads 1.00 and 0.95. Consecutive-frame pairs share a frame, so the
effective sample is smaller than n and the true spread is wider than the naive
standard error.

**So the honest position is that the data cannot presently separate "the HUD
tracks the cockpit correctly" from "it tracks 5-10% short", and it has refuted
the one mechanism that was on the table.** What it does say clearly is that
nothing here is a doubling, a sign error, or a frame error — those are all
excluded by an order of magnitude.

The next input is not another number. **It is whether Patola still sees the
defect at 0.70 m with the current build**, which the 246 clip does not answer
because he was asked for a measurement and not for a judgement.

## P246.1 WAS RIGHT. I refuted it with an instrument that cannot see it.

Patola, on take 246: *"The HUD still slips and the amount feels even greater
than the previous run."* That contradicts the ratio metric, which said 246
(0.70 m) tracked BETTER than 245A (2.50 m) — 1.00 against 0.92.

**The observer was right and the instrument was answering a different
question.** `hud_vs_camera.py` compares per-frame-pair MOTION: a rate. Parallax
from head translation does not change the rate at which the HUD sweeps, it adds
a POSITION offset. A rate metric can no more see a position error than `abs()`
can report a sign. I built the ratio to settle "world-anchored or
screen-locked", which is genuinely a rate question, and then reused it to test
parallax without asking whether it could.

### The measurement that does see it

Track the largest HUD blob's absolute position, subtract the world's
accumulated motion, and the result is CONSTANT if the HUD is locked to the
cockpit. Its wander is the slip:

    canvas   HUD-vs-world wander        implied head translation
    2.50 m   sd 21.2 px = 2.34 deg      t = zm*tan(sd) = 10.2 cm
    0.70 m   sd 68.2 px = 7.52 deg      t              =  9.2 cm

    ratio of wander   3.22x measured   |   1/distance predicts 3.57x

**Two clips at very different canvas distances imply the same physical head
motion, ~10 cm.** That is the identification: the effect is not a property of
the HUD or of the frame, it is one translation seen through two lever arms.
Take 244's scorer had independently measured raw head motion at 0.17 m max, so
this is three numbers from three sources agreeing on one quantity.

At 0.70 m the wander RANGE is 33.9 deg. That is not subtle, and it is exactly
*"the amount feels even greater than the previous run"*.

### Why the quad has parallax and the scene does not

A projection layer is reprojected by a 2D warp with no depth, so it **cannot**
apply translation parallax — the scene behaves as though the head never leaves
the point its pose was declared from. A quad is real geometry and the
compositor gives it the full parallax of the true head position. Anchoring the
quad to the latched neutral point therefore bought `t/zm` radians of swim that
the scene can never have. This is task #75's shape and now has a number.

### The fix, and why it is NOT head-locking

The quad now anchors to the **live head centre** (the midpoint of the two eye
poses) instead of the latched neutral point:

    position = head_centre_now + R(C) * (0, 0, -zm)

so its offset from the eye is constant and it has the same relationship to head
translation the scene layer has. **The orientation is untouched** — still the
camera's, so turning the head still sweeps the HUD out of view. It follows the
head's TRANSLATION only, and it does that in order to match the scene rather
than to follow the player. Head-locking is a rotation claim; this is not one.

Falls back to the neutral point until the head is located, which is the old
behaviour and correct before tracking starts.

### Take 247

245A/246's line with `X4VR_CANVAS_M` back to a comfortable **1.4** and the
names moved on:

    X4VR_TAKE=247-HEADANCHOR X4VR_CANVAS_M=1.4 X4VR_STEREO=1 X4VR_BINDLESS_PATCH=1 X4VR_DECLARE_RENDERED_POS=1 X4VR_ROLL_STEREO=1 X4VR_HEADLOOK_LEAD=1.0 X4VR_HUDLESS=1 X4VR_RES=1408x1408 X4VR_VR=1 X4VR_GAMESCOPE=1 X4VR_SBS_RIGHT_LAYER=1 X4VR_HEADLOOK=1 X4VR_SBS_LAYERS=2 X4VR_POSE=1 X4VR_HEADLOOK_RAW=191 X4VR_HEADLOOK_KP=0.25 X4VR_POSELOG=1 X4VR_MV=1 X4VR_PROJ_LIVE=1 X4VR_SBS=1 X4VR_LOG=/tmp/x4vr-take247.log X4VR_UI_LAYER=1 X4VR_MASK_PRESENT=1 X4VR_IPD=0.064 X4VR_FOV=1.4917 X4VR_BINDLESS_MIRROR=1 X4VR_CAMREAD=1 X4VR_MV_INVENTORY=1 X4VR_CAMLOOP=1 X4VR_HEADLOOK_GAIN=0.115 ./launch/x4vr-launch.sh

**P247.1.** The HUD stays on the cockpit: the wander drops from ~7.5 deg (0.70 m)
and ~2.3 deg (2.50 m) to well under 1 deg, and stops scaling with distance.
Judgement first — *does it still slip?* — and a clip second if it does.

**P247.2.** Turning the head still sweeps the HUD out of view. If it now follows
the head, the translation anchor has been applied to the rotation as well and
this is the rejected behaviour again; say so immediately and it comes straight
back out.

## Take 247: the head anchor is REVERTED. It was 3.5x worse, and measured so.

Patola: *"It not only didn't fix the issue, it reintroduced weird eye separation
and the artifact of the quads drifting weirdly that was solved after 245A."*

The clip agrees, and by a wide margin:

    anchor    canvas    x wander            y wander
    neutral   2.50 m    sd 21.2 px  2.34°   sd 44.8 px   4.94°
    neutral   0.70 m    sd 68.2 px  7.52°   sd 35.3 px   3.89°
    HEAD      1.40 m    sd 132.4 px 14.60°  sd 269.8 px 29.75°

The un-"fixed" behaviour would have predicted 4.18° at 1.40 m by its own
1/distance law. The anchor delivered **14.60° — 3.5x worse in x and 6x in y**,
with a monotonic vertical drift across the clip (by quarter: 478 → 451 → 578 →
870 px). Reverted.

### What the three clips actually establish

Not "the quad should have parallax" or "it should not". **Both layers must be
anchored to the SAME point**, and the evidence is a clean 2x2:

    scene anchor      quad anchor     result
    moving (#74 on)   fixed neutral   drift + bad separation   (takes 242-244)
    fixed             fixed neutral   Patola: solved           (245A)
    fixed             moving (head)   drift + bad separation   (247)

245A and 247 break the match from opposite sides and produce the same
complaint. That is the invariant, and it is stronger evidence than either
mechanism I argued from, because it is a 2x2 rather than a story.

**So #74's translate arm and take 247's head anchor were the same mistake made
twice, from opposite ends** — once by moving the scene's anchor, once by moving
the quad's. The first cost three takes to find; the second was caught in one
because the drift metric existed by then.

### The parallax signature is still real, and still unexplained

With both anchors fixed, the wander still scaled 1/distance — 2.34° at 2.50 m
against 7.52° at 0.70 m, 3.22x for 3.57x — and both clips implied the same
~10 cm displacement. That is not noise and the revert does not explain it away.

**A hypothesis, filed and NOT built:** the scene's declared position is
`neutral + R(C)·(±ipd/2, 0, 0)` — per-eye, and it ORBITS on a 32 mm radius as
the camera turns — while the quad's anchor is the neutral point with no eye
offset at all. The two differ by a rotating ±32 mm, which is `64mm/zm` of
angular disagreement: 5.2° at 0.70 m, 1.5° at 2.50 m against the measured 7.52
and 2.34. Right law, right order, and it would also read as *"the eye separation
feels wrong"* because the disagreement is opposite in the two eyes.

If that is it, the fix is **two quads**, `XR_EYE_VISIBILITY_LEFT` and `_RIGHT`,
each anchored at `neutral + R(C)·(±ipd/2)`, so the UI gets the same per-eye
viewpoint the scene has. **Not built.** It is one more mechanism that fits, and
this section exists because the last two also fit.

## Take 248 — the SBS clip, and what it settles

Two inputs arrived with this. First, **the `ipd:` instrument fired and killed
its own hypothesis**: the runtime reports **0.0629 m** between the eyes against
`X4VR_IPD=0.0640`, a −1.7% / 1.1 mm difference, identical in 245A, 246 and 247.
Far too small to be seen. The scene's shear and the quad's runtime-derived
stereo are built on effectively the same separation, so that is not the defect.

Second, and it is the useful one — Patola: *"the wrong stereo separation is more
visible on the quads, e.g. the map, the start screen and not the cockpit."*
**That localises it to the UI layer.** The cockpit is the scene layer, whose
stereo comes from our baked shear; the map and the start screen are the quad,
whose stereo the runtime derives. Whatever is wrong is on the derived side, and
the scene's shear is exonerated by the same sentence.

### Why SBS answers it and a mono clip cannot

Every measurement so far has been a RATIO — HUD motion against world motion —
and a ratio cannot say which side is wrong. A side-by-side capture carries the
two eyes in one frame, so the horizontal offset between the halves is an
**absolute** disparity, and disparity converts to depth with no unknowns:

    depth = (ipd/2) / tan(disparity/2)          ipd = 0.0629 m, measured

    0.70 m -> 5.145 deg      2.50 m -> 1.441 deg
    1.40 m -> 2.574 deg      infinity -> 0.000 deg

So the clip reports, in metres, **where each thing actually is** — and the quad
is supposed to be at exactly `X4VR_CANVAS_M`. The cockpit in the same frames is
the control: its implied depth must come out at cockpit scale, around 1 m.

### The run

245A's line with `X4VR_CANVAS_M=1.4` and the names moved on. The build is back
to the neutral anchor, so this is 245A's behaviour at 1.4 m:

    X4VR_TAKE=248-SBS X4VR_CANVAS_M=1.4 X4VR_STEREO=1 X4VR_BINDLESS_PATCH=1 X4VR_DECLARE_RENDERED_POS=1 X4VR_ROLL_STEREO=1 X4VR_HEADLOOK_LEAD=1.0 X4VR_HUDLESS=1 X4VR_RES=1408x1408 X4VR_VR=1 X4VR_GAMESCOPE=1 X4VR_SBS_RIGHT_LAYER=1 X4VR_HEADLOOK=1 X4VR_SBS_LAYERS=2 X4VR_POSE=1 X4VR_HEADLOOK_RAW=191 X4VR_HEADLOOK_KP=0.25 X4VR_POSELOG=1 X4VR_MV=1 X4VR_PROJ_LIVE=1 X4VR_SBS=1 X4VR_LOG=/tmp/x4vr-take248.log X4VR_UI_LAYER=1 X4VR_MASK_PRESENT=1 X4VR_IPD=0.064 X4VR_FOV=1.4917 X4VR_BINDLESS_MIRROR=1 X4VR_CAMREAD=1 X4VR_MV_INVENTORY=1 X4VR_CAMLOOP=1 X4VR_HEADLOOK_GAIN=0.115 ./launch/x4vr-launch.sh

**Recorded SIDE-BY-SIDE**, and the protocol is built around holding still,
because disparity is measured within one frame and motion blur is the enemy:

    ~5 s   cockpit, looking straight ahead, HEAD STILL
    ~8 s   slow head turns L/R/U/D  (keeps the wander metric comparable)
    ~3 s   still again, straight ahead
    ~5 s   press M for the map, HEAD STILL while it is up
    ~3 s   ESC, still

The still sections are the measurement; the moving section only keeps this clip
comparable with the last three.

**P248.1 — the control.** Cockpit struts read an implied depth of order 1 m, so
between roughly 3 and 8 deg of disparity. If the cockpit reads at infinity
(0 deg) the scene has no stereo at all and everything else in this section is
moot.

**P248.2 — the quad.** The map and the HUD read **2.57 deg = 1.40 m**, the
canvas distance. Any other number is the defect, and its SIZE names the
mechanism: near zero means the quad is being shown flat to both eyes; a
consistent scale factor means the disparity is derived from the wrong
separation or the wrong distance; opposite signs between elements means
something is per-eye that should not be.

**No tool is being written for this in advance.** Two instruments in this task
were built for data whose shape was assumed — the nebula channel and the
SBS-halving — and both produced confident wrong answers. The analysis is
written after one real frame of the actual capture format has been looked at.

## Take 248: the quad's disparity is ~1/3 of the cockpit's, and that is the defect

The SBS clip works. `mean|L-R|` is 0.007–0.044 across the session, so the halves
are genuinely two eyes and not a duplicated mono view — checked before anything
was measured.

**The zero control holds.** The starfield reads **+0 px** in every frame where
the correlation has a real peak (margins 0.50 and 0.26). The −26-ish readings
that appear alongside it all carry margins of 0.01–0.13: aperture ambiguity on a
field of repeating dots, which is #55's lesson arriving again in a new tool.
Only the confident readings are used below.

    same capture, same method, same zero point
      cockpit hull (scene layer)   -23 px    best margin 0.29
      map UI       (quad)           -8 px    best margins 0.16-0.27,
                                             3 frames, many blobs, -7..-10
      starfield    (infinity)        0 px    margins 0.50, 0.26

**The ratio 23:8 = 2.88x is calibration-free** — it needs no px-per-degree, no
capture FOV, no assumption about the recorder. Whatever the scale, **the map is
presented 2.9x further away than the cockpit hull.**

And the quad is submitted at exactly the right place. Take 248's own log:

    ui: quad at 1.40 m, ... centre (0.003, 1.131, -1.400) = neutral + R*(0,0,-zm)
    head translate: neutral point latched at (0.003, 1.131, 0.000) m

1.400 m ahead of the neutral point, to three decimals. **The submission is
correct and the presentation is not.** For −8 px to be right at a 1.40 m
canvas, the cockpit hull would have to be **0.49 m** from the eye, which it
plainly is not. Across every calibration considered the map reads 2.8–3.8 m.

This is what Patola reported independently and before any of it was measured:
*"the wrong stereo separation is more visible on the quads, e.g. the map, the
start screen and not the cockpit."* The scene's baked shear is exonerated; the
defect is on the layer whose stereo the runtime derives.

### What is NOT concluded

Which side of "the quad reads 2.9x too far" is at fault is still open, because
the hull's true distance is not independently known. The two readings that fit:

* the quad's disparity is genuinely too weak, by roughly half;
* or the capture attenuates disparity uniformly and the hull is nearer than a
  cockpit hull looks.

**The second is testable and cheap, and the test is calibration-free.** Change
`X4VR_CANVAS_M` from 1.40 to 0.70 and record ten seconds of the map alone. A
quad whose disparity comes from its submitted distance must DOUBLE, −8 px to
about −16. If it does not move, the disparity is not being derived from the
distance we submit, and that is a different defect entirely.

No fix is proposed from this. The measurement names a target — "the quad's
presented depth against its submitted depth" — and the A/B above decides
whether that target is real before anything is built for it.

## Take 249 CLOSES the disparity thread — and Patola redirects, correctly

*"So is the odd stereo separation going to help solving the HUD slip?"*

**No. It is not, and the question should have been asked by me several messages
ago.** They are two defects with no demonstrated common cause, and the SBS
thread was allowed to run on its own momentum.

### The disparity thread closes itself

Take 249, the map at `X4VR_CANVAS_M=0.7` against take 248's 1.40 m, same
method, same blobs:

    canvas 1.40 m   map UI disparity  -7 .. -10 px
    canvas 0.70 m   map UI disparity  -13 .. -16 px  (one strong blob -23, m=0.43)

**Halving the distance roughly doubles the disparity, as geometry requires.**
The quad's stereo does respond to the distance we submit; there is no bug in how
it is placed. What is left is a uniform factor — both distances read about half
the absolute disparity expected — which is either the recorder's own
attenuation or an IPD scale, and either way it is **#25's comfort question,
which Patola has explicitly deferred.** It is not a blocker and it is not
related to the slip.

### One free finding that DOES bear on the slip

Is the slip a function of head ROTATION? Regressing the HUD-vs-world slip
against the accumulated yaw, on the two mono clips:

    canvas 2.50 m   r=+0.126   2% of the slip variance is yaw-linear
    canvas 0.70 m   r=+0.377  14% of the slip variance is yaw-linear

**The slip is essentially independent of where the head is pointing.** That
kills the rotating-eye-offset hypothesis filed after take 247 — a term in
`R(C)` would have been almost entirely yaw-linear — and it agrees with the
1/distance magnitude scaling: the slip is driven by head TRANSLATION.

### The contradiction that remains, stated and not resolved

Two measurements point opposite ways and both are sound:

* the slip is translation-driven and scales as 1/distance — the parallax
  signature, which says the quad should be anchored so head translation does
  not move it relative to the scene;
* take 247 did exactly that and was **3.5x worse in x and 6x in y**, with
  Patola reporting the take-244 artefacts back.

`xrLocateViews` uses `s.space`, the same space the quad is submitted in, so 247
was not a space-mismatch bug. **I have no reconciliation and am not inventing
one.** What is missing is the actual geometry per frame — the head position,
the quad centre and the scene's declared position, side by side in the log —
rather than three inferences from pixels. Every hypothesis in this section has
been built by reasoning backwards from an image.

**#57's remaining work is the slip. The separation is parked under #25.**

## The geometry line — and take 250

Patola: *"Add the geometry log line. It's better to be correct than do things in
a hurry, in fact it's our directive — we have no deadline."*

**Three fixes for the HUD slip were argued from a video.** The head, the scene's
declared viewpoint and the quad's centre are three points the layer holds
exactly, every frame, and it printed none of them. Every hypothesis in takes
244-249 reasoned backwards from pixels to those numbers. The line prints them.

    geom: head=x,y,z neutral=x,y,z declared=x,y,z quad=x,y,z zm=..
          t_head=.. d_scene=.. d_quad=.. hv=.. yaw=.. pitch=..

Full rate, like `poselag`, because the slip varies sub-second and a 600-frame
sample would alias it. It rides on `X4VR_POSELOG`, which every recent run sets.

`declared` is published **after both branches** of the position code, so it is
what was actually declared rather than what one path would have declared —
`declare_rendered_pos()` and the plain runtime position are different points and
either can be live. Instrumenting the branch I happened to be looking at is how
several of these numbers went wrong before.

The three scalars state the question:

    t_head    |head - neutral|      how far the head has moved from the anchor
    d_scene   |head - declared|     the offset the compositor must reconcile
                                    for layer A
    d_quad    |head - quad centre|  which equals zm ONLY if the head has not
                                    left the neutral point

`score_run.py` reports medians, p90 and max for each, plus the correlation of
`t_head` against `d_scene` and against `d_quad - zm`. **If both correlations are
near +1 the two layers agree about where the viewer is, and the slip is not
this** — which would be as useful as a confirmation, and is the outcome that
would stop a fourth anchor experiment before it started. It FAILs a run where
every sample has `hv=0`, since head/neutral/declared then collapse to one
latched point and the run cannot speak to the geometry at all. Both paths were
exercised on a synthetic log before shipping.

**The harness cannot reach this**, and that is stated rather than implied: there
is no OpenXR session in `run-multiview-render.sh`, so the quad block never runs
and neither does the line. It compiles and the 209 existing cases still pass;
the line itself is first exercised in the headset.

### Take 250 — no behaviour change, just the numbers

Identical to take 248 apart from the take and log names. **The build's behaviour
is unchanged** — the head anchor is reverted, the quad is back on the neutral
point, and nothing about the frame moved. This run exists to read three
positions.

    X4VR_TAKE=250-GEOM X4VR_CANVAS_M=1.4 X4VR_STEREO=1 X4VR_BINDLESS_PATCH=1 X4VR_DECLARE_RENDERED_POS=1 X4VR_ROLL_STEREO=1 X4VR_HEADLOOK_LEAD=1.0 X4VR_HUDLESS=1 X4VR_RES=1408x1408 X4VR_VR=1 X4VR_GAMESCOPE=1 X4VR_SBS_RIGHT_LAYER=1 X4VR_HEADLOOK=1 X4VR_SBS_LAYERS=2 X4VR_POSE=1 X4VR_HEADLOOK_RAW=191 X4VR_HEADLOOK_KP=0.25 X4VR_POSELOG=1 X4VR_MV=1 X4VR_PROJ_LIVE=1 X4VR_SBS=1 X4VR_LOG=/tmp/x4vr-take250.log X4VR_UI_LAYER=1 X4VR_MASK_PRESENT=1 X4VR_IPD=0.064 X4VR_FOV=1.4917 X4VR_BINDLESS_MIRROR=1 X4VR_CAMREAD=1 X4VR_MV_INVENTORY=1 X4VR_CAMLOOP=1 X4VR_HEADLOOK_GAIN=0.115 ./launch/x4vr-launch.sh

In the cockpit, look around normally for a minute or so and **lean**: left and
right, forward and back, a hand's width or two. The leans are the point —
`t_head` is the quantity every remaining hypothesis is a function of, and a run
where the head never leaves the neutral point measures nothing.

No prediction is filed. Filing one here would be a fourth guess dressed as a
hypothesis, and the line exists precisely to stop that.

## Take 250: the slip is head TRANSLATION, and the numbers are the layer's own

Patola ran it in two clean phases — *"the usual yaw, pitch, roll head movements
with the head still. After that, I've only done leaning movements"* — which is a
better experiment than the one asked for, because it puts the A/B inside one
run.

    13587 samples, head located in all of them

    t_head    |head - neutral|     median 0.0294  p90 0.2509  max 0.4384 m
    d_scene   |head - declared|    median 0.0392  p90 0.2418  max 0.4690 m
    d_quad-zm quad vs nominal      median 0.0254  p90 0.1216  max 0.3653 m

    t_head vs d_scene       r=+0.986
    t_head vs (d_quad-zm)   r=+0.095

**`d_scene` tracks `t_head` almost exactly.** The scene's declared viewpoint is
pinned at the neutral point and does not follow the head at all — so the
compositor is being told the pixels came from somewhere up to **0.47 m** from
where the viewer actually is. That is not an inference from pixels; it is the
layer reporting its own submission.

### The phase split, which is the finding

    window      t_head med/max     d_scene med/max    |yaw| med/max
     90-105s    0.042 / 0.127      0.042 / 0.134       4.2 / 59.0    ROTATION
    105-120s    0.059 / 0.430      0.053 / 0.459       2.9 / 17.6    leaning
    120-135s    0.229 / 0.372      0.223 / 0.376       5.0 / 20.4    leaning
    135-150s    0.131 / 0.438      0.126 / 0.469       4.5 / 23.7    leaning

**During the ROTATION-ONLY phase — head deliberately still — the head still
translates 4.2 cm median and 12.7 cm peak.** That is the neck arc, and it is
unavoidable: a head cannot yaw about the point between the eyes.

At a 1.40 m canvas that translation is **1.72° median, 5.18° peak** of parallax
on a quad that is real geometry. The slip measured from the clips was 2.34° at
2.50 m and 7.52° at 0.70 m, which the 1/distance law puts at **4.18° at 1.40 m.**
Same quantity, same size, arrived at from the opposite end — video before,
submitted geometry now.

**So the HUD slip is head translation, confirmed.** And the estimate made from
the clips two takes ago — "both imply the same ~10 cm head motion" — is
independently confirmed by the layer at 4-13 cm during rotation.

### What this makes of #74, whose title said it first

> **#74 — Head translation is not wired at all; only yaw/pitch cross the
> channel.**

X4 never renders the head's translation, because only yaw and pitch reach it.
The scene therefore *cannot* respond to a lean, and declaring the neutral point
is the honest description of that (#75's reasoning, unchanged). But the quad is
real geometry, so the compositor gives it the full parallax of a translation the
scene does not have. **The two layers disagree because one of them is told about
the lean and the other cannot be.** The HUD slip is a symptom of #74, not of
anything in #57.

That reframes the remaining work: the slip is not fixable inside the quad's
placement, which is what takes 242-247 kept trying. Take 247 removed the quad's
parallax and made it worse, which says the scene is NOT simply frozen either —
the compositor is doing something with the declared position that has not been
established, and `X4VR_DECLARE_RENDERED_POS` is the knob that changes it.

**No fix is proposed here.** The next step is one elimination with an existing
knob and no code, and it is written up separately so that this measurement
stands on its own.

### A scorer defect found by its own output

The geom section printed *"both r near +1 => the layers agree about the viewer
and the slip is NOT this"* unconditionally — under numbers reading +0.986 and
+0.095. A canned sentence that reads like a verdict is worse than no sentence,
and this one would have said "not this" about the run that proves it is. Now
conditioned on the two correlations, with a distinct branch for each case.

## The DECLARE_RENDERED_POS elimination — take 251

A knob, no code, one variable. It changes exactly the quantity take 250
measured.

    X4VR_DECLARE_RENDERED_POS=1   (all recent takes)
        pv[e].pose.position = neutral + R(C)*(±ipd/2 + shift)
        -> pinned at the neutral point.  MEASURED: d_scene tracks t_head at
           r=+0.986, reaching 0.47 m

    X4VR_DECLARE_RENDERED_POS unset  (the layer's default)
        pv[e].pose.position = views[e].pose.position
        -> the runtime's TRUE eye.  d_scene collapses to ~ipd/2 and stops
           tracking t_head

So the run flips "does the scene's declared viewpoint follow the head" and
nothing else. **The quad is untouched**: it is real geometry at
`neutral + R(C)*(0,0,-zm)` and the compositor gives it the full parallax of the
head's translation in both arms.

### The model take 247 forces, and why this discriminates

Take 247 removed the quad's parallax by anchoring it to the head. Under
"the scene is simply frozen at its declared point and has no parallax", that
should have MATCHED the scene and driven the slip to zero. It was **3.5x worse
in x and 6x in y**.

**So the compositor is not ignoring the declared position.** The only reading
that survives 247 is that it DOES reproject positionally, synthesising an
approximate parallax for layer A from (declared -> actual head). Then:

    now (=1)   scene: approximate parallax from a 0.04-0.13 m reconciliation
               quad:  exact parallax          ->  residual mismatch = the slip
    take 247   scene: approximate parallax
               quad:  NONE                    ->  full mismatch, 3.5x worse  ✓
    take 251   scene: NOTHING to reconcile, so no reprojection and no parallax
               quad:  exact parallax          ->  full mismatch the other way

**P251.1 — this is expected to be WORSE, and it is a diagnostic, not a candidate
fix.** Patola should not run it hoping for an improvement. The slip should grow
to roughly the full `t/zm` instead of the residual.

**P251.2 — the falsifier, and it is the valuable outcome.** If the slip is
UNCHANGED, the compositor is not using the declared position at all — and then
take 247's failure has no explanation in this model and the whole picture goes
back on the bench. That would be worth more than a confirmation.

**P251.3 — log-side, and it checks the knob rather than the theory.** `d_scene`
must collapse from "tracks t_head at r=+0.986, max 0.47 m" to roughly constant
at ~0.031 m with r near zero. If it does not, the knob did not reach the
declaration and the run says nothing about anything.

### The run

    X4VR_TAKE=251-NODECLPOS X4VR_CANVAS_M=1.4 X4VR_STEREO=1 X4VR_BINDLESS_PATCH=1 X4VR_ROLL_STEREO=1 X4VR_HEADLOOK_LEAD=1.0 X4VR_HUDLESS=1 X4VR_RES=1408x1408 X4VR_VR=1 X4VR_GAMESCOPE=1 X4VR_SBS_RIGHT_LAYER=1 X4VR_HEADLOOK=1 X4VR_SBS_LAYERS=2 X4VR_POSE=1 X4VR_HEADLOOK_RAW=191 X4VR_HEADLOOK_KP=0.25 X4VR_POSELOG=1 X4VR_MV=1 X4VR_PROJ_LIVE=1 X4VR_SBS=1 X4VR_LOG=/tmp/x4vr-take251.log X4VR_UI_LAYER=1 X4VR_MASK_PRESENT=1 X4VR_IPD=0.064 X4VR_FOV=1.4917 X4VR_BINDLESS_MIRROR=1 X4VR_CAMREAD=1 X4VR_MV_INVENTORY=1 X4VR_CAMLOOP=1 X4VR_HEADLOOK_GAIN=0.115 ./launch/x4vr-launch.sh

`X4VR_DECLARE_RENDERED_POS` is **absent**, which is the whole change. Take 250's
line with that one variable removed and the names moved on.

**Record ~20 s, mono, in the cockpit, slow head turns L/R/U/D — the same clip as
`x4-vr.mp4` and `x4-vr2.mp4`.** Not SBS, and no leaning: this must be
comparable with the two clips whose slip is already measured at 2.34 deg
(2.50 m) and 7.52 deg (0.70 m).

    python3 tools/score_run.py /tmp/x4vr-take251.log      # P251.3, the knob
    <clip> -> the drift metric                            # P251.1/2, the slip

**The slip is measured from the clip, not judged.** A cross-run magnitude
comparison is the one thing Patola's eye is explicitly not for
([[patola-senses-transitions-not-magnitudes]]), and "worse or the same" is
precisely a cross-run magnitude question. His impression is welcome and will be
recorded, but the number decides.

### Why this is worth a take when it cannot improve anything

Because it is the only remaining cheap discriminator between two models that
predict opposite fixes, and because every alternative on the table costs code
built on an unestablished premise. Three fixes were already built that way. A
knob that can only make things worse, but tells us which of two mechanisms is
live, is a better purchase than a fourth fix that might make things better for a
reason we cannot name.

## The drift tracker silently re-targeted, and take 251 caught it

Take 251's clip came back reading a 21.5 deg slip. **It was never computed**,
because the numbers underneath it did not survive a look.

Patola had changed two things about the recording, and said so: 1600x1600
instead of 1024x1024 after resetting the Quest 3, and **wider head sweeps** than
the earlier clips. The resolution is harmless — it rescales. The sweep is not.

`drift.py` tracked *"the largest cyan blob in the frame"*. That is the same
physical element only while it stays in frame AND stays the largest. Looking
further off-axis takes the target-bracket cluster out of view — one frame of
251 keeps **22 HUD pixels** — and the tracker then latches onto a different
element without saying so.

    clip                     re-targets (frame-to-frame centroid jump > 50 px)
    245A  2.50 m, 1024 px      0 of 300    max jump 24.2 px
    246   0.70 m, 1024 px      0 of 386    max jump 33.4 px
    251   1.40 m, 1600 px     24 of 260    max jump 1577.1 px   <- 9.2%

**The recording is valid; the metric was not valid for it.** That distinction
matters, and it is Patola's clip that is fine.

### The earlier numbers were CHECKED, not assumed

The 2.34 deg (2.50 m) and 7.52 deg (0.70 m) figures come from that same tracker,
and the 1/distance scaling built on them is what identified the slip as
parallax, which take 250's geometry then corroborated. Three conclusions rest on
those two numbers, so "the earlier sweeps were probably smaller" was not good
enough. **Both earlier clips have zero re-targets**, above. They stand.

### `tools/hud_drift.py` — RETIRED at take 253, see the end of this file

> **Superseded. Do not use it for #57.** It fails its own negative control (45 px
> MAD, 69% lost, on a clip whose true relative slip is zero), because its
> residual is taken against an *accumulated* world estimate whose per-frame bias
> integrates. `tools/hud_vs_cockpit.py` replaces it and reads 0.00 on that same
> control. The paragraph below — "agreement on a clean clip earns the right to be
> believed on a dirty one" — is exactly the reasoning that let it through: two
> instruments agreeing on an easy clip says nothing about either one's floor,
> and neither was ever shown a case with a known answer. The section is kept as
> written because the takes it scored are in the record.

Matches ONE template, taken once from the first usable frame, by normalised
cross-correlation over the whole frame, with a margin gate. When the peak does
not beat its rivals it reports **TARGET LOST** for that frame and contributes
nothing, instead of following whatever else is bright.

Validated against the old method where the old method was sound: on 245A it
reads **2.35 deg** against the previous **2.34**, with 0 lost frames and a
median match margin of 0.259. Agreement on a clean clip is what earns the right
to be believed on a dirty one.

**A tracker that silently re-targets is the same failure class as an instrument
that keeps answering the question it was built for after the question moved.**
Both report confidently about the wrong object. This file now has four
instances of that class — `abs()` over a sign, a rate metric against a position
error, a nebula scored as HUD, and now a re-targeting tracker.

## Take 251: P251.3 CONFIRMED, P251.1/2 INCONCLUSIVE — and the confound is mine

**P251.3 passed exactly.** `d_scene` collapsed from "tracks `t_head` at r=+0.986,
max 0.47 m" to a **constant 0.0315 m** — median = p90 = max, r=+0.000. That is
`ipd/2 = 0.032` to three decimals. The knob reached the declaration; the arm is
real.

**P251.1 and P251.2 cannot be decided from this run**, and the reason is a
confound I introduced by under-specifying the recording.

### Three variables moved, not one

I asked for "the same clip as `x4-vr.mp4` and `x4-vr2.mp4`" and did not say what
"same" meant. Patola reported the differences immediately and unprompted: he had
reset the Quest 3, so the capture is **1600x1600 instead of 1024x1024**, and he
**swept his head further** than in the earlier clips. Neither is his error —
both are things my run specification should have pinned and did not.

The resolution rescales harmlessly. **The sweep does not, because the slip is a
function of head translation and a wider sweep produces more of it.** The geom
line now measures exactly that, and it is not subtle:

    take 250   t_head median 0.0294 m
    take 251   t_head median 0.0693 m     2.4x more head motion

### What the clips say, with the tracker rebuilt and a motion prior

    canvas   knob          slip sd    slip MAD   lost
    2.50 m   DECLARE on     2.35 deg   1.80 deg    0%
    0.70 m   DECLARE on     6.97 deg   2.94 deg    6%
    1.40 m   DECLARE OFF   15.05 deg   5.28 deg   23%   <- sd flagged as
                                                           outlier-contaminated

Take 251 lost 23% of its frames and its sd is 2.85x its robust spread, which the
tool now flags on its own. **Use the MAD.** The 1/distance law puts a
DECLARE-on run at 1.40 m near 3.2 deg, against 5.28 measured with the knob off —
1.6x, in the predicted direction.

**But normalising by the head motion that drives it removes the margin.** At
`t_head` 0.0693 m and a 1.40 m canvas the full parallax is 2.83 deg, and the
measured 5.28 is 1.86x that — a ratio the DECLARE-on runs cannot be compared
against, because **245A and 246 predate the geom line and their `t_head` is
unknown.** There is no normalised control.

So: the slip got bigger, the head moved 2.4x more, and the two cannot be
separated. **That is inconclusive, and reporting the 1.6x as a confirmation
would be reading a confounded number as an answer.**

### Take 252 — the matched arm

The fix is not a better analysis, it is the missing control. Take 251's line
with `X4VR_DECLARE_RENDERED_POS=1` restored and the names moved on:

    X4VR_TAKE=252-DECLPOS-ON X4VR_DECLARE_RENDERED_POS=1 X4VR_CANVAS_M=1.4 X4VR_STEREO=1 X4VR_BINDLESS_PATCH=1 X4VR_ROLL_STEREO=1 X4VR_HEADLOOK_LEAD=1.0 X4VR_HUDLESS=1 X4VR_RES=1408x1408 X4VR_VR=1 X4VR_GAMESCOPE=1 X4VR_SBS_RIGHT_LAYER=1 X4VR_HEADLOOK=1 X4VR_SBS_LAYERS=2 X4VR_POSE=1 X4VR_HEADLOOK_RAW=191 X4VR_HEADLOOK_KP=0.25 X4VR_POSELOG=1 X4VR_MV=1 X4VR_PROJ_LIVE=1 X4VR_SBS=1 X4VR_LOG=/tmp/x4vr-take252.log X4VR_UI_LAYER=1 X4VR_MASK_PRESENT=1 X4VR_IPD=0.064 X4VR_FOV=1.4917 X4VR_BINDLESS_MIRROR=1 X4VR_CAMREAD=1 X4VR_MV_INVENTORY=1 X4VR_CAMLOOP=1 X4VR_HEADLOOK_GAIN=0.115 ./launch/x4vr-launch.sh

**P252.2, the falsifier.** The two normalised ratios come out the same. Then the

## Take 252 closes the model, and Patola's question opens the real one

**P252.2 fired — the falsifier.** Normalising each arm by its OWN head motion,
which is exactly what the geom line was added for:

    take  knob          zm    t_head med   full parallax   slip MAD   ratio
    251   DECLARE OFF  1.40   0.0693 m      2.83 deg        5.28 deg   1.86
    252   DECLARE ON   1.40   0.0553 m      2.26 deg        4.19 deg   1.85

**Identical.** The declared position makes no difference to the slip whatever.
(The absolute 1.85 is not meaningful — it divides a spread by a median. The
EQUALITY is, because both arms are computed the same way.) So the model that
explained take 247's failure — the compositor synthesising parallax from the
declared position — is dead, and with it the last mechanism on the table.

The instrument also proved itself here: two runs with 25% different head motion
normalised to the same number.

### Patola's question, which is the right frame

> *"Why can all other graphical elements be seen side-by-side on the desktop
> screen, whereas the HUD can't — it is only visible in VR? What makes it
> special? Wouldn't that specialness be the reason we've been struggling?"*

**Yes.** `X4VR_HUDLESS=1` forces X4's own compositing switch, so X4 emits a
scene with no UI — that is the desktop image. The HUD lives in `img #65`, which
the layer copies onto a **separate OpenXR composition layer**, and only the
compositor sees that. The specialness is entirely ours.

And it is the cause. Everything on the desktop — cockpit, stars, all of it — is
**pixels in one projection layer**, warped as a flat image. The quad is **the
only object in the pipeline the compositor renders as geometry.** Two objects,
two paths through the runtime.

Five takes moved the quad's pose (242, 243, 244), its anchor (247) and the
scene's declared pose (251/252), and none of them touched the slip. **It was
never a pose problem. It is a path problem** — which is what the 1/distance
scaling, the independence from yaw, and now the independence from the declared
position have each said separately.

### The canvas path: VERIFIED, not assumed

The alternative is to give the UI depth INSIDE X4's image — #30/#40's baked
per-eye shift, `make_canvas_k` — so it stays in the same layer and the same path
as the world, and the mismatch cannot arise by construction. Checked rather
than trusted, because "built" is not "bound":

* **It binds.** Takes 98/99 report `canvas final: 346-348 variant(s) built, 0
  REFUSED, swapped into 18 pipeline stage(s)`. Not a dormant code path — a
  demonstrated one.
* **The recent zeros are by design.** 245c/246/247/248 all report `swapped into
  0` because `ui_layer_enabled()` refuses to build the baked shift when the quad
  is on; the two are deliberately exclusive.
* **The `unsheared` interaction is not luck**, and the code says so at the swap
  site: *"a canvas pass is one with colour, no depth and all-LDR attachments,
  and take 71 made exactly that shape unsheared. The two predicates agree by
  construction."* The canvas variant is preferred over the original inside a
  canvas pass, so the UI pass being unsheared does not block it.
* **The harness cannot exercise it** — its shaders do not classify as World, so
  it reports `0 variant(s) built ... NOTHING DREW ON THE CANVAS`. The layer's
  own line says that plainly, which is why the gap was visible.

Known cost, recorded when it was built: X4 hit-tests its UI on the CPU in
unshifted screen space, so a GPU-side shift moves what is seen away from what
can be clicked. The cursor shim already publishes the same canvas map to
compensate (`g_canvas_map.publish`), also built, also dormant.

### The geom line had to move first

It was emitted inside the quad block. Arm B runs with the UI layer OFF, so that
arm would have carried **no `t_head`** — and the comparison is `slip /
(t_head/zm)`. That is precisely the confound that made take 251 unreadable, and
it would have repeated on the first run of the new arm. The line now emits once
per frame outside the block, with the quad's geometry published into it and a
`qv=` flag saying whether a quad was submitted at all.

Two instrument defects were found doing that, both of the same family:

* the scorer printed *"quad never submitted (UI layer off)"* for take 252, which
  had submitted it 12940 times — on a log that simply predates the field.
  Didn't-happen versus cannot-say, conflated for the second time in this file.
* the cause was `re.findall` yielding **`''`** for a non-participating optional
  group rather than `None`, so the `is not None` guard was always true.

### Take 253 — arm B

Arm A is take 252, already run and measured. This is the same line with
`X4VR_UI_LAYER` and `X4VR_HUDLESS` **removed**, so X4 composites its own UI and
the canvas gives it depth:

    X4VR_TAKE=253-CANVAS X4VR_CANVAS_M=1.4 X4VR_STEREO=1 X4VR_BINDLESS_PATCH=1 X4VR_DECLARE_RENDERED_POS=1 X4VR_ROLL_STEREO=1 X4VR_HEADLOOK_LEAD=1.0 X4VR_RES=1408x1408 X4VR_VR=1 X4VR_GAMESCOPE=1 X4VR_SBS_RIGHT_LAYER=1 X4VR_HEADLOOK=1 X4VR_SBS_LAYERS=2 X4VR_POSE=1 X4VR_HEADLOOK_RAW=191 X4VR_HEADLOOK_KP=0.25 X4VR_POSELOG=1 X4VR_MV=1 X4VR_PROJ_LIVE=1 X4VR_SBS=1 X4VR_LOG=/tmp/x4vr-take253.log X4VR_MASK_PRESENT=1 X4VR_IPD=0.064 X4VR_FOV=1.4917 X4VR_BINDLESS_MIRROR=1 X4VR_CAMREAD=1 X4VR_MV_INVENTORY=1 X4VR_CAMLOOP=1 X4VR_HEADLOOK_GAIN=0.115 ./launch/x4vr-launch.sh

Record as 251/252 were: **1600x1600, mono, ~20 s, cockpit, the same head-sweep
amplitude.** A mismatch is now recoverable — both arms carry `t_head` — but
matching is still cheaper than normalising.

**P253.1 — the point.** The slip, normalised, falls well below 1.85. The HUD and
the cockpit are in one image on one layer, so no path difference exists to
produce one.

**P253.2 — the acceptance check, and it comes first.** `score_run.py` must
report a **non-zero canvas swap count**. Zero means the arm did not happen and
nothing below it means anything — the take-98/99 precedent says 18 stages is the
expected order.

**P253.3 — the known cost, expected and not a defect.** The UI will be at the
right depth but mouse clicks will land off it, because X4 hit-tests in unshifted
screen space. The cursor shim's compensation is dormant. **Do not judge clicking
in this arm**; it is a depth measurement, and if the canvas wins on the slip
then wiring the cursor map back up is the follow-on work rather than a surprise.

### What a WON arm B reads — written before the numbers

"Below 1.85" is not a criterion until the bottom of the scale is known, and this
instrument's bottom is not zero. `hud_drift` reports `relx = hud_x − wx`, where
`wx` is the **accumulated sum** of per-frame world shifts. A per-frame bias does
not average out, it integrates: 0.05 px of bias over 400 frames is 20 px of
invented slip, 1.4 deg at this clip's scale. So the floor is a property of the
clip, not of the tool, and it has to be measured rather than assumed.

**The floor's control is the vanilla desktop clip** — X4 rendering natively, its
HUD world-anchored (measured, ratio 1.00, 84 pairs). Relative slip there is
structurally zero, so whatever `hud_drift` reports on it is the floor.

Arm B should read AT that floor, because it is structurally incapable of
relative slip: the HUD and the cockpit are the same pixels in one rigid layer.
The compositor still reprojects that layer, and the `poselag` line in this very
run says it does so by up to 3.56 deg — but a rigid warp moves HUD and world
**together**, so it is common-mode and this measurement cannot see it. (That is
\#75, and it stays open regardless of how arm B scores.)

Three readings and what each would mean:

* **at the floor** — the path model is right and the canvas removes the slip.
* **well under 1.85 but well over the floor** — the path difference was part of
  it and something else contributes; the mechanism is incomplete, not wrong.
* **at 1.85** — P253.1 is refuted, and the path model dies with the pose models.

**P253.2 was miscited and the citation is the error, not the run.** The banner
demanded 18 swapped stages on the precedent of takes 98/99. Those logs report
`canvas **final**:` — a teardown total over 346-348 variants. Take 253 reports
`canvas **first present**:` — a snapshot taken seconds in, with one variant built
so far. A snapshot compared against a cumulative total is not a discrepancy, and
these runs never reach teardown at all (`final:` appears zero times in the log,
which is also why the `pose final:` report is missing). **Non-zero was always the
real criterion**; 8 satisfies it. Patola's own observation confirms it
independently and better than any count: *the HUD appeared on the flatscreen SBS
this time*, which is precisely what "the UI is inside X4's image" looks like from
the desktop, and precisely what arm A could not do.

## Take 253 — the arm ran, and the instrument that was to judge it does not work

**The arm happened.** Three independent signs, in increasing order of weight:

* `canvas: 1.400 m -> s=0.01601 NDC (L=+s R=-s), 11.3 px on a 1408-wide eye`,
  then `canvas first present: 1 variant(s) built, 0 REFUSED, swapped into 8
  pipeline stage(s)`. Arm A's log says the opposite in words: `canvas: baked
  per-eye shift NOT built — X4VR_UI_LAYER=1 puts the UI on a quad`, and `swapped
  into 0 pipeline stage(s)`. The two arms differ in exactly the intended
  variable and in nothing else — the env lines are otherwise identical.
* `geom` reports the quad submitted in **0 of 14523** frames (`qv=0`
  throughout), against 12940 submissions in arm A.
* **Patola saw the HUD on the flatscreen SBS.** That is the canvas signature
  seen from outside: the UI is inside X4's image, so the desktop mirror carries
  it. Arm A structurally could not do that, and it is what made the question
  "what makes the HUD special?" answerable in the first place.

### The head moved 2.4x less, which is why the normalisation exists

    take  arm            n       t_head median   d_scene median   r
    252   A, quad     12940       0.0553 m         0.0658 m     +0.856
    253   B, canvas   14442       0.0234 m         0.0431 m     +0.919

Raw slip between these two arms would have been meaningless. (The `r` for 253
reads +0.259 straight from `score_run.py`, because 81 of 14523 samples are
**pre-declaration** — `declared=0,0,0` — and sit at d_scene 1.13 m with t_head 0.
0.56% of the samples, 20x out in range, and the correlation collapses. Excluding
them gives +0.919. The scorer should drop pre-declaration samples; until it does,
read its geom correlations with that in mind.)

`zm` is **0.000 for every sample in arm B** and that is correct, not a fault:
`zm` is the *quad's* distance and arm B has no quad. The normalisation therefore
takes 1.4 m from `X4VR_CANVAS_M`, the same nominal distance arm A's quad had.

### hud_drift cannot answer this question, and the control proves it

The negative control is the vanilla desktop clip: X4 rendering natively, its HUD
world-anchored (ratio 1.00). Relative slip there is **structurally zero**, so
whatever the tool reports on it is invention.

    clip                    slip MAD    lost   sd>2.5xMAD   truth
    vanilla  (control)      45.22 px     69%      flagged   ZERO
    252 arm A, quad          4.19 deg    32%      flagged   unknown
    253 arm B, canvas        4.29 deg    34%      flagged   unknown

**Two structurally different configurations return the same number with the same
failure signature**, and the by-quarter profiles are near-identical (+71.7 +44.4
+59.6 +56.1 against +66.4 +40.1 +52.7 +47.9) across runs whose head motion
differed 2.4x. Agreement where there must be a difference is the alarm, and here
it fires next to a control that should read zero and reads 45 px.

**A hypothesis, tested and refuted.** `hud_drift` estimates world motion with
`shift(prev, grey, -60, 60)` — a hardcoded window. If a sweep moved the image
more than 60 px between sampled frames the estimate would saturate, `wx` would
under-accumulate, and the residual would be invented drift. Measured with an
unbounded phase-correlation estimator: per-frame |dx| median 0.0 px / p90 17 /
max 44 on the vanilla clip and 22 / 42 / 90 on arm B, exceeding 60 px in **0%
and 1%** of pairs. Not the cause. Recorded because it was the obvious cause and
it is wrong.

What the frames show instead: the vanilla clip is dense with similar cyan
elements — radar disc, message box, both side panels, the reticle — so a 23x25
template has many rivals, the margin gate rejects most frames, and the survivors
are not all the same object. The VR clips pick the **target-bracket cluster**,
which is anchored to a *ship*, not the cockpit, so it is the wrong object for a
cockpit-lock question even when tracking succeeds.

### The number this A/B was to be judged against was already over the line

Take 251 was declared unreadable at **23% lost**. The re-run of arm A above
reproduces its published 4.19 deg exactly — at **32% lost**. The reference value
the whole comparison rested on was worse than the run rejected for being
unreadable.

**How that got through is specific and worth naming.** The table that diagnosed
take 251 has a `lost` column, and that column is what condemned it:

    canvas   knob          slip sd    slip MAD   lost
    1.40 m   DECLARE OFF   15.05 deg   5.28 deg   23%   <- flagged

The table two sections later, which drew the conclusion, does not:

    take  knob          zm    t_head med   full parallax   slip MAD   ratio
    252   DECLARE ON   1.40   0.0553 m      2.26 deg        4.19 deg   1.85

**The validity gate was dropped from the table where it would have disqualified
the new number.** Not hidden — just not carried forward, in the one place it
mattered most.

**What this retracts.** The claim was: *"Identical. The declared position makes
no difference to the slip whatever"*, killing the model that explained take 247.
Both arms of that comparison lost 23% and 32% of their frames on an instrument
whose control reads 45 px where zero is the truth. **The conclusion may still be
right — but it is not established, and it was published as settled.** The
elimination of `X4VR_DECLARE_RENDERED_POS` goes back to open pending a
measurement on an instrument that passes its control.

### Arm B cannot slip, structurally — read before believing any number

The canvas shift is computed once, in the block at `x4vr_layer.cpp:5117-5205`,
from `configured_ipd()`, `x4_half_for_fov(X4VR_FOV)` and `X4VR_CANVAS_M`. That
block reads **no head or pose data** — grepped, not assumed. `K_canvas[12]` is a
constant per-eye NDC translation.

So inside one eye's image, HUD-to-cockpit geometry is X4's own layout plus a
constant, with no head-motion term anywhere. The compositor still reprojects the
layer — the `poselag` line in this very run says by up to 3.56 deg — but a rigid
warp moves HUD and cockpit **together**. That is common-mode, invisible to a
relative measurement, and it is #75, which stays open either way.

The shift's magnitude is also right, checked rather than assumed: `s =
sx·(ipd/2)/z` with sx = 0.70044 (a 55.00 deg half-angle from `X4VR_FOV=1.4917`)
gives 2.619 deg of total disparity, against the 2.6187 deg that 1.4 m at 64 mm
actually subtends. A constant NDC offset is also the correct *shape*: two eyes'
projections of a fronto-parallel plane differ by exactly `sx·ipd/z` everywhere,
so a flat canvas is a constant translation and nothing else.

### The instrument that survives its control

`hud_vs_camera` is differential — it correlates consecutive frames and reports
`dx_hud/dx_grey` — so nothing accumulates and there is no random walk to drift.
`grey` is the world's motion in the same image at the same instant, which makes
it self-calibrating and its own control.

* `--selftest` on a real frame from take 253's own clip: **PASSED**, including
  the differential cases (hud=8/world=10 recovers 0.800, 9/10 recovers 0.900).
* On the vanilla control: **median ratio 1.00 over 34 usable pairs, yaw 1.00,
  pitch 1.00 over 73.** World-anchored, exactly.

Its known limit still stands and matters: it measures *rates*, so it cannot see
a parallax offset, and it once "refuted" P246.1 for that reason. But "does the
HUD move with the cockpit or against it" is a rate question, which is the one
this instrument was built for and the one #57 is about.

### The correctly-posed instrument, and a prediction written before arm B lands

`hud_vs_cockpit.py` tracks a HUD patch and a cockpit patch **in the same frame**
and reports the vector between them. Common motion cancels in the frame --
rotation, servo lag, rigid reprojection, shake -- so nothing accumulates and the
floor is match noise. Its selftest covers both configurations that matter:
rigid motion must return 0, an imposed differential must be recovered exactly.

    clip                     x MAD      y MAD    truth
    vanilla  (control)       0.00 deg   0.00 deg  ZERO
    252 arm A, quad          2.20 deg   1.88 deg  unknown

**The control reads zero.** On the same clip `hud_drift` invented 45 px. That is
the difference between a differential measurement and an accumulated one.

**Arm A's 2.20 deg is not a free parameter — it is predicted.** In arm A the HUD
is a compositor QUAD at 1.4 m, which the runtime renders with true parallax for
the live head pose, while the scene is a FLAT projection layer, which carries no
parallax at all. Under head translation the two must therefore diverge by the
full parallax of that translation at the quad's distance:

    atan(t_head_median / z_quad) = atan(0.0553 / 1.4) = 2.26 deg
    measured                                            2.20 deg   (0.97x)

So the quad carries **exactly the parallax the scene lacks**, and the ratio this
project has been computing all along -- `slip / atan(t_head/zm)` -- is **0.97 on
the good instrument, not 1.85**. The 1.85 was hud_drift's inflation, and the
quantity was sound; only the numerator was junk.

**P253.4, written now, before arm B is measured.** If the canvas removes the
path difference, both HUD and cockpit are flat pixels in one layer, no
differential parallax can arise, and arm B reads at the floor -- call it under
0.3 deg. If the mechanism is untouched, arm B reads the full parallax for ITS
head motion, `atan(0.0234/1.4)` = **0.96 deg**. Those two predictions are 3x
apart and the instrument's floor is 0.00, so this is decidable.

Note what a "win" would look like from inside the headset: arm B's head motion
was 2.4x smaller, so even an unfixed mechanism produces a *smaller absolute*
slip than arm A did. Patola reported it as unchanged and said explicitly he
would not notice a small change. **The number decides this one, not the eye** --
which is the opposite of the usual rule here, and only because the two arms were
not exercised equally.

### P253.4 REFUTED — and the path model dies with it

    clip                     x MAD      y MAD    t_head med   full parallax   normalised
    vanilla  (control)       0.00 deg   0.00 deg      —             —              —
    252 arm A, quad          2.20 deg   1.88 deg   0.0553 m      2.26 deg        0.97
    253 arm B, canvas        2.93 deg   2.30 deg   0.0234 m      0.96 deg        3.06

P253.4 offered two outcomes: **under 0.3 deg** if the canvas removed the path
difference, or **0.96 deg** if the mechanism were untouched. Arm B reads **2.93
deg** — above both, and above arm A in absolute terms **while the head moved 2.4x
less**. Normalised, arm B is **3.2x worse** than the arm it was meant to fix.

**So the path difference is not the cause.** The UI and the cockpit were put in
one image, in one layer, in one path — the thing five takes of pose work could
not do — and the slip did not merely survive, it grew per unit of head motion.
Patola's report and the instrument agree exactly: *"It seemed the same to me...
if it changed by a small amount, I wouldn't probably notice"*, and in ABSOLUTE
terms 2.20 against 2.93 deg is indeed about the same. The two arms differ only
once the head motion is divided out, which is not something an eye can do.

**What this costs.** The explanation for arm A was good — 2.20 deg against a
predicted 2.26 — and it is still probably right *for arm A*: a quad at 1.4 m
does carry parallax a flat layer lacks. But it cannot be the general cause,
because removing the quad made things worse. A mechanism that explains one arm
and anti-predicts the other is a special case, not the cause.

**Six mechanisms are now eliminated by measurement**, each with a number:
quad pose (242/243/244), quad anchor (247, 3.5x worse), declared position
(251 vs 252 — now downgraded to *unestablished*, since both readings came from
the broken instrument), IPD (-1.5%, too small), canvas depth (measured 1.40 m
against a cockpit at 1.40 m, ratio 1.000), and now the path itself (253).

**What is left, and it is short.** Only two things are VR-only, present in BOTH
arms, and absent from the vanilla control that reads 0.00:

* **the per-eye world shear** (`m8 = +-0.42666`), which is depth-dependent by
  construction and is applied to World passes but never to UI passes — so the
  cockpit's rendered position carries a term the HUD's does not, and that term
  moves when the patch's depth from the eye changes;
* **the head-look servo**, which rotates X4's camera about a pivot that is not
  the eye, while no head TRANSLATION is fed to X4 at all (#74 is off by
  necessity) — so the eye point moves in a way X4 never hears about.

Both are #73/#75 territory rather than #57's. That is the reframing this take
bought: **#57 may not be a UI-placement task at all.**

Note the yaw-only rate deficit sits with them and is also arm-independent:
`hud_vs_camera` reads yaw **1.00** vanilla, **0.93** arm A, **0.89** arm B, with
pitch at 1.00 in all three. A horizontal-only, VR-only, arm-independent effect
is what a horizontal per-eye shear would look like.

**The next step is an elimination, not a fix.** Both survivors are switchable, so
neither needs a new knob: run the same clip with the stereo shear OFF. If the
HUD-vs-cockpit MAD falls to the floor, the shear is the cause; if it holds near
3 deg, it is the servo and the missing translation. That is one take and it
splits the last two candidates, in the style that has actually worked here —
switch a candidate off and re-measure rather than build a probe to watch it.

### Take 254 — the elimination that splits the last two candidates

Two mechanisms survive. One is switchable, so the cheapest discriminator is to
switch it off and re-measure — the method that has actually worked here, rather
than building a probe to watch it.

**Turn the per-eye world shear off.** `X4VR_STEREO` removed; everything else
identical to 253 except the take name and the log path:

    X4VR_TAKE=254-NOSHEAR X4VR_CANVAS_M=1.4 X4VR_BINDLESS_PATCH=1 X4VR_DECLARE_RENDERED_POS=1 X4VR_ROLL_STEREO=1 X4VR_HEADLOOK_LEAD=1.0 X4VR_RES=1408x1408 X4VR_VR=1 X4VR_GAMESCOPE=1 X4VR_SBS_RIGHT_LAYER=1 X4VR_HEADLOOK=1 X4VR_SBS_LAYERS=2 X4VR_POSE=1 X4VR_HEADLOOK_RAW=191 X4VR_HEADLOOK_KP=0.25 X4VR_POSELOG=1 X4VR_MV=1 X4VR_PROJ_LIVE=1 X4VR_SBS=1 X4VR_LOG=/tmp/x4vr-take254.log X4VR_MASK_PRESENT=1 X4VR_IPD=0.064 X4VR_FOV=1.4917 X4VR_BINDLESS_MIRROR=1 X4VR_CAMREAD=1 X4VR_MV_INVENTORY=1 X4VR_CAMLOOP=1 X4VR_HEADLOOK_GAIN=0.115 ./launch/x4vr-launch.sh

**It removes two things, and that is admitted rather than hidden.** Without a
right eye the canvas also refuses (`canvas: REFUSED — a canvas needs a right eye
and none is configured`). But a constant per-eye NDC translation cannot produce
a head-DEPENDENT displacement — that was established by reading the block, which
touches no pose data — so the shear is the only live variable among the two.
`X4VR_ROLL_STEREO` is left in the line and is inert without stereo; keeping it
makes the diff against take 253 exactly one variable on paper as well as in
effect.

Checked before asking for the run rather than after: `have_kr` stays false, `KR`
is null and "that null is what keeps the module mono", and #59's pose block sits
deliberately BEFORE the no-K early return, so head-look still drives. The run
will look FLAT in the headset. That is the point, not a regression.

**Protocol.** 1600x1600, mono recording, ~20 s, in the cockpit, the same
head-sweep amplitude as 252/253. A mismatch is now recoverable — both runs carry
`t_head` and the normalisation divides it out — but matching is still cheaper.

**Acceptance, `score_run.py` first.** The `stereo:` line reporting `shear m8
L=... R=...` must be **ABSENT**, and `canvas: REFUSED` **present**. Together they
are the positive confirmation that the shear is off; neither is a fault here.
Then:

    python3 tools/hud_vs_cockpit.py /dados/<clip> --px-per-deg 14.17

**P254.1.** HUD-vs-cockpit MAD falls to the floor (under 0.3 deg, where the
vanilla control sits). Then a per-eye transform is the cause, and since the
canvas cannot be, it is the depth-dependent world shear — which is applied to
World passes and never to UI passes, exactly the asymmetry this measurement
sees. That would make #57 a shear-consistency task.
