**P254.2, and it is the one to expect if the yaw-only signature is a coincidence.**
The MAD holds near 2-3 deg. Then per-eye transforms are exonerated altogether,
and what is left is the servo rotating X4's camera about a pivot that is not the
eye while no head translation ever reaches X4 — #73, #74 and #75. **#57 would
then be a symptom of those, not a task of its own**, and the honest move is to
renumber it rather than keep fixing the UI.

**Cost:** one take, about five minutes of Patola's time, and it eliminates
whichever way it lands.

## RETRACTION — `hud_vs_cockpit` fails a MATCHED control, and today's #57 numbers go with it

The replacement instrument was validated on the vanilla clip, which reads 0.00.
**That control was unmatched**: the vanilla clip's median per-frame motion is
**0.0 px** — it is nearly static. It showed the tool invents nothing when nothing
moves. It never showed the tool TRACKS under motion, which is the failure that
retired `hud_drift` one section earlier.

The matched control is two COCKPIT patches on the same clip. They are bolted to
the same rigid cockpit, so the true answer is **exactly zero**, with the same
head motion, the same 64x64 templates and the same tracking difficulty:

    take 254 clip          x MAD      y MAD    truth
    HUD vs cockpit         2.93 deg   0.63 deg  unknown
    cockpit vs cockpit     2.41 deg   5.02 deg  ZERO

**The floor is 2.4-5.0 deg and every number reported today sits at or below it.**
In y the "signal" (0.63) is EIGHT TIMES SMALLER than the floor (5.02). There is
no measurement here at all.

### What this retracts

Everything derived from `hud_vs_cockpit`, without exception:

* **"P253.4 refuted, the path model is dead."** WITHDRAWN. 2.93 against a 2.41
  floor establishes nothing about the canvas.
* **"The canvas is 3.2x worse normalised (0.97 vs 3.06)."** WITHDRAWN — and it
  was already doubtful on its own terms: across takes 252/253/254 the x MAD
  reads 2.20 / 2.93 / 2.93 while `t_head` runs 0.0553 / 0.0234 / 0.0913. A
  quantity flat across a 3.9x range of its supposed driver is not proportional
  to it, so **dividing by `atan(t_head/zm)` was never licensed**. A floor is
  exactly what "flat regardless of the input" looks like.
* **"Arm A's 2.20 deg is predicted, not fitted"** (against `atan(0.0553/1.4)` =
  2.26). WITHDRAWN. It was a noise floor landing near a number I had computed in
  advance — the most seductive shape a wrong result can take, because I wrote the
  prediction down first and it *matched*.
* **"P254.2 fired, per-eye transforms are exonerated."** NOT ESTABLISHED. The
  shear was genuinely off — both gates passed — but the measurement that was to
  judge it cannot resolve the difference.

### What still stands

* **Log-side facts.** Arm B ran (canvas swapped into 8 stages, quad submitted in
  0 of 14523 frames, and the HUD appeared on the flatscreen SBS). Take 254 ran
  with the shear off (no `stereo:` line, `canvas: REFUSED` present).
* **Patola's reports**, which never depended on my tools: the HUD moves wrongly
  in the quad arm, in the canvas arm, and with the shear off. The eliminations
  that rest on his perception stand; the ones that rest on my two trackers do
  not.
* **`hud_vs_camera`**, which has passed every control it has been given —
  selftest on a real take-253 frame, a built-in per-pair `grey` control, and
  1.00 on vanilla. Its readings: yaw **1.00** vanilla, **0.93** arm A, **0.89**
  arm B, pitch **1.00** everywhere. Small samples (14 and 17 pairs), so treat
  the 0.93/0.89 as suggestive, not settled.
* **`sbs_depth`'s 1.40 m.** Its match is far easier — same frame, same instant,
  a small horizontal disparity searched in a band — and many frames agreed
  exactly (-24/-24, -26/-26, -34/-34). It still owes a control before it is
  quoted as settled.

### The real lesson, which is one level up from the last one

Two instruments have now died on this task, and they died the same death:
**NCC template matching on a self-similar, moving scene, losing 50-75% of its
frames.** The class is wrong, not the parameters. `hud_drift` accumulated its
reference; `hud_vs_cockpit` did not accumulate but still had to track a single
small patch through motion, and could not.

`hud_vs_camera` is the survivor, and the reason is structural: it correlates
**whole regions** between **consecutive** frames. Many pixels, small
displacements, nothing carried forward. Its one known flaw is the reference —
`grey` mixes the cockpit with a starfield at infinity.

**So the instrument #57 needs is `hud_vs_camera` with a COCKPIT mask in place of
`grey`** — region-wise, differential, and answering the question about the
reference frame Patola actually uses. It gets a matched control before it is
believed: correlate the cockpit mask against itself split in halves, which must
read 1.00.

**And the rule this session earns:** a negative control must match the
DIFFICULTY of the real measurement, not merely have a known answer. A control
run on easy data licenses nothing about hard data. The cheapest matched control
is usually already inside the data — here, a second patch on the same rigid
object.

### The tracker's floor is not even stable — all three clips, matched control

`--control` tracks two COCKPIT patches, which are the same rigid object, so the
answer is **zero** on every clip:

    clip   HUD-vs-cockpit (reported)   matched control (truth ZERO)   usable
    252    2.20 deg / 1.88 deg          0.42 deg / 0.42 deg           25 of 360
    253    2.93 deg / 2.30 deg          UNMEASURABLE                  16 of 404
    254    2.93 deg / 0.63 deg          2.41 deg / 5.02 deg          107 of 315

Not one high floor but **three different failures**: a floor of 0.42, an outright
inability to complete, and a floor that exceeds the signal on both axes. A tool
whose noise level swings by an order of magnitude between clips cannot be
corrected by subtracting a floor, because there is no floor to subtract — only a
per-clip one that must be measured every time and is sometimes unmeasurable.

Take 252's control at 0.42 against its 2.20 reading is the one case that might
still be real. It rests on **25 tracked frames of 360**, so it is a hint, not a
measurement, and it is not enough to reinstate anything.

### Building the replacement, and what only rendering it revealed

`hud_vs_camera` gets a `cockpit` reference so its ratio is against the frame #57
is posed about, instead of `grey`, which mixes the cockpit with a starfield at
infinity. Two faults in the mask were found by drawing it over a frame and
LOOKING, and neither was reachable by argument:

* **The star boxes.** I reasoned that a star is "one bright pixel in 961, so tiny
  variance". Wrong: a point source against black is a *high*-variance
  neighbourhood, and the box filter smears it out to the filter's footprint. The
  first mask outlined the canopy correctly and stamped a little box on **every
  star** — the infinity reference walking back into the channel built to exclude
  it. Fixed by dropping connected components below ~4 footprints.
* **The HUD leaking into its own reference.** `grey` zeroes HUD pixels, so each
  glyph leaves a hard-edged hole, and holes are high variance. The mask grew
  blobs sitting exactly on the target bracket and the speed gauge. Left alone,
  the reference channel would partly track the HUD, dragging the ratio toward
  1.00 and **manufacturing the verdict "world-anchored"** — the answer under
  test. Fixed by excluding a neighbourhood of the HUD, not just its pixels.

Both would have produced a confident, plausible, wrong number. The general
lesson is cheap and was earned expensively today: **when a channel decides what
counts as the reference, render it and look at it.**

## The rate instrument fails its matched control too — video is the wrong substrate

`hud_vs_camera --control` correlates one half of the cockpit against the other.
Same rigid object, same clip, same motion: the answer is **1.00 by
construction**. On take 254's clip it reads **0.830** (quartiles 0.75-1.00).

That is a larger departure from truth than any measurement it was to judge:

    clip                     yaw ratio   pairs
    vanilla                    1.00        34
    252 arm A, quad            0.93        14
    253 arm B, canvas          0.89        17
    254 no shear               1.00        15
    254 MATCHED CONTROL        0.83        17   <- truth is 1.00

**So the 0.93 and 0.89 cannot be distinguished from the instrument's own error**,
and the tidy "shear ON = 0.93/0.89, shear OFF = 1.00" table is not a finding.

### The lag hypothesis is REFUTED — by its own sign

Splitting each run at its median rate, a temporal lag predicts the FAST bucket
sitting materially below the SLOW one, in every run, in the same direction:

    clip                 slow    fast    fast-slow
    vanilla              1.000   0.970    -0.030
    252 arm A            1.000   0.830    -0.170
    253 arm B            0.800   0.915    **+0.115**
    254 no shear         1.000   0.860    -0.140
    254 CONTROL          0.775   0.860    +0.085   <- truth is flat 1.00

**Take 253 has the opposite sign**, and the matched control — whose truth is a
flat 1.00 at every rate — swings by +0.085 on its own. With 5-10 pairs per
bucket, the -0.14 and -0.17 are the same size as the control's noise. The
attractive story that #57 is X4's HUD lagging its own camera does not survive
its first honest test, and it was mine, not the data's.

One result IS clean and worth keeping: **vanilla's fast bucket reads 0.970
against 1.000 slow.** So the correlator does not systematically underestimate a
sparse HUD at these displacements. The tool is not inherently rate-biased; it
simply cannot resolve 10% on these clips.

### The real problem: 95% of every clip is unmeasurable

Every run yields **14-17 usable pairs out of 300-350 frames**. The margin gate
throws away almost everything, and the reason is the substrate: these are
**H.264 headset recordings**, and compression destroys exactly what the HUD
channel needs — thin, sparse, high-frequency cyan strokes on a dark field. The
`grey` channel survives it (whole-image structure), which is why world motion
measures fine and only the HUD is starved.

**And the tool always said so.** Its own usage line is a PNG glob:

    tools/hud_vs_camera.py '/tmp/x4vr-t245-present-n*-layer0.png'

and its defaults were, in its own words, "sized for dumps 4 s apart". It was
built for **lossless present dumps** and has been fed compressed video all day.
Three instruments were then rebuilt to fix a problem that is in the input.

**So: no more video analysis for #57.** The next measurement uses
`X4VR_MV_DUMP_PRESENT` — lossless per-eye PNGs, at a cadence, during a head
sweep — and the existing dump sets (t180-t245b) do not substitute, because they
predate the sweep protocol: t237's log shows X4's camera at 0.00 for its whole
session and 245b was recorded holding still.

### Process failure, recorded because Patola had to catch it

Six background waiters sat for ~3 hours while the work they were waiting on had
already finished. Five used `pgrep -f "hud_vs_camera.py /dados"`, which **matches
the waiter's own shell command line**, so the count could never reach zero; the
sixth waited for a string in a file whose job had crashed. I diagnosed this exact
self-match bug earlier in the same session, wrote it up, and then wrote three
more of them.

Two rules, both cheap:

* A watcher must not be able to observe itself. Match on a PID, or a marker file
  the job writes on exit — never a pattern that appears in the watcher's own
  argv.
* Every concurrent job needs its OWN `--frames-dir`. Sharing one silently killed
  a control mid-run, because `frames_from_video` clears the directory before it
  extracts.

### Take 255 — lossless dumps, because the substrate was the problem

**The configuration is NOT free to choose, and this is the one fact that decides
it.** `X4VR_MV_DUMP_PRESENT` writes the PRESENTED EYE IMAGE. In the quad arm the
HUD is not in that image at all — it is a separate OpenXR composition layer,
which is exactly why Patola could not see it on the flatscreen SBS in take 252.
Dumping the quad arm would produce a series of HUD-less frames and a confident
null. So this run must be the **canvas arm**, take 253's line, where X4
composites its own UI and the HUD is in the pixels being dumped.

    X4VR_TAKE=255-DUMPS X4VR_MV_DUMP_PRESENT=45 X4VR_MV_DUMP=/tmp/x4vr-t255 X4VR_CANVAS_M=1.4 X4VR_STEREO=1 X4VR_BINDLESS_PATCH=1 X4VR_DECLARE_RENDERED_POS=1 X4VR_ROLL_STEREO=1 X4VR_HEADLOOK_LEAD=1.0 X4VR_RES=1408x1408 X4VR_VR=1 X4VR_GAMESCOPE=1 X4VR_SBS_RIGHT_LAYER=1 X4VR_HEADLOOK=1 X4VR_SBS_LAYERS=2 X4VR_POSE=1 X4VR_HEADLOOK_RAW=191 X4VR_HEADLOOK_KP=0.25 X4VR_POSELOG=1 X4VR_MV=1 X4VR_PROJ_LIVE=1 X4VR_SBS=1 X4VR_LOG=/tmp/x4vr-take255.log X4VR_MASK_PRESENT=1 X4VR_IPD=0.064 X4VR_FOV=1.4917 X4VR_BINDLESS_MIRROR=1 X4VR_CAMREAD=1 X4VR_MV_INVENTORY=1 X4VR_CAMLOOP=1 X4VR_HEADLOOK_GAIN=0.115 ./launch/x4vr-launch.sh

Diff against take 253: the take name, the log path, and **two added knobs**.
Nothing else moves.

**`X4VR_MV_DUMP=/tmp/x4vr-t255` is not cosmetic.** The default prefix is
`/tmp/x4vr`, which is where takes 180-245b already wrote 540 dumps. Without a
per-take prefix this run would overwrite data that cannot be regenerated.

**This is a MEASUREMENT run, not an interaction run.** Each dump does a
`QueueWaitIdle`, a full read-back of both eye layers and two PNG compressions, so
the game will stutter badly throughout. That is the instrument's price, it is
expected, and **nothing about feel, performance or comfort should be judged from
this take** — including the HUD's behaviour, which is what the dumps are for.

**Protocol.** In the cockpit, ~60 s, slow and smooth continuous sweeps: left,
right, up, down, then a slow roll. Slow because the stutter makes fast sweeps
useless, and continuous because pairs are what the tool consumes. Then quit.
Expect roughly 300 dumps x 2 layers, about 2.5 GB in /tmp (9 GB free after
clearing 6.1 GB of my own extracted video frames, which are re-derivable from
the clips in /dados).

**Acceptance, `score_run.py` first**, then the dump-mode invocation the tool was
actually written for — note the glob is quoted and there is no `--fps`, because
these are frames, not video:

    python3 tools/hud_vs_camera.py '/tmp/x4vr-t255-present-n*-layer0.png' --log /tmp/x4vr-take255.log --control
    python3 tools/hud_vs_camera.py '/tmp/x4vr-t255-present-n*-layer0.png' --log /tmp/x4vr-take255.log --reference cockpit

**P255.1 — THE GATE, and it comes first.** The `--control` run (one cockpit half
against the other, truth 1.00 by construction) must read **1.00**. It read 0.83
on video. If it still reads 0.83 on lossless dumps then compression was NOT the
problem, the whole ratio approach is wrong for this question, and no number from
the second command means anything. **Do not read the measurement before the
control.**

**P255.2 — the yield.** Usable pairs should rise from the 14-17 of 300-350 video
frames to a large fraction of the dumps. If the yield stays at 5%, the HUD
channel is starved for some reason other than compression and that is the next
thing to find.

**P255.3 — only if 1 and 2 pass** does the HUD-vs-cockpit ratio finally mean
something, and #57 gets a number instead of an argument.

**Bonus, at no extra cost:** the dump writes BOTH eye layers (`-layer0` and
`-layer1`) of the same instant, losslessly. That is a free, exact measurement of
the per-eye separation Patola reported as "visibly wrong" on the menu text and
the savegame loadscreen — `sbs_depth.py`'s question, on data far better than the
SBS clip it was run on, and it needs no calibration constant.

### Take 256 — the same run at cadence 10, because the gap was the problem

Take 255's dumps are lossless and healthy (`PASS`, 87 of 120 frames with parallax,
all 662 displaced tiles sheared the right way). The failure was **the interval**,
not the images, and Patola caught it: *"from my own visual assessment of the
pictures, 52 to 114 would be usable"*. He was right.

Measured with an unbounded phase-correlation estimator, the displacement between
consecutive dumps is **bimodal**: median 8 px, p90 218, max 564. At ~1.3 s apart
a pair is either parked in a menu (0 px) or mid-sweep (100-500 px), with little
in between — and only **3%** exceed the +-400 px search bound, so the bound was
never the main fault. **41 pairs do sit in the workable 8-120 px band**, which is
why the pictures look fine and the tool still reported 1-2 usable pairs.

The cadence was chosen for disk and stall cost and never checked against how far
a head sweep travels in that time. Take 255 prices both honestly:

    per dump           3.05 MB  (240 files, 366 MB, both eye layers)
    frame time         6.88 ms without dumps -> 8.11 ms at cadence 45
    so per dump        ~55 ms of stall, amortised 1.23 ms/frame at 45

At cadence 10 that is ~5.5 ms/frame amortised — about 80 fps, dumps ~125 ms
apart, ~713 dumps and ~2.2 GB. To land in the 8-120 px band at 125 ms the sweep
wants 5-75 deg/s, which any comfortable continuous motion satisfies.

    X4VR_TAKE=256-DUMPS10 X4VR_MV_DUMP_PRESENT=10 X4VR_MV_DUMP=/tmp/x4vr-t256 X4VR_CANVAS_M=1.4 X4VR_STEREO=1 X4VR_BINDLESS_PATCH=1 X4VR_DECLARE_RENDERED_POS=1 X4VR_ROLL_STEREO=1 X4VR_HEADLOOK_LEAD=1.0 X4VR_RES=1408x1408 X4VR_VR=1 X4VR_GAMESCOPE=1 X4VR_SBS_RIGHT_LAYER=1 X4VR_HEADLOOK=1 X4VR_SBS_LAYERS=2 X4VR_POSE=1 X4VR_HEADLOOK_RAW=191 X4VR_HEADLOOK_KP=0.25 X4VR_POSELOG=1 X4VR_MV=1 X4VR_PROJ_LIVE=1 X4VR_SBS=1 X4VR_LOG=/tmp/x4vr-take256.log X4VR_MASK_PRESENT=1 X4VR_IPD=0.064 X4VR_FOV=1.4917 X4VR_BINDLESS_MIRROR=1 X4VR_CAMREAD=1 X4VR_MV_INVENTORY=1 X4VR_CAMLOOP=1 X4VR_HEADLOOK_GAIN=0.115 ./launch/x4vr-launch.sh

Diff against take 255: the take name, the log path, the dump prefix, and the
cadence. Nothing else.

**Protocol — and "keep moving" is the whole point.** In the cockpit, ~40 s of
CONTINUOUS motion: swing left, then right, then up, then down, then a slow roll,
taking roughly 3 s per swing and **never pausing**. A parked pair reads 0 px and
is discarded, and take 255 lost most of its dumps to exactly that. Then quit
promptly — dumps keep being written in menus and cost disk for nothing.

**Acceptance, and the control is the gate.** `score_run.py` first, then:

    python3 tools/hud_vs_camera.py '/tmp/x4vr-t256-present-n*-layer0.png' --log /tmp/x4vr-take256.log --control --range 150
    python3 tools/hud_vs_camera.py '/tmp/x4vr-t256-present-n*-layer0.png' --log /tmp/x4vr-take256.log --reference cockpit --range 150

**P256.1 — yield.** Usable pairs should rise from 1-2 into the dozens. If it
stays in single figures with the gaps this small, the HUD channel is starved for
a reason that is not the interval, and that is the next thing to find.

**P256.2 — the control, checkerboard.** Must read **1.00**. Note the earlier
left/right-half control was NOT matched — content flows across a screen-space
boundary between frames, making it harder than the measurement, and a control
harder than the measurement cannot condemn it. That flaw is why the 0.83 that
voided the rate readings is itself withdrawn. The checkerboard split follows the
content.

**P256.3 — only then** does HUD-vs-cockpit mean anything.

**Still void regardless:** every `hud_vs_cockpit` tracker number. Its control WAS
matched (two 64x64 cockpit patches tracked exactly like the HUD patch) and it
read 2.41/5.02 deg where the truth is zero.

### STANDING DEFECT, reported by Patola across takes 253-256: UI per-eye separation is wrong

His words, unprompted and repeated: *"the last few runs have the HUD and
interface elements like the menu text and savegame loadscreens with the per-eye
separation wrong."* Reported at 253, restated at 255, restated again at 256. It
is not a passing impression and it is not the slip; it is a second, independent
defect and it has been sitting under the slip work all week.

**It is measurable from data already on disk, with no further take.** Every
present dump writes BOTH eye layers of the same instant, losslessly:
`-layer0` and `-layer1`. And the canvas makes a falsifiable prediction — the log
of every one of these runs says

    canvas: 1.400 m -> s=0.01601 NDC (L=+s R=-s), 11.3 px on a 1408-wide eye

**and 11.3 px is the PER-EYE shift, not the disparity.** `L=+s, R=-s`, so the
separation between the two layers is **22.5 px**, and writing 11.3 into a
prediction would have made a correct result look like a factor-of-two defect.
Checked independently against the physics rather than by re-reading the same
line: at the image centre the angular scale is `704*sx` = 8.60 px/deg (NOT the
12.8 px/deg the full field averages to — `x_ndc = sx*tan(θ)` compresses the
centre), and 1.4 m at 64 mm subtends 2.619 deg, giving 2.619 * 8.60 = **22.5
px**. The two derivations agree.

So the UI's horizontal disparity between the layers must be **22.5 px**, flat
across the whole element, with **zero** vertical disparity. Anything else is the
defect, quantified:

* wrong magnitude -> the UI sits at the wrong depth (but note `sbs_depth`
  already measured the COCKPIT at 1.40 m against a HUD set to 1.40 m, so a gross
  depth error is unlikely and something else is moving it);
* magnitude varying across the element -> it is not being treated as a flat
  canvas at all;
* any vertical component -> the eyes are asked to diverge vertically, which does
  not fuse and is the "cross-eyed" half of #52.

The scorer's `eye` section already tile-matches the two layers, but it reports
the WORLD: *"884 displaced tile(s) move left and 4 move right, shift -39..+0
px"*. That is the scene's parallax across many depths, not the UI's. The UI has
to be isolated by the cyan channel first — the same `hud` mask
`hud_vs_camera.channels()` builds — and measured on its own.

**This is now a task in its own right, not a footnote to #57.** It has a
prediction (11.3 px, flat, no vertical), the data exists, and it costs no run.

## Take 256 measured: the canvas is CORRECT on menus, and the cockpit channel is contaminated

### The one solid result of the day

On the 32 dense menu/loadscreen frames — 160k UI pixels, correlation peak 0.98,
the two eye layers of the SAME instant differing by a pure translation, which is
the one configuration where NCC is unambiguous:

    UI disparity   dx median -23.0 px   quartiles -23.0 .. -23.0   dy +0.0
    predicted      dx  -22.5 px                                    dy  0.0
    => 1.02x, and the cockpit in the same frames also reads -23.0 px

**Flat, exact, no vertical component, and the cockpit agrees.** Both sit at
1.40 m, which is what the canvas is for. `X4VR_CANVAS_M=1.4` is right, and
`sbs_depth`'s independent 1.000 ratio agrees with it.

**This does not confirm Patola's report on those screens**, and that is stated
plainly rather than smoothed over: he named menu text and savegame loadscreens
specifically, at takes 253, 255 and 256, and those frames measure correct to 2%.
Either the defect is something a disparity number does not capture — a plane at
1.4 m spanning 110 deg puts its corners at 2.44 m, geometrically right but
perhaps not right to look at — or the frames he reacts to are not among the 32.
Unresolved, and his report stands as data.

### RETRACTED within the hour: the "cockpit HUD is 3.33x too separated"

The cockpit-phase frames read -75 px against 22.5 predicted, which looked like a
large, quantified defect. **It is mask contamination.** Rendering the `hud` mask
over frame n94 — the same look-at-it step that caught the star boxes and the
HUD-hole leak — shows the red covering scattered STARS across the upper field
and COCKPIT CONSOLE elements at the bottom, both of which are world geometry.
Console parts sit close to the eye and therefore carry large disparity by
construction, which is the whole of the 3.33x.

The channel's own docstring predicted this in writing: *"A colour test alone
still catches blue-white stars, which are WORLD content and would bias the
answer toward world-anchored — the very verdict being tested."* It was right,
and the warning was ignored for a whole day of measurements.

### Which also unsettles the 0.45

The rate result — HUD at **0.45x** the cockpit in yaw, **0.30x** in pitch,
against a cockpit-channel control of exactly 1.00/1.00 — was measured on cockpit
frames with **that same contaminated channel**. Both controls (cockpit
checkerboard and HUD checkerboard) read 1.00, but a checkerboard control proves
only that **the channel correlates with itself**. It says nothing about whether
the channel IS the HUD. A clean audit of the wrong quantity, for the fourth time
in this file.

Direction of the bias is worth noting: the contaminants are console (moves with
the cockpit, ratio 1) and stars (move with the world, ratio 1), so both drag the
number TOWARD 1.00. A true HUD ratio would then be **below** 0.45, not above.
Suggestive, not established.

### There is no colour rule that separates them, measured not assumed

    known-good UI (menu n51, 160k px)   G/R median 2.35   G median 0.144
    contaminated (cockpit n94, 2.4k px) G/R median 3.08   G median 0.578

The G/R distributions overlap. Brightness separates these two frames, but it
cannot be used: the menu UI is dim because the menu is dim, while the cockpit
HUD is a bright cyan stroke. There is no threshold that survives both contexts.

### The clean path: dump the UI target ALONE

`img #65` is the UI render target, and `X4VR_MV_DUMP_IMG=65` writes it directly
— **no scene, no stars, no console, nothing to separate.** It is capped at
`kMaxDumps = 6` per image, which is far too few for a rate measurement.

**But disparity does not need pairs.** It is measured WITHIN one dump, layer0
against layer1, so six dumps are six independent measurements of the pure UI's
per-eye separation in the cockpit — exactly the question the contaminated
channel could not answer. That is the next measurement, and it is cheap.

The rate question (#57's slip) still needs many pairs of a clean UI channel, and
the 6-dump cap blocks it. Raising that cap is a small, contained layer change,
and it should be made deliberately rather than folded into a take.

### The 6-dump cap is now a knob — `X4VR_MV_DUMP_IMG_MAX`

`kMaxDumps` was a hardcoded 6, "capped so a long run cannot fill /tmp" — a good
reason that had become a wall. It now reads `X4VR_MV_DUMP_IMG_MAX` and **keeps 6
as the default**, so a run that does not ask still cannot fill the disk. Sized
against measurement rather than fear: take 256 priced a dump at 3.05 MB for both
layers, so 200 dumps of one image is about 600 MB. Built, and the 13
self-running tests still pass. (`x4vr_test_spirv_patch` is a CLI tool that exits
2 on its usage banner and `x4vr_test_xr_probe` needs a live runtime — neither is
a regression, and neither is a test that runs itself.)

### A trap found while writing the command, NOT after spending the take

`X4VR_MV_DUMP_IMG` fires from `probe_collect`, and its callers are gated on

    probe_hooks_wanted() = g_mv_probe || dump_after_rp() >= 0

**Take 256 set neither.** Adding `X4VR_MV_DUMP_IMG=65` to that command line
would have dumped nothing at all, and the run would have come back empty for a
reason having nothing to do with the question. The sweep probe also costs: it
arms every `kProbeEvery = 30` presents and drains the GPU each time — take 176
froze for 30 s at a stretch with ~10 usable frames between.

I could not verify the path end-to-end offline. `tests/multiview_render.cpp`
never presents and does not exercise `MV_DUMP_IMG`, so the headless harness that
has saved takes before cannot reach this one without new harness code.

### Patola's tint is the better instrument, and it should be built before another take

His words: *"if what you need is to clearly separate the HUD from the cockpit and
background/skybox, tint them differently. You already did that once."* He is
right on both counts — `B_csmdebugcolor` is exactly that trick, used for the
shadow cascades.

**Why it beats the img-dump path.** Marking the UI AT THE SOURCE removes the
whole classification problem instead of fighting it downstream. The cyan channel
cannot be fixed by any threshold — measured, not assumed: known-good UI has
G/R median 2.35 and the contaminated cockpit mask 3.08, the distributions
overlap, and brightness cannot separate them because the menu UI is dim while
the cockpit HUD is a bright stroke. A tint written by the canvas variant is
unambiguous by construction.

And it lands on the CHEAP path: the present dumps that already work at 3.05 MB
and +1.2 ms/frame, with no probe, no queue drain, and no 6-dump cap. That answers
**both** open questions with one instrument — the UI's per-eye disparity in the
cockpit (currently unknown; the 3.33x reading was contamination) and the rate
question (#57's slip, currently 0.45 on a dirty channel), because a tinted
channel gives as many pairs as there are dumps.

The machinery exists: the layer already does fragment-side SPIR-V patching
(`patch_fragment_force_block_uint`, `g_frag_patch_ok/refused`,
`g_mod_frag_patched`), and the canvas variant already singles out exactly the UI
passes. The work is a fragment transform on the colour store in the canvas
variant, behind a knob, defaulting off. **That is a contained change and it
should be made deliberately, not folded into a take at the end of a long day.**

## Take 277 — the jitter is a 30 Hz temporal INVERSION, locked to X4's render rate

Patola: *"the video goes beyond what I was looking and then bounces back to my
actual head rotation"*, plus ghosting on fast motion. Nauseating. 90 fps stereo
capture at `/dados/x4-vr-stutter.mp4`, 2160x1080, 6.2 Mbit/s, 145 s.

**Measured on the left eye, 270 consecutive frames at 90 fps (t=24..27 s):**

    per-frame dx            sd 7.3 px
    9-frame smoothed dx     sd 1.7 px      -> the NET head sweep IS smooth
    roughness / trend       4.4x
    sign reversals          83.0% horizontal, 81.5% vertical
    residual oscillation    30.4 Hz (2.96 captured frames)
    X4 GAMEPLAY in take 277 33.47 ms = 30 fps
    display                 90 Hz

**The oscillation frequency IS X4's render rate.** Each rendered frame is shown
about three times, and the presented motion inside one render period reads

    +13  -3  +2      +14  -4  +1      +12  -15  +3      +10  -5  +2

— a large jump when new content lands, then **backwards**. Not "fails to
update" (which would be +13, 0, 0) but an actual reversal. Head motion is
smooth: the 9-frame trend has sd 1.7 px, and 30 Hz is far above any human head
frequency, so **this is not the servo and not the head.**

**This is #75, and it is OURS, not the runtime's.** If we declared, for each
submitted image, the pose that image was actually rendered with, reprojection
would produce smooth motion — that is what reprojection is for. It does not, so
the pose we hand the runtime does not correspond to the image we hand it.
`poselag` has been saying exactly this for many takes: *"the declaration LEADS
the pixels ... the compositor is warping each frame by an angle it was not drawn
with."*

**Eliminated, with the A/B verified in the log**: the head-look LEAD. Take 276
ran `X4VR_HEADLOOK_LEAD_AB=20` and logged `lead ARMED` at phases 1/3/5/7/9 —
five armed arms against five controls — and Patola could not tell the arms
apart. #73's anticipation is not the cause, which the 30 Hz signature now
explains: the lead acts on head-motion timescales, the defect is at 30 Hz.

**Discarded, before it became a finding:** blits/submitted ~= 0.5 looked like
"half our frames re-present a stale image". It is just X4's render rate over the
display rate (56/90 = 0.62 against a measured 0.603). Reprojection filling that
gap is what reprojection is for.

**A range failure caught in the act, the third this session.** The first pass
measured frame-to-frame motion by NCC over +-12 px and returned `dx range
-12..12` — pinned at both ends of its own search, producing an alternating
+-max pattern that LOOKS exactly like the real defect. Re-measured with FFT
phase correlation, which has no search range to saturate: -26..24 against a
+-90 limit, and the reversal rate went UP (75% -> 83%). Had the first number
been reported, the conclusion would have been right by accident and the
magnitude wrong. See [[range-failures-have-two-ends]],
[[state-the-instrument-range]].

### The two eyes are in temporal lockstep — #75 is ONE defect, not two

Patola: *"the ghosting looked the same in both eyes as far as I could notice."*
Measured on take 277's capture, same 270-frame window, both eyes:

    L per-frame dx sd 7.31 px      R per-frame dx sd 7.29 px
    cross-correlation of the two eyes' motion series:
        lag -1  -0.5356
        lag  0  +0.9996   <-- peak
        lag +1  -0.5389
    per-frame motion sign agrees 268/269 frames (99.6%)
    per-frame |L-R| motion difference: median 0.0 px, p90 0.0 px

**The null discriminates**, which is what makes it worth anything: a one-frame
eye offset would have peaked at lag +-1, and those lags read **-0.54** against
+0.9996 at zero. The test had every chance to find an offset and found none.

So there is no per-eye timing skew, and both eyes carry the SAME 30 Hz inversion
at the same magnitude. #75 is a single shared frame-delivery defect, not a
per-eye rivalry defect stacked on one — which is consistent with the mechanism
being the pose declared per SUBMITTED FRAME, a per-frame quantity that cannot
differ between eyes.

### #75, where the fix has to go — and why take 278 was NOT specified

The declared orientation is built at `x4vr_layer.cpp:~12590` as **X4's camera
angle from a read-back, plus the servo's residual** (`decl_yaw = x4 + ay`). Two
properties of that make it the prime suspect for a 30 Hz inversion:

* the read-back is **stale by a varying amount** — `poselag` reports age median
  15.6 ms, p90 33.4 ms, which at 90 Hz is 1.5 to 3 display frames; and
* the residual is applied to the PIXELS by the shader as well as to the
  declaration, so any disagreement between the two is a warp by an angle the
  image was not drawn with.

`X4VR_DECLARE_RENDERED_POS` already fixes #75's **position** half and says so in
its own log line. **The orientation half is untouched**, and orientation is what
a yaw/pitch inversion lives in.

**There is no clean single-variable knob that nulls the residual.** Its budget
comes from `pose_budget_establish()`, which derives it from `X4VR_FOV`: unset
the field and the budget goes to 0, but the rendered field changes with it. That
is two variables, and [[vary-them-independently]] is explicit about what that
buys.

**So the next step is reading the servo's angle path, not a take.** Three
previous X4VR attempts died as good-state -> fix-cascade -> dead-end, and
[[three-fixes-one-unmeasured-number]] records three takes that each fixed one
defect a different way and failed identically because all three rested on a
guess at the same unmeasured quantity. A patch written now would be a fourth.
The quantity to measure first is which of the two terms — the stale read-back or
the residual — carries the 30 Hz component, and `poselag` already logs both at
full rate in takes 275/276/277.

## #75 SOLVED offline — the declaration is 20% of the way to the head, and take 278 tests the fix

**No run was spent on any of this.** Takes 275/276/277 already logged every term
at full rate; the work was reading them with a control attached.

### What the terms actually are

`poselag` builds the declared orientation as `cam_yaw_deg + residual`.

* **`residual` is identically zero** — 31481/31481 samples in take 275,
  18045/18045 in 276, 23189/23189 in 277. It was half of what the previous
  commit called "the two terms"; it is not a term at all.
* So `declared == cam_yaw_deg`, the head-look servo's **command**, while the
  pixels came from **`cam_raw_yaw_deg`**, X4's actual camera.

### The number, and how it was checked

Joining take 276's `lagsample` (`head=`, `x4=`) to `poselag` (`declared=`) on
timestamp — 2943 rows, median join error 0.00 ms:

| head speed | \|head−cmd\| (warp applied) | \|head−x4\| (error in the image) | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| slowest half | 0.223 deg | 0.287 deg | **0.78x** |
| 50–90 pct | 2.379 | 2.921 | **0.81x** |
| fastest 10% | 19.874 | 24.888 | **0.80x** |

**A constant ratio across every speed bin is a gain error, not a lag.**
Rearranged, `cmd = 0.2*head + 0.8*x4`: the declaration sits a fifth of the way
from the camera that drew the pixels towards the head, so the compositor is
asked to undo 80% of the error in the image and **leaves 20% standing** —
median 0.345 deg, p90 4.566 deg.

Confirmed a second, independent way. Fitting `x4[i+k] ~ declared[i]` puts the
best k at **+2 frames (22.2 ms)**, 34% better than k=0; and the error scales
with speed as `4.830 deg / 229.2 deg/s = 21.1 ms`. Two routes, one number.
The lag fit's controls behave: self-vs-self returns k=0, self-vs-self+4 returns
k=−4.

### Why this is the 30 Hz inversion

Within one 30 Hz period the content and the declaration are both frozen while
the head moves at 90 Hz, so the reprojection is smooth. At each boundary the
content steps by `Δx4` and the declaration steps by `0.8*Δx4 + 0.2*Δhead`. The
mismatch `0.2*(Δhead − Δx4)` is a **discontinuity at every 30 Hz boundary**, and
its sign follows whether the servo over- or under-shot — which is the
alternating per-frame dx the take-277 video shows.

### Two hypotheses of mine that the data killed, before they reached a run

* **"Which term carries the 30 Hz spectral peak"** — the question the previous
  commit posed. Its instrument failed its own control: a synthetic smooth 0.25 Hz
  sweep, which has no 30 Hz by construction, read a 29.5 Hz peak at 4.98x,
  higher than any real term. `age` peaks at 30.8 Hz, so the **sample clock**
  carries 30 Hz and interpolating anything onto a uniform grid injects it. The
  instrument shared a parameter with the effect. Both terms are 30 Hz staircases
  anyway — that is X4's render rate, not a defect.
* **"Two unsynchronised 30 Hz clocks beating"** — refuted directly. Lock
  fraction **1.00**: x4 never steps without the declaration stepping (0.0% of
  frames). Both are written by the same injector tick. There is no beat.

### The fix, and why it is ONE knob and not two

`X4VR_DECLARE_RENDERED_ROT=1` declares X4's own camera, read **on the
submitting thread at submission time** via `GetCameraRotation` (already resolved
and called in-process by the injector; its FFI declaration was read before use).

Both error sources had to go together, and the arithmetic says so:

| head speed | gain error (cmd vs x4) | staleness (v × age) | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| slowest half | 0.115 deg | 0.025 | 0.22x |
| 50–90 pct | 0.575 | 0.382 | 0.66x |
| fastest 10% | **4.830** | **4.640** | **0.96x** |

At speed they are the **same size**. Declaring `cam_raw_yaw_deg` alone — the
obvious one-line change — would have taken 7.88 deg to 4.64 and read as "still
jitters", refuting a correct hypothesis. That is why the fix reads the camera
fresh instead of taking the injector's copy, whose `age` is 18.2 ms median /
35.7 ms p90.

### PREDICTIONS FOR TAKE 278, recorded before the run

* **P278.1** The jitter/inversion at ordinary looking-around speeds is markedly
  reduced or gone. This is the claim; the mechanism above is only worth
  something if Patola's eye says so on an A/B within one run.
* **P278.2** Nothing perceptible changes with the head still — the error there
  was already 0.115 deg.
* **P278.3 (predicted REGRESSION, and the reason to watch for it).** The warp
  gets *bigger*, not smaller: from `0.8*(head−x4)` to the full `(head−x4)`, so
  ~20 deg becomes ~25 deg at the fastest 10%. More of the periphery must be
  reprojected from outside the rendered frame, so **peripheral smear or black
  edge on fast head turns may get worse** even as the judder goes.
* **P278.4** This fix does **not** touch the servo lag itself. X4's camera is
  median 1.15 deg and p90 17.6 deg behind the head (max 80.7) — that is #78/#71
  and it stays. If the fast-turn complaint is dominated by the lag, this fix
  will not remove it.

### What would REFUTE the fix

`score_run.py` reports `#75 fix ACTED` and Patola still reports the same jitter
at ordinary speeds. That would put the cause outside the declaration entirely,
and the next suspect is the content clock — not another declaration knob.

**The scorer was rewritten for this and both arms were tested on synthetic logs
covering all four intent x outcome cells.** Under the fix, `|declared − X4|`
stops meaning "gain error" and starts meaning "the injector's copy is stale", so
the old rule would have reported a healthy run as "the declaration LEADS the
pixels" — this scorer failing a healthy run for the third time. `cmd=` and
`rot=` now ride on every `poselag` line so one scorer reads both arms, and a run
that sets the knob without it acting is a loud FAIL rather than a quiet
"control arm".

## Take 279 prices the instrument and picks the sample — atdraw, not atsubmit

**camstamp costs nothing, and that is measured, not assumed.** Take 279's first
perf window read **1.87 ms/frame (534 fps) with 980 camstamp lines already
emitted**; take 278's matched first window, camstamp absent, read 2.05 ms. The
instrumented run was faster. The 33.06 ms gameplay phase is scene load — Patola
flew closer to a station — and the bound above rules the instrument out.

### The median could not express the answer

X4's camera is a 30 Hz staircase and the draw->submit gap is 13-22 ms, so **in
76.5% of frames the camera has not stepped and dyaw is exactly 0**. The median
therefore reads 0.000 in EVERY speed bin, including one whose p90 is 9.896 deg
and whose max is 15.040. Take 279 was first scored "0.00x — SMALL, look
elsewhere" on that median and the conclusion was wrong. Same failure as take
257's, recorded in [[statistic-cannot-express-the-alternative]].

### Corrected, on matched statistics inside the one run

| | dyaw | gain error |
|---|---|---|
| p90, all frames | 1.367 deg | 6.555 deg |
| **p90, given a step** | **6.658** | **6.555** |
| median, given a step | 1.031 | 0.920 |

Two ratios, because one cannot say this: **0.21x over all frames** (atsubmit
beats the command — it is EXACT in 76% of frames, where the command is wrong in
nearly all of them) and **1.02x given a step** (when atsubmit is wrong it is off
by a FULL camera step).

**dyaw-given-a-step IS the gain error, to within noise, and that is structural
rather than coincidental**: the servo's command is what makes X4's camera step,
so step size and gain error are one quantity seen at two points in the loop.

### So the declaration is the ATDRAW sample

`X4VR_DECLARE_RENDERED_ROT` now takes 0 / 1 (at-submit, what take 278 ran) /
2 (at-draw). **1 is kept rather than replaced** so take 278's arm stays
reproducible; silently redefining it would make that log incomparable.

### PREDICTIONS FOR TAKE 280, recorded before the run

* **P280.1** The jitter at ordinary looking-around speeds is markedly reduced or
  gone in the at-draw phases, and the improvement does NOT narrow with head
  speed the way take 278's did (0.28x -> 0.80x across the speed bins).
* **P280.2** `dyaw` is unchanged by the knob — it is a property of X4's frame
  pipeline, not of what we declare. If it moves, the stamp is being taken
  somewhere other than where it is believed to be taken.
* **P280.3 (regression, unchanged from 278)** The warp grows, so peripheral
  smear on fast turns may worsen even as the judder goes.
* **P280.4** This still does not touch the servo lag. X4's camera is p90 17.6
  deg behind the head; that is #78/#71 and it stays.

### What would REFUTE it

`score_run.py` reports `#75 fix ACTED [at-draw]` and the at-draw phases feel no
different from the control ones. That puts the cause outside the declaration
entirely, and the next suspect is X4's own 30 fps content clock against the
90 Hz display — not another declaration knob.

## Take 280 REFUTES the declaration — and names the shared input

**P280.1 is refuted on the channel that decides it.** The A/B ran (20 phases,
11008 at-draw frames against 12347 control, logged and balanced) and Patola
could not tell the phases apart: *"There were no phases... There was still
jitter."* The declaration is now provably exact and the jitter is unchanged, so
**#75's declared orientation is ELIMINATED as its cause.**

**P280.2 is confirmed**, which is what makes the refutation trustworthy rather
than a null from a knob that did nothing: `dyaw` is identical across arms
(median 0.458 deg in BOTH, p90 1.146 vs 1.260, stepped 26.6% vs 28.6%). The knob
does not move it, so the stamp is taken where it is believed to be taken.

### What take 280 did establish

`camstamp` logs `atdraw` on every frame in both arms, so the declaration error
against the rendered-from pose is computable the SAME way in each — the first
like-for-like version of this number:

| head speed | at-draw | control (`\|cmd - atdraw\|`) |
|---|---|---|
| 0-10 deg/s | 0.000 | 0.461 |
| 10-30 | 0.000 | 0.805 |
| 30-60 | 0.000 | 1.144 |
| 60-100 | 0.000 | 1.265 |

Frame counts are matched across arms in every bin, so take 278's speed confound
is gone. The at-draw column being 0.000 is **partly a tautology** and is not
offered as more: in that arm `declared` and `atdraw` come from one source, so it
verifies the plumbing and says nothing about whether `atdraw` is the pose the
pixels came from. See [[x4vr-guard-that-cannot-fail]].

### The shared input, which is the real finding

We submit at **90.9 Hz**. X4's camera, through `GetCameraRotation`, changes on
**28.6% of rendered frames (26 Hz)** — 42.9% while the head moves (39 Hz). About
**2.3 rendered frames share each camera value.**

**Every declaration tried is a function of that one channel**: `cmd` is the
servo driven by it, `raw` is it, `atsubmit` and `atdraw` are it sampled at two
instants. Four interventions, four identical outcomes, one shared input — the
pattern [[three-fixes-one-unmeasured-number]] exists to catch, one level up from
where it caught it before.

### THE QUESTION FOR TAKE 281 — and no fix until it is answered

**Does X4's renderer move smoothly between its 26 Hz camera updates?**

* If X4 renders a staircase, the content steps and a correct declaration lets
  the compositor smooth it — but then take 280 should have worked, so something
  downstream is not reprojecting.
* If X4 **interpolates** — 90 smooth frames from a camera re-read 26 times a
  second — then we have been declaring a staircase against smooth content all
  along and **no sample from this channel can be right**. This fits every
  observation: jitter that survives all four declarations and scales with head
  speed.

The instrument is NOT a dump burst: dumping slows the game, each rendered frame
then gets a fresh camera, and the staircase would vanish as an artifact of the
instrument. The measurement has to be passive — the per-object model-view
rotation X4 uploads per frame, whose change cadence can be compared directly
against `GetCameraRotation`'s. `M_view` cannot serve: it is IDENTITY under X4's
camera-relative rendering, which is why the rotation lives in the per-object
blocks.

### What stays

The at-draw declaration is kept and is strictly more correct (0.000 against
0.46-1.27 deg) at no measured cost — take 280 ran 11.36 ms against take 278's
11.38. It is not the jitter fix and is not presented as one.

## Take 281 — a recording that can answer the matrix question without the matrix

Take 280 measured X4 rendering at **88 fps while its camera changes on 28.6% of
frames (26 Hz)**. Whether that staircase reaches the pixels is the whole
question, and a capture can settle it because it shows the image rather than the
channel we have been sampling.

**The discriminator is CONSTANT ANGULAR VELOCITY, and it is why the protocol
matters more than the length.** Under a steady sweep:

* a smoothly interpolated render gives **equal per-frame displacement** — the
  image moves on ~100% of frames;
* a 26 Hz staircase gives **0, 0, X, 0, 0, X** — the image moves on ~29% of
  frames, in gaps of 3.

Random movement cannot separate those: a step and a genuine change of velocity
look identical frame to frame. Take 280's "uniform speed, random direction" was
the right instinct for an A/B and is the wrong substrate for this.

**Single condition, no A/B.** `X4VR_DECLARE_RENDERED_ROT=2` with no `_AB`, so
every frame of the recording is comparable. Alternating here would split the
capture into arms too short to fit a steady sweep.
See [[x4vr-instruments-perturb-interaction]].

### Where in the chain the capture sits decides WHICH question it answers

Checked from the file, never by asking — post-warp frames carry lens distortion
and dark corners, pre-warp frames are rectilinear to the edge:

* **pre-warp** (what take 273 turned out to be): the capture IS X4's submitted
  frame, so the declaration cannot touch it and the stepping it shows is X4's
  renderer directly. **That answers the matrix question outright** and the
  passive per-object instrument is not needed.
* **post-warp**: the capture is after reprojection, so stepping there means the
  compositor is not smoothing a staircase it should be smoothing — a different
  and equally useful answer.

Either way it informs the next step, which is why it is worth doing before the
instrument.

### PREDICTIONS FOR TAKE 281, recorded before the capture

* **P281.1** During a steady sweep the image moves on **~29% of frames in gaps
  of 3**, matching the logged camera cadence. X4 renders a staircase, the content
  steps, and the jitter is X4's 26 Hz sim rate reaching the eye.
* **P281.2 (the alternative, and the one that would reframe #75 again)** The
  image moves on **~100% of frames** while the log says 28.6%. X4 interpolates,
  every declaration we have sampled is a staircase against smooth content, and
  the fix is to stop taking the orientation from `GetCameraRotation` at all.
* **P281.3** The per-frame displacement during a steady sweep is *equal* in
  whichever frames do move. Unequal steps under constant velocity would mean a
  third thing is modulating it and neither P281.1 nor P281.2 is clean.
* **P281.4** The logged camera cadence is unchanged from take 280 (~26 Hz, 39 Hz
  while moving). If it is not, the recording changed the thing it measures and
  the capture is priced wrong.

## WITHDRAWN, then INVERTED — X4 INTERPOLATES, and the channel is the defect

**The take-281 analysis above is withdrawn.** It was run on a convenience
re-encode, not on the capture. Patola flagged the original and the numbers are
not close:

| | original | re-encode |
|---|---|---|
| frames | **7536 / 125.6 s = 60 fps**, VFR | 11162 at a constant 90 fps |

**The transcode padded 60 fps up to 90 by DUPLICATING frames** — 32.5% inserted
duplicates — and duplicate frames were the entire signal the measurement was
about. I checked the file's rate and took `avg_frame_rate=90` as a property of
the capture; it was ffmpeg's output setting.
See [[check-provenance-before-measuring]].

**The capture rate was also read wrong.** 90 fps was asked for and assumed
delivered. WiVRn captures on the 90 Hz clock but DROPS about one frame in three:
the intervals alternate **11.11 / 22.22 ms**, exactly 1x and 2x a display frame.
The data survives, but only through the PTS, using pairs exactly one display
frame apart.

### Re-measured on the original, 1-display-frame pairs only

| | re-encode (void) | **original** |
|---|---|---|
| frames moving >1 px | 40.7% | **79.3%** |
| median displacement | 0.187 px | **4.857 px** |

Negative control, the pause at 01:34: median **0.073 px**, 7.9% moving — so the
sweep motion is the camera and not the ship or the scene, and the ~16% of
sweep frames below threshold are direction reversals.

### P281.1 REFUTED, P281.2 CONFIRMED — and #75 moves

**X4 renders smooth ~90 fps camera motion while `GetCameraRotation` reports a
~38 Hz staircase** (41.7% of frames while moving). The image moves on ~80% of
consecutive display frames; the channel we sample changes on 42%.

**So every declaration this project has ever tried — `cmd`, `raw`, `atsubmit`,
`atdraw` — is a sample of a staircase that X4's renderer does not use.** We
declare a staircase against smooth content, the compositor warps by the
difference, and that difference oscillates at ~38 Hz. That is the jitter, and it
explains what four takes could not:

* it survives every declaration variant, because all four sample one channel;
* it scales with head speed, because the staircase's step size does;
* it is ~30-38 Hz, which is what take 277's video measured as 30.4 Hz.

The `[[three-fixes-one-unmeasured-number]]` pattern was called correctly at take
280 — four interventions, one shared input — but the shared input was not the
cadence of X4's camera. It was **the assumption that `GetCameraRotation`
describes what X4 draws.** It does not.

### THE FIX IS NO LONGER A CHOICE OF SAMPLE

`GetCameraRotation` must stop being the source of the declared orientation. The
rendered camera has to come from what the shaders actually use — the per-object
model-view matrices, since `M_view` is IDENTITY under X4's camera-relative
rendering. The passive instrument proposed after take 280 is now the FIX, not a
diagnostic.

Declaring the head pose instead is NOT the answer: past the yaw clamp X4's
camera stops while the head keeps going, which is the case the original comment
at the declaration site was written to avoid.

## Take 282 — X4VR_CAMDIFF locates the smooth camera

`GetCameraRotation` is retired as a source. The smooth camera must be read from
what the shaders actually use, and rather than guess which of the 11 per-view
mat4s carries it, `X4VR_CAMDIFF=1` diffs the whole 704-byte block per frame and
reports, per member, on what fraction of frames it changed.

**Sampled at end-of-frame on X4's own thread**, not at the first render pass:
the credit map is built during the frame, so at the first pass there is nothing
populated to read. One camera, the most-drawn credited slot, NAMED in the report
with its draw count — pooling several would repeat the defect #53 exists to fix.

**The verdict is not hardcoded to a member name.** Naming the expected winner in
advance is how an instrument confirms the guess it was built around.

### PREDICTIONS FOR TAKE 282, recorded before the run

* **P282.1** Exactly one family of members changes on ~80-90% of frames with
  real magnitude, and it is NOT `M_view` — `M_view` is IDENTITY under
  camera-relative rendering, which also empties `M_viewinverse` and collapses
  `M_viewprojection` onto `M_projection`. The shadow matrices are the standing
  hypothesis because world-to-light cannot be camera-relative, but the
  instrument exists so that this does not have to be assumed.
* **P282.2** `M_jitter` changes on ~100% of frames with a magnitude near 1e-6.
  It is TAA dither, not camera motion, and the max-delta gate must reject it.
  If the report calls it the smooth channel, the gate is wrong and the run says
  nothing.
* **P282.3** At least one member changes at ~40%, matching
  `GetCameraRotation`'s cadence — another view of the staircase.
* **P282.4 (the outcome that would move #75 again)** NO member reaches 70% with
  real magnitude. Then X4's smooth camera is not in the per-view block at all
  and is baked per-object CPU-side, which makes the object blocks (#66's walk)
  the next place to look and makes the fix substantially harder.

### What this run does NOT do

It changes nothing the player sees. The declaration still reads the at-draw
sample, which take 280 showed is not the jitter. This is a locate, not a fix,
and the jitter is expected to be exactly as Patola last reported it.

## Take 282: X4 does NOT interpolate — and take 281's capture was POST-reprojection

**The "X4 interpolates" conclusion is withdrawn. That is twice on take 281.**

`camdiff`, reading the bytes X4 uploads, from inside X4:

| member | changed on | max delta |
|---|---|---|
| `M_view` | **44.6%** | 13755.35 |
| `M_viewprojection` | **44.6%** | 9632.02 |
| `M_viewinverse` | **44.6%** | 11834.48 |
| `M_projection`, `_uj`, `M_jitter`, `M_prevjitter` | 0.1% | — |
| `M_shadowCSM0/1` | **0.0%** | 0.000000 |

This run rendered at **58 fps**; a ~26 Hz camera against 58 fps is 45%. **The
view matrix the shaders use steps at the camera rate.** X4 renders a staircase,
and `GetCameraRotation` was describing it correctly all along.

* **P282.1 REFUTED** — the shadow matrices never change. The standing hypothesis
  was wrong, which is what the instrument was built to allow.
* **P282.2 partly refuted** — `M_jitter` did not change on ~100% of frames
  either; it moves with everything else at the block's rewrite rate.
* **P282.3 CONFIRMED** — three members move at the staircase rate.
* **P282.4 fired**, but its stated consequence does NOT follow: no member reaches
  70% because **there is no smooth camera to find**. `M_view` is also NOT
  identity for this camera (max delta 13755 m), so #53's "identity in every one"
  is a per-camera fact, not a global one.

### Where take 281 went wrong the second time

I called the capture **pre-warp from the absence of lens distortion and dark
corners**. That was an inference from an appearance, not a measurement, and
`camdiff` contradicts it: X4's content steps on 44.6% of frames while the
capture moves on 79-84%. Nothing downstream of X4 can ADD motion except the
compositor, so **the capture is post-reprojection** — WiVRn records the
composited frame before the lens pass, not X4's submitted frame.

The capture's interval pattern is a strict `22, 11, 22, 11` — it takes two of
every three display frames and never three in a row, so the longest run of
consecutive display frames is **one pair**. A per-frame smoothness sequence
cannot be built from it at all.

### What this leaves standing

1. X4's content is stale for 2-3 display frames (44.6% step rate, measured
   inside X4).
2. **Reprojection IS working** — the post-reprojection capture moves on 79-84%
   of frames where the content moves on 45%.
3. The declared orientation is exact (take 280, `|declared - atdraw|` = 0.000).
4. Patola still sees jitter.

So the surviving mechanism is that **rotation-only reprojection cannot repair
content staleness for anything that is not pure rotation about the eye**: scene
motion, the ship's own translation, and cockpit parallax all freeze for 2-3
display frames. X4's camera rotates about the ship's pivot rather than the eye,
so even pure head-look produces parallax the warp cannot undo — which is why it
scales with head speed.

### camdiff PRICED — under 1%, and the 58 fps was my reading, not the instrument

Priced the way `camstamp` was: matched phases, instrument on against off. Three
takes share the same two scene phases.

| phase | take 280 (off) | take 281 (off) | **take 282 (ON)** |
|---|---|---|---|
| ~17 ms phase | 17.76 ms (8 win) | 17.16 ms (8 win) | **17.19 ms (7 win)** |
| ~11.4 ms phase | 11.35 ms (27 win) | 11.36 ms (13 win) | **11.44 ms (4 win)** |

**0.08-0.09 ms, under 1%** — and in the 17 ms phase take 282 lands BETWEEN the
two instrument-free runs, so the difference is smaller than the run-to-run
spread with it off.

**The 58 fps GAMEPLAY figure was a composition artifact and I should have read
it as one.** That number is a median over windows whose scenes differ by 3x.
Take 280 spent 27 of 31 gameplay windows in the 11.35 ms phase; take 282 spent 4
of 8 there and the rest at 17.19 / 23.04 / 32.71. Same per-phase cost, different
mix, and the median moves from 11.36 to 17.14 without any setting changing.

The scorer prints *"session-wide, so it compares scenes, not settings"* directly
above that line. I quoted the aggregate against a previous run's aggregate
anyway, which is the cross-run comparison the per-phase table exists to replace.
See [[x4vr-aggregates-hide-local-defects]] and [[one-number-several-cameras]].

`camdiff` may be carried into a take whose number matters.

## Take 283 — is the 26 Hz camera OURS or X4's?

The rate is not a fixed sim clock. Across three runs the camera changes on a
near-constant fraction of RENDERED frames:

| run | render | camera changes | rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| 280 | 88 fps | 42.9% | 39.0 Hz |
| 281 | 88 fps | 41.7% | 37.9 Hz |
| 282 | 58 fps | 44.6% | 25.9 Hz |

**~43% of rendered frames, whatever the frame rate.** That is tied to the frame
loop, and it splits into two hypotheses whose fixes point in opposite
directions:

* **OURS** — the servo emits a delta on only ~43% of ticks. A count needs
  **0.23 deg** of error (`kp` 0.25, gain 0.115, `lround`) while the dead zone
  sits at **0.15**, and `lround` DISCARDS the residue. Fixable here: carry it.
* **X4's** — we send on nearly every tick and X4 samples the mouse at its own
  rate. Not fixable from this side; the staleness would have to be hidden.

`X4VR_HEADLOOK=1` now emits `inputrate` every 600 ticks, COUNTED at full rate.
Not sampled: the `headlook:` line fires every 30 ticks AND on every clamp, and
reading a rate off that biased subset is how its 12.4%-zero-delta figure misled
me once already.

`cam_moved` here is the same event `camdiff` counts from the other side of the
process. **They are expected to agree, and disagreement means one is wrong** —
that is the cross-check, not a redundancy.

### PREDICTIONS FOR TAKE 283, recorded before the run

* **P283.1** The tick rate is ~the render rate, because the layer publishes one
  head pose per submitted frame and the servo gates on `fresh`. If it is
  materially lower, the publish is the bottleneck and everything above is moot.
* **P283.2** `delta sent on` lands near **43%**, matching the camera rate —
  i.e. OURS, and the residue-carrying fix applies.
* **P283.3** `X4 camera moved on` agrees with `camdiff`'s per-frame figure to
  within a couple of points. Disagreement invalidates one instrument and the
  run says nothing until that is settled.
* **P283.4** Nothing the player sees changes. This is a counter.

## Take 283 — the bottleneck is OUR tick rate, and my scorer read a diluted number

**The `inputrate` verdict printed "X4's" and is WITHDRAWN.** It read a counter
cumulative over 209 s that included ~100 s in which `cam_moved` was 0.0%.
Differenced into per-window rates, with no new run:

| window | t(s) | tick Hz | sent% | camera moved% |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1-2 | 17-24 | **87-90** | 100 | **0.0** |
| 3-9 | 34-100 | 49-62 | 100 | **0.0** |
| 10-19 | 110-209 | 52-58 | ~99 | **70-77** |

During gameplay X4's camera moves on **~73% of ticks**, not 33.4%.

### Two defects in my own instruments, both found by the cross-check

1. **`cam_moved` conflates "did not move" with "could not be read."** It only
   increments inside `if (have_cam)`, so a run with no readback reports 0.0% --
   indistinguishable from a stationary camera. Windows 1-9 are almost certainly
   the latter. Same shape as [[x4vr-identical-inputs-different-verdicts]].
2. **The counters are cumulative and never reset**, so every percentage is an
   average over phases that differ by 3x in frame rate. The per-window table
   above is the only honest reading, and the scorer must difference consecutive
   lines rather than quote the last one.

**And `camdiff` is not the cross-check I claimed.** It diffs all 16 floats of
`M_view`, which carries TRANSLATION (max delta 13767 while the ship flies);
`inputrate` counts yaw only. They measure different quantities and I labelled
them the same event. P283.3's "disagreement invalidates one instrument" did not
apply -- the mislabelling was mine.

### The corrected chain

| stage | rate |
|---|---|
| display | 90 Hz |
| X4 render | 88 fps |
| **head-pose tick** | **~52-57 Hz** (87-90 Hz in the early windows) |
| delta sent | ~99% of ticks |
| X4 camera acts | ~73% of ticks -> **~40 Hz** |

That ~40 Hz agrees with `camdiff`'s independent 37.9-39.0 Hz at 88 fps, so the
two sides of the process do corroborate once the quantities are matched.

**X4 honours nearly three-quarters of what we send. The binding constraint is
that we only tick at ~55 Hz while X4 renders at 88 and the display runs at 90.**
P283.2 is refuted (the emit side is not sparse; the residue-carrying fix would
have bought nothing) and so is the "X4's, not fixable from this side" verdict.

### NEXT: why does the tick rate fall from ~88 Hz to ~55 Hz?

`head_share_write` sits in the VR thread's frame loop, one write per located
view, gated on `have`. The early windows tick at 87-90 Hz and gameplay ticks at
52-58, so the publish -- or the injector's consumption of it -- loses about a
third somewhere. **This is ours and it is the lever**: at 73% acceptance, a
90 Hz tick would put X4's camera near 65 Hz instead of 40.

Note 56/90 = 0.62 was already recorded earlier in this file as the
blits/submitted ratio and dismissed as "render rate over display rate". It may
be the same 55 Hz showing up twice. Worth checking before assuming a new cause.

### The 56/90 lead is REFUTED — the loss is between our own two components

Measured, not assumed: take 283's submit rate is **89.6 Hz** (18688 poselag
lines over 208.7 s; median dt 11.00 ms), and **89.3 Hz** over the last 100 s.

The earlier `56/90 = 0.62` was X4's render rate over display rate **at that
time**, when X4 rendered at 56 fps. Take 283 renders at 88 fps and submits at
89.6 Hz. Same magnitude, different quantity — a coincidence, and the reason to
check it rather than build on it.

So the chain is tighter than it looked:

| stage | rate |
|---|---|
| head pose PUBLISHED (`head_share_write`, once per submitted frame) | **~90 Hz** |
| head pose CONSUMED (injector tick) | **~55 Hz** |

**We drop ~39% of head poses between the layer and the injector.** Nothing about
X4 is involved in that step.

The injector's tick runs from the `SDL_PeepEvents` hook and gates on
`fresh = updates != last_updates`, so several publishes landing between two
polls collapse into ONE tick. The narrow question is therefore: **how often does
X4 call `SDL_PeepEvents` during gameplay?** The 18 kHz figure in
`x4vr_headlook.hpp`'s comment was measured at take 119, in a different phase,
and must not be carried forward — if the real gameplay rate is ~55 Hz, that hook
cannot carry 90 Hz and the tick needs a different driver.

**This is the one lever left that is entirely ours.** At the measured 73%
acceptance, a 90 Hz tick would put X4's camera near 65 Hz instead of 40.

### The hook named in that question is the wrong one — corrected before take 284

The paragraph above says "the injector's tick runs from the `SDL_PeepEvents`
hook". **It does not, and has not since take 118.** Left standing as written
because wrong turns stay in this file, but nothing should be built on it.

`injector/x4vr_inject.cpp` calls `headlook_tick()` from two places:

| site | condition |
|---|---|
| `SDL_PumpEvents` | `this_is_the_game()` — and it sets `g_pump_seen` |
| `SDL_PeepEvents` | `this_is_the_game() && !g_pump_seen` |

`g_pump_seen` is set on the first `SDL_PumpEvents`, and the line
`sdl: SDL_PumpEvents is called` appears in **all eight** of takes 276-283. So the
`SDL_PeepEvents` tick site has been **dead code in every take ever measured**,
and the "~18 kHz" in `headlook_tick`'s comment is a fact about a hook that drives
nothing. It was true when it was written — at take 119 `SDL_PeepEvents` *was* the
driver — and the comment simply outlived its architecture, which is the third
time a stale comment in this project has cost or nearly cost a take.

**Reading the gate order gave a second correction, and this one is about the
measurement rather than the prose.** `inputrate` counts at a point *after* two
early returns:

```
head_share_read fails  -> return        (pose invalid, or the seqlock retried out)
!fresh                 -> return        (this publish was already seen)
...                                     <- inputrate counts here
```

So `inputrate`'s ~55 Hz is **not** a hook rate and **not** a publish rate. A slow
hook, a `valid == 0` pose, and several publishes collapsing into one poll all
produce the same 55 Hz there — and they want three different fixes. The question
as posed could not have been answered by the instrument that raised it.

### P284 — committed before the run

`pumprate` counts each step at its own site and prints the layer's own `updates`
delta on the same line as the `fresh` count it should equal, so the accounting
closes inside one line with no cross-log arithmetic.

- **P284.1** `pump` ≈ X4's render rate (~88 Hz), not ~18 kHz, and not ~55 Hz.
  `SDL_PumpEvents` is a once-per-frame call in every engine that has one; the
  18 kHz was `SDL_PeepEvents` being looped until the queue drained.
- **P284.2** If P284.1 holds, `fresh` ≈ `published` ≈ 90 Hz and **`pumprate`
  reports NO loss** — which would mean the ~55 Hz of take 283 was the *publish*
  rate being low in those windows, not poses being dropped, and relocates the
  defect to the layer's submit rate. This is the outcome I consider most likely,
  and it contradicts the "we drop 39%" headline above.
- **P284.3** The alternative: `pump` measures ~55 Hz, the hook is frame-locked to
  something slower than the display, and the fix is to give the tick a driver
  that is not X4's event loop.
- **P284.4** `nopose` is ~0. If it is large instead, the loss is pose *validity*
  in the layer, and neither of the above applies.

P284.2 and P284.3 are distinguished by one number — `pump` against `published`,
both on the same line. There is no threshold to tune and no subset to select.

**Two instrument defects fixed in the same commit**, both identified as bugs
rather than findings, so that neither survives into the next reading:

- `inputrate` printed **cumulative** totals since the first tick. Take 283's last
  line said the camera acted on 33.4%; per-window differencing said 73%, the
  ~100 s of startup being the entire difference. I printed the 33.4% as a
  verdict. Both `inputrate` and `pumprate` now emit fixed **2 s windows** — fixed
  in *time*, not in ticks, because a per-N-ticks window has its length set by the
  very rate being measured.
- `cam_moved` only incremented where `have_cam` held but was divided by **all**
  ticks, so "the camera did not move" and "the camera could not be read"
  produced the same number — and a run with `X4VR_CAMREAD=0` would have reported
  0% and read as a frozen camera. The denominator is now `reads`, printed beside
  the rate so a low read rate cannot be mistaken for a low move rate, and a gap
  in the readings breaks the pair instead of being compared across.

The scorer recognises the **old** `inputrate` shape and names it rather than
silently matching nothing, because a regex that quietly finds zero lines reads as
"the instrument was not running". On take 283's log it now refuses to quote
either old figure and says why.

The `inputrate` verdict's 0.75 boundary sits at ~74% for a run sending on ~99% of
ticks, and take 283 measured **73%** — 1.2 points from flipping. The scorer now
prints that margin. `pumprate` decides the same question without a threshold.

### Take 284 — the accounting closes, and P284.2 is refuted

225 s, 112 windows, log-only. Every number below is per-window or a total; no
medians of components that must sum.

| quantity | measured |
|---|---|
| poses **published** by the layer | 20243 = **89.9 Hz**, range 87.5–90.9, **zero** windows below 10 Hz |
| `pump` (= `entered`) | 17145 = 76.1 Hz, range **24.3–422.3** |
| `peep` | 17145 — **equal to `pump` to the count in 111/112 windows** |
| `fresh` (servo ticks) | 10482 = 46.5 Hz |
| `skipped` | 6663 = 29.6 Hz |
| `nopose` | **0**, whole run |
| poses that produced a tick | **51.8%** |

- **P284.2 REFUTED.** The publish rate is 89.9 Hz in every window. The ~55 Hz of
  take 283 was not a low publish rate; poses really are being dropped.
- **P284.4 CONFIRMED** exactly: `nopose` is 0. Pose validity is not involved.
- **P284.1 REFUTED as stated.** `pump` is not X4's render rate. `pump == peep`
  to the count means X4 calls them as a **pair**, which is what
  `while (SDL_PollEvent(&e))` does — `SDL_PollEvent` is `SDL_PumpEvents` plus one
  `SDL_PeepEvents(GET)`. So `pump` counts **drain-loop iterations**, and the loop
  runs until the queue empties. Our own synthetic mouse events lengthen it, so
  `pump` is partly our own signal and must never be read as X4's poll rate.
- **The ~18 kHz is retired by measurement, not by argument.** It was this same
  drain loop spinning on take 119's 3.2 million queued key events. With a normal
  queue the pair rate is 24–422 Hz.

**P284.3 CONFIRMED, with the mechanism corrected.** Not a hard rate cap:

| window | polls | publishes | fresh | caught |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| typical over-polling | 136 Hz | 89.5 Hz | 54.9 Hz | 0.61 |
| hardest-polling | **422 Hz** | 90.0 Hz | **90.0 Hz** | **1.00** |

`fresh / min(pump, published)` has median **0.79**. If polls were evenly spaced
that ratio would be 1.00 — every publish interval would contain one. It is not,
because **the polls arrive in bursts**: 2.6 polls per tick at the usual rate,
4.7 at the extreme. Over-polling *saturates* — the hardest-polling window caught
every single publish — so **nothing caps the tick below 90 Hz.** The deficit is
phase, not capacity.

That also means the obvious lever is the forbidden one: the way this run reached
422 Hz was our own events lengthening the drain, which is take 119's runaway in
miniature. **The fix is to stop deriving the tick from the drain at all** — give
it a cadence we own — not to make X4 drain harder.

#### Four instrument defects, three of them mine from this session

1. **My scorer printed medians of `fresh`, `skipped` and `entered`** — components
   that must sum. The line read `60.5 = 51.7 + 23.0` and looked broken while the
   data was exact in 112/112 windows: the median of a sum is not the sum of
   medians. Rates now come from totals.
2. **My first reading of the log indexed regex groups positionally** and got
   `fresh`/`nopose`/`skipped` shifted by one, printing "fresh = 0.0 Hz in every
   window". Caught only because that contradicted the scorer's own total. This is
   the fourth time in this project that reading a list positionally has produced
   a wrong number; named groups now.
3. **My new "fast windows vs slow windows" branch compared two self-selected
   groups.** The fast-polling windows are also the fast-head-movement and
   high-frame-rate windows, so the difference could not be attributed to
   polling. Replaced with the per-window `fresh / min(pump, published)` ratio,
   which needs no grouping — and which then *refuted* the "second ceiling"
   hypothesis that branch had been built to support.
4. **`inputrate`'s `sent` counted `d.dx != 0`, not what was sent.** `d` is
   computed ~160 lines before `steering` is known and `send_mouse_delta` is gated
   on `steering`. Take 284 printed "delta sent on 100.0%" against "camera moved
   on 13.1%" and concluded *"X4's — not fixable from this side"*. **That verdict
   is WITHDRAWN**: the run's protocol deliberately contained a 20 s still segment
   and a 21 s map segment (HUD down 180–201 s), which is exactly when nothing was
   being sent. This is the **same defect as `cam_moved`/`have_cam`, in the same
   code block, which I fixed in the same commit** — one instance fixed, its twin
   left in place.

Also not usable: `corr(fresh/published, camdiff M_view%) = −0.744`. The run has
two phase clusters at opposite ends of both axes, so that coefficient describes
the clustering, not a relationship. Do not cite it.

### The threading question, settled — and what it forced the design to be

`headlook_tick` makes two foreign calls and keeps a great deal of non-atomic
state. Those are three separate questions and only one was ever open.

| what the tick touches | verdict |
|---|---|
| `last_updates`, `stale`, the inputrate counters, **all of `g_headlook`** | **Not a question — a constraint.** Two threads in the tick corrupt the servo command, not merely a statistic. The knob must MOVE the tick, never add a caller. |
| `SDL_PushEvent` | Safe. SDL's queue is mutex-protected and push is the producer-side call. The real hazard is RATE: takes 119 and 124 livelocked X4's `while (PollEvent())` drain with 18 kHz of pushes. 90/s is 2x today's ~46/s and 200x under that. |
| **`GetCameraRotation`** | **Open, and not settleable by reading** — X4 is closed source. Its failure mode is a crash. |

So the design is forced, not chosen:

- The drain's call is **suppressed** when `X4VR_TICK_HZ` is set, and a guard in
  the tick compares the thread now inside it against the one that was and names
  both. A guard that merely set a flag could not tell "moved" from "called
  twice", which is the one mistake this knob must not make.
- The unknown gets its own probe rather than a VR take. `X4VR_CAMPROBE_HZ` runs a
  thread that does nothing but call the getter and bound-check the result, so it
  can be run **flatscreen with no headset** — the cheapest configuration in which
  it can fail. It is deliberately *not* part of the tick: the tick reads the
  camera only after the freshness gate, and with no layer publishing there are no
  fresh poses, so a flatscreen run of the tick would never reach the call under
  test. An instrument that cannot execute the thing it measures has already
  failed twice in this project.

**Verified offline before handover**, because compiling is not running:

- The cadence arithmetic, as a standalone program with a fake tick of controlled
  duration: 90 Hz asked → **90.0 Hz achieved** (89.6 with 8 ms of work per tick).
  With a 20 ms tick — longer than the 11.1 ms period — it degrades to 49.7 Hz
  with a **minimum gap of 20.00 ms**, i.e. it drops ticks and never bursts. That
  mattered: absolute deadlines make `clock_nanosleep` return immediately once the
  deadline is past, so without the re-phase an overrunning tick would become a
  busy loop pushing SDL events — take 119's livelock, rebuilt by accident.
- The two-thread guard: 0 firings on 1000 single-thread calls, exactly 1 on
  10000 calls across two threads.
- `tests/headlook.cpp`: all cases pass, including the windup, spin-crossing and
  #74 shift-frame sets.

#### Why the tick rate is worth raising at all — checked first

A driver that cannot act is the mistake this project has made most often, so
before building it: does X4's camera rate follow **our tick** or **X4's frame
rate**? From take 284's own log, restricted to windows where the camera was
actually being driven:

| t | tick | X4 fps | camera moved | moved/tick |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 129 s | 51.0 Hz | 88.3 | 38.3 Hz | 0.76 |
| 145 s | 58.5 Hz | 86.5 | 41.3 Hz | 0.72 |
| 177 s | 28.8 Hz | 29.5 | 28.2 Hz | 0.98 |

At 129–145 s the camera moves at ~0.7x the **tick** while X4 renders at 88 fps.
**Tick-locked, not frame-locked** — so the fix can act, and at ~0.7–1.0 per tick a
90 Hz tick should put X4's camera near 65–90 Hz instead of 40.

That comparison also exposed a fifth instrument defect, from the same family as
the other four: `inputrate`'s camera-movement figure is **bimodal** — take 284's
deciles are 0, 0, 0, 0, 6.5, 51.8, 77.2, 92.7, 98.3 — and its median of 13.1%
names the **empty valley between the two modes**, a value no window ever had. The
zero mode is the first ~90 s, during which X4's camera did not move at all. The
scorer now sets non-steering windows aside, reports the two modes, and says so.

### P285 — committed before the run

- **P285.1** `camprobe` survives. `GetCameraRotation` is a small getter over
  cached state and I expect no crash and no out-of-range reading. If it *is*
  unsafe, the tick driver must sample on X4's thread and pass the value across,
