  and that is a different and larger change.
- **P285.2** `tickdrv` holds 90 Hz with **zero** re-phases, and `pumprate`
  reports `acted on` above 95% — up from 51.8%. This is near-certain if the
  driver runs at all: the cadence is ours and the publish rate is 90 Hz.
- **P285.3** `inputrate`'s steering windows still show X4 acting on 0.7–1.0 of
  our ticks, so X4's camera rate lands near 65–90 Hz instead of 40. **This is the
  prediction that can fail**, and the one the whole change rests on: if X4's
  consumption turns out to be frame-locked after all, `acted on` will read 99%
  while the camera rate does not budge, and the win is nil.
- **P285.4** The jitter is reduced but NOT gone. Rotation-only reprojection still
  cannot repair content staleness for motion that is not pure rotation about the
  eye, and X4's camera rotates about the ship's pivot. P285.3 bounds how much of
  the jitter was ever the tick rate.

P285.2 and P285.3 are independent: the first says the poses arrive, the second
says X4 acts on them. Only the second is a fix.

### Take 285b — the tick driver works, and X4's camera rate nearly doubled

183 s, 91 windows, log only. `X4VR_TICK_HZ=90`, otherwise take 284 exactly.
Compared in the **driven mode only** — windows where X4's camera was actually
moving — because the aggregate is bimodal and its median names the empty valley.

| | take 284 (drain) | take 285b (ours@90) |
|---|---|---|
| servo tick, driven windows | 28.8 Hz | **68.5 Hz** (2.4x) |
| **X4's camera** | 28.2 Hz | **54.5 Hz** (1.9x) |
| poses acted on, whole run | 51.8% | **88.5%** |
| X4 acted per tick | 92.8% | 79.3% |
| gameplay frame time | 11.36 ms | **11.26 ms** |

- **P285.3 CONFIRMED — the prediction that could have failed.** X4's camera rate
  is tick-locked, and raising the tick raised it: 28.2 → 54.5 Hz. This is the
  first change in #75 that moved the defect's own quantity rather than
  relocating it.
- **P285.1 holds, but measured the expensive way.** The flatscreen `camprobe` run
  was not taken; 285b itself is the evidence, because with `X4VR_CAMREAD=1` and
  the tick on our own thread, `GetCameraRotation` was called ~79 times a second
  from a foreign thread for 183 s. No crash. 486 `camread` samples span yaw
  −63.94…+62.80 and pitch −35.00…+35.00 — **exactly X4's own documented clamps**
  (`maxyaw="65" maxpitch="35"`), with nothing outside ±200°. That is evidence the
  call neither crashes nor tears; it is still not a proof of thread-safety, and
  `X4VR_CAMPROBE_HZ` remains the cheap way to re-check it after any X4 update.
- No `TWO THREADS` line: the drain suppression worked, so the tick moved rather
  than gaining a caller.
- **The driver is free.** 11.26 ms against take 284's 11.36 ms.
- `tickdrv` held **90.0 Hz** (range 89.9–90.1), 0% of wakeups late, **zero
  re-phases**, over all 91 windows.

#### P285.2 was wrong, and foreseeably so

I predicted `acted on` above 95%; it is **88.5%**, with 10.7 Hz of ticks seeing no
new pose. The cause is not a defect: our tick runs at 90.0 Hz and the layer
publishes at 89.7 Hz, so **two free-running clocks at the same nominal rate beat
against each other** — sometimes two ticks fall inside one publish interval and
one is wasted; sometimes two publishes fall inside one tick interval and one is
skipped. Choosing exactly the publish rate is the *worst* case for phase, and I
chose it because it looked like the natural match. Sampling theory says the same
thing the log says directly, in a line that was already printing before this run:

> Hardest-polling window: 193 Hz of polls against 90 Hz of publishes caught
> 89.9 Hz (1.00 of them), at 2.1 polls per tick.

About 2x oversampling captures everything. **The tick rate should be above the
publish rate, not equal to it.**

#### The new open question: is X4's consumption saturating?

Two points now exist for X4's camera rate against the servo tick:

| servo tick | X4 camera | acted per tick |
|---|---|---|
| 28.8 Hz | 28.2 Hz | 92.8% |
| 68.5 Hz | 54.5 Hz | 79.3% |

Linear would have put the second at ~66 Hz. It is 54.5, and the per-tick
acceptance fell from 92.8% to 79.3% — consistent with **X4's own consumption
approaching a ceiling somewhere near 55–60 Hz**, which would mean further tick
rate buys progressively less. Two points cannot distinguish a ceiling from a
shallower slope; a third at a much higher tick rate can, and the same run closes
the 11.5% phase loss. That is one single-variable change.

**Unknown, and the only thing that matters:** P285.4, whether the jitter actually
improved. Nothing in this log speaks to it, and it must not be settled by asking
for a comparison against the memory of an earlier take — that channel is reliable
for transitions inside one run, not for magnitudes across runs.

### Take 285a — P285.1 confirmed properly, in the cheap configuration

16607 off-thread `GetCameraRotation` calls, 7448 non-zero, **0 outside ±200°**,
no crash. The flatscreen probe is now the standing cheap re-check after any X4
update. (The sliding HUD in that run is expected and not a finding: 285a carries
none of `X4VR_CANVAS_M`, `X4VR_UI_WGATE`, or the declaration knobs.)

### Take 285b, second session — X4VR_TICK_HZ=90 makes the camera oscillate clamp to clamp

**This is a regression introduced by the tick driver.** The second run appended
to the same `X4VR_LOG`, so the file holds two sessions and the scorer refuses it;
split at the second `env: run =` line, session 1 reproduces the published numbers
exactly, and **the two env lines are identical in all 39 variables**. Same
configuration, different outcome — an intermittent fault, which is what a race or
a marginal loop looks like.

The episode runs **t = 110–138 s** and ends exactly at the map open (HUD down at
t = 139.4), which is what Patola reported: head movement started it, holding the
head still did **not** end it, opening and closing the map did.

What the frames show, at t = 136.2:

```
       t    x4_yaw     dyaw  declared   cmd_yaw   x4-cmd  val
 136.116    65.000    0.000    65.000    53.040   11.960    1
 136.149    58.697   -6.303    65.000    46.737   11.960    1
 136.181    28.674  -30.023    58.697    16.715   11.960    1
 136.227   -30.913  -59.588    28.674   -27.233   -3.680    1  <<<
 136.272   -65.000  -34.087   -30.913   -53.040  -11.960    1
```

- The camera slams **+65 → −65, clamp to clamp, in ~150 ms**, repeatedly.
- The per-frame jumps are **exact integer multiples of 11.918°**: 3x = 35.753,
  4x = 47.670, 5x = 59.588. `max_step_deg` is 12.0, which quantises to 11.96 at
  `gain 0.115`. So X4 is applying **three to five maximum-size commands in a
  single frame**.
- `x4 − cmd` is pinned at **exactly ±11.960** for dozens of consecutive frames:
  the servo's error sits at exactly one max step, tick after tick.
- `cam_valid = 1` on all 2521 frames of the episode and `declared` is non-zero
  throughout, so this is not the not-steering path and not a declaration fault.
- `clamped%` is **0.0** through the episode — `d.clamped` reports the *target*
  being clamped to `yaw_limit`, not the *step* being limited to `max_step`, so
  it cannot see this. An instrument that cannot express the failure it is next
  to.

**Leading explanation, not yet established: the servo re-commands while its
previous commands are still in flight.** During the episode X4's camera moves on
only 24% of ticks (against 70–86% outside it) while we tick at 89.5 Hz, so
delivery takes about four ticks. The servo sees a 12° error, commands max step,
sees the camera unmoved next tick, commands max step again — four times — and
then X4 applies all four at once for a ~48° overshoot. The error reverses, still
saturated, and the oscillation sustains itself without any further head movement.
The rates agree: 90 ticks/s x 11.96° is 1076 °/s of command, and 21 bursts/s x
~50° is ~1050 °/s observed.

Under the old drain-driven tick this could not happen, because the tick *was* the
drain: delivery took one tick by construction, and the command rate was
rate-matched to X4's consumption for free. Raising the tick rate above the
consumption rate turns the SDL event queue into an unmodelled integrator.

Note the queue does **not** need to grow for this: `pump` is *lower* during the
episode (119.6 vs 145.4 Hz), so events are not piling up unboundedly. A delivery
latency of several ticks is sufficient on its own.

**Status and safety.** `X4VR_TICK_HZ` is **off by default** — `tick_hz()` returns
0 unless the variable is set — so the default path is exactly the pre-285b
behaviour and is unaffected. The knob must not be used again until the servo
accounts for in-flight command.

> **Superseded — the conclusion held, the reason did not.** "Until the servo
> accounts for in-flight command" names a fix that would unlock the knob, and
> take 292 showed that fix is the wrong one: in-flight accounting was refuted by
> `servo_rate.cpp` section 8, and the real cost is that the knob moves the servo
> off X4's event drain and buys ~17 ms of queue latency. See
> *"`X4VR_TICK_HZ` is harmful"* at the end of this file. Left in place because
> wrong turns are not edited away. Session 1's measurement (camera 28.2 → 54.5 Hz)
still stands as a measurement, but the win is **unusable** in this form: a camera
slamming between clamps is a far worse VR defect than the jitter it was meant to
reduce.

**Next, and it must not be a take.** `tests/headlook.cpp` already models a plant
and a servo. The in-flight mechanism should be *reproduced offline there first* —
a plant that delivers command in bursts of N ticks — and the fix (subtract the
pushed-but-unconsumed command from the error before stepping) demonstrated
against it. Only then is another run worth spending. Designing the fix and its
hypothesis in one step is how three earlier attempts each needed a full
re-measurement to refute.

### The offline reproduction FAILED — and that is the result

`tests/headlook.cpp` now carries a burst-delivery plant: commands accumulate and
every `burst` ticks the whole accumulation lands at once, which is what X4 does
when it drains queued mouse events on its own loop rather than on our cadence.
Built **before** any fix, exactly so the mechanism had to be confirmed first.

Varied as a 2x2x2 — and the amplitude is not a free parameter, take 285b's own
`headlook` lines show the head reaching −70.0…+63.9°, past X4's 65° clamp:

| burst | lead | amp | worst_err | worst_jump | max\|cam\| | reversals |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.0 | 45 | 4.71 | 1.61 | 44.73 | 0 |
| 1 | 0.0 | 70 | 7.21 | 2.41 | 64.86 | 0 |
| 1 | 1.0 | 45 | 0.11 | 1.61 | 45.08 | 0 |
| 1 | 1.0 | 70 | 5.14 | 2.42 | 64.86 | 0 |
| 4 | 0.0 | 45 | 7.07 | 6.32 | 45.08 | 0 |
| 4 | 0.0 | 70 | 11.03 | 9.77 | 65.00 | 0 |
| 4 | 1.0 | 45 | 2.48 | 6.44 | 45.20 | 0 |
| **4** | **1.0** | **70** | **5.05** | **9.77** | **65.00** | **0** |

**All eight cells are stable.** The worst is 11.03° of error and 9.77° jumps,
against a real episode of 59.6° jumps and sustained clamp-to-clamp reversals. The
bottom row is take 285b's exact setting, including reaching X4's clamp.

So **the oscillation is not in the servo arithmetic.** Burst delivery, the #73
lead, and driving into the 65° clamp are innocent individually and jointly, over
the ranges the real run exercised. **The in-flight-command compensation proposed
in the previous entry would not have fixed it** — building it would have cost a
take to learn that. This is what the offline step was for.

The assertions are now flipped to the invariant that *is* true, so the file keeps
its value as a regression guard. It must not be cited as a reproduction.

#### A new lead, and it is AMBIGUOUS — recorded as such

Take 285b logs X4's camera read from **two different threads** on the same frame:
`poselag x4=` is the injector's read from our tick thread, `camstamp atdraw=` is
the layer's read at the first render pass, on X4's render thread. Over 21461
frames carrying both:

| window | n | median | p90 | max |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **episode 110–138 s** | 2509 | 0.000 | **29.794** | **59.588** |
| before 0–100 s | 8902 | 0.000 | 0.000 | 1.490 |
| after 145–240 s | 7848 | 0.000 | 1.146 | 9.167 |

During the episode the two threads disagree about the same camera by up to
**59.588°** — the *same number* as the largest frame-to-frame jump — while
outside it they agree to within 1.5°.

**This cannot distinguish cause from effect, and must not be reported as if it
could.** Two readings:

1. **Staleness (cause):** the off-thread read returns a value X4's own thread has
   already moved past, so the servo steers on a camera that is wrong by tens of
   degrees and commands max step in the wrong direction.
2. **Fast motion (effect):** the camera genuinely slews at ~1000 °/s in bursts,
   and the two threads simply sample either side of a burst, so the disagreement
   is the burst size and nothing more.

Both predict a disagreement equal to the jump size. Take 285a established that
the off-thread call does not crash and returns in-range values; it said **nothing
about freshness**, which is a different property and the one that matters here.

**What separates them** is a pair of reads taken close together in time with the
gap recorded — same camera, both threads, known Δt. If the disagreement persists
as Δt goes to zero it is staleness; if it scales with Δt it is motion. The
`camprobe` struct already has the `drain_yaw`/`drain_seen` fields for exactly
this comparison and they were never exercised, because 285a ran without
`X4VR_HEADLOOK` so the tick never wrote them.

**Do not design a fix before that measurement.** The last hypothesis died to a
harness; this one has two live alternatives with opposite fixes.

### The staleness matcher — and the version of it that would have lied

`common/x4vr_camring.hpp` answers the one question take 285b left open: is an
off-thread `GetCameraRotation` returning a value X4 has already moved past, or is
the camera genuinely slewing at ~1000 °/s? It matches a reading against the
**time series X4's own thread recorded**, because fast motion spreads that
series' values apart and makes the match *sharper* — it cannot make the matched
entry *old*. Only staleness does.

The header exists so `tests/camring.cpp` drives the **same code the injector
uses**, not a copy of it.

**The control is the instrument.** A reading taken on X4's own thread, run
through the identical matcher with the newest entry excluded, scores ~one poll
period. That is what "current" looks like *through this matcher*; without it the
probe's number is a bare quantity of milliseconds with nothing to be read
against. Control and measurement print on one line so the lag can never be quoted
without its scale.

#### The first version reported 500 ms of lag for a perfectly current reading

Closest-in-value across the window is wrong, and confidently so. Driven with a
monotonic ramp it is exact at every depth — which is precisely why a single
happy-path case would have passed it. But a real camera **revisits** every angle:

| sweep | reported lag for a CURRENT reading |
|---|---|
| 0.5 Hz | 11.11 ms — correct |
| 2.0 Hz | **500.00 ms** |
| 5.0 Hz | **1200.00 ms** |

Take 285b's camera oscillated between X4's clamps several times a second. Pointed
at it, that matcher would have reported enormous staleness *whatever the truth
was* — confirming the hypothesis it was built to test. This is the third
instrument in this project that would have answered its own question.

Fixed by scanning from the **newest** entry backwards and taking the first match
within a tolerance derived from the camera's own per-sample motion, then walking
to the local minimum. Returning the first in-tolerance entry instead was one
frame early at every depth — a systematic 11 ms bias, the same order as the
staleness being hunted, so it would have read as signal.

**Validated before the run**, all exact:

| planted | reported |
|---|---|
| 0.0 ms | 0.0 ms |
| 11.1 ms | 11.1 ms |
| 44.4 ms | 44.4 ms |
| 100.0 ms | 100.0 ms |
| 200.0 ms | 200.0 ms |
| 500.0 ms | **REFUSED** — beyond the 300 ms window, stated not pinned |

And the two properties that make the answer meaningful rather than merely
present: a current reading scores **0.00 ms at 50, 200, 600 and 1200 °/s**, so
speed alone never manufactures a lag and the alternative stays distinguishable;
and a near-static camera is **refused**, because with every entry matching
equally the reported age is whichever tie happened to win.

### P286 — committed before the run

- **P286.1** `camlag` reports OURS within a frame or two of CONTROL, i.e. **not
  stale**. The getter almost certainly reads a plain cached field. If so,
  staleness is refuted, take 285b's 59.588° two-thread disagreement was genuine
  fast motion, and — with the servo arithmetic already cleared by
  `tests/headlook.cpp` — **both** of my explanations for the oscillation are
  dead and the cause is somewhere I have not yet looked.
- **P286.2** If instead OURS runs tens of milliseconds behind CONTROL, the fix is
  forced and is not the one I proposed earlier: sample the camera on X4's thread
  and pass the value across, never call the getter from the tick's own thread.
- **P286.3** The control itself lands near one X4 poll period. If it does not,
  the matcher is mis-scaled and nothing else on the line may be quoted.

**Caveat, stated up front:** this runs flatscreen, where the drain rate and
thread structure differ from the gamescope+VR configuration the episode occurred
in. A *stale* result there is conclusive. A *not stale* result is strong but
wants one VR confirmation before #75's staleness branch is closed, because the
oscillation has only ever been observed under the VR configuration.

### Take 286 — staleness REFUTED, and both standing explanations are now dead

284 s flatscreen, camera swung on free-look throughout. Read **per window**, not
off the last cumulative line — that is the dilution defect that made take 283's
`inputrate` report 33.4% where differencing said 73%, and I had already fixed it
in two instruments before writing it a third time here. It mattered: the
cumulative means are 18.41/13.13 ms against per-window medians of 11.22/6.71,
inflated by matches saturated at the 300 ms window edge.

| | per-window median | range |
|---|---|---|
| CONTROL (X4's own thread) | **11.22 ms** | 6.79 – 55.68 |
| OURS (off-thread) | **6.71 ms** | 2.80 – 51.40 |
| OURS − CONTROL | **−4.04 ms** | −17.86 … **+1.83** |

- **P286.3 holds**: CONTROL's 11.22 ms sits on one 90 Hz frame, which is its
  structural floor, so the matcher is correctly scaled and the rest of the line
  may be read.
- **P286.1 CONFIRMED.** In the **worst of 90 windows** the off-thread read is
  **1.83 ms** behind X4's own — not a mean that could hide a bad stretch. At the
  ~1000 °/s the oscillation reached, that bounds the servo's input error at a few
  degrees. The episode needed ~60.
- 25639 off-thread calls, 17055 non-zero, **0 outside ±200°**, no crash.

**A structural asymmetry, recorded rather than left to flatter the result:**
CONTROL excludes the entry it just wrote, so its floor is one poll period while
OURS' floor is zero. A perfectly current off-thread read should therefore score
about a frame *better*, not equal — which is roughly what −4.04 ms is. The
defensible claim is the **bound**, not the sign.

#### Both of my explanations for take 285b are now dead

| explanation | status |
|---|---|
| servo re-commands while commands are in flight (burst delivery) | refuted offline — `tests/headlook.cpp`, all 8 cells of burst x lead x amplitude stable |
| the off-thread camera read is stale | refuted here — worst window 1.83 ms |

I proposed both, in that order, each as the leading explanation. Neither
survived, and **neither cost a take**: one died to a harness written before the
fix, the other to a 3-minute flatscreen run. That is the pattern to keep.

**What has NOT been examined** — the difference between the drain-driven tick and
the thread-driven one, minus the two pieces now cleared. What remains is the
*coupling* rather than the arithmetic: `SDL_PushEvent` called from a foreign
thread while X4 drains, the free-look key re-assertion now issued at 90 Hz from
that thread, and whatever ordering X4 sees between our synthetic motion events
and its own frame boundaries. None of that is modelled anywhere, and none of it
should be guessed at: the next step is to characterise what X4 receives, not to
propose a third mechanism.

`X4VR_TICK_HZ` stays unused meanwhile. It is off by default, so nothing is
broken while this is open.

### The event census — what X4 actually receives

Two mechanisms proposed and refuted, so this counts rather than guesses. `evflow`
instruments **both ends of the one channel that carries our commands into X4**:

| counted | where | what it settles |
|---|---|---|
| `pushed` motion/key | `push_our_event` | how much we emit |
| `got` motion/key | the `SDL_PeepEvents(GET)` walk | how much X4 **takes** |
| queue time | the event's own `timestamp`, stamped before the push | how long a command sits before landing |
| ours-per-drain histogram | one `SDL_PeepEvents(GET)` call | whether X4 gets several commands at once |
| the player's own motion | same walk, non-ours | what competes for the same channel |

`pushed` and `got` are counted **at their own sites, never inferred from one
another**: "delayed" and "DROPPED" want opposite fixes, and one counter cannot
separate them. Counted only on GET — a peek leaves the event queued and would
credit X4 with receiving it twice.

**The one assumption, pinned against the real library.** The whole queue-time
measurement rests on SDL preserving a `timestamp` we set ourselves.
`tests/sdl_push_timestamp.cpp` links real SDL3 and asserts it, because a version
that overwrote the field would leave `evflow` reporting a latency near zero with
no other symptom — a plausible number, silently wrong. Against **SDL 3.4.16**:

- a non-zero timestamp **survives** the push;
- a zero one is filled in by SDL, so zero cannot be mistaken for one of ours;
- the marker field and the payload survive;
- the queue is **FIFO**, and one `SDL_PeepEvents(GET)` returned all eight queued
  events — so "several of ours in one drain" is a real backlog, not reordering.

X4 ships its own SDL, so this can still fail there. The scorer detects exactly
that: non-zero `got` with every queue time reading zero is reported as **the
timestamp did not survive**, with the queue time declared void and the counts
left standing, rather than as "no delay".

### P287 — committed before the run

- **P287.1** `pushed ≈ got`. Nothing is dropped; SDL's queue is reliable and X4
  drains it to empty. If instead `got` is well under `pushed`, commands are being
  discarded, the servo's error can never close, and that is a third defect
  distinct from both refuted ones.
- **P287.2** The ours-per-drain histogram has real mass at **2 and above** while
  the thread driver runs, and essentially none at the drain-driven rate. This is
  the one I expect to carry the answer: it is the direct measurement of the
  backlog that take 285b's 3–5x max-step jumps imply, and nothing has measured it
  yet.
- **P287.3** Queue time is tens of milliseconds during fast motion. At the
  ~1000 °/s the oscillation reached, 40 ms is 40° of command in flight that the
  servo has no knowledge of.
- **P287.4** The player's own motion is ~0 Hz. If it is not, the run was
  contaminated and P287.2 cannot be read.

**If P287.1–P287.3 all come back clean, the channel is innocent too**, and every
mechanism proposed for take 285b is dead. That would be a real result and not a
failure — it would mean the difference is in X4's own handling of *when* input
arrives relative to its frame, which nothing on our side has ever looked at.

### Take 287 — the channel is innocent, and the cause is finally located

#### First: 287a's ghosting was MINE

`push_our_event` stamped `timestamp = mono_seconds() * 1e9` — CLOCK_MONOTONIC
**since boot**, about 6.4e14 ns — into a field SDL fills from `SDL_GetTicksNS`,
which counts from `SDL_Init` and was around 1e10. **Four orders of magnitude
out, in a field handed straight to X4.** 287a ghosted for its whole length in the
drain-driven configuration that has never had a problem.

`tests/sdl_push_timestamp.cpp` proved SDL *preserves* a value we set. It never
asked whether X4 *reads* it — and that was the question that mattered. Verifying
the wrong property is how an instrument comes to perturb the thing it measures;
the test passed, and gave me confidence in exactly the wrong direction.

Fixed by leaving the field at **zero so SDL stamps it**, and reading it at the
drain with `SDL_GetTicksNS` at both ends. The queue time was always available for
free by reading; writing was never necessary.

#### Second: the scorer read 2 lines out of 94 and printed a verdict

The log prints `%+lld`, so the in-flight count arrives as `(+0 in flight/lost)`,
and the pattern had `-?\d+`, which does not match a leading `+`. It matched
**only the windows where the count went negative**: 2 of 94 in 287a, 9 of 95 in
287b — and "CLEAN" was printed from that. A regex that silently matches a biased
subset is worse than one matching nothing, because nothing is visible as nothing.
The scorer now compares its match count against the raw line count and says
`PARSE DEFECT` when they differ.

#### The census, read properly — restricted to windows actually pushing commands

| | 287a (drain) | 287b (thread, 90 Hz) |
|---|---|---|
| pushed → took | 1389 → 1390 | 3138 → 3136 |
| queue time median | 0.01 ms | 6.56 ms |
| drains carrying **≥2** of ours | **0 of 2898** | **0 of 6513** |
| player's own motion | 0.0 Hz | 0.0 Hz |

- **P287.1 CONFIRMED** — 1:1, nothing dropped.
- **P287.2 REFUTED outright** — 100.00% of drains carry exactly one command.
  There is no backlog in the queue. This was the prediction I expected to carry
  the answer.
- **P287.3 REFUTED** — 6.56 ms, not tens.
- **P287.4 confirmed.**

**So the channel is innocent too.** Servo arithmetic, camera-read freshness, and
now the event channel: three mechanisms, three refutations, none of which cost a
take beyond the ones that produced the data.

#### And the cause, which none of the three was

The episode is located exactly: X4's camera first moves at **t = 99.4 s**, goes
wild at **104–122 s** with 47–59° jumps, and the map cycle at **122.6–124.4 s**
ends it permanently — matching Patola's report that it could never be re-triggered
afterwards.

At engagement the servo was **perfectly converged** — `cmd ≈ head ≈ −1°`, dx of
2–4 counts — so accumulated startup windup is refuted as well. And at t=104.66,
head +9.8 with `cmd` 53.04 and dx +104 is the servo *correctly* driving a camera
already pinned at +65 back toward the head. **The servo is responding, not
causing.**

What the `camread` lines show through the whole run-up:

```
camread: X4 -0.00,0.00 deg (raw 0.0000,0.0000) | cmd 0.46,1.73 | head 1.50,7.19 CLOSED
camread: X4 -0.00,0.00 deg (raw 0.0000,0.0000) | cmd 0.46,1.84 | head 2.01,7.31 CLOSED
```

**X4's camera reads EXACTLY zero, for seconds, while the head moves and the servo
commands.** `head_look_observe` therefore pins the estimate to 0 every tick, the
error never closes, and the servo keeps sending. X4 is not in free-look yet, so
those deltas go somewhere else or accumulate; when free-look finally engages,
what has piled up lands at once and slams the camera into the ±65 clamp — and the
oscillation follows from there.

That explains every observation at once: why it is always *early*, why holding
the head still does not end it, why a map cycle cures it permanently (a clean
idle→steering transition establishes free-look properly), and why the 90 Hz tick
makes it far worse than the drain — twice as many commands are pumped into the
dead window.

The servo already has a stall detector for "commanding into a dead camera", and
`tests/headlook.cpp` reports it firing **twice in 300 frames**. At 90 Hz that
leaves hundreds of commands going out during the dead window. **The detector is
not wrong, it is too permissive for this rate** — and that is a hypothesis about
a fix, so it gets tested offline before any take, like the last two.

`X4VR_TICK_HZ` stays unused until then; it is off by default.

### The withdrawal: the camera was never being commanded

**Everything under "And the cause, which none of the three was" above is wrong,
and this is how.** The `camread` lines quoted there are real, and X4's camera
really does read exactly `0.0000,0.0000` for the whole run-up. The causal story
built on them is not: **we were not sending anything during that window.**

`send_mouse_delta` is gated on `steering`, and `inputrate` counts that same
variable. In take 287b every window from t=0 to t=98.8 s reads `steering on 0.0%
of ticks`. The camera comes alive at t=100.60 and tracks the head immediately and
well — X4 +0.11 against head +0.15, X4 −9.28 against head −8.89, X4 −3.67 against
head −3.65. **The first blow-up is at t≈103.5, three seconds after engagement,
with the camera live and non-zero throughout.** Nothing accumulated, because
`head_look_observe` re-pins `cmd` to X4's zero at the top of every tick and the
step is re-derived from the head — which is why the log prints the same `cmd
0.46,1.73` over and over instead of a rising number.

I read `camread` lines from the idle phase and attributed them to the wild phase.
The steering state was in the same log, in a line the scorer already parses. This
is `window-from-system-state` exactly: a verdict whose measurement window came
from somewhere other than the program's own record of its state.

#### So the dead-camera gate was not built

Swept across every take carrying an `inputrate` line — **1245 s** of instrumented
ticks, 669 s of it live steering — the number of 2 s windows that sent a delta
into a frozen camera is **zero**. The single near-miss is one 2 s window of take
287a at 1.0 Hz of sending. The `steering` predicate (cockpit ∧ HUD ∧ relative
mouse) already covers the hazard completely, and a new gate in the servo's
control path is the exact shape of thing that broke head tracking three times.

#### What the poselag stream actually measures

`camread` prints one tick in 30 and was aliasing a full oscillation. `poselag`
runs at frame rate and carries `x4=` and `cmd=` together, so the loop can be read
per camera update. Servo ticks per camera update, and camera updates moving more
than 20° — the slam itself:

| take | tick driver | Patola's report | cam Hz | N med | N max | slam |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 278–284 | none | — | 30–48 | 1.0 | 4–6 | 0.0–0.5% |
| 287a | drain | ghosting, camera fine | 29.4 | 1.0 | 4 | **0.0%** |
| 285b-s1 | 90 Hz | no wild report | 62.5 | 1.0 | 6 | **0.0%** |
| 285b-s2 | 90 Hz | **went wild** | 58.8 | 1.0 | 11 | **7.1%** |
| 287b | 90 Hz | **went wild** | 55.6 | 1.0 | 7 | **7.5%** |

The statistic agrees with his eye on 4 of 4 labelled sessions, and 285b-s1 is the
control that makes it worth something: same binary, same knobs, same tick driver,
0.0%.

#### P288.1 and P288.2 — the rate mismatch, refuted offline

X4 reports at 30–60 Hz while `X4VR_TICK_HZ` steps the servo at 90, and
`head_look_observe` overwrites `cmd` every tick — so on the ticks between two
camera updates the servo re-observes a reading it has already acted on and sends
the same correction again. M commands per intended correction is a loop gain of
M·kp. `tests/servo_rate.cpp` drives the real `head_look_step` against a plant
whose *report* rate is decoupled from the step rate (`tests/servo_lag.cpp` steps
its plant once per servo step, so it cannot express the question at all).

Both predictions were committed in the file before it was run, and both hold:

- **P288.1 confirmed.** The first period that slams is **11** (loop gain 2.75).
  The measured median is 1–2. The control passes: period 1 is calm, matching the
  takes without the driver.
- **P288.2 confirmed.** With the head frozen and the camera thrown to the +65
  clamp, the model settles to **0.000°/update** at every period up to 4. Patola
  held his head still mid-oscillation and it did not cure it, so his observation
  refutes this mechanism on its own.

#### The gain mismatch, refuted from the logs

The same harness shows a **8.7×** gain error is enough on its own with the rates
matched. Measured instead of assumed: realised move over commanded move, on the
updates where exactly one command acted and the axis was not on X4's stop, binned
by command size across takes 280–287b — **1.00 at every size in every take**,
including 8–12° commands in 287b. X4 applies what we send, at the gain we
believe, across the whole range. A constant gain error is also refuted by the
calm phases of the same runs.

#### What is left standing

Six mechanisms are now dead: servo arithmetic, in-flight commands, the stale
off-thread read, the event channel, the dead camera, the rate mismatch, and the
gain. The residual is this, from the onset of 287b's first slam:

```
    t(s)   x4_yaw   x4_pit |  step_y  step_p |   dx4_y   dx4_p
 103.475    -6.99    -4.24 |    1.38   -1.38 |    1.15   -3.78
 103.509    -4.47   -10.54 |    1.04    0.00 |    2.52   -6.30
 103.552    -0.46   -19.82 |    0.46    2.07 |    4.01   -9.28
```

At 103.509 the servo commanded **0.00** of pitch and X4's camera moved **−6.30°**;
at 103.552 it commanded **+2.07** and the camera moved **−9.28**, the other way.
Across the updates where the command was under half a mouse count and the axis was
off its stop, the median motion is one count (0.115°) everywhere — but the maximum
is 1.5–3.7° in the calm takes and **11.9 / 17.8 / 33.0°** in 284, 285b and 287b.
**Something other than our servo moves X4's camera, by tens of degrees, and it is
largest in exactly the sessions that went wild.**

It is not #78's auto-recentre: that would pull toward zero, and the correlation
between the uncommanded motion and the camera's position is +0.02 to +0.45 — the
wrong sign, and weak.

**Caveat, stated before the next step is chosen:** `cam_raw_yaw_deg` and
`cam_raw_pitch_deg` are two separate atomics written without a seqlock, so a
layer-side read can mix yaw from one tick with pitch from the one before. While
the camera is moving 20–30° per frame that tear can fabricate a large single-axis
"move", and this residual is measured from exactly those pairs. The slam itself is
**not** in doubt — `camread` sees it through one single-threaded `X4Rotation`, and
reports X4 at +65.00,+35.00 against a head at −3.78,−0.64 — but the size of the
uncommanded component is only as good as that pairing. Closing that hole is
cheaper than a take and comes before any mechanism is built on this number.

### The seqlock hole, closed — and the residual survives it

The camera block of `Shared` had **no seqlock at all**, while the file's own
opening note says two floats "would tear harmlessly in practice, but 'in
practice' is how a reader ends up with x from one frame and y from the next
exactly once, during the measurement that matters." The block was added
underneath that note without one.

Two sites were exposed, and the second is the one that made me flag the residual:

- **the declared pose** — a yaw from one tick with a pitch from the next is an
  orientation the frame was never rendered from, and the compositor reprojects
  by it;
- **`poselag`** — the layer loaded the readback near the top of its submission
  block and `cam_yaw_deg` again a hundred lines further down, two independent
  loads, so one line could carry `x4=` and `cmd=` from different ticks.

Closed with `cam_seq` + `share_write_camera`/`share_read_camera`
(`kShareVersion` 2 → 3). `tests/share.cpp` drives it with a writer thread and a
**negative control that runs first**: the old two-load read, reproduced exactly,
tears on **207917 of 400000** reads. Without that arm the guarded one would pass
for want of contention rather than because the seqlock works.

Two defects of my own, found by the test rather than by reading:

- The first guarded arm **refused 98%** of its reads and asserted only on the
  survivors — a pass bought by not looking. `share_read_camera` gave up after
  eight attempts while the writer holds the block open for seven stores. Raised
  to 32; the arm now completes 57125 reads with zero tears, and a second arm at
  a realistic write cadence reports **0.000% refused**.
- I wrote a header comment promising that a refused read "reports the last
  complete snapshot instead — a frame stale, never inconsistent", and then wrote
  callers that passed a fresh `CamSnap` and got **zeroes**. At the declaration
  site that drops the pose to identity for a frame: the world lock popping,
  which is a bigger artefact than the tear being fixed. Both callers now hold a
  static snapshot, which is what makes the sentence true. See
  [[stale-comment-is-misinformation]] — this time I wrote the comment and the
  code that contradicted it in the same edit.

#### Re-measured: the tear did NOT contaminate #75

No take needed — the tear is detectable in the logs already on disk. The servo
sets `cmd = raw + sign·dx·gain` with `dx` a **whole** mouse count, so on an
untorn line `(cmd − x4)` is an exact multiple of the gain. A torn line took `cmd`
from a different tick and picks up X4's own camera motion in between, which is
not a multiple of anything.

| | |
|---|---|
| `poselag` lines, takes 280–287b | **239 668** |
| observed torn | **0** |
| detector sensitivity, measured on 92 386 planted tears | **16.0%** |
| true tear rate, Rule of Three at 95% | **< 0.0078%** |

The sensitivity number is the point: a tear is only visible when X4's camera moved
by a non-multiple of the gain between the two ticks, so the detector misses 84% of
them and the bound is widened to match. **The 100%-untorn column on its own would
have been a guard that cannot fail** — every value in this system is quantised to
0.115°, and I checked whether differences are too before believing it.

So the gap between the two loads was microseconds, not a frame, and my caveat on
the previous entry was right to raise and wrong by three orders of magnitude.
**The uncommanded motion is not an artefact of the tear**: 11.9 / 17.8 / 33.0° in
takes 284, 285b and 287b stands as measured, and remains what #75 has left.

The fix is still worth having — 0.0078% of frames at 90 Hz is a wrong declared
pose roughly every twenty minutes, and [[no-cosmetic-defects-in-vr]] applies — but
it is not the cause of the slam and must not be reported as one.

### What moves the camera uncommanded — the answer needs `plantid`, which has never run

X4's own `libraries/parameters.xml` already names a candidate, in the same node
as #68's clamp:

    <internal maxpitch="35" maxyaw="65" anglespeed="200" angleacc="500" .../>

`angleacc` is an angular **acceleration**. A plant with acceleration has
velocity, and a camera with velocity keeps moving after the command stops —
which is what "moves uncommanded" looks like from the current command alone. And
this project already measured it once: the section *"What is established, and
what is not"* above records **"the camera carries momentum (commanded ~nothing
while moving, it still travelled ~77% of the previous step, n=128)"**, and in the
same breath that the form of the response was **NOT established**.

#### Three instruments, three answers I could not use

- **Differentiating the camera twice** gave velocities to 3164 °/s and
  accelerations to **217 219 °/s²** against X4's declared 200/500. A maximum 400×
  the median is noise, not a plant: `age` is quantised to 0.1 ms and the line
  stamp to 1 ms, and a second derivative multiplies that.
- **A least-squares FIR fit** of camera motion on the last six commands returned
  h[0] = **−1.086** with coefficients alternating sign and summing to 1.9, at
  R² 0.88. Physically impossible, and the reason is collinearity: consecutive
  commands are nearly the same number.
- **The aggregate realised/commanded ratio** reads 1.00 and always will —
  momentum redistributes motion in time without changing the total.

All three fail for one reason, and it is written in this document already: **the
data is closed-loop.** The command is computed from the camera position, so no
regression of one on the other identifies the plant. That is the exact sentence
that justified building `plantid` — *"Everything take 212 established about X4's
camera was inferred through a closed loop, which chooses its command from the
very error it is trying to measure."*

I rebuilt, badly, what the project already has in a form designed to work. See
[[read-the-existing-report-first]].

#### `plantid` is built, tested, wired — and has never been run

Zero `plantid:` lines in any log on disk. The sequence drives X4 open-loop with
a known signal and the head out of the loop entirely: RESET, SETTLE, **IMPULSE**,
**COAST** (14 steps of commanding nothing — "an integrator stops dead, a smoother
decays, momentum overshoots"), SUSTAIN, DECAY. 7 sizes × 2 directions × 3 passes
= 2642 ticks, about **53 s** at the measured 50 Hz drain rate.

#### The acceptance check now discriminates, which it never did

`score_run.py`'s plantid block carried a comment crediting `tests/plantid.cpp`
with validating it. That file checks **its own** statistics on **its own**
in-memory trace and never emits a line the scorer can read — two separate pieces
of arithmetic, one tested, and the untested one is the one that names the plant
on the day. `tests/run-plantid-scorer.sh` closes it: the real `plant_id_step`
drives an integrator, a smoother and a per-step cap, emits the injector's exact
log format, and the real scorer must name each. It does, **3 of 3**:

| planted | scorer's verdict | coast | fade |
|---|---|---|---|
| integrator | PURE INTEGRATOR | 0% | 1.00x |
| smoother (k=0.25) | **SMOOTHED / MOMENTUM** | **75%** | — |
| per-step cap | PER-STEP CAP | 0% | 0.33x |

The smoother reads **75%** coast against take 212's measured **77%**. That is a
prior, not the answer, and it is written here before the run rather than after.

Two things this found that would have cost the take:

- `score_run.py` refuses any file with no render-pass inventory **before** it
  reaches any instrument block, so the run must carry `X4VR_MV=1` or the scorer
  prints UNSCORABLE and never scores the thing the take was spent on.
- `tests/run-plantid-scorer.sh` reported `SKIP  not built` with the binary
  present: Patola's `CDPATH=.:/home/patola:/dados` makes `cd` **print** the
  directory, so `$(cd … && pwd)` captured two lines. That is
  [[workaround-hid-the-defect]] reproduced in a brand-new script — fixed with
  `CDPATH=` inside the script, and a missing binary in an existing build tree is
  now a FAIL rather than a silent skip.

**P288.3, committed before the run:** the coast will read above 35% and
`score_run.py` will say SMOOTHED / MOMENTUM. If it says PURE INTEGRATOR instead,
then X4 applies exactly what we send and the uncommanded motion has a source
outside the mouse channel entirely — a different search, and this prediction
should be read as refuted rather than explained.

### Take 288 — the plant is an INTEGRATOR WITH DEAD TIME, and the first verdict was wrong

The run completed: 2900 ticks, 43 element-passes, sequence COMPLETE. The camera
swept 83.9 deg peak-to-peak and never came within 23 deg of X4's stop, so no
measured sample is a clamp measurement.

**What X4 actually is**, from the open-loop sequence:

```
impulse response   +0: 0.00  +1: 0.16  +2: 0.15  +3: 3.45  +4..+7: 0.00
delivery           99.7 99.6 99.6 99.6 99.6 99.6 99.6 %   (2 -> 104 counts)
```

92% of the response arrives in **one** tick, **three ticks late**, and exactly
**0.000** arrives after it. Delivery is 99.6% at every size across the whole
range. That is a faithful integrator with a transport delay — **no momentum, no
cap, no nonlinearity.** An independent stack of the 42 isolated impulses,
computed outside the scorer, gives the same shape and a total of 0.996.

#### P288.3 is REFUTED, and the scorer said the opposite

I predicted coast > 35% and SMOOTHED / MOMENTUM. The scorer duly printed
**"coast 100% => SMOOTHED / MOMENTUM"** — and it was wrong, for a reason the same
output contained: **during COAST a delayed integrator is still paying out the
impulse from three ticks back.** It moves with nothing commanded, so coast reads
100%, identically to momentum and with the opposite fix.

The scorer checked coast *first and alone*, under a comment claiming it "is the
one number that separates a smoothing plant from a stiff one whatever the
delivery curve looks like". It does not separate either from dead time.

**Why the validation missed it:** the three plants I validated against were
Integrator, Smoother and Capped, and **not one had a transport delay**. A control
set that excludes the answer cannot catch a wrong answer. Adding
`delayed-integrator` to `tests/run-plantid-scorer.sh` reproduces the failure
exactly — the old scorer calls it SMOOTHED / MOMENTUM, the same as a delayed
smoother.

**What separates them was already printed and thrown away:** the response
*width*. Delay moves the response; smoothing widens it.

| planted | in one tick | old verdict | new verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| integrator | 100% | PURE INTEGRATOR | PURE INTEGRATOR, no delay |
| smoother | 28% | SMOOTHED / MOMENTUM | SMOOTHED / MOMENTUM |
| capped | 100% | PER-STEP CAP | PER-STEP CAP |
| **delayed integrator** | **100%** | **SMOOTHED / MOMENTUM** ✗ | INTEGRATOR WITH TRANSPORT DELAY |
| **delayed smoother** | **72%** | SMOOTHED / MOMENTUM | SMOOTHED / MOMENTUM |
| **take 288** | **92%** | **SMOOTHED / MOMENTUM** ✗ | **INTEGRATOR WITH TRANSPORT DELAY of 3** |

5 of 5 on the planted set after the fix.

#### What Patola saw, and why it was correct

He expected the camera to move independently of his head. Instead the cockpit
stayed at his head's angle while **"the frustum was what was moving — a black
band from the right eating more of the visible scene, then moving back."**

That is the sequence working. The layer's shader conjugation applied **0.00 deg
for all 16950 frames** of the run; the sweep reached his eyes entirely through
the *declared* pose, which followed X4's camera to the digit (median
|declared − x4| = 0.000, over 7992 frames, 83.9 deg peak-to-peak). The compositor
therefore placed each frame up to 42 deg from where he was looking, and the
uncovered side is black. The band growing and shrinking **is** the sweep.

#### The mechanism is still not in hand — and the test says so

`tests/servo_rate.cpp` now drives the real servo against the measured plant.
At kp = 0.25 the loop reaches X4's clamp at a dead time of **6 ticks**; at the
**measured 3** it is completely calm — max excursion 20.24 deg, zero reversals.
So dead time *at the rate it was measured* does not explain 285b/287b either.

That section also caught a defect in its own statistic: at one tick per camera
update a single update can move at most `max_step_deg` = 12 deg, so the log's
">20 deg per update" slam measure **read 0.0% on a run pinned to both clamps with
113 reversals.** It cannot express the failure at that period, and max excursion
and reversal count are now reported beside it.

**P289 — the one question left, and one run answers it.** Take 288 measured 3
ticks at its 30.3 Hz tick rate. Whether that is **99 ms of wall clock** or
**3 of X4's frames** cannot be told from a single rate, and it decides everything,
because stability depends on the dead time in *ticks*:

- **fixed in TIME** — 99 ms is 3 ticks at 30 Hz, 5 at 50, **9 at 90**, walking
  straight past the threshold of 6. That ordering matches all four labelled
  sessions: 287a (drain, ~50 Hz) calm, 285b-s1/s2 and 287b (90 Hz) wild.
- **fixed in FRAMES** — it stays 3 at every rate, the loop never crosses, and the
  oscillation has a cause still unfound.

One `plantid` run with `X4VR_TICK_HZ=90` reports 9 ticks or 3. Nothing else
changes, and the servo is off throughout so it cannot go wild.

### Take 289 — P289 is NOT answered: the run is unmeasurable

Same command as 288 with `X4VR_TICK_HZ=90` added. The driver ran (90.0 Hz median
over 76 windows) and the sequence completed, 3873 ticks, 43 element-passes. The
scorer then printed **"only 38% of the response in one tick → SMOOTHED /
MOMENTUM"** — flatly contradicting take 288 on the same game, the same build and
the same plant.

**The delivery column is what settles it:**

| counts | take 288 (30 Hz) | take 289 (91 Hz) |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | 99.7% | 83.0% |
| 4 | 99.6% | 49.8% |
| 8 | 99.6% | 83.0% |
| 16 | 99.6% | **124.6%** |
| 32 | 99.6% | 64.4% |
| 64 | 99.6% | 87.7% |
| 104 | 99.6% | 49.8% |

**124.6% is impossible** — nothing in this system delivers more than it was
commanded. Take 289 is not a plant measurement.

#### Why, and it is plantid's own design

`plantid`'s phases are counted in **ticks** — IMPULSE is one tick, COAST is
fourteen — but the plant is only observable when X4's camera readback *changes*.

| | tick rate | camera changes | ticks per update |
|---|---|---|---|
| take 288 | 30.3 Hz | 12.1 /s | **2.5** |
| take 289 | 90.9 Hz | 16.0 /s | **5.7** |

Tripling the tick rate barely moved the readback rate, so each phase now covers
less than half as many updates and the one-tick impulse usually falls entirely
*between* two readbacks. The response looked "wider" purely because it was being
sampled three times faster than the thing it was sampling —
[[instrument-inherits-its-question]]: the width discriminator I added yesterday
was derived from a run where tick ≈ camera rate, and it does not survive a rate
change.

This also contradicts take 285b's banked claim that `X4VR_TICK_HZ=90` raises X4's
camera rate from 28.2 to 54.5 Hz. Here it went 12.1 → 16.0. Flagged, not chased.

#### The gate that should have stopped me, and the gate that was wrong

`score_run.py` now refuses to name a plant when the run cannot support one. My
**first** version gated on the delivery column spanning more than 25 points —
which is exactly the signature of a **PER-STEP CAP**, so it declared two of the
three plants it exists to name "unmeasurable". `tests/run-plantid-scorer.sh`
caught that immediately; a gate that rejects the answer is worse than no gate.

What survives is one genuine impossibility (>110% delivered) plus the direct
measurement of the cause (ticks per camera update > 3). 5 of 5 planted plants
still pass, take 288 still reads INTEGRATOR WITH TRANSPORT DELAY of 3, take 289
now reads UNMEASURABLE.

#### Where P289 stands

**Unanswered.** The question — is the 3-tick delay fixed in time (≈99 ms, so
9 ticks at 90 Hz and past `servo_rate.cpp`'s threshold of 6) or fixed in frames
(3 ticks always, and not the cause) — needs a run where the sequence and the
readback are on comparable cadences at BOTH rates. The fix is plantid's phase
lengths: they must be expressed in camera updates, not ticks, so a 90 Hz run
covers the same number of observations as a 30 Hz one. That is a change to
`common/x4vr_plantid.hpp` and it is testable offline against
`tests/plantid.cpp`'s existing plants before any further take is spent.

Take 288 remains the only valid plant measurement.

### The fix: plantid now runs in the readback's time base

`plant_id_step` stepped once per servo tick. It now steps once per **camera
update** and sends nothing on the ticks in between — one command per observation,
every phase counted in observations. The same experiment at any tick rate, which
is what P289 needs in order to compare two of them.

Three things this required, each of which broke something first:

- **A `Calibrate` phase, because a value change is not a refresh.** During SETTLE
  and COAST the camera is genuinely still, so "the readback did not change" and
  "the readback did not refresh" are the same observation with opposite meanings.
  The ratio has to be measured where the camera is certainly moving, so one short
  phase drives a constant command and counts changes. Excluded from the
  measurement, like Reset.
- **That phase alternates direction.** 40 ticks × 16 counts is 73.6°, against
  X4's 65° stop — and a clamped camera stops changing, so the ratio would have
  read the clamp, silently, and every phase length after it would have been
  wrong. Reversing every 10 ticks bounds the excursion at 18.4°.
- **The ratio is comparisons ÷ changes, not ticks ÷ changes.** The first tick has
  nothing to compare against, so 40 ticks give 39 comparisons, and 40/39 = 1.026
  for a readback that refreshes *every* tick. The fractional accumulator then
  skipped one step in 39 and smeared the impulse response — which turned the
  `delayed-integrator` control back into "SMOOTHED / MOMENTUM" in the validation
  run. Caught there, not in the field.

The injector logs only the ticks where the sequence advanced, so one logged line
is one observation and the scorer's lag profile is indexed by observation rather
than by tick. Logging the idle ticks would put the tick rate straight back into
the measurement.

#### The proof: the same plant, sampled at two rates, gets the same name

`tests/plantid.cpp` grew a `Sampled` wrapper that holds the published angle for
N steps while the plant integrates underneath — exactly what
`GetCameraRotation` does between X4's camera ticks, and exactly take 289's
condition. `tests/run-plantid-scorer.sh` now drives **seven** plants end to end
through the real `score_run.py`:

| planted | verdict |
|---|---|
| integrator | PURE INTEGRATOR, no delay |
| smoother | SMOOTHED / MOMENTUM |
| capped | PER-STEP CAP |
| delayed integrator | INTEGRATOR WITH TRANSPORT DELAY of 3 |
| delayed smoother | SMOOTHED / MOMENTUM |
| **delayed integrator, sampled 3×** | **INTEGRATOR WITH TRANSPORT DELAY of 1** |
| **smoother, sampled 3×** | **SMOOTHED / MOMENTUM** |

The last two are the ones that matter. Under-sampling no longer changes what a
plant is called, and the delay is reported in **camera updates** — 3 ticks of
dead time sampled every 3 ticks is 1 update, the same physical lag stated in the
one unit that does not move with our own tick rate.

#### What it costs, and why both arms must be re-run

2418 measured updates: **200 s at 12.1 Hz** (take 288's readback rate) or 151 s
at 16.0 Hz, plus ~264 reset steps. A run now costs the same wall clock at any
tick rate — that is the point, and it is also why it is longer than take 288's
97 s.

**Take 288 cannot serve as the 30 Hz arm.** It was measured with tick-counted
phases and a tick-indexed lag profile; comparing it against an update-counted run
would be the cross-instrument arithmetic that produced this whole detour. Both
arms get the new code.

**P289 restated in the unit that now carries it:** take 288's 3 ticks at 2.5
ticks per update is ~1.2 updates. If both arms report ~1 update, the lag is fixed
in X4's own frame, the servo sees the same dead time at any tick rate, and the
"9 ticks at 90 Hz" branch is dead. If the 90 Hz arm reports ~3 updates instead,
raising the tick rate really does multiply the dead time and
`tests/servo_rate.cpp`'s threshold of 6 is in reach.

### Takes 290a/290b — P289's premise is dead, and so is dead time as the mechanism

Both arms completed with the update-counted sequence. **The fix worked on its
target:** delivery is **99.6% flat at every one of the seven sizes in both arms**,
against take 289's 49.8–124.6%.

| | tick rate | calibrated | peak lag | delivery | coast |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 290a | 28.2 Hz | 1.39 ticks/update | +2 steps | 99.6% flat | **0%** |
| 290b | 75.1 Hz | 1.30 ticks/update | +2 steps | 99.6% flat | **0%** |

#### P289 answered, in the negative

It asked whether take 288's 3-tick delay was fixed in **time** (→ 9 ticks at
90 Hz, past `servo_rate.cpp`'s threshold of 6) or in **frames**. It is neither:

```
290a   2 steps x 1.39 ticks/step = 2.78 ticks   at 28.2 Hz =  99 ms
290b   2 steps x 1.30 ticks/step = 2.60 ticks   at 75.1 Hz =  35 ms
```

**Constant in OUR ticks, not in time.** X4 does not know our tick rate, so a lag
that counts ~2.7 of our ticks however fast we tick is in our own sampling path —
command out at the top of tick N, camera read at the top of tick N+1 or N+2 —
not in X4's plant. Either way it is nowhere near 6, so **transport delay is
refuted as the mechanism for 285b/287b's oscillation.**

The calibration also settles a standing question: **1.39 and 1.30 ticks per
camera update at a 2.7× difference in tick rate.** X4's readback tracks our tick
rate rather than sitting at a fixed ~12–16 Hz, which is what take 288's
`inputrate` line claimed and take 289's 12.1 → 16.0 appeared to contradict. The
apparent contradiction was the still-camera phases: over the whole run the ratio
reads 8.6 and 14.3, but that is "how often the camera had anything to report",
not staleness.

#### Two hard facts, each now measured three times

- **Delivery is 99.6% flat from 2 to 104 counts** (288, 290a, 290b). No cap, no
  sub-linearity, no direction asymmetry. Take 212's "delivery falls from 95% to
  71% as the command grows, 87–126% continuing against 21–49% reversing" is
  **dead** — it was closed-loop inference, exactly as the header of
  `x4vr_plantid.hpp` warned.
- **Coast is 0% in both arms.** With the sequence in the readback's time base the
  camera stops dead when commands stop. **Momentum is refuted**, and take 288's
  coast of 100% is confirmed as the transport-delay artefact it was called.

#### Two more scorer defects, both mine

- **The ticks-per-update gate refused 290b.** It computed `len(S)/changes` over
  the logged lines — correct while the injector logged every tick, wrong the
  moment it began logging one line per sequence step. Most of the sequence is
  SETTLE/COAST/DECAY, where the camera is still because nothing was commanded,
  not because the readback is stale. It read 3.7 and threw away a run whose
  delivery column was flat at every size. Removed; the >110% impossibility is
  sound on its own and still catches take 289. **An instrument that re-derives a
  quantity the log already states can end up evaluating a different one** — the
  injector prints the calibrated ratio, and that is what should have been read.
- **290b printed SMOOTHED / MOMENTUM against its own coast of 0%.** A smoother's
  defining property is that velocity persists; coast near zero refutes momentum
  whatever the width says. The verdict now reports **CONTRADICTORY** and names
  nothing, rather than letting the width win. The bands were set from planted
  plants and moving one to break a tie in live data would be fitting the
  instrument to the answer — which is how this file got SMOOTHED / MOMENTUM onto
  a delayed integrator in the first place.

#### Where #75 stands

Seven mechanisms are now dead: servo arithmetic, in-flight commands, the stale
off-thread read, the event channel, the dead camera, the rate mismatch, the gain,
momentum, and dead time. The plant is a **faithful integrator** — it delivers
99.6% of every command at every size and stops when told.

The oscillation of 285b/287b is therefore **not in the plant**, and
`tests/servo_rate.cpp` says it is not in the servo at the measured parameters
either. What remains unexplained is 290b's response *width* — 49% in one step
with no coast — which is neither smoothing nor a clean delay, and the isolated
0.50 bump at lag +7 that goes with it.

### The width difference, characterised: it is bucket size, and the real quantity is JITTER

Decomposing the impulse response per lag instead of reading the pooled mean:

```
take 290a   lag  0    1     2     3..7          take 290b   lag 0..3        4..7
  MEAN         0.18 0.72  2.87  0.00              MEAN        0.09 .. 0.49  0.005 .. 0.50
  MEDIAN       0.00 0.00  0.46  0.00              MEDIAN      0.00 .. 0.00  0.00  .. 0.00
```

**The median is 0.000 at every lag in both takes.** Each impulse's response lands
in exactly ONE step — whichever one the camera happened to move in — and zero in
all the others. The "impulse response" is a mean over 42 sparse windows, so what
it measures is the *distribution of arrival step*, not a plant shape. In 290b,
three windows supply **77%** of all the mass past lag 4; one of them is the whole
11.918 deg command landing at lag 7.

Measured in milliseconds instead of bucket indices — per impulse, bracketed by
the step's own timestamps:

| | tick | step size | latency median | p10 | p90 | max | **p90−p10** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 290a | 28.2 Hz | 35 ms | 108.8 ms | 39.0 | 139.5 | 162 | **100.5 ms** |
| 290b | 75.1 Hz | 11 ms | 52.8 ms | 38.5 | 128.0 | 167 | **89.5 ms** |

The medians differ because the buckets differ; **the spread agrees**. All 42
impulses resolve in both arms, and there is no dependence on command size —
correlation **+0.03** and **−0.18** across 2 to 104 counts, with every size
spanning roughly 25–165 ms.

**So X4's input-to-camera latency is not a constant to be compensated. It wanders
over roughly 40–165 ms, about 90–100 ms of jitter, at both tick rates.** The
"width" difference between the arms was 35 ms buckets against 11 ms buckets and
nothing else.

#### My control table was built on windows where the servo was not running

Restricting `inputrate` to windows with steering above 50% **and** deltas going
out above 5 Hz — the windows where the servo was actually working:

| take | tick rate | Patola's report |
|---|---|---|
| 287a | **28.0 Hz** | ghosting, camera fine |
| 285b-s1 | 68.6 Hz | no wild report |
| 285b-s2 | 70.7 Hz | **WENT WILD** |
| 287b | 69.7 Hz | **WENT WILD** |
| 280–284 | *no such window exists* | — |

Two corrections to what this document said before. Take 287a ran at **28.0 Hz**
where it mattered, not the 50.1 Hz median I quoted over all windows — the idle
windows were dragging it up. And takes 280–284 **never exercised the servo at
all**, so their "0.0–0.5% slam" was the slam rate of a servo that was not
running. They are silent on this question, not evidence for it. Same error as
[[x4vr-window-from-system-state]]: a measurement window chosen by something other
than the program's own record of what it was doing.

#### P291 — the jitter, not the delay, and it was committed before the run

`tests/servo_rate.cpp` section 5 swept a **fixed** delay: calm to 5 ticks, at the
clamp by 6. The measured 40–165 ms in ticks is 1–5 at 28 Hz and 2–12 at 70 Hz.

Driven with the measured distribution — order preserved, since X4 applies deltas
in the order it dequeues them — against the real `head_look_step`:

| tick Hz | delay range | slam | max \|cam\| | reversals | |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 28.0 | 1–5 | **0.0%** | 20.47 | 0 | 287a: calm |
| 50.0 | 2–9 | 12.6% | 65.00 | 12 | no take ran here |
| 68.6 | 2–12 | 14.8% | 65.00 | 6 | 285b-s1: not reported wild |
| 70.7 | 2–12 | **14.9%** | **65.00** | 7 | 285b-s2 / 287b: **WENT WILD** |

**Both halves of P291 confirmed.** A latency that jitters over a fixed band in
*milliseconds* spans more *ticks* the faster we tick, and crosses section 5's
threshold between 28 and 70 Hz — which is exactly the variable that separates the
calm session from the wild ones.

**What does not fit, stated rather than smoothed over:** 285b-s1 ran at 68.6 Hz,
the same rate as the two wild sessions, and was not reported wild. The model
calls it 14.8%. A marginally unstable loop needs excitation to show it, and "no
wild report" is weaker evidence than "went wild" — but it is one of only four
labelled sessions and it does not support the model. #75 is not closed on this.

### P292 — excitation is NOT why 285b-s1 stayed calm, and the model is refuted

Head angular rate per session, from `camread` (cadence `% 30` only, so it does
**not** oversample the wild moments the way `headlook` does — that one fires on
`% 30 || clamped`):

| take | tick | p50 | p90 | max | report |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 287a | 28.0 Hz | 3.9 | 56.3 | 113.9 | calm |
| 285b-s1 | 68.6 Hz | 6.2 | 69.4 | 117.5 | calm |
| 285b-s2 | 70.7 Hz | 33.4 | 103.7 | 161.9 | **WILD** |
| 287b | 69.7 Hz | 5.3 | 87.7 | 160.6 | **WILD** |

**287b went wild with a quieter head than s1's** — p50 5.3 against 6.2. The
peak-rate split (118 calm / 161 wild) is a threshold fitted to four points and is
not evidence.

**P292 was committed before the sweep and is confirmed.** Sweeping the head's
peak rate at each measured tick rate, amplitude held at 20° and only the
frequency varied:

| peak °/s | 28.0 Hz | 68.6 Hz |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | 0.0%, max 20.1 | **14.2%, max 65.0** |
| 62.8 | 0.0%, max 20.6 | 15.0%, max 65.0 |
| 118 | 0.0%, max 23.0 | 15.5%, max 65.0 |
| 220 | 0.0%, max 31.6 | 14.7%, max 65.0 |

At 68.6 Hz the model reaches X4's clamp at **5 °/s — the lowest rate swept** —
and at 28 Hz it never does, at any rate up to 220. **The model needs no
excitation at all.**

The control settles it: with the head **frozen**, 68.6 Hz still slams (15.0%,
max 65.00) while 28 Hz stays at 8.16°. This is not a marginally unstable loop
waiting for a trigger; it is an unconditional oscillator above some tick rate,
and then excitation can never be the reason a session stayed calm.

A second control separates two things I had been treating as one:

```
68.6 Hz, frozen head:  jitter 2-12  slam 15.0%  max 65.00
                       FIXED    7   slam  0.0%  max 65.00
```

**The mean delay decides whether it fails; the jitter decides how violently.** A
fixed delay of the same mean still walks to the clamp, but smoothly — no slams.
Section 5's threshold on the mean was the whole instability story; section 6's
jitter is what turns a slow walk into 20°+ steps.

#### s1 and s2 differ in nothing measurable

Restricted to servo-active windows:

| take | windows | tick Hz | camera moved | ticks per camera move | report |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 287a | 46 | 28.0 | 27.4 Hz | 1.02 | calm |
| 285b-s1 | 41 | 68.6 | 54.5 Hz | 1.26 | calm |
| 285b-s2 | 73 | 70.7 | 52.0 Hz | 1.36 | **WILD** |
| 287b | 44 | 69.7 | 50.1 Hz | 1.39 | **WILD** |

s1 and s2 are the same configuration at the same rates. And s1's calmness is not
merely an absent report: the independent slam statistic reads **0.0%** for s1
against 7.1% and 7.5% for s2 and 287b.

**So the jitter model is refuted for s1.** Something damps the real loop that the
model lacks. The quantity it is most sensitive to is the latency band, which has
only ever been measured in `plantid` runs (290a/290b) and never during ordinary
play — closed-loop data cannot give it. If that band is not constant across
sessions, s1 having a shorter one would explain everything, and nothing measured
so far excludes it. That is a hypothesis, not a finding, and it is written here
as one.

The one practical conclusion that survives all of this unchanged: **`X4VR_TICK_HZ`
is the variable that moves the loop between the calm and unstable regimes, and it
stays off by default.**

### Measuring the latency band during ordinary play — NOT ACHIEVED

`plantid` needs the servo out of the loop for four minutes, so it cannot run
while anyone is playing, and the session that refutes the model — 285b-s1, calm
at 68.6 Hz where s2 went wild at 70.7 with every other measured variable
identical — differs, if it differs at all, in exactly this band.

The route is an **exogenous dither**: a few mouse counts the servo does not know
it is sending, drawn from an LFSR so it is uncorrelated with the head, the camera
and the command. That is what makes closed-loop identification valid, and it is
the only thing that does.

**The signal is demonstrably there.** With a planted delay D, the two correlation
sequences satisfy `b[L] = a[L−D]` to four decimals — for a fixed 2-tick delay,
`b[2..] = a[0..]` reading −0.11522 against −0.11527, 0.05787 against 0.05793,
−0.01586 against −0.01593. The plant is in the data.

**Turning that into a band is not solved.** Four estimators, four failures, each
diagnosed rather than patched:

| estimator | failure |
|---|---|
| `corr(dither, camera)` | recovers **P/(1+PC)**, not P — the servo corrects the dither and its reaction is inside the answer. Planted 5.00 came back 11.35; a band of width **zero** reported a spread of 4.10. |
| deconvolution, instrument = injected **delta** | a differenced white sequence is MA(1), not white, so `a` is non-causal and forward substitution from L=0 is invalid. |
| deconvolution, instrument = white **offset** | correct in principle — but the injection is itself a first difference, so `a` inherits that shape and deconvolving a difference is an **integration**. The tail drifts: −0.04, −0.05, −0.07, −0.08 over successive lags. |
| match filter, b against a | fixed delays recover with a constant +1.2 bias and a correct **zero** width; jittered bands collapse — the only quantity wanted. |

Holding each dither level past the lag range, to separate `a`'s two lobes, made
it worse.

`tests/dither_id.cpp` keeps the harness and the diagnosis. It carries **one**
assertion — that with the dither off the recovery refuses rather than building a
band out of the loop itself — and prints the rest as diagnosis. Asserting on a
number I cannot recover would be a guard that cannot fail, and the file says in
its banner that it is not a measurement.

**No take on this.** The rule this project runs on is that the acceptance check is
shown to discriminate *before* the run is spent, and here it demonstrably does
not. The next attempt starts from the table above rather than from scratch; the
most likely fix is an injection whose position offset is white in its own right,
so that `a` carries no difference structure at all — every failure above traces
back to that one choice.

### The bounded PRBS — the in-play estimator WORKS, within a stated range

The previous entry recorded four failed estimators and traced every one to a
single choice: injecting the *difference* of a white position sequence, to keep
the accumulated offset bounded. The relation being inverted is
`Δcam[i] = Σ P[k]·u[i−k]` — a convolution against the **delta** sequence — so the
instrument has to be a white **delta**, and differencing put that difference into
the input correlation, where deconvolving it becomes an integration.

**The reason a white delta looked impossible was wrong.** Its accumulated offset
does not run free, because the servo is a regulator: it drives the camera back to
the head, so the disturbance is suppressed. Two corrections followed, each
measured rather than argued:

- **The cap has to go.** Reflecting a draw to bound the offset destroys
  whiteness: at ±3 counts inside ±6 the reflection fired on **12.6%** of draws, a
  planted fixed delay came back 2.51 instead of 2.00, and a band of width zero
  reported a spread of 3.33. Without the cap the same case is **exact**. The
  injection counter does random-walk — 141 counts at amplitude 1 — but that
  counter is not the camera; the view costs a few tenths of a degree.
- **Taps below 5% of the peak are noise, and summing them was a systematic bias.**
  Counting every positive tap gave a thin tail at large lags, each contributing
  its own large L to the first moment and its large (L−mean)² to the second.
  Every planted band came back **+1.5 ticks in the mean and +2.3 in the spread —
  all in the same direction**, which is what marks a bias rather than a wobble.

Recovered through the running servo, head moving, kp 0.25:

| planted | true mean | recovered | true sd | recovered | sum P |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2–2 | 2.00 | **2.00** | 0.00 | **0.00** | 1.00 |
| 3–3 | 3.00 | **3.00** | 0.00 | **0.00** | 1.00 |
| 1–5 | 3.00 | 3.47 | 1.41 | 1.09 | 1.00 |
| 2–6 | 4.00 | 4.59 | 1.41 | 1.38 | 1.02 |
| 1–7 | 4.00 | 5.10 | 2.00 | 1.86 | 1.02 |

Worst error: **1.10 ticks in the mean, 0.32 in the spread**. With the dither off
it refuses. **2 counts — 0.230° — is enough**, chosen from the table rather than
guessed into a headset.

#### The range, and it is a limit rather than a caveat

The deconvolution needs the camera inside its clamp. Past a mean delay of ~6
ticks this servo slams between X4's stops (`servo_rate.cpp`), and a clamp is the
one nonlinearity no deconvolution sees through. A planted 2–8 band reads **7.20**
where 5.00 is true — and its recovered **mass goes to 1.09** where every in-range
case sits at 1.00–1.02. **That mass is the instrument's own statement that it is
out of range**, and it is asserted at 0.05.

What that means for #75, stated before any run: the band measured open-loop in
takes 290a/290b is ~40–165 ms. At the drain rate near 28 Hz that is **1.1–4.6
ticks and in range**; at 70 Hz it is 2.7–11.3 ticks and is **not**. So this can
measure a calm drain-rate session during ordinary play. It cannot yet read one at
90 Hz — which is precisely where the loop is already unstable, for reasons that
have nothing to do with the instrument.

The injector side is not built. `X4VR_DITHER` does not exist yet, and no take is
proposed: what exists is the recovery, proven against planted bands, with its
range measured and its own validity gate.

### The dither is wired: `X4VR_DITHER`, and the run it enables

`X4VR_DITHER=N` adds N mouse counts per tick, sign from a 16-bit LFSR, **after**
`head_look_step` has run — so the servo's estimate never contains it and it is a
disturbance rather than a command. Gated on `steering`, and that gate is
load-bearing: a delta sent while not steering never reaches X4, so recording it
as plant input would put a term in the correlation the plant never received.

Each tick logs `dither: v=±N dx=±M cam=…`, with `cam` read at the TOP of the
tick, before anything is sent — the state the logged command acted on. The scorer
differences consecutive lines for the motion, so no tick may be skipped.

**The scorer's recovery is a SECOND implementation**, in Python, of arithmetic
that already exists in C++ — and it is the one that reads the take.
`tests/run-dither-scorer.sh` drives it against bands planted by
`tests/dither_id.cpp --emit`:

| planted | recovered | mass |
|---|---|---|
| fixed 2 ticks | **2.00 ± 0.00** | 1.00 |
| fixed 3 ticks | **3.00 ± 0.00** | 1.00 |
| 2–6 (4.00 ± 1.41) | 4.82 ± 1.99 | 1.03 |
| 1–7 (4.00 ± 2.00) | 5.06 ± 2.02 | 1.05 |

Fixed delays come back with **zero width** — a recovery that invented a spread
could not tell a jittering plant from a steady one, which is the entire question.

The scorer refuses rather than reporting when the run is out of range: mass away
from 1.0 means the deconvolution drifted, most likely because the camera reached
X4's clamp, and a mean past 6 ticks is the regime where this servo slams between
the stops whatever the mass says.

**Take 291 is the drain-rate run.** At ~28 Hz the 40–165 ms measured open-loop is
1.1–4.6 ticks and in range; at 70 Hz it is 2.7–11.3 and is not. So this measures
the band during ordinary play at the drain rate. It does **not** settle 285b-s1
against s2 — those ran at ~70 Hz, where the instrument cannot follow — and that
limitation is stated here before the run rather than discovered in its results.

## P291 — committed before take 291 exists

Take 291 is the first attempt to measure X4's input-to-camera latency **with the
servo running**. `X4VR_DITHER=2`, drain rate, ordinary play. The log is
`/tmp/x4vr-take291.log`; the acceptance check is
`python3 tools/score_run.py /tmp/x4vr-take291.log`, and the `dither` block is the
whole of it.

**The reference to compare against:** takes 290a/290b measured **40–165 ms**
open-loop with `plantid`, ~90–100 ms of jitter, no dependence on command size.

**P291.1 — the run will read IN RANGE.** At the drain rate near 28 Hz (35 ms
ticks) the open-loop band is 1.1–4.6 ticks. The scorer's range is a mean under 6
ticks with recovered mass within 0.05 of 1.0, so this should sit comfortably
inside it. If it reads OUT OF RANGE the likely cause is the camera reaching X4's
clamp during play, and the band must not be read — that is the instrument
working.

**P291.2 — the mean will land between 40 and 165 ms and the spread will be
large.** If in-play agrees with open-loop, #75's plant model is confirmed on a
second, independent instrument and the ~90–100 ms of jitter is a property of X4
rather than of `plantid`. **A small spread (under ~20 ms) would be the
interesting result**: it would mean the jitter is something `plantid`'s own
sequence provokes, and the open-loop band would have to be re-examined.

**P291.3 — this does NOT settle 285b-s1 against s2.** Those ran at ~70 Hz, where
the same physical band is 2.7–11.3 ticks and the instrument cannot follow. Anyone
reading take 291 as an explanation for why s1 stayed calm is reading it wrong.

### What is already dead, so it is not re-proposed

Servo arithmetic; in-flight commands; the stale off-thread read; the event
channel; the dead camera; the rate mismatch; a gain mismatch; momentum; transport
delay at the measured depth; and excitation as the reason s1 stayed calm. The
plant is a **faithful integrator** — 99.6% of every command at every size from 2
to 104 counts, and it stops when told.

What stands: X4's latency **jitters**, the mean delay in *ticks* is what decides
stability, and `X4VR_TICK_HZ` is the variable that moves the loop between the calm
and unstable regimes. It is off by default and stays off.

### Where the pieces are

| | |
|---|---|
| the knob | `X4VR_DITHER=N` counts/tick, injector, after `head_look_step`, gated on `steering` |
| the log line | `dither: v=±N dx=±M cam=…`, `cam` read at the TOP of the tick |
| the recovery (C++) | `tests/dither_id.cpp` — planted bands, range, amplitude table |
| the recovery (Python) | `tools/score_run.py`, the `dither` block — **this is what reads the take** |
| the check that the Python copy works | `tests/run-dither-scorer.sh` — 4 planted bands through the real scorer |
| the open-loop instrument | `common/x4vr_plantid.hpp`, `tests/run-plantid-scorer.sh` |
| the stability model | `tests/servo_rate.cpp` — clamp reached at a mean delay of 6 ticks |

## Take 291 — the verdict, and the instrument was the defect

**In-play latency: 50–90 ms, with the servo running.** Mass 0.93, mean 3.03 ticks
at 43.5 Hz. That sits inside the 40–165 ms `plantid` measured open-loop, so the
two instruments agree. At 43.5 Hz it is 3.0 ticks, and `servo_rate.cpp` puts the
clamp at 6 — the loop was in its calm regime, which is what Patola reported.

### P291.1 REFUTED, and the reason it gave was wrong

The run read `OUT OF RANGE. Recovered mass 1.46 … most likely the camera reached
X4's clamp during the run.` **It did not reach the clamp.** From the same log:
zero samples were commanded outward at |cam| > 55 without moving, and the camera
peaked at 62.91 against a 65 stop. The scorer named a cause it had never
measured, and acting on it would have bought a take with a lower yaw limit to fix
a clamp that was not there. Same shape as [[report-without-its-guard]]: a report
that names a risk without naming the check generates work against a fiction.

Four candidates were eliminated from take 291's own data before anything was
rebuilt — no new run:

| candidate | measurement | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| gaps where steering stopped | max gap 105 ms, one of them | dead |
| the camera hit X4's clamp | 0 stuck samples, peak 62.91 of 65 | dead |
| servo saturation | 0.27% of ticks at ±104 | dead |
| uncommanded camera motion | 0 steps exceed 10 ticks of command budget | dead |

That last row is worth keeping. The largest single step was **22.1° in one tick
against a 1.84° command**, which looks exactly like the uncommanded motion #75
has been hunting — and it is not. Summed over the preceding ten ticks, every one
of those steps is covered by commands already in flight. X4 was paying out its
backlog. 30.2% of moving samples step *against* the current tick's command, which
is what a latency band does, not a defect.

### What actually produced 1.46: 28 taps
