Replaying take 291's **own timestamps and own command sequence** with a healthy
40–165 ms band planted in place of X4 read **mass 1.43**. The take read 1.46. The
forward substitution is sequential, so `P[0..12]` are bit-identical at ML=28 and
ML=12 — the tap count only decides how many enter the sum, and past the plant's
support those taps are noise that the 5%-of-peak floor cannot remove *because the
floor is relative to a peak the noise can itself set*. Re-read at ML=8, 10 and 12
the take gives the identical 3.03 ± 1.43 ticks with 0% of its mass in the tail.

ML=28 was chosen against `dither_id.cpp`'s synthetic sessions: a 20° 0.3 Hz sine
at a metronome-uniform 70 Hz. Take 291 was ordinary play. **The player's own
steering carried 51× the instrument's variance and the tick wandered from 9 to
51 ms**, and nothing in the control set had ever run there. Third time this
project has shipped an instrument validated only in its easiest configuration.

### The old gate was calibrated on the wrong regime too

`abs(mass - 1.0) > 0.05` was read off quiet synthetic runs where the mass sits at
1.00–1.02. Planting known bands on take 291's real data, at its real amplitude:

| truth ms | 25 | 50 | 70 | 90 | 110 | 140 | 180 | 220 | 300 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| read ms | 41 | 64 | 63 | 88 | 109 | 124 | 148 | 121 | 138 |
| mass | 1.14 | 1.07 | 0.87 | 0.81 | 0.76 | 0.53 | 0.35 | 0.14 | 0.23 |

Every healthy row fails the old gate. Mass falls monotonically with the mean and
separates reachable (0.53–1.14) from past-the-window (0.14–0.41) with no overlap,
so it is now a two-sided gate: below 0.45 the answer is out of reach, above 1.35
the deconvolution diverged. **The upper bound was missing from the first draft**,
and a mass of 3.92 sailed through a lone floor into a branch that announced "the
mass is fine" about a number it had never looked at.

### P291.2 half-confirmed — and the width is NOT measurable here

The mean is confirmed inside 40–165 ms. **The spread is not measured, and the tap
spread is not it.** P291.2 said a spread under ~20 ms would be the interesting
result; take 291 prints 33 ms, and that number cannot be read that way:

* planting **the same mean with widths from 0 to 35 ms sd** moved the recovered
  spread less than changing the random seed did (0.66–1.00 at one width);
* planting **the same width with means from 60 to 120 ms** moved it cleanly
  (0.90 → 0.52).

It is a second reading of the mean wearing a spread's units. I had already
written "0.93 sits in the fixed regime, not the jittered" before running the
fixed-width control — which is the whole of [[vary-them-independently]], caught
one step before it was published.

So the open-loop 40–165 ms band stands unchallenged, because take 291 cannot
challenge it. Resolving the width needs more amplitude: at 2 counts the sweep put
the useful floor near 8 counts, which is **0.92°/tick in a headset**.

### P291.3 holds, as written

Take 291 ran at 43.5 Hz. s1 and s2 ran at ~70 Hz, where the same physical band is
2.7–11.3 ticks and straddles the clamp threshold. Unchanged, and the run does
nothing to it.

### What changed in the tree

`tools/score_run.py`: ML 28 → 12; the two-sided calibrated gate; the spread
demoted to diagnostics with the reason printed beside it.
`tests/dither_id.cpp`: a `play` regime — wandering tick plus steering that reaches
X4's 65° stop — and two fixtures, `slam-fixed` and `slam-band`, that the scorer
must **refuse**. An instrument that cannot decline is not an instrument, and the
old one answered take 291's clamped-loop twin with a confident 222.1 ms.

## Take 291, second reading — the delay is not a pure transport delay

Take 291 can be asked one more question for free: **its tick wandered 9→51 ms
inside the run**, so a delay fixed in wall time and a delay fixed in our own ticks
make different predictions about the same 10853 samples.

Recovering the impulse response in tick-lag, with both plants built as controls so
the answer cannot come from the estimator:

| plant | concentration in the peak tick |
|---|---|
| fixed in TIME, 70 ms | 0.36 |
| fixed in TIME, 120 ms | 0.36 |
| fixed in TICKS, 3 | 1.00 |
| fixed in TICKS, 5 | 1.00 |
| **take 291** | **0.61** |

**X4's response is neither.** It sits between a pure time delay and a pure
tick-locked one, which means the servo model's assumption of a transport delay —
one number, in one unit — is wrong in a way no amount of tuning fixes.

Fitting a mixed plant (n ticks of our cadence, then τ ms of X4's own response)
against the two tick-domain observables:

* **τ = 0 is excluded**: best misfit 14.93 against 0.27 for the mixed fit. X4
  contributes a real component in *time*, and every acceptable fit puts it at
  **20–30 ms** — about two of X4's own ~99 fps frames.
* **n is 1–4 and not pinned**, and n = 0 scores 4.14, which this data cannot
  reject. How much of the delay is ours is **open**.

### A discriminator that only worked at the bin width I chose

The first version of this measured concentration on a **millisecond grid** as
well, and the two domains together appeared to pin the split at 3 ticks + 20 ms
with a misfit of 2.0 against 83 for the worst of the grid. Sweeping the bin width
afterwards:

| bin ms | TIME 70 | TIME 120 | TICKS 3 | TICKS 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 12 | 0.31 | 0.40 | 0.29 | 0.44 |
| 17 | 0.44 | 0.47 | 0.35 | 0.44 |
| **23** | **0.49** | **0.67** | **0.42** | **0.33** |
| 30 | 0.68 | 0.59 | 0.60 | 0.51 |

The families separate at **23 ms and nowhere else** — and 23 ms is take 291's
median tick, the one width at which the millisecond grid *is* the tick grid. The
separation was the alignment, not the plant. Half the fit's observables were
noise, and the conclusion they bought — *"most of the latency is ours"* — is
withdrawn. The tick-domain column has no bin-width parameter and is what the table
above rests on.

I had also written that 290a and 290b "both read 2 of our own cadence steps, so
the wall-clock difference was never X4" and offered it as independent
corroboration. It corroborated the part that did not survive. It is left here
because it was said.

### What separates n from τ, and take 291 cannot do it

Varying the tick rate: at 43.5 Hz our n ticks are n×23 ms, at 90 Hz they are
n×11 ms, while τ does not move. The in-play latency at a second tick rate pins n
directly. Take 291's own internal tick variation is not a controlled variable and
the domain test above is exactly what fails on it.

**P292.1** — if n ≈ 3, take 292 at 90 Hz reads roughly 20 + 3×11 = **53 ms**. If
n ≈ 0 it reads **20–30 ms**, near 291's 70 ms only if n is large. A reading at or
above 70 ms would refute the mixed model altogether.

**P292.2** — the loop may go unstable at 90 Hz and the scorer refuse with
ILL-CONDITIONED. That is a real outcome, not a failure: 285b-s2 went wild at
70 Hz, and a run that slams at 90 is the same phenomenon with an instrument
attached. Committed before the run.

## Take 292 — the scorer refused, and the run answered anyway

Patola: *"most of the time of this run I had the frustum rapidly spinning and
sometimes I couldn't even see where I was heading. There were some brief moments
of stability."* **P292.2, as written.** The loop went wild at 90 Hz.

`dither` read `OUT OF REACH, mass 0.11` — the refusal path added after take 291,
firing correctly on its first real run. At ML=12 and an 11 ms tick that window is
132 ms, so the only thing the block can say is that the delay **exceeded 132 ms**,
against 70 ms at 43.5 Hz. **P292.1 is unanswerable**: the model predicted 53 ms if
n≈3 and 20–30 ms if n≈0, and an unstable loop has no transport delay to report.
The n-versus-τ split stays open.

### What the run did answer

| | tick | camera update | steps per update | queue time |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| take 291, calm | 38.5 Hz | 34.5 Hz | **1.12** | **0.01 ms** |
| take 292, wild | 75.8 Hz | 45.5 Hz | **1.67** | **16.43 ms** |

X4's camera rate is **not** invariant — it rose 34.5 → 45.5 Hz — but it rose
**sub-linearly**: doubling our tick bought 1.3× the camera. (The `inputrate` line
reports 28.0 and 28.5 Hz for the same quantity, over its own restricted windows.
Two measurements of one number disagree; the table above is the direct one, over
all 10853 and 22602 samples.)

### A mechanism proposed and refuted in the same hour

`head_look_observe()` overwrites the estimate with the readback unconditionally —
confirmed at the call site, there is no freshness check on the camera. So on the
40% of ticks where the readback has not changed, the servo re-derives the same
error and **re-sends a correction already in flight**. Section 1 of
`servo_rate.cpp` already models that as a loop-gain multiplier. It looked
conclusive: take 291 at 1.12 × 3.0 ticks = 0.78, take 292 at 1.67 × 5.3 = 2.2,
either side of the 1 where a proportional loop lets go.

**Section 8 sweeps the pair and the boundary does not move: dead time 6 at period
1, 6 at period 2, 6 at period 3.** Period and dead time do not multiply. Section 1
needed period 11 to slam *at zero dead time*, and that gain multiplication does
not survive contact with a plant that has any. The mechanism is refuted, by the
assertion written to be able to refute it.

> **This refutation was wrong, and the fault was the statistic.** `max_excursion`
> is dominated by the 20 deg the head is asking for and only moves once the loop
> reaches a stop, so it cannot see a loop that is oscillating and has not got
> there yet — the *same* blindness that made the log's slam counter call take
> 285b-s1 calm. Re-run on p99 of the per-update move over its smooth-tracking
> baseline, the boundary *does* move. See *"Making the model show the period
> mechanism"* below. Left as written: I refuted a correct hypothesis with a blind
> instrument and it took the log analysis to notice.

Worth naming why it was missed twice: section 1 swept period at dead time 0 and
section 5 swept dead time at period 1, so each cleared the other's factor while
holding it at the value where it cannot bite. Two sweeps, both honest, and the
pair never tried.

### What is left needs no new mechanism

The term the model lacked is measured, and was measured for something else.
`evflow` puts our motion events' time in X4's queue at **0.01 ms in take 291 and
16.8 ms in take 292** — at 72 Hz we push faster than X4's drain takes them.

Restricted to windows that **actually pushed motion**, because the summary line
averages idle windows in and happily prints a queue time next to
`motion pushed 0.0 Hz`, with a `max` that is a running maximum and never resets.
The restriction makes the gap larger, not smaller — 0.01 ms over 140 motion
windows in 291 against 16.79 mean / 19.89 median over 149 in 292 — and it was
checked before the account below was built on it.
Against section 5's existing 6-tick threshold:

    take 291   (70.00 + 0.01) ms / 26.0 ms tick = 2.7 ticks   calm side
    take 292   (70.00 + 16.43) ms / 13.2 ms tick = 6.5 ticks  wild side

**This is an account, not a test.** It was assembled after seeing which take went
wild and every number in it was taken for another purpose. It earns a prediction,
not a conclusion — and the prediction is that the queue time, not the tick rate,
is the controlled variable.

### Uncommanded motion past X4's own stop

`clamp` reports **max |X4| yaw 76.79°** against a maximum command of 65.00, and
pitch 38.39° against stock `maxpitch="35"`. `<internal>` declares
`trackmaxyaw="85"`, so 76.79 may simply be a mode with a wider stop rather than
anything uncommanded — but take 291 reached only 58.16 with a 53.86 command, and
nothing yet says which. Recorded, not explained.

## The queue model — refuted, then replaced by measurement

**The model I set out to build is wrong, and it was refuted before a line of it
was written.** "Our event waits for X4's next drain at rate D" predicts:

| | drain rate | predicted 1/(2D) | measured |
|---|---|---|---|
| take 291 | 38.9 Hz | 12.85 ms | **0.01 ms** |
| take 292 | 79.9 Hz | 6.26 ms | **19.89 ms** |

Wrong by 1000x one way and 3x the other, and across the 140 and 149 motion
windows the per-window correlation between prediction and measurement is
**-0.05 and +0.04**. There is no relationship. `ours per drain` never exceeds 1
in either take, so nothing is accumulating and it is not a backlog either.

### What 0.01 ms actually is, from the call site

`headlook_tick()` is called from **inside** the injector's `SDL_PeepEvents`
interception:

```c
if (this_is_the_game() && !g_pump_seen.load(...)) {
    ...
    if (!tick_hz())
        headlook_tick();      // runs INSIDE X4's drain
```

Without `X4VR_TICK_HZ` the servo pushes its event while X4 is in its own
`while (SDL_PollEvent(&e))` loop, and that loop consumes it immediately — hence
0.01 ms. With `X4VR_TICK_HZ` the servo runs on our own thread and the event waits
for X4's next drain, which `pumprate` independently measures as **clustered**, so
the wait is far longer than half a drain period: 19.89 ms against the 6.26 a
uniform drain predicts. **This is structural, not a tuning choice** — the tick
driver moves the servo off X4's drain and buys ~20 ms for it.

### Section 9: the measured operating points, with nothing invented

Four measured numbers per take — servo rate, X4's camera publish rate, transport
delay, queue time — driving the real `head_look_step()` in a time base:

| | delay | slam% model | slam% **measured** | Patola |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| take 291 | 2.70 tk | 0.0% | **0.0%** (2 of 10031) | calm |
| take 292 | 6.58 tk | 32.3% | **20.3%** (2358 of 11639) | wild |

It reproduces the split and the slam statistic to within 1.6x, having been given
no free parameter to fit. That is the falsifiable form of the section 8 account.

### It does NOT reproduce the excursion, and a check that could not fail

Take 292's camera reached **79.64 deg** with one update moving **81.57**. The
model's max move is 23.92 at any stop.

I ran the model at `trackmaxyaw="85"` to test whether that explains it, and wrote
a check that the excursion would "land near the measurement". **It passed, and it
could not have done otherwise**: the model pins at 65.00 given 65 and 85.00 given
85 — it saturates at whatever stop it is handed, so the assertion tested my choice
of constant. Hand it 100 and it reads 100. Same shape as
[[a-guard-that-cannot-fail]], caught one run later.

What survives without a model: **79.64 exceeds 65 by 14.6 deg, and a position
limit cannot be exceeded.** So `maxyaw=65` is not the operative stop in take 292,
and `trackmaxyaw=85` is *consistent* — the camera never reached it. Consistent is
not confirmed, and this model cannot get further, because a run pinned at its own
clamp says nothing about where X4's is. The 81.57 deg single update remains
unexplained and the suite now asserts that it is unexplained.

## `X4VR_TICK_HZ` is harmful — the verdict, and why it is kept

**Symptom.** The camera slams between X4's stops, the frustum spins, and the view
becomes unusable. Every session that has ever done this had `X4VR_TICK_HZ` set.

**Do not set it.** It is kept in the tree only so takes 285b, 287b and 292 can be
reproduced. It is off by default and stays off, and this is stronger than "off by
default" — it is a knob that is known to break the thing it was added to improve.

### What it does, and why that is the defect

It does exactly what it claims: it moves the servo tick off X4's event drain onto
a thread of our own at the requested rate. **That move is the whole problem.**

`headlook_tick()` is normally called from *inside* the injector's
`SDL_PeepEvents` interception, so the mouse event it pushes is consumed by the
very `while (SDL_PollEvent(&e))` loop it was pushed into. Take it off that drain
and the event has to wait for X4's next one — and `pumprate` measures those as
clustered, so the wait is much longer than a drain period would suggest.

Measured over the windows that actually pushed motion:

| | servo runs on | queue residency |
|---|---|---|
| take 291, default | X4's drain | **0.01 ms** mean, 0.01 median |
| take 292, `=90` | our own thread | **16.79 ms** mean, 19.89 median |

That is ~17 ms of pure added latency, and it lands on a loop whose stability
depends on total delay counted in **ticks** — so raising the rate shortens the
tick and charges the same milliseconds twice over. `tests/servo_rate.cpp`
section 9 drives the real `head_look_step()` from those measured rates, with no
fitted parameter, and reproduces both outcomes: 0.0% slam at the default against
a measured 0.0%, and 32.3% at 90 Hz against a measured 20.3%.

### The record

| session | rate | outcome |
|---|---|---|
| 285b-s2 | 70.7 Hz | **WILD** (7.1%) |
| 287b | 69.7 Hz | **WILD** (7.5%) |
| 292 | 75.8 Hz | **WILD** (20.3%) |
| 285b-s1 | 68.6 Hz | calm (0.0%) — **unexplained** |
| every take without the knob | — | calm |

**285b-s1 is still open** and nothing measured separates it from s2 — same
binary, same knobs, same tick driver. It is not a reason to use the knob; it is
the remaining question in #75.

### The win it was added for is real and unusable

Session 1 measured X4's camera rate going 28.2 → 54.5 Hz, and that measurement
still stands. Take 292 measured the same effect more carefully — 34.5 → 45.5 Hz,
**sub-linear**: doubling our tick bought 1.3x the camera. Either way the rate does
rise. It is bought with a camera that slams between X4's stops, which is a far
worse VR defect than the jitter it was meant to reduce, and
[[no-cosmetic-defects-in-vr]] applies in both directions — the cure must not be
worse than the complaint.

### If the camera rate is wanted again

Not with this knob. The thing to change is what the servo does *on* X4's drain,
not where it runs — the drain is the only place a pushed event is consumed for
free. Any future attempt has to keep the queue residency at the 0.01 ms the
default achieves, and `evflow`'s queue time restricted to motion windows is the
number that says whether it did.

## #75 ANSWERED — s1 and s2 do not differ, and the variable is ticks per camera observation

> **SUPERSEDED AGAIN — this whole section's conclusion is now withdrawn, not
> just its magnitudes.** The note below was written after one correction; two
> more followed (pitch-only publishes, and the pitch stop), and together they
> remove the effect entirely — in 287b the corrected ratio is *lower* when wild.
> See *"Take 292's 28 Hz — it was never 28 Hz"* at the end of the file. The
> paragraph below is kept as the intermediate position it was.
>
> **Magnitudes in this section are WITHDRAWN; the shape is not.** Every `tk/obs`
> figure below is computed from "camera moved on N% of READS", and a camera
> pinned on its stop reports no change — so the denominator collapses exactly
> when the camera slams. Corrected, 285b-s2's wild/calm ratio is 1.22x rather
> than 2.25x and 287b's is 1.09x rather than 2.09x; the "3.01 against 1.30"
> headline is an artefact and the threshold sits near 1.5–1.7, not 2.2. The
> pooled 2x2 stays monotone once redone. See *"Modelling the camera-rate halving
> — there was nothing to model"* at the end of this file. Left as written: the
> analysis was right about the shape and wrong about the size, and it cited
> [[a-ratio-against-its-own-denominator]] in the same session it walked into it.

**The question was malformed.** "What makes 285b-s1 different from s2" presumes
wildness is a property of a session. It is not. s2 contains a contiguous ~40 s
episode and the remaining 55 windows are indistinguishable from all 41 of s1:

| | windows | tick | camera | **tk/obs** | X4 fps | p99 \|dyaw\| |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 285b-s1, all | 41 | 68.5 | 52.9 | **1.29** | 89.6 | 3.86 |
| 285b-s2, calm | 55 | 69.7 | 53.6 | **1.30** | 89.4 | 4.76 |
| 285b-s2, WILD | 18 | 82.6 | 27.4 | **3.01** | 89.7 | 44.69 |
| 287b, calm | 34 | 69.0 | 51.1 | **1.35** | 89.3 | 4.74 |
| 287b, WILD | 10 | 80.3 | 27.1 | **2.96** | 89.8 | 56.97 |

s1 is s2's calm phase. Nothing about the session was ever going to explain it.

**X4's frame rate is 89–90 in every group**, wild and calm alike, so the scene and
the load are not it either — that hypothesis is refuted in the same table.

### Two instruments had to be replaced first

*The severity statistic was blind.* The log's ">20 deg per camera update" counter
reads 0.0% on a camera **pinned to its stop**, because a pinned camera does not
move — `servo_rate.cpp` section 5 already recorded it doing exactly that on a run
with 113 reversals. That counter is what labelled s1 "calm". Replaced with p99 of
|dyaw| over `camstamp`'s per-frame `atdraw` stream: 3.86 for s1, 44.69 for s2's
episode, an order of magnitude with no threshold to argue about.

*The window set was chosen by the log's extent.* Averaged over its whole span s1
looks like 21.5 fps and s2 like 88.6 — an artefact of s1's span holding 8 minutes
of menus. Windows now come from `inputrate`'s own record: steering above 50% of
ticks and deltas going out above 5 Hz.

*And a field that sounds right and is not:* `inputrate`'s `clamped %` counts **our
servo's** command hitting its own ceiling, not X4's camera reaching its stop. Read
as the latter it says s1 clamped *more* than s2 (24% of windows above 20% against
22%) and anti-correlates with every wild report. The camera's own position, from
`atdraw`, says 0.1% against 7.7%.

### A threshold that passed on the training set and failed held out

Pooling 285b and 287 alone, the **tick rate** looked decisive: 0% wild below
40 Hz, 6–7% from 60–75, and **100% (18 of 18) above 80 Hz**. Applied to takes 291
and 292, which set none of it, the relation **inverts** — take 292 is 85% wild at
60–75 Hz and only 35% wild at 80–95.

Take 292 settles it internally, with no cross-session comparison at all:

    292 WILD windows   tick 74.8 Hz   camera 28.3 Hz   tk/obs 2.64
    292 calm windows   tick 80.0 Hz   camera 64.4 Hz   tk/obs 1.24

**Its calm windows run at a higher tick rate than its wild ones.** Tick rate only
looked causal because within any one session it is collinear with tk/obs.

### The 2x2, over 491 windows from six sessions

`tools/wildness.py` reproduces this from the logs.

| tk/obs | tick 20–60 | 60–70 | 70–78 | 78–95 | **row** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.9–1.3 | 3% (149) | 0% (66) | 0% (35) | 4% (28) | **2%** (278) |
| 1.3–1.7 | 0% (7) | 12% (43) | 12% (34) | 43% (7) | **13%** (91) |
| 1.7–2.2 | — | 100% (1) | 20% (5) | 100% (1) | **43%** (7) |
| 2.2–4.5 | — | 92% (13) | 97% (67) | 100% (35) | **97%** (115) |
| **column** | 3% | 15% | 50% | 56% | |

Down a column the tick rate is held and tk/obs varies: 0 → 12 → 100 → 92, and
0 → 12 → 20 → 97, and 4 → 43 → 100 → 100. Across a row tk/obs is held and the tick
rate varies: 3, 0, 0, 4 — flat; and 92, 97, 100 — flat. **The controlling variable
is how many commands the servo issues per camera reading.** Below 1.3 it is 2%
wild; above 2.2, 97%.

### This contradicts `servo_rate.cpp` section 8, and the data wins

Section 8 swept `period` against dead time and found the clamp boundary unmoved —
6 at period 1, 2 and 3 — and I wrote there that the re-issued-command mechanism
was refuted. **491 windows across six sessions say `period` is the variable.** The
refutation was of the model, not of the world: the model reproduces calm-versus-
wild from the delay term alone and therefore never needed period, which is not the
same as period having no effect. Section 8's assertion stands as written and is
now known to be a statement about the model's blind spot. Finding the mechanism by
which period destabilises, and making the model show it, is the open work.

The practical rule needs no model: **keep ticks per camera observation near 1.**
That is what the default path does (1.05–1.35 in every calm group) and what
`X4VR_TICK_HZ` breaks.

## Making the model show the period mechanism

`servo_rate.cpp` section 8 said `period` does not interact with dead time, and
491 windows of game data said `period` is *the* variable. The disagreement was
the model's **statistic**, not its physics.

### The same blindness, one file over

Section 8 scored itself with `max_excursion` and the ">20 deg per update" slam
counter. Both are blind in exactly the way the log's slam counter was blind:
max excursion is dominated by the 20 deg the head is asking for and moves only
once the loop reaches a stop, and the slam counter cannot fire below 20 deg per
update. A loop oscillating harder and harder but not yet at the clamp reads
identical to a calm one.

That is the defect I had just found in the *log*, fixed in `tools/wildness.py`,
and left standing in the model. [[x4vr-fixed-here-broken-next-door]] — the class
was known, and I still shipped it one file over the same day.

### The statistic, and why it is a ratio

p99 of the per-update move, **divided by what smooth tracking would give**:
a camera sampled every `period` ticks shows `period` times as much motion per
update from tracking alone, so the raw p99 would credit `period` with an
instability that is only a coarser sample. The head asks for at most
`amp·2π·hz` = 62.8 deg/s, so the baseline is `62.8·period/90` deg per update. The
ratio reads 1.0 for a loop that is merely tracking, at any period.

### The mechanism is there

| dead time | period 1 | period 2 | period 3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0–4 | 0.99 | 1.07 | 1.04–1.15 |
| **5** | **1.15** | **1.56** | **2.25** |
| 6+ | 17.13 | 17.13 | 17.13 |

At dead time 5, just under the clamp, the ratio grows monotonically with period,
and period 3 passes "moving twice as far as it was asked" **one whole tick of
dead time earlier** than period 1. `max_excursion` could not see any of that,
because all three reach the stop at 6.

### It is the right mechanism at the wrong weight, and that is the open work

In the game, holding the tick rate and varying only ticks-per-observation moves
the wild share from **2% to 97%**, while holding ticks-per-observation and varying
the tick rate leaves it flat (3/0/0/4, and 92/97/100). So `period` dominates and
the delay in ticks is nearly irrelevant.

In the model it is the reverse: dead time decides, and tripling the period buys
one tick. Section 8 now asserts **both** — that the effect exists
(`cross[3] < cross[1]`) and that it is still only ~1 tick (`cross[1] - cross[3]
<= 2`) — so the gap is bounded from both sides and cannot be quietly closed by a
model that later overclaims.

**What the model still lacks is a reason for `period` to dominate.** Two things it
does not have: X4's camera readback rate is an *input* here, set by hand, where in
the game it halved (53 → 27 Hz) during the episodes for reasons nothing has
measured; and the plant integrates every command the instant its dead time
expires, with no queue, where `evflow` measures ~17 ms of queue residency whenever
the servo is off X4's drain. Either could carry the missing weight. Neither is
modelled, and guessing which before measuring is what
[[hypothesis-and-fix-in-one-step]] costs.

## Modelling the camera-rate halving — there was nothing to model

Asked to model the halving (53 → 27 Hz during the wild episodes) so the model
could show `period` dominating, the first thing to check was whether it is real.
**In two of the three sessions it is not.**

`tk/obs` = tick ÷ camera rate, and the camera rate comes from `inputrate`'s
"camera moved on N% of READS". **A camera pinned on its stop does not change
value, so it counts as not moving** — the same blindness that made the slam
counter call 285b-s1 calm, now in the *denominator of the predictor*. During the
wild episodes the camera sits on its stop 23–30% of the time, and 71% of samples
show no change against 45% when calm.

Counting a sample as an update when it changed **or** sat on that session's own
saturation value:

| | tk/obs raw, wild ÷ calm | corrected |
|---|---|---|
| 285b-s2 | 3.22 / 1.43 = **2.25x** | 1.72 / 1.41 = **1.22x** |
| 287b | 3.15 / 1.51 = **2.09x** | 1.65 / 1.51 = **1.09x** |
| 292 | 2.66 / 1.26 = 2.11x | **unchanged** — no clamp dwell found |

**Most of the contrast in the two sessions the finding was built on is an
artefact.** [[a-ratio-against-its-own-denominator]] — I correlated a ratio with
something that depresses its denominator, which is the exact failure that memory
records, and I walked into it the day after citing it.

Take 292 is different: its camera never *sat* near its peak, so its 28 Hz is real
and is not explained by pinning. That is unexplained.

### What survives, and what does not

**Survives.** s1 has no wild window and s2's wildness is one contiguous episode;
that is measured from p99 |dyaw| on the camera stream and never involved tk/obs.
The pooled 2x2, redone with the corrected ratio over the same 491 windows, is
still monotone down the rows (3%, 13%, 67%, 93%) with the top row flat-low
(3/3/0/4) and the bottom flat-high (83/92/100) across every tick band.

**Does not survive.** The magnitudes. "3.01 against 1.30" was inflated by
pinning; corrected it is 1.72 against 1.41, and the threshold sits near
**1.5–1.7**, not 2.2. Any statement of the form "the wild episodes run at three
times the ticks per observation" is withdrawn.

### Two defects in `tools/wildness.py`, both caught by disagreeing with itself

*Mixed populations.* The first correction took `raw` from `inputrate` (counted at
the servo tick) and `corr` from `camstamp` (per submitted frame) and printed them
side by side. A correction that can only ADD updates came out **lower** than what
it corrected, which is how it was noticed. Both now come from `camstamp`.

*A stop that was not a stop.* Detecting the clamp as "the most-repeated value"
gave 285b-s1 a stop of **24.52 deg** — somewhere the camera happened to rest in a
session that never clamped at all — and credited it with updates it never had. It
now also has to sit at the edge of the range actually visited, and the correction
is a no-op in the three sessions that never reached a stop.

### And so the modelling question dissolves

There is no halving to put in the model for 285b-s2 or 287b: X4's camera kept
publishing and the stop stopped it moving. The model already treats `period` as
an input, and the corrected inputs are 1.4 against 1.7 rather than 1.3 against
3.0 — a difference `servo_rate.cpp` section 8 already spans (1.15 at period 1
against 1.56 at period 2, at dead time 5). What is left to explain is take 292's
28 Hz, which is real, and why a shift of 1.4 → 1.7 flips a session.

## Take 292's 28 Hz — it was never 28 Hz, and #75's answer is withdrawn

The camera rate is **48.7 Hz** in take 292's wild windows, not 28.1. The 28 was
three stacked defects in my own tooling, each found only because fixing the
previous one exposed it.

A readback that does not change counts as "no update", and three separate things
make a change vanish **exactly when the camera is slamming**:

1. the camera is **pinned on X4's yaw stop** at 65 deg — no change to report;
2. it is **pinned on the pitch stop** at 35 deg — likewise;
3. only **pitch** moved, and every measurement so far read yaw alone.

Counting a publish as an update when either axis moved or either sat on its stop:

| | camera, wild | tk/obs wild | tk/obs calm | |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 285b-s2 | 25.6 → **63.4 Hz** | 3.22 → **1.30** | 1.22 | above its own calm rate |
| 287b | 25.5 → **63.7 Hz** | 3.15 → **1.26** | **1.33** | **inverted** |
| 292 | 28.1 → **48.7 Hz** | 2.66 → **1.54** | 1.22 | |

**In two sessions of three the camera rate is HIGHER during the wild episode than
during that session's own calm windows**, and in 287b the corrected ratio is
*lower* when wild. There is no halving, in any session, and `tk/obs` does not
separate the two states.

### #75 ANSWERED is WITHDRAWN

The claim "the controlling variable is ticks per camera observation" is retracted
in full — not just its magnitudes, as the earlier annotation said. Every version
of that ratio had the wildness in its denominator; each correction shrank the
effect, and the third removed it. A quantity that changes this much under three
successive fixes to how it is *counted* was never measuring X4.

**What survives** is description only: s1 has no wild window, s2's wildness is one
contiguous episode, s1 matches s2's calm phase, and p99 |dyaw| separates the two
states cleanly (3.86 against 44.69). That is measured from the camera stream and
never used tk/obs. **Nothing measured so far explains what starts an episode.**

### Three stop-detection rules, each right on half the sessions

Worth recording because each looked principled:

* *largest repeated value* — gave 285b-s1 a stop of **24.52 deg** in a session
  that never clamped;
* *largest repeated value at ≥0.90 × peak* — fixed s1 and then excluded **take
  292's real stop**, because 292 sits at 65.00 for 1442 samples while its peak is
  79.64, so the rule demanded dwell above 71.68 and found none. That is what made
  292's rate look real and produced the question this section answers;
* *most-repeated value away from zero, holding ≥1% of samples* — separates
  cleanly: 3.77 / 2.82 / 3.86% for the three sessions with episodes against
  0.27 / 0.12 / 0.09% for the three without.

Position does not identify a clamp; **dwell mass does**. And 292's 79.64 deg peak
is still unexplained: the camera reaches it but never sits there, so it is not a
stop — [[a-guard-that-cannot-fail]] applies to the earlier attempt to confirm
`trackmaxyaw=85` from a model that pins at whatever limit it is handed.

## What starts an episode — the player does not

Taking "episode" to mean the **severe** state (p99 |dyaw| >= 40 deg), which is one
population: 14 of 18 wild windows in 285b-s2, 8 of 10 in 287b, 80 of 100 in 292.
The handful of marginal windows (15–25 deg) have **no clamp contact at all** and
are most likely fast head turns, not the same thing. Clamp contact tracks severity
monotonically — 0–0.6% calm, 0–9.8% marginal, 10.8–25.8% mid, 22.9–35.1% severe.

### The head is NEARLY STILL during an episode

`camread` carries the servo's own input, `| head yaw,pitch`, one sample in 30.
I nearly declared this an instrument gap — `geom`'s `yaw=` is
`last_decl_yaw`, X4's camera under `DECLARE_RENDERED_ROT=2`, which is why it
matched `camstamp` to two decimals — and the head was logged all along.
[[read-the-existing-report-first]]

| | \|head\| median | max | past 65 deg |
|---|---|---|---|
| 285b-s2 severe | **9.0** | 50.9 | **0.0%** |
| 285b-s2 calm | 25.1 | 69.8 | 0.4% |
| 287b severe | **3.6** | 21.0 | **0.0%** |
| 287b calm | 17.4 | 54.3 | 0.0% |
| 292 severe | **4.1** | 50.3 | **0.0%** |
| 292 calm | 10.0 | **75.8** | 1.1% |

**The camera slams to ±65 deg while the head sits within 10 deg of centre**, and
the head passes X4's stop *only during calm windows*. The obvious mechanism — the
player turns past the clamp, the error never closes, the servo winds up — is
refuted, and refuted backwards: the head is further out when nothing is wrong.

This is what P288.2 saw from the other side. Patola held his head still
mid-oscillation and it did not stop.

### Nor does head RATE before the onset

Angular rate over the 3 s before each severe onset, against the same session's
calm baseline (deg/s, median):

    285b-s2   40.5 before onset   against  51.3 calm
    287b       7.5 before onset   against  34.3 calm
    292        3.4 before onset   against   6.2 calm

Lower in all three. The two single-episode sessions give only n=8, but 292 gives
n=82 and agrees. Sampling is ~2.6 Hz, so this resolves a sustained turn and not a
flick — stated because it bounds what the null covers.

### What could NOT be measured, and why

**Whether the clamp or the oscillation comes first is unanswerable from these
logs.** Only 1 of 13 severe episodes has 15 s of calm before it, and that one puts
both events 30 s before onset, inside windows classified as calm. The episodes are
not isolated: take 292 is severe in 68% of its windows.

The first attempt at this reported a clean ordering for 9 of 11 episodes in 292.
It was an artefact — the search started 6 s before each onset and both events
landed at −5.87 to −6.00 s, i.e. **on the search boundary**, because both were
already under way before the window opened. [[range-failures-have-two-ends]] The
tell was the numbers clustering at the limit, and it is why the table above says
"cannot order" instead of an answer.

### Where that leaves it

The player is eliminated as the trigger — by angle and by rate. Whatever starts an
episode is internal to the loop or to X4, which is consistent with
`servo_rate.cpp` section 2: the model reaches its stops **with a frozen head**
once the period is high enough. Answering it needs a take whose episodes are
isolated by construction, not more analysis of these six.

## The ordering question, ANSWERED without a run — and P293

Asked to design a run with isolated episodes, the first step was a better onset
detector. The old one keyed on a single >=20 deg jump and fired **6 s early** on
an isolated pair in 285b-s2 that was followed by six seconds of quiet. An onset
is *sustained* growth: the first of >=5 consecutive moving samples above 10 deg.
On that definition four episodes have enough clean calm before them to order:

| episode | calm before | clamp reached | \|cam\| just before onset |
|---|---|---|---|
| 285b-s2/0 | 12.1 s | **+0.66 s after onset** | 61.0 |
| 292/6 | 14.1 s | **never** | 61.2 |
| 292/7 | 10.0 s | **+0.17 s after** | 66.6 |
| 292/10 | 44.2 s | **+0.19 s after** | 33.4 |

**The oscillation always starts first.** 292/6 is the negative control: a severe
episode that never touches the clamp, so contact is not necessary. The clamp is a
consequence.

285b-s2's onset at full sample resolution: the camera is driven smoothly out to
**60.50 deg** by ordinary tracking — steps of 0.2-4 deg, decelerating to 0.23 near
the top — then reverses, and the swings grow 3, 12, 25, 41 deg over about a
second before reaching -65.00. That is a loop losing stability from a small
perturbation, not a jolt.

### The lead that replaces it: the camera is NEAR the stop when it starts

Three of the four were at **61-67 deg** when the oscillation began, just inside
X4's 65. The head is already eliminated — during episodes it sits nearer centre
than when calm, and never passes 65 — so the region just short of the stop is
what is left.

**P293, committed before the run.** `X4VR_HEADLOOK_YAW_LIMIT_AB` alternates the
servo's own yaw limit between the shipped 65 and 40 every 45 s. At 40 the servo
never asks the camera past 40 deg, so it cannot approach X4's stop.

* **Severe share drops to near zero in the NARROW arm** -> the near-stop region is
  the trigger, and capping the servo's reach below X4's clamp is a fix that costs
  only head-look range.
* **Severe share is unchanged** -> the trigger is elsewhere and proximity to the
  stop was a coincidence of three episodes. The run still bounds it.
* **292/10 already argues against**, at 33.4 deg — one of four did not start
  anywhere near the stop, so a partial effect is the outcome to expect.

### Why it alternates inside one run

Episodes are rare (~1 per 2 min of steering) and their rate varies between
sessions for reasons this project has spent days failing to pin. 285b-s1 and s2
were the same binary and the same knobs, and comparing them produced a finding
withdrawn in full. **Two takes would repeat that exact mistake.** The statistic is
the severe share of servo-active windows per arm, not episode count, so ~3 min per
arm is enough.

### What the design had to discard

*An arm/idle A/B, so every episode began from rest.* Refuted before it was
written: **X4's camera does not return to centre when steering stops.** It sits at
65 -> 56 deg after 8-12 s in 285b-s2, and 65 -> 67.4 in 292. Re-arming would have
started hard against the clamp with a large error and provoked an episode by
construction — the contamination the design existed to avoid.

*Provoking episodes with a gain mismatch.* It would study gain-mismatch
instability, not X4's.

*90 Hz.* Take 292 was severe in 68% of its windows, which is why nothing in it
could be ordered. 70 Hz gives 23-25%, which is where episodes are isolated
naturally.

### The instrument, checked against a planted answer both ways

`tools/wildness.py` splits by the run's own `headlook: yawlimit` phase lines —
read from what the run ASKED for, never re-derived. Two synthetic logs, one where
narrowing removes the episodes and one where it changes nothing, are scored
100% -> 0.0% and 100% -> 100%. A 5 s guard band after each switch drops windows
where an episode from the previous arm is still running; episodes last 18-72 s, so
without it a spill-over would look exactly like "narrowing does not help".

The first version of the split rebuilt the window list in a second function and
zipped the two together. `windows()` also drops windows with no camera movement,
so the lists drifted and rows were scored against the wrong arm — reading one list
positionally against another, which is a recurring defect here. The window's start
time now travels inside the row and there is only one list.

## Take 293 — P293 is UNMEASURABLE, and the protocol was mine

The A/B engaged: 13 phases, 45 s each, alternating correctly over 9 minutes,
verified from the log's own `headlook: yawlimit` lines.

**The arms differ.** Severe share 56.2% control against 42.0% NARROW, and within
matched head-angle bands 65% -> 47% (0–30 deg) and 55% -> 24% (30–50 deg). Time
spent past 45 deg halves, 38.1% -> 20.3%.

**But the cap was never enforced, so none of that can be attributed to it.**
Restricted to CALM windows, where the loop is tracking rather than overshooting
and a 40 deg ceiling should be plainly visible:

| arm | \|cam\| p99 | \|cam\| max | % past 45 deg |
|---|---|---|---|
| control (asks ≤65) | 71.6 | 78.8 | 38.1% |
| NARROW (asks ≤40) | **71.6** | **79.3** | 20.3% |

A servo whose target is capped at 40 deg left the camera at **79.3 deg**, the same
as control. The knob did *something* — the time past 45 deg halved — but it did
not do the thing P293 tested, which was to keep the camera away from X4's stop.
**"Is the near-stop region the trigger" is therefore not answered**, and the 56→42
difference has no established mechanism. [[x4vr-knob-null-refutes-the-knob]] in
reverse: an effect exists, and the knob cannot be shown to have caused it.

This also connects to a defect already on the record and still unexplained: X4's
camera reaching **76.79 deg in take 292 against a maximum command of 65.00**. A
camera that routinely overshoots the servo's target makes any ceiling-based
manipulation untestable until it is understood. That is the blocker.

### The run was 83% wild, and that is my fault

Designed for the 23–25% regime that 285b-s2 and 287b sat in at ~70 Hz. It came
back at **83%**, with Patola reporting *"almost the entire time was the frustum
going wild, trembling, rotating, bouncing around"*.

The tick rate was not the cause — 63.4/61.6 Hz here against 69–70 in those takes,
**lower**. What differed is the protocol: I wrote *"look around naturally —
including well out to the sides, since that's where episodes start."* Head yaw
reached **135.8 deg**, against a maximum of 75.8 across every earlier take. I
changed the input distribution while asking whether a change in the servo mattered,
and the run was too continuously unstable for anything to isolate.
[[x4vr-instruments-perturb-interaction]] — the instruction is part of the
instrument.

Patola also could not perceive the range halving. With the view spinning for 83%
of the run that is expected and says nothing either way.

### What the take did establish

*Episodes are most likely when the head is NEAR CENTRE* — 65% severe in the
0–30 deg band against 0% above 70 deg. That is the third independent confirmation,
after 285b-s2, 287b and 292, that the player is not driving this.

**`max|head|` per window is not a clean covariate**, because a wild camera is
exactly what stops a player turning their head. The banded table above is the best
available control and is still partly circular; it is reported as such.

## The overshoot past the commanded ceiling — X4's stop is not 65/35 in every run

X4's own readback, not the declared pose:

| take | camread max \|yaw\| | max \|pitch\| |
|---|---|---|
| 285b-s2 | **65.00** | **35.00** |
| 287b | **65.00** | **35.00** |
| 292 | **76.79** | **38.39** |
| 293 | **78.79** | **48.87** |

Two takes pin to X4's documented `maxyaw="65" maxpitch="35"` to the centidegree.
Two exceed both, and everything seen is inside the `trackmaxyaw="85"
trackmaxpitch="85"` that `<internal>` declares alongside them.

### It is not ours

*Not the declared pose.* `camstamp`'s `atdraw` is `decl_yaw + g_residual.applied_yaw`,
so it is X4's camera **plus** a rotation we add — a real reason to distrust it
here. Measured, the residual is **0.00 at p99 and at max** in both takes. It
explains nothing, and the small camread/atdraw gap (76.79 vs 79.64) is sampling
density, 1103 samples against 37335.

*Not configuration.* `config:` and `inputmap:` are byte-identical across all four
takes — 3822 bytes with 0 overrides, 48160 bytes — and all four ran
`DECLARE_RENDERED_ROT=2 DECLARE_RENDERED_POS=1`.

### It is #68's clamp extension, and the scorer already said so

`score_run.py`'s own clamp block, on take 293:

    clamp  MOVED ✓ — X4 reached 78.79 deg of yaw, past the 65.00 stop every
           stored take pins to. The override reached X4 and the limit is data,
           confirmed live

That verdict exists for #68 and has been there all along. I read the first four
lines of the block and went off to build a theory. [[read-the-existing-report-first]]
— for the second time in this task, the answer was in output I had already
generated. It did not print for take 292 only because that verdict is gated on
the servo having *asked* past 66 deg, and 292's command peaked at 65.00; 293's
reached 66.83, so it fired.

So X4's clamp extension is installed and active, somewhere between take 287b and
take 292.

### Why this made P293 unmeasurable

Take 293 capped the servo at 40 deg to keep the camera **away from X4's stop**,
which the design assumed was 65. The stop was about **79**. The manipulation left
39 deg of room below the limit it was meant to probe, so the NARROW arm never
tested the hypothesis — which is exactly what the calm-window check found, a
camera at 79.3 deg under a servo asking for at most 40.

**Any knob set relative to "the stop" is wrong until the stop is read from the
run.** `tools/wildness.py` already detects it per session by dwell mass and is
unaffected; `score_run.py` now prints a loud `!!` line whenever X4's readback
exceeds the stock 65/35, so the next design cannot quietly inherit the wrong
number.

### One thing for Patola, not for me to change

#68 records the extension's cost as `modified="1"` on the savegame, and keeping
saves at `modified="0"` is a standing constraint of this project. If the extension
is installed for testing that is a deliberate trade; if it arrived by accident it
wants removing. Flagged, not touched.

## Two paths, and the stock clamp was hiding a defect of ours

Patola keeps #68's extension installed deliberately, and the project has to
support **both** paths: with it (`modified="1"`, X4's own supported mechanism) and
without it, for players who will not run a modified game. That is a product
requirement, not a preference, and it means every measurement has to record which
path it ran on.

*(Ventures is not a reason for it — `venture="1"` is dead and must not be weighed
in a trade-off. The requirement stands on the unmodified-install audience alone.)*

### The 65.00 everywhere is OURS, not X4's

`g_headlook.yaw_limit_deg` defaults to 65, so the servo's own target never exceeds
65 in any of these takes. Every "camera sitting at 65.00" is the servo having
converged on its own ceiling. X4's clamp is a *second*, independent limit at the
same number by coincidence of the default.

### The overshoot is the servo exceeding its own target

X4's readback, split by whether the loop was unstable:

| take | severe: max \|yaw\| / past 65.5 | calm: max \|yaw\| / past 65.5 |
|---|---|---|
| 285b-s2 | **65.00 / 0.00%** | **65.00 / 0.00%** |
| 287b | **65.00 / 0.00%** | **65.00 / 0.00%** |
| 292 | 79.64 / 7.27% | 70.56 / 1.24% |
| 293 | 81.68 / 10.65% | 79.31 / 5.37% |

The two stock takes read exactly 65.00 in **both** groups. X4's hard clamp
contained the overshoot completely, even mid-slam, which is why nothing before
take 292 ever saw it.

**So the extension did not cause the overshoot. It removed the wall that was
hiding it** — and the overshoot appears in CALM windows too (1.24%, 5.37%), so it
is not only an instability artefact. Our servo overshoots its own target by up to
14 deg in ordinary operation, and that is a defect of ours that three months of
takes could not see.

### The correction to what was said one entry ago

That entry concluded "it is #68's clamp extension" from `score_run.py`'s
`MOVED ✓`. **That verdict cannot distinguish an installed extension from any
other reason X4's limit might be higher** — it fires whenever X4 exceeds 65 while
the servo asked past 66. The conclusion happened to be right because Patola
confirms the extension is installed, but it was not established by the line cited.
A verdict that assumes its conclusion is not evidence for it.

### Detection is ASYMMETRIC, and the scorer has to say so

A take **proves** the clamp is raised when X4's readback exceeds 65.5 — nothing
else can produce that. A take **cannot prove** the clamp is stock: with the
servo's own ceiling also at 65, a camera pinned at 65.00 looks identical either
way. Distinguishing them requires the servo to ask past X4's stop, i.e.
`X4VR_HEADLOOK_YAW_LIMIT` above 65, which no ordinary run sets.

**So "stock" is never confirmed by a normal take, only unrefuted.** Any A/B across
the two paths must set the servo limit above 65 in both arms, or it is comparing
a measured state against an assumed one.

## The servo's overshoot — a law, and no free fix

With the plant unclamped (the extended path) and the servo's `yaw_limit_deg` at
65, the real `head_look_step` sails past its own target:

| dead time | 0 | 1 | **2** | **3** | 4 | 5 | 6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| overshoot | −0.14 | −0.03 | **+6.30** | **+17.80** | +29.76 | +41.72 | +53.68 |

Against X4's readback: take 292 reached 76.79 (+11.79) and take 293 78.79
(+13.79), so the effective dead time in play is ~2.5–2.8 ticks — consistent with
take 291's measured 3.03.

### The law

Sweeping `max_step` at dead time 3, the ratio is flat at **0.49–0.53**:

    overshoot ≈ 0.5 x dead_time_in_ticks x max_step_deg

12 deg of step and 3 ticks of delay give 18, which is what the model reads and
the right order for the game's 12–14. **It is exactly zero at a dead time of 1 or
less**, so this is dead time spending a saturated command, not a tuning error:
while the step is clamped the loop has no feedback authority and is running open
at full rate.

### Three levers, one curve

| lever | overshoot | what it costs |
|---|---|---|
| `max_step` 12 → 6 | 17.80 → 8.83 | a 65 deg sweep goes 127 → 206 ms |
| `max_step` 12 → 3 | 17.80 → 4.46 | 381 ms |
| `kp` 0.25 → 0.15 | 17.80 → 3.77 | tracking lag, which #73's lead exists to fight |
| `kp` 0.25 → 0.10 | 17.80 → **−0.14** | more of the same |
| in-flight accounting | 17.80 → **−0.14** | **rms tracking error 0.40 → 3.57 deg** |

**In-flight accounting is not the free fix it looks like.** Crediting commands
already sent is arithmetically close to lowering the gain, which is why it lands
on the same −0.14 as `kp` 0.10, and on a moving head (60 deg, 0.4 Hz) it makes
tracking **nine times worse** and doubles the sweep time. Every lever here trades
overshoot against responsiveness; there is no direction that buys both.

It does at least fail gracefully. Crediting 3 ticks while the true delay is
larger: 4 → 3.31, 5 → 12.39, 6 → 21.60, against today's 29.76, 41.72, 53.68.

### Whether it is worth paying for depends on the path

*Stock path.* X4's own clamp at 65 absorbs the whole overshoot — the two stock
takes read exactly 65.00 with 0.00% past, in severe windows as well as calm. The
defect is real but has no visible consequence there.

*Extended path.* The camera goes ~14 deg past where the servo asked. Note which
direction: with the head at 80 and the servo capped at 65, the overshoot lands the
camera *nearer* the head, not further. The condition that exercises it is the
servo's limit sitting **below X4's** — which is a configuration inconsistency, and
exactly what take 293's NARROW arm maximised by asking 40 while X4 allowed ~79.

**So the first thing to fix is not the servo but the pairing:**
`X4VR_HEADLOOK_YAW_LIMIT` has to match the path. #68 already warns that raising
it alone changes nothing unless X4's file is overridden too; the converse is now
also true — leaving it at 65 when the extension has raised X4's is what puts the
servo in the regime where its overshoot is visible.

## Pairing vs changing the servo — not a choice, and lag decides which servo lever

They fix different defects and neither substitutes for the other.

**Pairing is not optional and does not fix the overshoot.** With the servo capped
below X4's limit the camera stops short of the head by the difference, at *every*
head speed — a standing 15 deg error in the 65-against-80 case, not a transient.
But with the limit paired (servo 85, head to 60, never near the stop) the
overshoot is still there, because the law needs **saturation**, and the error
exceeds `max_step/kp` = 48 deg on any fast turn:

| head deg/s | max_step 12 | 6 | 3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 60 | 3.02 | 3.02 | 3.02 |
| 200 | 8.42 | 8.42 | 4.40 |
| 350 | **22.00** | 10.15 | 4.40 |
| 500 | **27.17** | 8.77 | 4.40 |

### Overshoot alone picks the wrong lever

Both overshoot and lag are disagreements between the neck and the view, so the
honest score is the **larger of the two**. Paired, dead time 3:

| setting | 350 deg/s over / lag / **worst** | 500 deg/s over / lag / **worst** |
|---|---|---|
| today 0.25/12 | 22.00 / 16.70 / **22.00** | 27.17 / 23.81 / **27.17** |
| 0.25 / 6 | 10.15 / 16.70 / **16.70** | 8.77 / 31.64 / **31.64** |
| 0.25 / 3 | 4.40 / 36.08 / **36.08** | 4.40 / 45.05 / **45.05** |
| **0.15 / 12** | 16.59 / 16.70 / **16.70** | 17.63 / 23.81 / **23.81** |
| 0.10 / 12 | 5.90 / 17.16 / **17.16** | 0.49 / 29.57 / **29.57** |

**`max_step` 3 has the best overshoot of any row and is the worst setting on the
table.** It does not remove the error, it moves it from forward to backward, and
past 350 deg/s the lag it buys is larger than the overshoot it sold. Scoring on
overshoot alone would have shipped it.

### What the numbers actually recommend

**`kp` 0.25 → 0.15, `max_step` unchanged.** Tied-best at 350 deg/s, outright best
at 500, and identical to today at 120 where nothing differs. It costs no lag while
the step is saturated — both rows read 16.70 and 23.81, because a clamped step
does not care about `kp` — and it settles *faster* (143 ms against 413 at
500 deg/s) since there is less overshoot to unwind.

That it improves three axes and worsens none is exactly the shape that usually
means a missing cost, so it is a **candidate, not a conclusion**, and the missing
cost to look for is tracking a continuously moving head rather than a ramp-and-hold.

### Both, then, and in this order

1. **Pair `X4VR_HEADLOOK_YAW_LIMIT` to the path.** Free, fixes a persistent error,
   and is also the only way a stock run can prove it is stock.
2. **Then `kp` 0.15** as an A/B inside one run, against the standing-offset fix
   already in place, so the two are never confounded the way take 293 confounded
   the limit with the protocol.

## P294 — the kp A/B, committed before the run

Patola confirms the extension sets **maxyaw=85**, so the servo is paired to 85 and
the standing offset is gone before kp is touched. One variable at a time.

`X4VR_HEADLOOK_KP_AB=45` alternates kp between the run's own value (0.25) and
`X4VR_HEADLOOK_KP_B` (0.15) every 45 s, opening on the control arm.

**P294.1 — over 350 deg/s of head rate, the worst neck-vs-view disagreement falls
from ~22 deg to ~17.** Modelled at dead time 3. Below 150 deg/s the arms should be
indistinguishable; a difference there would mean kp is doing something the model
does not describe.

**P294.2 — if the fast band is thin the run says nothing.** The effect exists only
where the step saturates, above `max_step/kp` = 48 deg of error. The scorer says
so explicitly rather than reporting a null.

**P294.3 — kp also scales the lead**, `lead_scale * (1/kp - 1)`: 3.0x becomes
5.67x. The arms differ in anticipation as well as gain. That is what setting kp
does, so it is recorded rather than controlled, and #73 closed the lead as
imperceptible.

### The instrument already existed

`lagsample` logs head AND X4's camera every tick, gated on
`X4VR_HEADLOOK_LAGLOG`. I was about to build a duplicate because `camread` is
1-in-30 and `geom`'s `yaw=` is the declared pose, not the head.
[[read-the-existing-report-first]], third time in this task. It now also carries
`kparm=`, `kp=` and `ylim=`, **stamped from the branch the code took** rather than
joined by timestamp against the phase lines.

Setting `X4VR_HEADLOOK_KP_AB` auto-arms `lagsample`, because a kp run without it
cannot be scored at all — the failure take 293 already paid for. The handover sets
`LAGLOG=1` explicitly anyway: a take is too expensive to spend testing a
convenience.

### Scored on the WORSE of overshoot and lag

Both are the neck and the view disagreeing, and every lever trades one for the
other — `max_step` 3 has the best overshoot on the table and the worst worst-case.
The scorer bins by the head rate **3 ticks before** each sample, because the error
is paid out from commands issued a dead time earlier; binning on the current rate
filed a planted fast sweep's overshoot under "slow" the moment the head stopped,
leaking a p90 of 19.7 deg into a band where nothing should exceed 5.

Checked against two planted logs, one where ARM_B is better and one where it is
not: `22.90 -> 17.49, ARM_B is better` and `22.90 -> 23.49, no difference beyond
15%; a null here refutes it`.

### Still open, deliberately not in this run

Pitch. X4's pitch reached 48.87 deg, which a 35 deg clamp cannot produce, so its
limit moved too — but `pitch_limit_deg` stays at 35 here rather than changing two
things at once. The standing pitch offset survives this take by design.

## Take 294 — what it actually says

Run: `X4VR_HEADLOOK_KP_AB=45 X4VR_HEADLOOK_KP_B=0.15 X4VR_HEADLOOK_YAW_LIMIT=85
X4VR_HEADLOOK_LAGLOG=1`, no `X4VR_TICK_HZ`. 20667 lagsamples, 14376 cockpit with
steering and a live read-back, 9 A/B phases (5 control, 4 ARM_B) over 395 s.

### The kp A/B is NOT scorable, and the scorer's null must not be acted on

The pooled `kpab` block printed *"no difference beyond 15%; the model predicted
22.00 -> 16.70, so a null here refutes it"*. **Do not act on that line.** Split by
phase — which is the unit of replication, because the A/B alternates every 45 s
and an episode lasts tens of seconds — the arms interleave:

    phase  arm       under-150 p90    WORST
      2    control          1.68      62.66
      3    ARM_B           11.61      49.49
      4    control          4.25      27.57
      5    ARM_B            3.19      36.80
      6    control          5.34      49.22
      7    ARM_B            2.50      19.55
      8    control         45.16     100.66

Three of the four comparable control phases sit at or below the ARM_B phases. The
pooled control p90 of 25.14 against ARM_B's 3.84 is **carried by phase 8 alone**,
and phase 8 is where the single read-back fault below happened. Four or five
draws per arm cannot support a pooled tail statistic when one draw contains an
outlier event two orders of magnitude larger than the effect.

Three further defects in the block, all of which must be fixed before another kp
take is specified:

**The rate bins are contaminated.** `band()` takes the head rate from
`use[i-4]`/`use[i-3]` **without checking those samples are adjacent in time**. A
menu, a view change or any steer=0 stretch puts two distant samples side by side
and manufactures a rate: the over-350 band contains "head rates" of 1738 and 2367
deg/s, against a human maximum around 500-800 and a whole-run measured maximum of
77 deg of travel. [[range-failures-have-two-ends]] — the gap test exists at the
top of the function for the error and was never applied to the rate.

**The magnitudes are not the modelled quantity.** The model predicts a worst case
of 22.00 deg; the block reports 89.67. A 4x disagreement means the tail is made of
something else — here, the episodes — so a null in it is not a null in the servo.
[[instrument-inherits-its-question]].

**The WORST column is a single sample.** Over 350 deg/s each arm has 148-159
samples spread over four phases; comparing two maxima drawn from that is an
extreme-value comparison, not a measurement.

### CONFIRMED: the servo acts on an invalid camera read-back

`head_look_observe` (common/x4vr_headlook.hpp:514) is two unconditional
assignments. Whatever `GetCameraRotation` returns becomes the servo's idea of
where the camera is, with no validity, freshness or plausibility test. The
snapshot path 400 lines away in the same tick **does** protect itself — it carries
`raw_valid` forward and its comment says overwriting a real angle with zero would
make "no answer" and "centred" the same value. The control path never got that
care.

One instance in 395 s, at t=920748.87, tick by tick:

    920748.828  head 16.852,9.345   x4   16.387,9.167    tracking, 0.5 deg error
    920748.873  head 17.954,9.556   x4   -0.000,0.000    <-- X4 answers EXACTLY zero
    920748.896  head 18.176,9.594   x4  104.123,63.783
    920748.982  head 18.379,9.648   x4  119.043,66.101   servo emits delta 104,104
    920749.190  head 16.655,9.726   x4   55.304,3.279
    920753.492  head  4.012,6.075   x4   51.458,5.996    4.6 s later, still 47 deg out

The head moved 2 deg across the whole event. The arithmetic of the servo's reply
is exact: cmd is pinned to the 119.04 read, the step saturates at -11.96 =
-`max_step`, so cmd becomes 107.08 and the delta is (107.08-119.04)/0.115 = -104
counts. **It never recovered** — 4.6 s on, the camera sat at 51 deg with the head
at 4, drifting the wrong way.

Note what this is NOT: the 104.12 read is not our command either — a 39-count
delta moves the camera 4.5 deg, not 88. Both reads are invalid. Those two frames
carry `draws=4` and `draws=16/8` against the usual 34-35, out of arena block #25
rather than the usual #3/#7/#8/#9/#11 — a different camera for ~150 ms while our
`view` gate still said cockpit. [[x4vr-one-number-several-cameras]],
[[record-the-branch-dont-recompute-it]].

### WITHDRAWN: "EXTENDED PATH — X4's stop is not the stock 65"

`score_run.py`'s clamp block reported *"!! EXTENDED PATH ... it read yaw 119.04
... MOVED ✓ ... the override reached X4 and the limit is data, confirmed live"*.
**That verdict is wrong and the block needs fixing.** It reads a MAX. Its evidence
is 4 samples out of 14376, and all four are inside the read-back fault above, with
the head at 18 deg. The other 20304 cockpit ticks pin at exactly 65.00-65.20 while
the head reached 77.40.

A max over a run containing view transitions and invalid reads is not a
measurement of a stop. The block must require a *plateau* — repeated dwell at a
value with the head demanding more — not an extremum.
[[verdict-that-fires-whatever-the-number-is]], and the second time a clamp verdict
has been believed on evidence that cannot distinguish the case
([[confidence-label-shields-a-claim]]).

This leaves #68's status genuinely unsettled again: 292 and 293 did read past 65
(76.79 and 78.79) but in runs of 1-7 samples out of 1103/1221, which is the same
shape as the faults, not a plateau.

### The episodes track X4VR_TICK_HZ

Count of **saturated commands issued while the head is inside 15 deg of centre** —
the servo slamming at `max_step` when the neck is not asking for it — per minute,
over every take that logs `headlook: ... delta`:

    take        TICK_HZ   per min
    285b-s1        90        0.0
    285b-s2        90       14.9
    287a            -        0.0
    287b           90        8.7
    288             -        0.0
    289            90        0.0
    290a            -        0.5
    290b           90        0.7
    291             -        0.0
    292            90       29.1
    293            70       52.7
    294             -        2.7

Every take above 2.7 had `X4VR_TICK_HZ` set. Every take without it reads 0.0-2.7,
and take 294's 2.7 is not spread out: 16 of its 18 events are the read-back fault
at t0+384 and the external-view stretch at t0+392-395, leaving two isolated
samples in 6.5 minutes.

The knob is **permissive, not sufficient** — 285b-s1, 289 and 290b had it at 90
and stayed near zero, and 285b-s1/s2 are one session split into a calm and a wild
phase. But it is the only setting common to every wild take, and the mechanism was
derived before this count: `X4VR_TICK_HZ` moves the tick off X4's drain and adds
~17 ms of queue, and overshoot is `0.5 x dead_time x max_step`, so a saturated
loop at that dead time goes to a limit cycle. Take 292 shows exactly that — the
head still at -5 deg for six seconds while the read-back flips -70 -> +25.9 ->
+65.6 -> -65.7 and the servo emits a saturated +-102 counts on every single
sample.

This is consistent with the knob already being documented HARMFUL, and it
sharpens that entry: it does not merely cost latency, it is present in every
session that went wild.

**Not claimed:** that `TICK_HZ` is the whole of #75. 285b-s1 and s2 share it and
differ, so something still selects the episode within a session. What is claimed
is that the two takes whose wildness Patola described most vividly (292, 293) are
the two highest rows in that table, and that the one take without the knob and
without a read-back fault would have scored zero.

## X4 ignores the PipeWire default sink — answered, not a PipeWire bug

`~/.config/EgoSoft/X4/96679891/config.xml` (and our intercepted
`config-x4vrmod.xml`):

    <sounddevice>CORSAIR VIRTUOSO SE Wireless Ga, USB Audio (CARD=Ga,DEV=0)</sounddevice>

X4 names an **ALSA card** directly. It never asks for the default, so no change of
default can move it. Other titles ask for `default`, which resolves through
PipeWire and follows.

Ruled out on the way: WirePlumber's `restore-stream` is not pinning it — X4's
saved keys are `channelMap`, `channelVolumes`, `mute`, `volume` and **no target**,
and across all 1330 saved applications there are zero target pins. The usual
"clear restore-stream" advice does not apply. X4 is one of ~90 pipewire-alsa
clients in that file, so "it uses ALSA" alone would not have separated it either —
the device NAME is what does.

Fix: X4's Settings -> Audio device -> the default/system entry, then restart X4.
Since the WiVRn sink is created on connect and destroyed on disconnect, connect
VR first and launch X4 second.

**Mod opportunity, not taken:** we already intercept the config load, and the
intercepted copy is ours to write. Pointing `<sounddevice>` at the VR sink when a
session is live would be in scope without touching the player's file. Filed, not
built.

## Take 294's residual, with the episodes removed

Patola on take 294: *"a bit better than the others with the frustum not going
through wild spins, but it still felt glitchy, jittery, with the visuals taking
time to follow up on the movement. It would be nauseating if I didn't have strong
VR legs."* Two complaints, measured over the 13765 clean cockpit steering ticks
(the read-back fault window 920748.80-920756.00 dropped).

### LAG: 85 ms, and the servo's own term accounts for 60 of it

Cross-correlating X4's camera against the head, both resampled to a uniform
200 Hz grid so the shift is a time and not a tick count:

    best alignment at tau = 85 ms (r = 0.954)

**The peak is broad and the instrument says so**: r is 0.945 at 40 ms and 0.948 at
140 ms, against 0.954 at the peak. Anything in 60-120 ms is indistinguishable
here; 85 is the argmax, not a resolution. r at zero shift is already 0.921, so
most of the signal is common-mode.

A proportional servo sampled every `dt` settles to a standing error of
`head_rate * dt * (1/kp - 1)`, i.e. an effective lag of `(1/kp - 1) * dt`
independent of how fast the head moves. Mean tick period is 19.9 ms, kp is 0.25:

    (1/0.25 - 1) * 19.9 ms = 60 ms   vs   85 ms measured

60 of 85. The remaining 25 ms is **not** attributed here — the candidates are the
pose already being ~11 ms old when the servo sees it (`poselag` read-back age
median 11.4 ms), X4's own input-to-camera share (20-30 ms, take 291), and
render-to-submit (`camstamp` median 9.7 ms) — and they sum to more than 25, so
assigning it would be arithmetic in search of a budget.
[[three-contradictory-measurements]].

### P294.1 was pointed the wrong way

The committed prediction wanted **kp 0.15**, to cut overshoot from 22 to 17 deg.
But lag is `(1/kp - 1) * dt`, so kp 0.15 gives `5.67 * 19.9 = 113 ms` against
today's 60 — **it would have made the complaint Patola actually has about 90%
worse**, to buy 5 degrees on a defect he no longer reports.

[[optimise-one-axis-move-the-error]] is in memory and it fired anyway. Lag WAS on
the trade table (16.70) — I scored it as a tie-breaker between servo settings
instead of asking which axis the player feels. The overshoot was real and
measured; it was simply not the live complaint once the episodes went.

Note the overshoot law `0.5 * dead_time * max_step` has no kp in it: kp does not
change the size of an overshoot, only how small an error has to be before the step
stops saturating (`max_step/kp` = 48 deg at 0.25, 30 deg at 0.40). So raising kp
buys lag directly and costs only saturation MARGIN — which matters because the
episodes are saturated limit cycles.

### JITTER: the first reading did not survive its control

Raw, `|d(error)|` per tick rises monotonically with the tick period — p50 0.110 ->
0.519 deg across five bins, a 4.7x increase. That looks like a mechanism and is
not one: divided by dt, the same bins read **11.67, 9.36, 10.05, 12.12, 12.76
deg/s at p50** — flat, and not even monotonic. At the median the tremble is
elapsed time and nothing else.

What DOES survive is the tail: `|d(error)|/dt` at p90 reads 96, 84, 116, 153, 155
deg/s — a 1.9x rise from the fastest bin to the slowest — **while the head is
moving SLOWER in the long-tick bins** (p50 head rate 9.8 deg/s in the fastest,
5.5 in the slowest). So long ticks are genuinely worse in the tail, and not
because the head is doing more during them.

A 1.9x tail effect, not a 4.7x one. [[a-ratio-against-its-own-denominator]].

### The tick period is the lever, but its accounting is already flagged broken

Mean 19.9 ms, p10 9.0, p50 15.0, p90 40.0, p99 56.0 — a **4.4x spread** in the
sample period of a proportional loop, against a layer publishing at 89.5 Hz
(11.2 ms). Both complaints point at it: lag is `3 * dt`, and the tremble tail
grows with it.

**Before anything is built on that**, `score_run.py`'s own pumprate block says:

> INCONSISTENT, and that is a defect of this instrument rather than a finding:
> pump runs at 103.7 Hz, above the 89.5 Hz publish rate, and nopose is only 0 — so
> every published pose should have been seen, yet only 58.3% were. Either
> `updates` advances more than once per publish, or the windows of the two
> counters are misaligned. Do not spend a take on this number until it is
> resolved.

The tick enters at 103.7 Hz and acts at 52.2 Hz because of `if (!fresh) return;`,
and whether that gate is discarding real poses or the counter is lying is exactly
the unresolved question. Resolving it is a code read, not a take.
[[read-the-existing-report-first]].

## Take 295 — the tick period, and three fixes that precede it

Predictions committed before the run, as always.

### RESOLVED: the pumprate "inconsistency" was neither suspect

`fresh` is `updates != last_updates` — an INDICATOR, not a count. Several
publishes landing between two polls collapse into one `fresh`, so it counts
*poll intervals that contained a publish*, and comparing it to the publish count
as a percentage compares two different quantities. Nothing was lost and no
counter was lying.

The honest reading: **the servo ITERATES at `fresh` Hz**, 52.2 in take 294.
Corroborated by a route that shares none of that arithmetic — the mean lagsample
tick period is 19.9 ms = 50.3 Hz. Every iteration reads the LATEST pose, so the
servo is never acting on stale data; what is lost is loop iterations, and lag is
`(1/kp - 1) * tick_period`.

### CONFIRMED and FIXED: the servo acted on invalid read-backs

`head_look_observe` now refuses a reading further than `observe_max_jump_deg`
(3 x max_step = 36 deg, the dead time times the step ceiling — not a free
parameter) from our own command, for at most `observe_max_refusals` = 8
consecutive ticks before resynchronising. **A guard that can never yield would
strand the servo pushing at a camera that has genuinely moved**, which is the
map-view accelerator again.

Four cases in tests/headlook.cpp, and the negative controls are the ones that
matter:

    take-294 replay        6 refused, worst command 15.64 deg (was 107.08)
    honest 250 deg/s sweep 0 refused of 400   <- the false-positive case
    head past X4's stop    0 refused of 200   <- standing 20 deg gap
    sustained real move    9 refused, 1 resync, cmd follows to 120

`X4VR_HEADLOOK_OBSERVE_JUMP=0` restores the unguarded behaviour so earlier takes
stay reproducible.

### WITHDRAWN: the clamp block's `MOVED ✓`

It read a MAX. Rewritten to find a **plateau**: the camera DID NOT MOVE while the
target was 2+ deg past it, reported as p95 of that population. Both halves are
needed — "target past camera" alone is true throughout ordinary lag, and scoring
that returned 53.94 deg on take 294 against a real stop at 65.

It now reads take 294 from `lagsample` (20308 cockpit ticks) rather than
`camread` (479), and says:

    PLATEAU yaw=65.00 deg, 248 sample(s) with the target 2+ deg past the camera
    !! the MAX is 54.0 deg past the plateau — that excursion is not a stop
    DID NOT MOVE — the command asked past 66 deg and X4 still stopped at 65.00

**So take 294's extension did NOT reach the cockpit camera**, and the previous
verdict was exactly backwards. An axis with no plateau now scores 0.0, not its
max, so an unmeasured pitch can no longer fire a verdict off four fault samples.

### FIXED: kpab's rate bins, and its verdict

The rate came from `use[i-4]`/`use[i-3]` with no check that they were adjacent
ticks, and used a fixed nominal 63 Hz against a tick that wanders 9-56 ms. Both
corrected; 316 samples now excluded as gap artifacts, and ARM_B's over-350 band
falls from 148 samples to 67 — **over half of it was manufactured by the gaps**.

The verdict now judges a p90 rather than two maxima at unequal n, and a new
per-PHASE line outranks the pooled one. On take 294 it says what the manual
analysis found:

    control  ph2:1.86  ph4:4.30  ph6:5.98  ph8:45.21
    ARM_B    ph3:18.64 ph5:2.97  ph7:2.38
    => the per-phase ranges OVERLAP ... **This run does not answer the kp
       question** whatever the pooled line above says.

### P295: what the rate fix is, and what it is not

`servo_kp` and `max_step_deg` are both PER TICK, and the tick wanders 4.4x. So:

    lag       = (1/kp - 1) * dt                 worse when dt is LONG
    slew      = max_step / dt                   worse when dt is LONG
    overshoot = 0.5 * (dead_time_s/dt) * max_step   worse when dt is SHORT

No fixed pair is right across that spread. `X4VR_HEADLOOK_RATEFIX=<nominal Hz>`
scales both by `dt/nominal`, which collapses them into one time constant
`tau = 1/(kp * nominal)`. **At exactly the nominal the arithmetic is unchanged**,
which is what lets the A/B measure the wander and nothing else — asserted as an
exact-equality test.

**P295.0 — the first check I wrote here FAILED and the check was wrong.** I
asserted the fix would take a quarter off the lag. It takes 14%, and the algebra
says it should: `lag = tau - dt`, and with the nominal set to today's mean rate
tau IS today's lag. The rate fix makes the loop the same controller at every tick
rate; it does not by itself make it a faster one. Consistency and speed are two
knobs and the fix is the first. Kept visible rather than retuned away.

Offline against take 294's REAL tick sequence — a contiguous 300-tick window
whose p10/p50/p90 match the whole run's — in tests/servo_rate.cpp section 11:

    nominal   tau ms   lag ms   overshoot
        50      80.0     80.4        1.07      today's equivalent
        70      57.1     60.4        1.64
       100      40.0     50.4        2.44      <- take 295's ARM_B
       140      28.6    137.4       62.59      UNSTABLE: tau under the 60 ms
                                               dead time. Do not ask for this.

**P295.1 — ARM_B at nominal 100 Hz should read ~50 ms against the control's
~80.** The harness reproduced take 294's independently measured 85 ms as 90.4
without being fitted to it, so the control arm is a check on the harness too: a
control far from 80 means the harness, not the fix, is what to doubt.

**P295.2 — the per-phase ranges must SEPARATE.** A median difference with
overlapping phases is what take 294 produced and it meant nothing. The `rfab`
block says so itself rather than reporting a winner.

**P295.3 — the read-back guard should show 0 or very few refusals.** Take 294 had
one fault in 395 s. A log full of `headlook: REFUSED` means the threshold is
wrong and that is the finding, not a nuisance.

`tests/run-rfab-scorer.sh` plants streams whose lag is known by construction and
checks the block recovers it (80/50, 80/80, 50/80 all recovered to the
millisecond) and reaches all three of its verdicts — because a scorer only ever
seen to print one of them is worth nothing, which is what take 294's kpab was.

## Take 295 — the rate fix is REFUTED, and the defect was mine

Patola: *"the spinning frustum came up again ... the glitching and jittering is
still intolerable for gameplay; I am only tolerating it because these are
measurement runs."*

    rfab   control (off)     5    122  48  153  52  41      ms of lag
    rfab   ARM_B @100Hz      4     564  448  2072  831
    rfab   => SEPARATED THE WRONG WAY — every ARM_B phase is worse.
    rfab   read-back guard: 901 refusal(s), 56 resync(s)

Everything localises to ARM_B: **898 of 901 refusals, all 56 resyncs, and 39 of
the run's 40 saturated-with-head-centred commands.** Commanded step p99 was 7.71
deg in the control arm and 29.33 in ARM_B, max 32.77 against a design ceiling of
12. P295.3 said a log full of REFUSED means the threshold is wrong and that is
the finding; it was, twice over.

### Cause 1: one knob was doing two jobs

`nominal_hz` set BOTH the gain and the step ceiling, because I derived both from
the same scale factor. So asking for tau 40 ms also doubled the slew:

    nominal  50   dt 40 ms   kp_eff 0.500   max_step_eff 24.0 =  600 deg/s
    nominal 100   dt 40 ms   kp_eff 0.600   max_step_eff 48.0 = 1200 deg/s

[[vary-them-independently]], inside the fix built to settle a question that
memory had already been written about. They are separate parameters now:
`rate_fix_tau_ms` and `rate_fix_max_rate_deg_s`, and `X4VR_HEADLOOK_MAXRATE`
is its own knob.

### Cause 2: the guard was calibrated against a constant the code stopped using

`observe_max_jump_deg` was a fixed 36 = 3 * `max_step_deg`. The rate fix scaled
the step to 48, so the guard spent ARM_B refusing **honest** read-backs: the
