servo held a stale belief, the error grew, the next step was larger, refuse
again. 56 times the budget ran out and it resynchronised. head_look_step now
keeps the threshold at 3 * the step ceiling actually in force.

### Cause 3: the offline test could not see either, and I knew better

Section 11 drove a smooth 0.35 Hz sweep whose error never reached
`max_step/kp`, so **the step never saturated and the ceiling was never
exercised at all**. A step-ceiling bug cannot appear in a test that never
reaches the ceiling. [[test-the-fix-where-it-can-act]], which is in memory and
says exactly this.

Section 12 now drives 1.4 Hz at +-70 deg (~615 deg/s, a real snap-glance) and
reproduces it offline:

                             worst step   slew deg/s  worst |cam|
           today (fix off)        11.96          997        81.42
       295 ARM_B (coupled)        20.24         1198        90.85
          tau 40, slew 600        24.04          604        96.49

### And the second correction failed too — which is the real finding

Separating the knobs does NOT rescue tau 40. Sweeping tau in the saturating
regime with the slew held at 600, against the measured 60 ms dead time:

    tau ms   worst |cam| against an 85 deg limit
       200         50.14   clean
       140         71.88   clean
       110         81.88   clean
        80         92.35   SPINS    <- TODAY'S EQUIVALENT
        60         95.45   SPINS
        40         96.49   SPINS

**Today's setting is already on the unstable side of the margin for fast head
motion.** A proportional loop with transport delay is stable only while its time
constant stays comfortably above the dead time, and 80 ms against 60 ms is not
comfortable. That is why the episodes are intermittent: the same constants are
fine for the gentle motion of section 11 and unstable for a snap-glance.

So **the safe direction is a LONGER tau, not a shorter one — more lag, not
less** — and P295.1's whole premise was backwards. Lag and spinning are one
knob pulled in opposite directions, and there is no setting of it that gives
Patola both.

### What this redirects the work to

Every row of that table is against a **60 ms dead time**, and tau must clear it
by roughly 2x. Halve the dead time and tau 55 ms becomes as safe as 110 is now —
that is the only way to buy lag back without buying spin.

The dead time is our tick period (19.9 ms mean, wandering 9-56) plus X4's own
input-to-camera share (20-30 ms, take 291) plus queueing. **The part we own is
the tick, and it is the larger part.** The servo iterates at 42-52 Hz because a
tick happens only when a drain poll finds a new pose, while the layer publishes
at 89.7 Hz — so roughly half the available rate is being left on the floor by
`if (!fresh) return;`, not by anything X4 does.

`X4VR_TICK_HZ` tried exactly this and made it worse, by moving the tick onto our
own thread and adding ~17 ms of queue — more dead time, which this table now
explains as the reason it spun. The untried option is to keep the tick on X4's
drain and remove only the freshness gate, or floor it on time.

**Not attempted in a take until it is measured offline in the saturating
regime**, which is the mistake this section exists to record.

## The freshness gate, removed and verified offline (take 296 pending)

`if (!fresh) return;` made a tick happen only when a drain poll happened to find
a new pose. Measured: the servo iterates at **41.9 Hz** (take 295) and 52.2 (294)
while the drain runs at 84.2 and 103.7 and the layer publishes at ~89.7. So about
half the available iteration rate was being left on the floor by our own gate,
not by anything X4 does — and lag is `(1/kp - 1) * tick_period`.

### A time floor, not a bare removal

Take 295 measured the drain between **25 and 325 Hz**. Ticking the servo at
325 Hz is take 119's shape again, and it would leave the period as irregular as
it already is. `X4VR_HEADLOOK_UNGATED=<ms>` acts on every drain entry but no more
often than that floor, which bounds the rate AND regularises it. 0 keeps the
gate, so every earlier take reproduces.

Nothing else moves: the gate sits *after* the stand-down (`stale > 5000`) and
after the mouselook key hold, and `stale` still counts non-fresh entries, so the
dead-pose-channel path is untouched.

### Verified in section 12, at take 295's own measured rates

                                tick ms   lag ms   worst |cam|
    gated (today), ratefix off     23.9    117.0         72.45   clean
          UNGATED, ratefix off     11.9     53.2         78.55   clean
    gated (today), ratefix tau110  23.9    112.3         71.30   clean
       UNGATED, ratefix tau110     11.9    106.8         68.08   clean

**Lag more than halves, 117 -> 53 ms, and the excursion grows to 78.55 while
staying inside the 85 limit.** The model is deliberately unkind: the head is
sampled-and-held at the publish rate, so the ungated arm really does see
repeated poses, and the dead time shortens by only half a tick — anything more
would be the harness inventing the answer.

Two checks, and the first is the one that matters:

* removing the gate with **today's per-tick constants** makes the excursion
  worse, because doubling the iteration rate doubles the motion in flight at a
  fixed per-tick step. That is the term that killed `X4VR_TICK_HZ`, and the
  model reproduces it rather than hiding it.
* with the rate fix on the step ceiling is per SECOND, so the same change costs
  nothing — but tau 110 then puts the lag back to 106.8, which is the trade
  section 12's sweep already established.

So the pairing to test is **ungated with the rate fix OFF**: the only
combination in the table that both halves the lag and stays clean.

**What the model cannot see:** our own injected events lengthen X4's drain, so
doubling the event rate may raise the drain rate that feeds the tick — take 119's
runaway in miniature. That is what the floor is for, and it is the first thing to
read in the log.

### Scored by `ugab`, with its own planted controls

Same stream and statistic as `rfab`, split on `ugarm`. Predicted: ARM_B roughly
halves the lag; the excursion and the count of samples with the camera 30+ deg
off a centred head are printed beside it, because **a halved lag bought with a
spinning frustum is not a win** and take 295 is why that is printed rather than
left for the player to notice.

`tests/run-rfab-scorer.sh` now plants six logs — three for each block — and
checks all three verdicts are reachable in both. Writing the new field into the
regex strictly broke take 295's own parse (it logs `rfhz=`, before the knob was
split, and no `ugarm=` at all); the control suite caught it on the first run, and
the pattern now accepts both spellings and a missing field.

## Take 297 — the ghosting is NOT in what we build

Patola recorded the monitor during a normal run and reported double/triple
images in the headset at 0:33-0:38, 1:05-1:16 and after 1:22, **absent from the
recording**. The recording turned out to contain the full side-by-side
composite letterboxed onto his 3440x1440 monitor, so both eyes are in it and the
stereo could be measured directly — no new run needed.

### Each eye is individually clean

A 3x magnification of one eye at 1:10, in the region he flagged: sharp station,
sharp cockpit strut, no doubling, no smear, no trailing. Whatever he is seeing
is not in the pixels we hand over.

### My first hypothesis was wrong, and the measurement says so

`X4VR_POSE=0` with `X4VR_ROLL_STEREO=1` has been printing as FAIL in the scorer
on EVERY take — 294, 295, 296b, 297 — and I read past it every time
([[read-the-existing-report-first]], fourth instance this task). Roll
compensation armed against a dead pose channel sends disparity VERTICAL under
head tilt, which is the classic fusion killer, so it looked like the answer.

Measured instead, by bounded normalised cross-correlation over a tile grid
(bounded because the first phase-correlation version wrapped at +-tile/2 and
reported its own failures as +-60 px — [[state-the-instrument-range]]):

    frame   VERTICAL |dy|            horizontal dx
    0:05    p50 0.00  p90 0.36 deg   p10 -3.02  p50 -1.39 deg
    0:35    p50 0.00  p90 0.24 deg   p10 -2.54  p50 -1.39 deg
    1:10    p50 0.00  p90 0.42 deg   p10 -2.84  p50 -1.15 deg

Vertical disparity is **zero at the median** and only 5-11 tiles of ~120 exceed
0.5 deg. The ROLL_STEREO defect is real and still unfixed, but it is **not** what
Patola is seeing. Horizontal disparity of 3.0 deg at a 64 mm IPD implies an
object at ~1.2 m, which is a plausible cockpit console — the stereo geometry is
broadly sane.

### And "triple" does not fit a fusion failure at all

Binocular disparity produces exactly TWO images. Three means a temporal
mechanism, not a geometric one.

### What the run does establish

The defect is introduced **downstream of the composite**. Two facts about that
path, neither yet a conclusion:

**WiVRn is a STREAMING runtime.** At `X4VR_RES=2816x2816` per eye, two eyes,
90 Hz, it is being handed **1.43 Gpixel/s — 2.9x a 4K60 stream** — to video
encode and ship to the headset. Encoder starvation at that load produces exactly
this class of artifact and is invisible to a local screen capture by
construction.

**This run ran at 57 fps against a 90 Hz headset** (17.68 ms, range
11.46-40.56). But `gpu-screen-recorder` was running, and take 294 without it read
10.29 ms / 97 fps — so the recording cost roughly 40% of the frame rate and
**this run's fps is not representative**. [[price-the-instrument]]. The repeat
rate in a normal run is a different and unmeasured number; the `blits` against
`submitted` ratio is NOT it either, because 294 reads 71% at 97 fps where a
simple repeat count would read ~0, so that counter's semantics are not what I
assumed.

### The decisive test is Patola's, and it is elimination not instrumentation

Switching to **SteamVR** changes the runtime, the compositor and — if wired —
removes video streaming entirely. If the artifact vanishes or changes character
it is the runtime path; if it is identical it is ours. Second knob in the same
direction: **halve `X4VR_RES`**. If it is encode bandwidth the artifact should
fall sharply; if it is unchanged, bandwidth is not it.
[[x4vr-eliminate-dont-instrument]].

## Take 298 — SteamVR crashes X4, and the bug is ours

`XR_RUNTIME_JSON` reached the process and the override worked:

    xr: runtime "SteamVR/OpenXR in Meta compatibility mode" 2.17.10
    xr: system "SteamVR/OpenXR : oculus" — max swapchain 8192x8192
    xr: view 0 — recommended 2528x2704
    xr: wants Vulkan 1.0.0 .. 1.2.0
    <SIGSEGV, 53.9 MB core>

Patola confirmed SteamVR itself is healthy by running another VR title, and
tried both the manifest path and the `active_runtime.json` symlink. Same crash.

### Infinite recursion through vkCreateInstance

`coredumpctl` gives a 14-frame cycle that repeats until the stack is gone:

    x4vr_CreateInstance (ours)
      -> gamescope_wsi -> MESA_device_select -> MND_timeline_semaphore
      -> steamoverlayvulkanlayer -> libvulkan vkCreateInstance
      -> SteamVR vrclient.so        <- creates its OWN VkInstance
      -> x4vr_CreateInstance again

We open the OpenXR runtime from **inside** `vkCreateInstance`, because the
runtime's required instance extensions have to be merged into the create-info
X4 wrote, and that has to happen before the instance exists. WiVRn lives out of
process and returns from `xrCreateInstance` without touching Vulkan, so this was
never exercised in 298 takes. SteamVR's client does it in process.

`vr_open_runtime()`'s existing early-out is `if (g_vrs.rt.ok()) return true;` —
and `rt.ok()` is still false during the first call, so it does not catch a
re-entry. `runtime_open` is simply called again.

**`app_is_target()` cannot separate the two calls and should not be asked to.**
It falls back to `/proc/self/exe`, and SteamVR's client runs inside X4's own
process, so the executable is X4 for both. Only re-entrancy distinguishes them.

### The fix — FIRST ATTEMPT, take 299, WRONG PLACE

A thread-local depth guard in `vr_open_runtime()`. **It never fired.** Take 299
crashed identically and the log had zero guard messages.

`vr_open_runtime()` opens with `if (g_vrs.rt.ok()) return true;` and by the time
the re-entrant call arrives the runtime IS open — the log proves it, printing the
runtime name, the system, both view configurations and the Vulkan requirements
before the crash. So the early-out short-circuits and the depth check below it is
never reached.

**The recursion was never in opening the runtime.** It is in what
`x4vr_CreateInstance` does *afterwards*: `vk_instance_extensions()` asks the
runtime what X4's instance needs, and SteamVR answers by calling
`vkEnumerateInstanceExtensionProperties` and `vkCreateInstance` itself. The full
backtrace is **6521 frames, 469 of them ours** — `bt 14` had truncated it, which
is why the second attempt looked shallow and I briefly believed it fixed.

### The fix — SECOND ATTEMPT, around the whole block

The guard belongs in `x4vr_CreateInstance`, wrapping everything from the runtime
open through the merge, not around the open alone. On re-entry: no query, no
merge, chain straight through.

Checked by modelling the nesting rather than by reasoning about it: under an
out-of-process runtime depth never exceeds 1, under an in-process one it reaches
2 and returns, and **in both cases X4's instance is merged exactly once** and the
depth unwinds to zero. That is the property that matters — a guard that stopped
the recursion by also skipping the real merge would start X4 flat and look like a
success.

**Not verified by a run yet.** It is reasoned from the backtrace, and it cannot
be exercised without an in-process runtime; the next take is its test. Two things
to watch in that log, in order:

1. **`vr: re-entered while the runtime was still opening`** — the guard firing,
   which is the fix working rather than a warning.
2. **`xr: wants Vulkan 1.0.0 .. 1.2.0`** — SteamVR accepts at most Vulkan 1.2.
   If X4 builds a 1.3 instance this is the next thing that can fail, and it will
   fail at the graphics-requirements check rather than in a stack overflow.

Predicted next failure point if it moves past both: `x4vr_CreateDevice`, which
looks up `dispatch_key(phys)` in `g_instances` and would treat a SteamVR-created
device as X4's. It is gated on `g_vrs.rt.ok()` and does not call
`vr_open_runtime()`, so it cannot recurse the same way, and SteamVR most likely
uses X4's device through the OpenXR graphics binding rather than making its own —
so this is flagged, not patched. Patching code that cannot be tested is how the
rate fix shipped broken.

### Why this is worth fixing on its own account

Patola: *"maybe not everybody will be able to use WiVRn, or even willing to do
it; SteamVR is more mainstream."* WiVRn as a hard requirement is a real limit on
who can run the mod, independent of what it does for the ghosting question.

## Take 300 — the crash is fixed; X4 now HANGS during load under SteamVR

The guard fired exactly once and everything downstream came up:

    vr: re-entered vkCreateInstance from inside our own — ... (1 occurrence)
    vr: instance extensions — X4 asked for 6, the runtime needs 5, added 3
    vr: this device has no spare graphics queue — the runtime shares X4's
        (family 0 index 0), serialised by the layer
    vr: session created on X4's own device — ... reference space STAGE
    vr: session -> XR_SESSION_STATE_FOCUSED
    xr: chose format 50 — X4's eye image is format 44, so the copy is
        byte-preserving
    sbs: composite recording on queue family 0

So the re-entrancy defect is CLOSED and SteamVR negotiates cleanly. The
remaining failure is different in kind.

### What the numbers say

    frames=489 located=489 submitted=397
    copy swapchain=1 blits=4 released=4 acquire_failed=0 refused=0
    log spans 173498.333 -> 173515.091 = 16.8 s

`acquire_failed=0` and `blits == released`, so nothing is stuck inside an
acquire and no image leaked — **we stopped asking**. The log then stops
entirely while X4 kept running (Patola heard music and had to kill both X4 and
gamescope), so our hooks stopped being called rather than the game exiting.

The last frames carry `valid=0`, `x4=-0.000,0.000`, `seq=7` and the final lines
are shader patches. **X4 never left the loading/menu screen.** The black monitor
is then expected rather than a second defect: `X4VR_MASK_PRESENT=1` masks the
flat present, and there was no VR content to replace it with.

### Ruled out, cheaply

* **SteamVR's compositor did not crash.** `coredumpctl` shows no `vrcompositor`
  core during take 300 — only gamescope's SIGABRT at 00:53, which is Patola
  killing it. An earlier `vrcompositor` core at 00:44 belongs to take 299.
* **Not a stall in shader patching.** Take 300 patched 4 fragment / 8 vertex
  against take 297's 7 / 12 — the patching is sparse in both, so stopping at
  vertex #250 is a symptom of a short run, not its cause.
* **`vr: submitting NO layers this run by design` is MISINFORMATION**, not a
  finding. It is unconditional and appears in take 297 too, which submitted
  35297 layers. A Milestone-A line that outlived its branch —
  [[stale-comment-is-misinformation]]. It cost a few minutes of chasing here and
  should be deleted or made conditional.

### The standing suspect

This device has **one graphics queue**. The runtime shares X4's (family 0 index
0) and the two are serialised by `VrQueueLock`. During take 300 the VR thread
submitted 397 frames while X4 was still loading, which is the most contended
this path has ever been — WiVRn runs may simply never have exercised it the same
way. `VrQueueLock` is already re-entrant per thread and deliberately excludes
`xrWaitFrame` (take 114c hung exactly there), so the obvious shapes are covered;
what is not established is how SteamVR's `xrEndFrame` behaves while held.

**Not diagnosed, and not to be patched on a guess.** gamescope also aborted in
all three attempts, and it wraps everything — so the one-variable next step is
`X4VR_GAMESCOPE=0`, which is cheaper than reasoning about a lock.

## The SteamVR hang — DIAGNOSED from a live backtrace

`gdb -p` on the wedged process while it hung. Three threads, and they form a
cycle across the boundary between our lock and SteamVR's:

**Thread 1, X4's own present thread**

    x4vr_QueuePresentKHR (ours)   <- holds g_vr_queue_mu via VrQueueLock
      -> vrclient.so              <- xrReleaseSwapchainImage
      -> pthread_mutex_lock       <- BLOCKED on a SteamVR-internal mutex

**Thread 20, our XR session thread**

    vr_session_thread -> vr_thread
      -> vrclient.so              <- inside xrEndFrame, holds SteamVR's mutex
      -> x4vr_QueueSubmit (ours)
      -> pthread_mutex_lock       <- BLOCKED on g_vr_queue_mu

**A third thread, X4's renderer**, also blocked in `x4vr_QueueSubmit`, waiting
behind the same lock.

So: X4's present thread holds OUR lock and wants SteamVR's; our XR thread holds
SteamVR's and wants OURS. Textbook ABBA, and neither side can see the other's.

### Why 298 takes never hit it

`VrQueueLock` is held across `xrReleaseSwapchainImage` — that is take 114c's
documented path, `QueuePresentKHR -> vr_finish_blit -> swapchain_release ->
xrReleaseSwapchainImage -> x4vr_QueueSubmit`, and 114c was fixed by making the
lock re-entrant **per thread**. Re-entrancy is the right fix for one thread
meeting itself and does nothing for two threads meeting each other.

With WiVRn the second thread is never there: the runtime is out of process, so
`xrEndFrame` does not call `vkQueueSubmit` inside X4 and our XR thread never
holds a runtime lock while wanting ours. SteamVR does both in process.

The existing comment above `g_vr_queue_mu` already states the principle for one
case — *"xrWaitFrame is deliberately NOT covered: it blocks until the runtime's
next frame boundary"* — and the correct generalisation is that **no call into
the runtime may be made while holding this lock**. `xrReleaseSwapchainImage` is
such a call and is made under it.

### Why the naive fix is wrong

Dropping the lock around `xrReleaseSwapchainImage` removes the deadlock and also
removes the serialisation the lock exists for, because that call SUBMITS to the
shared queue. #36 exists because this device has one graphics queue and external
synchronisation of `vkQueueSubmit` is the application's job. So the fix has to
keep two submissions apart while not holding our mutex across a runtime call —
those are in tension and it needs design, not a patch.

### The fix, and why it costs the serialisation nothing

**Narrow the lock to the queue operations and never hold it across a call into
the runtime.** The tension above dissolves once ordering and exclusion are
separated:

* **Ordering** — the release must follow the composite's submit — is program
  order on X4's present thread. It never needed a mutex, and the old comment
  said so while keeping it inside the scope anyway.
* **Exclusion** — two threads must not submit to one queue at once — is provided
  by locking each queue operation individually. Every path is covered:
  `g_sbs.composite()` submits through the dispatch table and now takes it;
  `d->QueuePresentKHR()` now takes it; and the runtime's own `vkQueueSubmit`
  arrives through `x4vr_QueueSubmit`, which already took it. Nothing is left
  unserialised.

Checked before touching anything: the ONLY global the XR thread and the present
hook share is `g_camstamp`, and `CamStamp` is entirely `std::atomic`. So the
mutex was providing no exclusion that anything depended on.

`tests/queue_lock.cpp` tests the SHAPE rather than the arithmetic, and its
negative control is the part that earns it — **the old nesting must deadlock**,
and it does, deterministically, via a rendezvous so both threads hold their
first lock before either reaches for its second. Then the new shape survives 20
rounds, and a third case confirms 4000 submits across two threads still take
exclusive turns.

WiVRn is unaffected: the lock is held strictly less, the serialisation is
identical, and out-of-process submits were never under it.

### Also removed: the line that cost an hour

`vr: submitting NO layers this run by design` was unconditional and false — take
297 printed it and submitted 35297 layers. Milestone-A wording that outlived its
branch, and it sent me looking for a mode that does not exist during the take-300
diagnosis. Deleted rather than made conditional.
[[stale-comment-is-misinformation]].

### Also settled, and it retires a proposed take

X4 **and** gamescope dump core at the end of EVERY run, working or not:
22:50:42/44 is take 295 and 23:43:28/29 is take 297, both of which produced full
scorable data. So gamescope aborting under SteamVR was never evidence, and the
`X4VR_GAMESCOPE=0` take it was about to justify is withdrawn —
[[x4vr-metric-must-discriminate]], caught before it cost a run rather than
after. That X4 segfaults on exit in every single run is a separate pre-existing
defect, harmless to the data because it happens at teardown, and it should be
recorded rather than kept as folklore.


## Take 302 — the same deadlock, other half

56ab22f narrowed the PRESENT side and shipped. Take 302 hung anyway, and the
backtrace shows the cycle simply swapped ends:

    X4's present thread  x4vr_QueuePresentKHR -> vrclient (the release)
                           -> x4vr_QueueSubmit -> BLOCKED on ours
                         ...so it holds SteamVR's mutex

    our XR thread        vr_thread -> vrclient -> BLOCKED on SteamVR's mutex
                         ...so it holds ours, across xrEndFrame

The comment on the site I missed said so outright: *"X4's submits and presents
take it here, the runtime's take it around xrEndFrame on the layer's XR
thread."* I fixed the first clause and left the second. It hung earlier than
before — `frames=1 submitted=0 swapchain=0 focused=0` — because the XR thread
now wedges before the session ever goes live.

The premise of that comment is right and its conclusion does not follow: the
runtime's compositor does submit, but it submits **through vkQueueSubmit**,
which means it arrives at `x4vr_QueueSubmit` and takes the lock there, per
submit. The outer lock never added serialisation.

**The rule, stated once and now applied at every site: nothing may hold
`g_vr_queue_mu` across a call into the runtime.** `xrWaitFrame` had already been
exempted for a different stated reason; it is the same rule. The three surviving
`VrQueueLock` scopes wrap `d->QueueSubmit`, `g_sbs.composite()` and
`d->QueuePresentKHR()` — queue operations only, audited one by one.

### The test was wrong about its own truth table

`tests/queue_lock.cpp` is now parameterised by lock ORDER rather than by four
hand-written bodies, and the table is:

    present        xr             result
    OURS_FIRST     RUNTIME_FIRST  deadlock   takes 298-301
    RUNTIME_FIRST  OURS_FIRST     deadlock   take 302, the half-fix
    OURS_FIRST     OURS_FIRST     safe
    RUNTIME_FIRST  RUNTIME_FIRST  safe       where the code is now

I had asserted three of four cells hang. They do not — a cycle needs the two
threads to DISAGREE on the order, so both matching cells are safe. **That is
also the explanation for 298 takes of silence**: on WiVRn the runtime never
submits in-process, so no RUNTIME_FIRST actor exists and no disagreement is
possible. A one-axis test could not have caught the half-fix;
[[vary-them-independently]] applied to a fix rather than a measurement.

Two harness defects found on the way, both worth recording because both would
have produced a confident wrong answer: the rendezvous spun unbounded (one
actor holds `ours` while waiting, so a partner blocked on `ours` never arrives
and the test hangs for reasons unrelated to its subject), and every acquisition
now has a timeout.

### And the mutex identity was an assumption until now

`x4vr_QueueSubmit` takes `g_mu` and then `VrQueueLock`, and a backtrace reading
`pthread_mutex_lock` inside it does not say which. Checked rather than assumed:
`g_mu` is scoped to the device-map lookup and released immediately, and
`vr_thread` never takes it at all. `g_vr_queue_mu` was the only candidate.

> happened: the deadlock prediction was RIGHT (read `blits` first; thousands
> means it is gone — it was 14778). The recording's stated purpose was
> WRONG in an instructive way: it was to decide whether the ghosting is in
> the pixels the compositor shows, and it could not, because the Quest
> captures POST-reprojection output. The take-304 bandwidth framing was

> its "cannot be an A/B" weakness is real and unchanged.

Written before any of the three exist, so none can be read backwards.

### A. Take 303 — SteamVR, does the deadlock survive two fixes?

    XR_RUNTIME_JSON=/home/patola/.local/share/Steam/steamapps/common/SteamVR/steamxr_linux64_patched.json X4VR_HEADLOOK_LAGLOG=1 X4VR_TAKE=303-STEAMVR X4VR_CANVAS_M=1000 X4VR_STEREO=1 X4VR_BINDLESS_PATCH=1 X4VR_H=2816 X4VR_DECLARE_RENDERED_POS=1 X4VR_W=5632 X4VR_ROLL_STEREO=1 X4VR_HEADLOOK_LEAD=1.0 X4VR_RES=2816x2816 X4VR_VR=1 X4VR_OFFAXIS=off X4VR_GAMESCOPE=1 X4VR_SBS_RIGHT_LAYER=1 X4VR_HEADLOOK=1 X4VR_SBS_LAYERS=2 X4VR_UI_WGATE=0.02 X4VR_POSE=0 X4VR_HEADLOOK_RAW=191 X4VR_HEADLOOK_KP=0.25 X4VR_POSELOG=1 X4VR_UI_WGATE_W1=0 X4VR_MV=1 X4VR_PROJ_LIVE=1 X4VR_SBS=1 X4VR_PROJ_INVPROJ=1 X4VR_CAMDIFF=1 X4VR_LOG=/tmp/x4vr-take303.log X4VR_CAMSTAMP=1 X4VR_DECLARE_RENDERED_ROT=2 X4VR_MASK_PRESENT=1 X4VR_UI_FOV=1.0 X4VR_IPD=0.064 X4VR_FOV=1.4917 X4VR_BINDLESS_MIRROR=1 X4VR_CAMREAD=1 X4VR_CAMLOOP=1 X4VR_HEADLOOK_GAIN=0.115 ./launch/x4vr-launch.sh

**Read `blits` FIRST.** Take 300 reached 4 and stopped; take 302 reached 0 with
`frames=1 submitted=0 focused=0`. Thousands means the deadlock is gone.

If it hangs, the capture goes to a PER-RUN name — `tee /tmp/x4vr-hang-303.txt` —
because the 301 and 302 captures both went to `x4vr-hang-bt.txt` and the second
overwrote the first. Read the FULL `bt`, never `bt 14`: that truncation is what
made take 299 look shallow and cost a wrong diagnosis.

**P303.1 — if it hangs a THIRD time with another arrangement of the same two
mutexes, the per-site approach is wrong.** The answer then is to stop sharing
the queue at all: reserve a dedicated one, or fall back to flat when none is
spare, rather than serialising two compositors onto one. Do not narrow a fourth
site.

### B. The WiVRn in-headset stereo recording — the objective instrument

This is the one that matters most, and the reason is a measurement already made.

Take 297's recording turned out to contain the whole SBS composite, so both eyes
were measurable **before submission**: each eye is individually sharp at 3x
magnification, vertical disparity is 0.00 deg at the median (p90 0.24-0.42), and
horizontal disparity implies a ~1.2 m console. **The pixels we hand over are
clean and the stereo geometry is sane.**

So a headset recording is not more of the same — it is the *other side* of the
submission boundary:

* artifact **absent** from the monitor capture and **present** in the headset
  capture ⇒ the compositor, the reprojection or the video stream introduced it,
  and nothing in our rendering is implicated;
* artifact in **both** ⇒ take 297's measurement was looking in the wrong place
  and the disparity work reopens.

A mono headset capture is still worth having — Quest recordings usually are —
because "is it in one eye" already splits the space. Do not reject a capture for
being mono.

**Provenance caveat, and it is not pedantry.** Ghosting IS duplicate/stale
frames, and a re-encode can manufacture exactly that:
[[check-provenance-before-measuring]] cost a wrong published conclusion once
already. So this recording is for CLASSIFICATION — doubling vs smearing vs
trailing vs strobing, one eye or both — and not for rates. If classification
points somewhere needing numbers, ask for a lossless constant-frame-rate capture
and say why.

### C. The X4VR_RES halving under WiVRn — weakest of the three, and why

    ...identical to take 297 but X4VR_RES=1408x1408 X4VR_W=2816 X4VR_H=1408
    X4VR_TAKE=304-HALFRES X4VR_LOG=/tmp/x4vr-take304.log

WiVRn is a STREAMING runtime and at 2816x2816 per eye, two eyes, 90 Hz it is
handed **1.43 Gpixel/s — 2.9x a 4K60 stream** — to video-encode. Halving the
dimension quarters that. If it is encode starvation the artifact should fall
sharply; if unchanged, bandwidth is not it.

**This one cannot be an A/B**, because `X4VR_RES` is fixed at init, so it is a
cross-run comparison against take 297 — and Patola's eye is reliable for a
switch WITHIN a run, not for intensity against the memory of an earlier one
([[patola-senses-transitions-not-magnitudes]]). Treat a "seems better" as a
hint, not a result. **The recording in (B) is what settles it**, because pixels
do not depend on anyone's memory.

Note also that take 297's own frame rate was NOT representative:
`gpu-screen-recorder` cost roughly 40% of it (57 fps against take 294's 97), so
do not compare 304's `perf` against 297's without accounting for that.

### Still open underneath all of this

**#75's residual.** With the episodes gone, take 294 measured **85 ms of lag**
(broad peak; 60-120 ms indistinguishable), of which the servo's own
`(1/kp - 1) * dt` accounts for 60 at a 19.9 ms mean tick. The jitter reading did
NOT survive its control — divided by dt the tremble is flat at the median; only
a 1.9x tail effect survives.

**The tick period is the lever and the ungate A/B is BUILT AND NEVER RUN.**
`X4VR_HEADLOOK_UNGATED=<ms floor>` plus `X4VR_HEADLOOK_UNGATED_AB=30`, scored by
the `ugab` block, with three planted controls in `tests/run-rfab-scorer.sh`.
Section 12 predicts lag 117 -> 53 ms with the excursion growing 72.45 -> 78.55
and staying inside the limit. Take 296 was specified for it and never ran — the
command line that arrived was take 295's, recalled from shell history.

**`X4VR_POSE=0` with `X4VR_ROLL_STEREO=1`** has printed as FAIL on every take
since 294 and is still unfixed. It is NOT the ghosting — measured, above — but
it is real.

**X4 segfaults on exit in EVERY run**, working or not. Harmless to the data
because it is teardown, but it is a defect and not folklore.

## Takes 303a-d — SteamVR runs, and the ghosting is not in any frame

Four takes on 2026-09-19, command line byte-identical apart from `X4VR_TAKE`
and `X4VR_LOG`, so the only variables are the runtime and the headset's
refresh setting. Tagged `take-303-steamvr`.

### The deadlock is gone, and this is the first SteamVR run

Takes 298-302 hung or cored. Take 303 reached **14778 blits, 18866 layers
submitted**, against 4 for take 300 and 0 for take 302. Narrowing
`g_vr_queue_mu` at BOTH sites — the present hook and `xrEndFrame` — is
confirmed by a run, not only by `tests/queue_lock.cpp`. The standing caution
"if it hangs a third time, stop narrowing sites and stop sharing the queue"
was not needed and is retired.

### The narrowing also fixed WiVRn, and the tail is where it shows

Same runtime, same knobs, only the lock change between them:

| WiVRn take | X4 fps | render->submit p90 | camera stepped | stale dyaw p90 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 294 before | **97** | 34.4 ms | 19.6 % | 3.39 deg |
| 297 before | 57 | 37.9 ms | 16.0 % | 7.71 deg |
| 303b after | 83 | **22.2 ms** | 2.7 % | 2.07 deg |
| 303c after | 76 | **21.5 ms** | 5.8 % | 2.05 deg |

Take 294 rendered FASTER than 303c and still had the larger tail, so this is
not the scene getting easier. The MEDIAN barely moved (9.7 -> 10.8 ms) while
the p90 collapsed — the signature of removing a contended lock rather than of
a faster frame.

**Do not read `dyaw` as a declaration error.** All four takes ran
`X4VR_DECLARE_RENDERED_ROT=2`, which declares the AT-DRAW camera, so the
declaration matches the pixels by construction. `camstamp`'s closing advice
("Declare the ATDRAW sample; it removes this residual") is STALE — it was
written while that choice was still open and still prints after it was made.
`dyaw` and "stepped %" are consequences of the latency, not defects beside
it. One quantity improved, and it is the render->submit tail.

### The ghosting is in no single frame, and the recording cannot see repeats

In-headset stereo capture, `/dados/x4-vr-stutter2.mp4`, 2160x1080 SBS at
59.99 fps, 7620 frames, **zero duplicate frames** — a genuine capture, not a
re-encode. Both eyes are sharp at the motion peak; no doubling within either.
With take 297 having already measured the pre-submission composite clean
(each eye sharp at 3x, vertical disparity 0.00 deg median), the ghosting is
in **no single frame anywhere in the chain**. It is temporal.

**But the recording cannot measure our repeat rate, and it was built to.**
Interframe-difference autocorrelation over the busy stretch: lag-1 **+0.533**,
decaying smoothly, no alternation, 0.00 % near-copy frames. If app-layer
repeats reached the capture, lag-1 would be strongly negative. The Quest
records the compositor's POST-reprojection output, where every frame is
freshly warped to the current head pose whether or not we supplied new
content. So the recording classifies (no doubling) and is blind to the
mechanism (repeats). Stated because a future reader will otherwise take
"no duplicates in the recording" as "no repeats in the pipeline".

### The repeat rate is real, and the denominator is the open question

`layer/x4vr_layer.cpp` says it outright: *"submitted counts headset frames,
blits counts X4 frames that reached it."* Over a matched 90 s gameplay window:

| take | runtime | X4 fps | blit Hz | Patola |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 303 | SteamVR | 92.6 | **88.1** | no ghosting |
| 303b | WiVRn | 81.5 | 68.3 | better |
| 303c | WiVRn | 77.4 | 67.2 | some ghosting |
| 303d | SteamVR | 76.2 | 72.4 | some, subtle |

New content reaches the headset at 67-88 Hz against a panel at 72-90, so a
quarter of displayed frames are a REPEAT in every run except 303 — the one
he called suspiciously clean. Reprojection corrects a repeat for head
rotation but NOT for scene motion, which puts the cost exactly where it was
reported: fast relative motion, close to a station.

**The honest caveat, and why take 304 exists.** Normalising blits by the
assumed 72/90 Hz panel orders the four runs as Patola ranked them;
normalising by our own measured submit rate does NOT. Two denominators, two
orderings, and the panel rate was a REPORTED headset setting, never measured
— `XR_FB_display_refresh_rate` is advertised by both runtimes and we never
called it. So the ordering is not evidence yet. Fixed by reading
`XrFrameState::predictedDisplayPeriod`, which is core, already received, and
costs no extra call; reported as `vr pace` and scored by the `pace` block,
with `tests/run-pace-scorer.sh` planting all of its verdicts. Every log
before take 304 prints "not measured" rather than assuming a rate.

### P304 — committed before the run

Take 304 raises the new-content rate instead of lowering the panel rate, at
`X4VR_RES=1408x1408` on WiVRn at 90 Hz.

- **P304.1** `vr pace` reads ~90 Hz. If it reads 72, the four takes above
  were NOT the 2x2 they look like and the table needs rebuilding.
- **P304.2** blits rise from 67 Hz to **>= 90 Hz**, repeats fall below 5 %.
- **P304.3** if repeats go below 5 % and the ghosting REMAINS, the frame
  deficit is refuted as its cause. That is the outcome worth having.
- **P304.4** confounded by construction: lowering `X4VR_RES` cuts both the
  render cost and the stream bandwidth. A pass does not separate them; only
  a sweep across the predicted threshold at ~1.0 does, and that is takes
  after this one.

Still open and NOT touched by any of this: #75's 85 ms servo lag, the ungate
A/B (built, never run), and `X4VR_POSE=0` with `X4VR_ROLL_STEREO=1` which
every one of these four takes still FAILs.

## Take 304 — the frame deficit is the trigger, WiVRn's handling is the severity

`X4VR_W`/`X4VR_H`, not `X4VR_RES` (see the launcher warning added for this).
Display period MEASURED for the first time: **90.0 Hz in both runs**, so the
panel assumption the 303a-d table rested on did hold at 90.

Per-5 s window, no window selected:

| take | starved | new content (median) | deficit run-wide | Patola |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 303c WiVRn 2816 | 98 % | 61.6 Hz | 26.4 Hz | some |
| 303d **SteamVR** 2816 | 97 % | 58.8 Hz | **30.9 Hz** | **subtle** |
| 304a WiVRn 2816 | 71 % | 63.2 Hz | 20.5 Hz | **a lot** |
| 304b WiVRn 1408 | 24 % | **138.1 Hz** | 8.4 Hz | virtually none |
| 304c WiVRn 2816 new client | 91 % | 57.4 Hz | 27.4 Hz | still there |

**P304.2 held, P304.3's premise did not.** Halving the render size took the
median new-content rate from 63 to 138 Hz and the ghosting went with it. But
the deficit alone does NOT set the severity: **SteamVR carried the LARGEST
deficit of all five runs (30.9 Hz, starved in 97 % of windows) and produced
the mildest artifact.** So repeats are the trigger and what the runtime does
with a starved stream is the severity. Updating the WiVRn client changed
nothing (304c).

At 2816x2816 per eye X4 delivers 57-63 Hz of new content into a 90 Hz
display **in every run, including the ones that felt fine**. That is the
standing condition, not a property of any one take.

### Two instrument defects found by this take, both mine

- **The `pace` block computed repeats from SESSION TOTALS** and printed
  "14.8 % ... not enough to explain a doubling complaint" for take 304a,
  whose flight phase was starved in 71 % of windows. Loading blits slowly and
  drags a total down. All nine planted controls were totals, so they tested
  the arithmetic and never the WINDOW. Now reports the per-window rate,
  the starved fraction and the run-wide deficit, and the totals verdict
  DEFERS when a series exists — with a control asserting the precedence.
- **My own analysis picked "the last 90 s" as a gameplay window** and read
  115.3 Hz out of a run whose first three minutes ran at 59.8. That is
  take 158's selector defect in the other direction: it found the fastest
  phase instead of the slowest. Describe the series; do not select from it.

### What this does NOT settle

304a vs 304b changed the render size AND the stream bandwidth together
(1.43 -> 0.33 Gpixel/s), so which of the two WiVRn is failing on is still
open. It is not worth a take: both point at WiVRn's streaming path, which is
not ours, and two mitigations we control already work — SteamVR at full
resolution, or a lower resolution on WiVRn.

## HANDOVER — the mouse shim (#71/#46/#64/#72), written before the work starts

### Where the code actually is

There is no separate shim binary. `cursor/README.md` is a **placeholder**; the
work lives in two places:

* **`injector/x4vr_inject.cpp`** — `LD_PRELOAD`, hooks SDL3. It owns the input
  channel (#19, done):
  - `SDL_GetKeyboardState` — copies the real array and forces the free-look
    scancode bit. Polled state, no event synthesis, no key-up to lose.
  - `SDL_PeepEvents` / `SDL_WaitEvent` — X4's drain. **`headlook_tick()` runs
    INSIDE this interception**, and `send_mouse_delta()` pushes a synthetic
    `SDL_EV_MOUSE_MOTION` with `xrel/yrel` into the very loop that is draining.
    That is why queue residency is 0.01 ms.
  - `SDL_GetMouseState` / `SDL_WarpMouseInWindow` — `fold_x()` for the SBS
    split, plus `publish_cursor()` for the layer's drawn cursor.
  - `SDL_SetWindowRelativeMouseMode` — tracked only, so `fold_x` stands down
    during mouse-look. Passed through untouched by design.
* **`layer/x4vr_cursor_draw.hpp`** — draws the cursor into the eye image (#17,
  done), because the real SDL cursor is hidden (`hide_sdl_cursor`).

X4 imports BOTH mouse idioms (`SDL_GetMouseState`+`SDL_WarpMouseInWindow` and
`SDL_SetWindowRelativeMouseMode`); the injector hooks all of them.

### The trap that must not be walked into again

**`X4VR_TICK_HZ` is HARMFUL and is kept only to reproduce the damage.** Moving
the servo tick off X4's drain onto a thread of our own measured:

    servo on the drain      take 291   0.01 ms mean queue residency
    X4VR_TICK_HZ=90         take 292  16.79 ms mean, 19.89 median

~17 ms of pure added latency, charged to a loop whose stability is counted in
TICKS. Every session that ever went wild had the knob set (285b-s2, 287b, 292),
and 285b-s1 is the one that did not and is still unexplained.

`tools/score_run.py` **told the reader to do exactly this** — "the fix is to
stop deriving the tick from the drain at all" — from before take 292 measured
the damage. It survived every scoring run since and changed a handover
recommendation in this session before anyone checked it against the code it
was recommending changes to. Now corrected to name `X4VR_HEADLOOK_UNGATED`
and say explicitly NOT to move the tick.

**Consequence for the ungate A/B: it does NOT belong to the shim work.**
Removing `if (!fresh) return;` keeps the tick on the drain and only stops it
skipping iterations — 117 -> 53 ms of servo lag (servo_rate.cpp section 12)
with the 0.01 ms residency intact. The gate and the cadence are separate
questions; the stale line had merged them. It can be run before, during or
after the shim, and it is still built and never run.

### #71 — what is OBSERVED and what is only supposed

**Observed:** Patola confirmed by hand that mouse steering is dead while
head-look is armed, and that arrow keys still work. Take 211 separately
confirmed by hand that steering is independent of head-look and that HUD
clicks work, at 4224². **Those two read as contradictory and are probably
reconciled by "armed or not" — take 211 likely had head-look disarmed. That
reconciliation is a GUESS and is the first thing to establish.**

**Not established: the mechanism.** The obvious story is that head-look and
the player share one channel (both are `SDL_EV_MOUSE_MOTION` with xrel/yrel)
and a closed-loop regulator on that channel cancels an open-loop contribution.
Plausible, unverified, and not to be built against until measured. Note that
`evflow`'s "player's own motion 0.0 Hz" in every recent take is NOT evidence
for it — every one of those takes was a measurement run in which Patola was
not touching the mouse. An instrument reporting zero for an input nobody
supplied says nothing.

### What the first step should be, and what it must not be

Measure before building, on a take where Patola DOES move the mouse while
head-look is armed, with `evflow` reporting ours/theirs separately (it already
splits them — the ours/theirs budget split exists since take 122).

The three candidate mechanisms, which need different fixes:

1. the player's events reach X4 and the servo steers the camera back
   (regulator cancellation) — fix is to give head-look its own channel, or to
   feed the player's delta into the servo's target instead of fighting it;
2. the player's events are dropped or overwritten before X4 sees them — fix is
   in our interception;
3. X4 itself ignores motion while the free-look key is held — fix is not ours
   at all, and would mean head-look must stop holding the key.

Nothing in the tree distinguishes these today. **Do not design a fix before
the take says which.** Three fixes for one unmeasured quantity is a pattern
this project has already paid for.

### Riding along

* **#78** — we zero the declared pose in ONE frame while X4 eases over ~0.9 s,
  disagreeing by up to 55 deg. The fix is a design choice, not a search, and
  was explicitly noted as able to ride #71's take.
* **#64** — pointer starts at (0,0) on savegame load.
* **#46** — cursor invisible over much of the eye image until moved down.
* **#72** — head-look keeps driving in external view while logging "idle"
  (command reached 163.80 there against 69.95 in cockpit).

## Take 305 — NOT SCORABLE, and the protocol was mine

The ungate A/B ran correctly — 15 phases, 8 gated / 7 ungated, alternating on
schedule. The lag it was run to measure cannot be read from it.

### Why: I asked for two incompatible things in one take

The handover said *"please turn your head a good way off-centre sometimes...
I want that exercised, not avoided."* That was for the overshoot half. It
drove **42 % of samples to the camera's 65 deg yaw stop**, with the head
reaching **176.7 deg**. The lag estimate is rms(command error) / rms(head
rate); at the stop the "error" is the head's excursion past a camera that
cannot follow and carries no timing at all. The block printed 229-850 ms
against take 294's 85, and a confident OVERLAP.

Dropping the saturated samples does not rescue it: the arms saturated by
**different amounts (52 % gated, 33 % ungated)**, so the survivors are two
different populations and the same data then reads SEPARATED THE WRONG WAY
(gated 14-16 ms, ungated 97-441). One dataset, four answers, selected by how
the contamination is handled — which means the instrument was what was being
measured. Neither number is reported as a result.

The excursion half the instruction was FOR reported `0 sample(s) with the
camera 30+ deg off a centred head` in both arms, because that check requires
a centred head and his was never centred during the big turns. The
instruction cost the measurement and bought nothing.

### What the take DOES establish

* **The premise did not hold in this configuration.** The gated tick was
  **12.7 ms**, not section 12's 23.9. Measured: pump 125.7 Hz, published
  85.1, fresh 71.7 — the gate costs ~16 % of iterations here, not 50 %. There
  was never 117 ms of gate-caused lag available to remove.
* **The ungated arm ticked SLOWER** — 14.0 ms against the control's 12.7 —
  and the code says why. The floor was applied to FRESH ticks as well as
  stale ones, so with the natural rate (12.7 ms) faster than the floor
  (11 ms) the ungated arm refused fresh ticks the control ran. The knob meant
  to raise the iteration rate lowered it. **Fixed**: the floor now bounds
  stale ticks only; fresh ticks are already capped by the publish rate.
* **SteamVR's `predictedDisplayPeriod` changed 14903 times** in one session.
  The pace line's headline 90.0 Hz is the last sample, not a constant. Only
  visible because the change counter was added with the instrument.

### Instrument defects fixed

* **`ugab` now REFUSES** when >10 % of samples sit at the yaw stop, prints
  the per-arm saturation share, and emits no lag verdict. `ylim` is captured
  from the log for this; it was matched and discarded before, so nothing
  downstream could tell a lag sample from a pinned one.
* **The excursion report was inside the lag branch**, so an unscorable run
  silently lost the half that does NOT depend on the head staying inside the
  ceiling. Now printed either way.
* **"too few complete phases per arm" printed underneath the refusal**,
  naming a second and wrong cause for the same silence.
* **Column collision**: at 6+ phases the phase count and the first lag value
  ran together, so `6 phases, first lag 630` printed as `6630`. I read it as
  n=6630 and started diagnosing a sampling defect that did not exist.
* `tests/run-rfab-scorer.sh` gained a **planted saturating case** plus a
  negative control, so the refusal is seen to fire on data whose
  contamination is known by construction — and seen NOT to fire on clean
  data, which is what stops it being an off switch.

### P306 — committed before the re-run

Same A/B, protocol corrected: **keep the head inside the servo's ceiling**,
turn smoothly and continuously, do not drive to the stop. No mouse.

* **P306.1** `ugab` scores (saturation under 10 %).
* **P306.2** the ungated arm's tick is now FASTER than the control's, not
  slower — this is the floor fix's first test and it is the precondition for
  reading anything else.
* **P306.3** the lag difference will be SMALL. At a 12.7 ms gated tick the
  gate costs ~16 % of iterations, so expect single-digit ms, not 117 -> 53.
  If `ugab` says OVERLAP with the ticks separated, the gate is not worth
  removing and #75's residual is elsewhere.

## Take 306 — the freshness gate is NOT the lever. #75's residual is elsewhere.

Protocol corrected (head kept inside the ceiling): **0.5 % saturation**, so
`ugab` scored and the refusal added after take 305 correctly stayed quiet.

| | tick | lag per phase | lagfit tau |
|---|---|---|---|
| control (gated) | 13.1 ms | 19 17 16 17 17 24 | 12.9 ms yaw |
| ARM_B (ungated) | **12.3 ms** | 18 18 17 18 17 18 | (one arm, whole run) |

**All three predictions held.**

* **P306.1** scored — saturation 0.5 % against the 10 % threshold.
* **P306.2** the ungated arm ticks **FASTER** than the control now, 12.3
  against 13.1 ms. Take 305 had it slower; the floor fix (bounding stale
  ticks only) is confirmed by a run.
* **P306.3** and the lag does not move. OVERLAP, gated 16-24 vs ungated
  17-18. Ungating buys ~6 % of tick rate and **zero ms of lag**.

**Decision: keep the gate.** `X4VR_HEADLOOK_UNGATED` stays off by default. A
default is not changed for a measured null.

### The number that reframes #75

Two independent estimators agree on this run: `ugab` ~17 ms both arms,
`lagfit` 12.9 ms tau yaw. Take 294 read 32.0 ms on the same `lagfit` at a
51.3 Hz pose rate; this run sits at 77.9 Hz. **The servo's own lag is now
12-17 ms** and is no longer a plausible cause of "the visuals take time to
follow the movement".

Budget for take 306, all measured in the same run:

    servo lag          12-17 ms
    read-back age       6.3 ms median
    render -> submit    6.3 ms median (p90 12.2)

Plus compositor, stream and display, which we do not measure. Nothing in the
servo is worth another take.

### What IS chronic, in the same run

**STARVED in 100 % of windows**, 12.3 Hz of new content missing run-wide, on
SteamVR at 85 fps into a measured 90 Hz display. The frame deficit of takes
303-304 is not a WiVRn phenomenon and not a resolution accident — it is the
standing condition at 2816x2816 per eye on both runtimes. That, not the
servo, is what remains of #75's felt symptom.

`predictedDisplayPeriod` changed **14947 times** again (14903 in take 305),
so SteamVR's pacing is genuinely variable, not a one-off.

### Why this matters for the shim

The question take 305/306 existed to answer was whether the shim would start
from a ~53 ms or a ~117 ms servo. The answer is **neither: ~13-17 ms, and the
gate has nothing to do with it.** The shim's parameters do not depend on a
servo change that does not exist, so #71 can be measured against the input
path as it stands. Nothing is blocked.

## #71 reopened on the tree, not on a take — and the handover above is wrong

No run was spent here. Everything below comes from the repo, X4's binary, and
Patola's own `inputmap.xml`. It contradicts the "HANDOVER — the mouse shim"
section above, which stays as written.

### What the handover got wrong

**1. "Nothing in the tree distinguishes these [three candidate mechanisms]
today."** It does, on one line. `injector/x4vr_inject.cpp` in
`SDL_PeepEvents`:

```cpp
if (consuming && e->type == SDL_EV_MOUSE_MOTION &&
    e->reserved != kOurEventMagic &&
    g_headlook_steering.load(std::memory_order_relaxed)) {
    e->xrel = 0.0f;
    e->yrel = 0.0f;
}
```

That is candidate (2) — the player's events overwritten before X4 sees them —
as our own deliberate code, from commit `503005b` (#33), with a comment giving
the reason: the player's mouse fought the head and the servo dragged the view
back.

**2. "`evflow`'s 'player's own motion 0.0 Hz' ... every one of those takes was
a measurement run in which Patola was not touching the mouse."** Six takes
carry non-zero foreign motion — 123.6 Hz in take 291, 76.6 in 292, 50.5 in
293, 42.5 in 304b. In take 304b three consecutive windows have foreign motion
AND `steer=1` on *every* `lagsample` in them, so those events were blanked by
the code above. `steer=` is stamped from the same local that arms the drop
(one function, ~200 lines apart), not re-derived. This is **executed**, not
merely emitted.

**3. It ignored what this same file already said.** The "#71 is STRUCTURAL,
not a bug" entry records that holding MOUSELOOK is how X4 suspends ship
control, that `GetCameraRotation` has no setter in 1931 FFI cdefs, and names
the cheap untested question. The handover was written into this file and did
not read it.

### And two claims I then made to Patola, both refuted by him

**"There is no keyboard pitch/yaw in your inputmap at all, only roll on
Q/E."** False. `inputmap.xml` lines 329-332:

    INPUT_STATE_STEER_LEFT   -> INPUT_KEYCODE_LEFT
    INPUT_STATE_STEER_RIGHT  -> INPUT_KEYCODE_RIGHT
    INPUT_STATE_STEER_UP     -> INPUT_KEYCODE_DOWN
    INPUT_STATE_STEER_DOWN   -> INPUT_KEYCODE_UP

I had grepped `<state .*(STEERING|YAW|PITCH|ROLL)`. The analog axes are
`INPUT_RANGE_STEERING_*`; the held keys are `INPUT_STATE_STEER_*`. One family
surveyed, the other reported absent from the game. Patola flies with these
daily and corrected it immediately.

**"Steam was never in the loop — we exec the binary directly."** False. X4
requests `SteamInput006` and `SteamController008` through
`SteamInternal_FindOrCreateUserInterface`, ships `lib/libsteam_api.so`,
imports `SteamAPI_IsSteamRunning`, and `launch/x4vr-launch.sh` exports
`SteamAppId=392160`. The client must be running and X4 has a genuine Steam
Input path.

### What is actually established now

* **A non-mouse steering channel already works under head-look.** Patola
  steers with the arrow keys while MOUSELOOK is held, across many takes. That
  confirms this file's own "only the *mouse* is suspended" and means **#71 is
  a quality-of-control defect, not a playability blocker.** His words for the
  arrow keys: *"far from perfect and not even close to using the mouse, but at
  least it allowed me to get close to stations and steer."*
* **Two mechanisms are live at once**, and they are not alternatives:
  (2) we blank the player's `xrel`/`yrel` while steering, and (3) X4 suspends
  mouse control while MOUSELOOK is held. **An A/B that only switches our drop
  off cannot restore mouse steering**, because X4 reads motion as LOOK
  regardless — it would be a null by construction. That is the take the
  handover was about to ask for.
* **Our inputmap rewrite is exonerated**: exactly one line differs from
  Patola's own file, `INPUT_STATE_CAMERA_MOUSELOOK` moved to `INPUT_KEYCODE_F13`.
  No joystick binding is touched.
* **X4 is a native Wayland client** — `vkCreateWaylandSurfaceKHR`,
  `SDL_GetCurrentVideoDriver()=wayland`, logged every run by #18. The X11-only
  CEF overlay cannot reach it, which is Patola's diagnosis and is correct.
* **X4 has TWO controller paths** — `SteamInput006` and the SDL3 evdev/udev
  one (`/dev/input/event*` through libudev, in X4's bundled `libSDL3.so.0`),
  tied together by its `SDL_GetGamepadSteamHandle` import. **Which one is live
  in our configuration is unknown and is not readable from the binaries.**
* Patola's X52 Pro and his sc-controller virtual pad both failed to fly the
  ship. His inputmap puts steering on `INPUT_JOYAXIS_RX`/`RY` (Xbox right
  stick) and strafe on `X`/`Y`, so a stick whose main axes are X/Y would
  strafe rather than turn. **That is a prediction from the file, not a
  measurement**, and it competes with "Steam Input captured the device".

### What must NOT be done next

Do not design #71's fix. Three mechanisms were listed in the handover, two are
now known live, and the arrow-key finding changes what the fix is even *for* —
it is no longer "restore steering" but "give back something better than
digital keys". See [[hypothesis-and-fix-in-one-step]] and
[[three-fixes-one-unmeasured-number]].

## #46/#64: the cursor channel is dead, and no log could have said so

Found by reading, before any take. Two defects, stacked — the first is
certain from stored logs, the second is a prediction.

### 1. `publish_cursor` has one caller, and X4 never calls it

`publish_cursor()` is called from exactly one place: our `SDL_GetMouseState`
interposer. X4 **imports** `SDL_GetMouseState` — and never calls it.

The proof is `note_extent`, which sits in the same interposer two lines above
the publish and logs on every *new extreme*, so a single call would emit a
line. Across takes 303b, 305 and 306 there is **not one**
`sdl: GetMouseState extent` line. The drain's own `note_mouse_event` fires in
the same runs under the same `this_is_the_game()` guard, so the guard is not
the explanation.

`SDL_WarpMouseInWindow` does **not** publish either — it folds x and passes
through. The mouse-shim handover said both idioms "do `fold_x` +
`publish_cursor`"; only one ever did, and it is the dead one.

**So the cursor position in shared memory is permanently (0,0).** Take 303b is
the only recent run whose overlay drew at all, and its one-shot says
`first at x=0.0 y=0.0`. That is not a savegame-load artifact: **#64 is not
"the pointer starts at (0,0)", it is "the pointer is never published".**

This is [[x4vr-imports-are-not-calls]] for the fourth time in this project —
after SDL_PollEvent (interposed for 47 takes, fired zero times) and
SDL_GetKeyboardState.

### 2. A factor of 2 between the pointer and the eye — predicted, not measured

The drain measures the pointer ranging **0..1408 in both axes**
(`sdl: motion extent x=0..1408 y=0..1408`). X4 believes its window is
**2816x2816** (`SDL_GetWindowSize -> 2816x2816`, after our halving) and the eye
image is **2816x2816**. Half, in *both* axes, so it is not the SBS fold, which
is x-only.

`cursor_rect()` maps the pointer against the eye extent. If the pointer is in
logical units and the eye in physical pixels, the cursor is confined to the
**top-left quadrant** — and the canvas map then contracts what is left.

**The canvas contracts; it does not magnify.** Measured in take 303b:

    canvas eye0 A=(0.5252,0.5252) B=(+0.00002,+0.00000)
      -> hotspot moves +668.6,+668.5 px

The header's own comment says "a scale of about 1.29 in x and 1.19 in y". The
run says 0.5252 in both. Quadrant plus contraction would leave the cursor
reachable only in an inner block of the upper-left quadrant — which is the
shape of #46's complaint, and is **not confirmed**: nothing can be confirmed
about placement while the position never updates at all. Fixing the publish
without settling the 2 would move the cursor from a corner to a quadrant and
look like progress. See [[x4vr-fixed-here-broken-next-door]].

X4 never calls `SDL_GetWindowSizeInPixels` either, so no stored log
distinguishes logical from physical. That is a question for the census below,
not for reasoning.

### A latent third: the cull asks a different question than the draw

`record()` culls on `cursor_rect()`'s `onscreen`, computed from the **unmapped**
position, then draws at the **mapped** one. With a contracting map the mapped
point is always nearer the centre, so a pointer outside the eye can be culled
while its drawn position would have been inside. It cannot fire at today's
0..1408 range. It is recorded, not fixed — the census will count it if it ever
does.

### What was built, and what it must not be used for

* **A cursor refusal census.** Every one of `record()`'s early returns was a
  bare `return false`; takes 305 and 306 both armed the overlay, never drew,
  and produced byte-identical logs. Now each branch tallies
  (`not-ready | no-channel | no-cursor-image | bad-pitch | format |
  no-pipeline | off-eye | drew`), reported periodically and at teardown with
  the pointer range and the eye extent on the same line, and an explicit
  **"NEVER MOVED — the channel is not being fed"** when the range is a point.
  `refuse()` makes a bare `return false` impossible to add without picking a
  bin, and `tests/cursor_place.cpp` fails the build if a reason has no name.
* **A controller census** (#71). `SDL_GetJoysticks` / `OpenJoystick` /
  `OpenGamepad` / `IsGamepad` / `GetJoystickAxis` /
  `AddGamepadMappingsFromFile`, all six checked with `nm -D` before being
  hooked and all six added to `tests/check-exports.sh`, whose comment is
  explicit that adding a hook means adding it there. It says what X4
  enumerates, what it opens, what those devices are NAMED, and — the part that
  discriminates — whether the axes are ever **read**. A device that never
  appears was never offered to X4, which no rebinding could fix; one that is
  opened and never polled is a different defect from one polled into the wrong
  binding.

**Neither is a fix, and neither justifies a take of its own.** Both ride the
next run of any kind. Do not touch the publish path until a census line says
what the pointer range and the eye extent actually are in the same run.

First run carrying the cursor and pad censuses. **No knob changes from take

isolates the question we want first — while sc-controller runs, Steam cannot
see his Steam Controller 2, so anything X4 sees arrived through SDL/evdev.

* **P307.1** The cursor census reports **THE POSITION CHANNEL IS DEAD**, with

* **P307.2** `off-eye` will be **0 or near it**. A pointer pinned at (0,0)

Nothing here reads the lag or overshoot estimators, so head position does not

## Take 307 — two of three predictions REFUTED, and Patola's hands beat my census

**Controller configuration 2** (sc-controller virtual Xbox pad, no HOTAS),
SteamVR. Scored with `score_run.py`'s new `cursor` and `pad` blocks.

### P307.1 REFUTED — X4 DOES call SDL_GetMouseState, in menus

39 `sdl: GetMouseState extent` lines in take 307; zero in takes 303b, 305 and
306. All three of those were **cockpit-only**. X4 polls the pointer when a
menu or the map is open, and take 307 was the first run to open one.

The silence was real and correctly read. **The quantifier was invented.** The
honest claim was "not in these three takes, none of which opened a menu" — and
I wrote "X4 never calls it" into this file, a commit message, and a memory.
Fifth instance of a survey complete over the wrong population.

**So "#64 is never published" is WITHDRAWN.** The position channel works; it
is fed only while X4 is polling, which is when a cursor is on screen anyway.

### P307.2 HELD — `off-eye` is 0

The pre-map cull is not what eats the cursor. It remains latent.

### #46 has a real number now, and it is not the factor of 2

    drew 4441 of 17194 presents (25.8%), rest no-cursor-image
    pointer x=0..1898 y=0..2024 against a 2816x2816 eye  =  67% x 72%

**The logical-vs-physical factor of 2 is REFUTED** — 67/72%, not 50/50, and
the scorer's own branch said so because the percentage was reported rather
than the prediction announced. What survives is a genuine reachability limit:
about a third of each axis the pointer cannot enter. Cause unknown; the
canvas contraction (A=0.5252) is not it either, since the cull never fired.

`no-cursor-image` at 74% is expected — cockpit flight selects no cursor.

### P307.3 REFUTED, and the verdict it printed was FALSE

The census said **"OPENED, NEVER POLLED ... no binding could have acted"**
while Patola was steering the ship with the pad perfectly well.

    pad  enumerate 0 (last saw -1 device(s)) | opened joystick 0 gamepad 1
         | axis reads 0 | mappings 0
    pad  opened gamepad id=2 "Xbox 360 Controller"

`SDL_OpenGamepad(2)` succeeded, yet `SDL_GetJoysticks` and
`SDL_GetJoystickAxis` were called **zero** times. X4 does not import
`SDL_GetGamepadAxis` at all. So the axis values arrive as **events through
`SDL_PeepEvents`** — the drain we have hooked since #19 and do not count by
type — and X4 learned the device existed from an ADDED event rather than by
enumerating.

**I built the census around a polling API for an event-driven channel**, then
published a confident negative from its zero. The instrument was the thing
that was wrong; the watcher was right.

### #71 IS ANSWERED — analog pad steering works under head-look

Patola: *"the controls just responded normally and I was able to steer the
ship with these controls just fine."* The log agrees that head-look was live
while he did it: **`steer=1` in 1860 of the final 2000 `lagsample` lines
(93%)**, which is the phase the pad was used in.

So MOUSELOOK suspends **the mouse**, not an analog pad, and the head-look
servo does **not** fight pad steering — the "expect something odd" I put in
the handover did not happen.

**"Stick to fly, head to look" is demonstrated rather than hypothesised.**
#71 stops being an investigation and becomes a control-scheme decision, and
his X52 failure is now most likely the `JOYAXIS_RX/RY` vs `X/Y` binding story
after all — testable with a rebind, no take.

### An instrument defect found in passing

`note_extent`'s range accumulator **and** its 64-line cap are function-level
statics **shared between its two callers** (`GetMouseState` positions and
motion-event positions). Take 307 hit exactly 64 (39 + 25), so the instrument
went silent while the real range kept growing: its last line reads
`x=0..1738 y=0..1806` against the census's measured 1898/2024. Its printed
range is both contaminated by the other caller and truncated. Trust the
cursor census.

## Runtime default: WiVRn from here on

Patola's decision, recorded so handovers stop defaulting to SteamVR: **WiVRn
is the default runtime for future takes** — it is more comfortable and lets
him interact with the flatscreen and VR at the same time, which SteamVR does
not. SteamVR stays useful as a *comparison* arm because it does not show the
ghosting/artifacts WiVRn does, so it is the reference for judging smoothness.

Mechanically: WiVRn needs `XR_RUNTIME_JSON` **UNSET**; SteamVR needs it
pointed at `steamxr_linux64_patched.json`. Since take 298 the injector records
`XR_RUNTIME_JSON` in the `env: run =` line, so which runtime a take used is
recoverable from its log.

## Instrument fixes after take 307, and P308

### The pad census now watches the channel the values arrive on

Take 307 proved the axis values reach X4 as **events**, not polls. The census
now counts, at **both** drains (`SDL_PeepEvents` and `SDL_WaitEvent` — this
file has already shipped a fix to one of two symmetric sites and had the
defect return through the other), and only on GET so a peek cannot be counted
twice.

`Sdl3AxisEvent` is read positionally and **asserted against the real SDL3
headers** in `tests/sdl_event_layout.cpp`, along with all six event-type
constants, because a renumber is exactly what an enum name cannot catch.

**One assert caught a live defect in my own first version.** SDL orders
*gamepad* axes `LEFTX=0, LEFTY=1, RIGHTX=2, RIGHTY=3` — which is NOT raw
joystick numbering. I had pooled both families into one array and labelled the
indices `X/Y/Z/RX/RY/RZ`, so an index would have meant different hardware
depending on which event carried it, and the X52 (likely a joystick) would
have been named with gamepad labels. Now kept **per family**, with the device
instance id recorded, and the joystick family carries **no invented labels at
all** — a raw index and its travel is a measurement; mapping it onto X4's
`INPUT_JOYAXIS_*` names would be the same guess that made the census wrong the
first time.

### `note_extent` had two defects, both of which flattered it

Its accumulator **and** its 64-line cap were function-level statics shared
between its two callers, so the printed "GetMouseState extent" was widened by
motion events and vice versa, and take 307 spent exactly 64 lines (39 + 25)
and went quiet while the range kept growing — last line `x=0..1738 y=0..1806`
against the census's measured 1898/2024. State is per caller now, the cap
bounds **lines and not the range**, and a `FINAL` line reports the true extent
on the periodic cadence.

### P308 — committed before the run

**Controller configuration: X52 Pro connected, sc-controller running with Xbox
emulation OFF** — one game controller present, and sc-controller still keeps
Steam from seeing the SC2, so Steam Input stays out of the picture. Compared
against take 307 (configuration 2, pad only), which makes this a one-device
run against a one-device baseline rather than a two-device run in which either
could be doing the steering.

**Runtime: WiVRn** (`XR_RUNTIME_JSON` unset), now the project default.

* **P308.1** X4 opens the X52. The census names it, and says whether it came
  through the joystick or gamepad family.
* **P308.2** The stick's main travel lands on **axis indices 0 and 1**, which
  the inputmap has on `INPUT_RANGE_STRAFE_LEFT_RIGHT` / `STRAFE_UP_DOWN` —
  while steering sits on `RX`/`RY`. So the ship **strafes rather than turns**,
  which is what "plugged it in and it didn't work" would look like from the
  cockpit. If the axes land somewhere else, this explanation dies and the
  census says where to look instead.
* **P308.3** The values arrive by **events**, with polled reads still 0, like
  take 307's pad.

If P308.2 holds the fix is a rebind, and it ships non-intrusively through the
inputmap rewrite that already moves `MOUSELOOK` to F13.

## Take 308 — VOID: the X52 was powered but never enumerated

Not an X4 defect, not a census defect, and not a stick defect. The run simply
had no joystick attached.

    take 308 ran   298254.6 -> 298440.8   (monotonic, 186 s)
    X52 enumerated 298750.19              (310 s AFTER the run ended)

dmesg carries **exactly one** X52 connect event and it is that one; the buffer
covers the whole period (Steam Ctrl at 298026, WayVR at 298232), and
`/proc/uptime` confirms the two clocks are the same. The build was current —
36 `cursor census` lines.

Patola plugged the stick in before launching and **it lit up**, both the
throttle and the stick. That is bus power; the kernel never saw it on the data
lines until it was re-seated. `jstest-gtk` showed nothing for the same reason
and would not have rescanned. The device is healthy now: `js5` + `event265`,
`crw-rw-rw-` with an explicit `user:patola:rw-` ACL, `joydev` loaded, and
`fuser` reports no process holding either node.

### The run recorded its own configuration — badly, so now it does

A take specified as "X52 connected" ran without one and **nothing in the log
said so.** The pad census was correctly silent, which is indistinguishable
from "a device was present and X4 ignored it". Stating the controller
configuration in the handover is necessary and is not sufficient: the handover
describes intent, and intent is what failed here.

So the injector now logs `pad present:` lines at startup, read from
`/proc/bus/input/devices` — no SDL, no open, no grab, nothing that can perturb
the device under test — naming every entry whose Handlers list a `js` node,
or an explicit **NONE** with the powered-but-not-enumerated hint. Every take
from here records what was actually plugged in.

### A verdict of mine was overclaiming, and take 308 is what showed it

The cursor block said **"CANNOT REACH THE WHOLE EYE"** from the pointer's
observed range. Take 308 read `x=0..1408 y=0..1408` — and **1408 is half of
2816, which is where X4 parks the pointer for mouse-look.** A cockpit-only run
reaches exactly that for an entirely uninteresting reason, and take 307's
menus took it to 1898/2024, so 1408 is no limit at all.

"Was not seen there" is not "cannot go there". The verdict now says **NOT SEEN
OVER THE WHOLE EYE**, states that it is where the pointer *went* rather than
where it *can* go, and names the mouse-look park so the number is not read as
a bound. The control suite gained a check that the word CANNOT cannot come
back.

**Consequence for #46: take 307's 67%x72% is not evidence of a limit either.**
It is where Patola happened to move the mouse. Measuring reachability needs a
protocol that drives the pointer deliberately into all four corners, and until
one runs, #46 has no measured extent.

| axis | swept | X4 name | bound to | what Patola saw |
